acc-position-l.name: Positioning and landmarks
acc-position-l.summary: Surface anatomy, lateral decubitus on a broken table, landmarks, the layers of the chest wall.

steps.title: Surface anatomy, supine
steps.body:
Count the ribs from the sternal angle (angle of Louis): the 2nd costal cartilage joins the sternum there, and the 2nd space lies just below it. In a man the nipple sits over the 4th space in the mid-clavicular line. The costal margin (cartilages 7 to 10) ends at the xiphoid.

Laterally: the anterior axillary line drops from the anterior axillary fold (lower border of pectoralis major), the mid-axillary line from the apex of the axilla, the posterior axillary line from the posterior fold (latissimus dorsi).

steps.title: Right lateral decubitus, left side up
steps.body:
Double-lumen tube placed and checked with the bronchoscope before turning; recheck after. Turn as a team, the head and neck with the trunk.

Table broken (flexed) with the break under the right flank, between the costal margin and the iliac crest: the left intercostal spaces open and the hip drops out of the way of the instruments. Axillary roll under the upper chest, a hand's breadth below the axilla (not in it), to take weight off the brachial plexus and the dependent shoulder.

Dependent arm forward on a board; upper arm on a rest, shoulder flexed about 90°, never hyperabducted. Pillow between the knees, lower leg flexed, upper leg straight; pad the fibular head (common peroneal nerve). Supports or a bean bag front (pubis) and back (sacrum), strapping across the hip.

ask.question: Where does the axillary roll go?

choices.text: Under the dependent chest wall, a hand's breadth below the axilla
choices.why: It lifts the chest off the dependent shoulder; placed in the axilla it compresses the brachial plexus and axillary vessels.

steps.title: Landmarks on the side you operate on
steps.body:
Tip of the scapula: about the 7th rib (7th space) with the arm at rest; the posterolateral incision passes 2–3 cm below it. Lifting the arm forward draws the scapula up and forward.

Mid-axillary line at the 4th–5th space: the site for a uniportal incision, a utility incision and a chest drain. Triangle of safety for a drain: lateral border of pectoralis major, anterior border of latissimus dorsi, a line at the level of the nipple (5th space), apex below the axilla.

Count ribs under the scapula from above with a hand: the highest rib felt is usually the 2nd; the 1st lies inside the curve of the 2nd.

steps.title: The muscle layers of the lateral chest wall
steps.body:
From outside in: skin and fat; latissimus dorsi behind and below (its anterior border is the posterior axillary fold); trapezius and rhomboids between the scapula and the spine; pectoralis major in front (its border is the anterior axillary fold); serratus anterior on the ribs from the 1st to the 8th, running back under the scapula; then the intercostal muscles, endothoracic fascia and parietal pleura.

The long thoracic nerve runs down the outer surface of serratus anterior near the mid-axillary line; the thoracodorsal nerve and vessels on the deep surface of latissimus dorsi.

The auscultatory triangle (latissimus, trapezius, medial border of the scapula) has no muscle over the ribs: the posterior limb of a thoracotomy enters there.

ask.question: A patient has a winged scapula after a lateral thoracotomy. Which nerve was injured?

choices.why: It runs on the outer surface of serratus anterior in the mid-axillary line; serratus paralysis lets the scapula wing.

acc-plt-standard-l.name: Thoracotomy incisions, left
acc-plt-standard-l.summary: Landmarks, the incision, each muscle layer, then the ribs.

steps.title: Standard posterolateral thoracotomy (serratus-sparing)
steps.body:
From the anterior axillary line along the line of the 5th space, curving 2–3 cm below the tip of the scapula, then up between the scapula and the spine as far as needed.

Latissimus dorsi is divided in the line of the incision. Serratus anterior is spared: its posterior border is freed and the muscle lifted forward. Trapezius and rhomboids are cut only if the incision is carried up behind the scapula.

Landmarks: tip of the scapula, the 5th space (count from above), the anterior and posterior axillary lines.

steps.title: Through the chest wall, layer by layer
steps.body:
Skin and subcutaneous fat → Latissimus dorsi: divided → Serratus anterior: freed and retracted forward → Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the 6th rib.

Press play to take each layer in turn.

Enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib: the intercostal vein, artery and nerve run in the groove under the lower border of the rib above.

layers.label: Serratus anterior: freed and retracted forward
Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the 6th rib

steps.title: Open the pleura and spread the ribs
steps.body:
Right lateral decubitus, table flexed, the arm forward. The incision curves from the anterior axillary line to a point midway between the tip of the scapula and the spine.

Divide latissimus dorsi, spare and retract serratus anterior, count the ribs from above under the scapula, and enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib so the neurovascular bundle under the 5th is spared. Open the space with the rib spreader, slowly.

steps.title: Closing and what each choice costs
steps.body:
Two drains through separate stab incisions below the wound. Pericostal sutures round the 5th and 6th ribs (or intracostal through the 6th, sparing the nerve below the 5th). Repair each muscle layer that was cut; with a muscle-sparing incision, lay the muscles back and drain the flaps.

Muscle-dividing: best exposure, most pain and shoulder weakness. Serratus-sparing: the usual compromise. Muscle-sparing: least pain, smaller field, seromas.

steps.title: Muscle-sparing lateral thoracotomy
steps.body:
A vertical incision of 10–12 cm along the anterior border of latissimus dorsi, from the axilla down. Raise skin flaps widely.

steps.title: Three-port VATS, anterior approach
steps.body:
Utility incision (4–5 cm, no rib spreading) in the 4th space, anteriorly, directly over the hilum and the superior vein. Camera low anterior, at the level of the top of the diaphragm (7th space). Working port at the same low level, further back.

Hilum first, from the front (Copenhagen). Anterior ports pass through serratus anterior and, near the fold, the edge of pectoralis major.

steps.title: What the port goes through
steps.body:
Skin and subcutaneous fat → Serratus anterior: passed through → Pectoralis major: passed through → Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the rib below.

Enter on the upper border of the lower rib; open the pleura with a finger and sweep for adhesions before the first instrument goes in.

layers.label: Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the rib below

steps.title: The view from inside
steps.body: From the camera the hilum sits in the middle of the screen, the instruments entering from separate ports at an angle to the camera (triangulation).

steps.body:
A single 3–4 cm incision between the anterior and mid-axillary lines: 4th space for upper lobes, 5th space for middle and lower lobes.

Serratus anterior is split along its fibres; a wound protector holds it open. The camera sits at the back of the wound, instruments below and in front of it, all working in the same plane as in open surgery. Staplers come in from the same incision, so angles for the superior vein and the bronchus need planning (curved-tip staplers help).

steps.title: What the port goes through
steps.body:
Skin and subcutaneous fat → Serratus anterior: split along its fibres → Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the rib below.

Enter on the upper border of the lower rib; open the pleura with a finger and sweep for adhesions before the first instrument goes in.

layers.label: Serratus anterior: split along its fibres
Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the rib below

steps.title: The view from inside
steps.body: From the camera the hilum sits in the middle of the screen, the instruments entering from the same incision, in line with the camera.

steps.title: Three-port VATS, anterior approach
steps.body:
Utility incision (4–5 cm, no rib spreading) in the 4th space, anteriorly, directly over the hilum and the superior vein. Camera low anterior, at the level of the top of the diaphragm (7th space). Working port at the same low level, further back.

Hilum first, from the front (Copenhagen). Anterior ports pass through serratus anterior and, near the fold, the edge of pectoralis major.

Skin and subcutaneous fat → Serratus anterior: passed through → Pectoralis major: passed through → Intercostal muscles, on the upper border of the rib below.

Enter on the upper border of the lower rib; open the pleura with a finger and sweep for adhesions before the first instrument goes in.

A utility incision of 3–4 cm in the 4th space (upper lobes; 5th for lower lobes) at the anterior axillary line, and a 1 cm camera port in the 7th or 8th space in the mid- to posterior axillary line.

All instruments and staplers go through the utility incision; the camera looks up from below, as in three-port VATS.

lul-anterior.name: VATS left upper lobectomy
lul-anterior.summary: Hilum first: vein, truncus, bronchus, remaining arteries, fissure last.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The left hilum you are about to meet
steps.body:
Look at the hilum from the front, as the anterior approach meets it. The superior pulmonary vein is the most anterior structure, with the truncus anterior just above and behind it, the first branch off the top of the pulmonary artery.

Behind the vein lies the upper lobe bronchus. The pulmonary artery arches over the left main bronchus, then turns down behind the upper lobe bronchus into the fissure.

Order of division from the front: vein → truncus → bronchus → remaining arteries → fissure.

steps.title: Case: an EGFR-positive adenocarcinoma in a never-smoker
steps.lead: A 58-year-old woman, never a smoker, cooked over a wood fire for 30 years. Six months of cough; given anti-TB treatment twice at a health centre without a positive sputum test. CT: a 3.4 cm mass in the left upper lobe, no enlarged nodes; biopsy: adenocarcinoma, EGFR exon 19 deletion. PET: no nodal or distant uptake. EBUS: stations 4L, 7 and 10L negative. FEV1 78%, DLCO 72% predicted.
steps.body:
Stage: T2a (3–4 cm) N0 M0 = IB. Why EBUS with a negative PET? A tumour over 3 cm (or central, or cN1) carries enough risk of occult N2 to justify invasive staging. Fitness: the left upper lobe (with the lingula) has 5 of the 19 segments: ppoFEV1 = 78 × 14/19 ≈ 57%, ppoDLCO = 72 × 14/19 ≈ 53%; both are in the 30–60% band, and she climbs three flights (over 22 m) without stopping: fit for lobectomy.

Plan: VATS left upper lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection, then adjuvant osimertinib for the EGFR mutation.

Evidence: VIOLET (HTA 2022; 503 patients): VATS lobectomy gave better physical function at 5 weeks and fewer in-hospital complications than open lobectomy, with no loss of nodal upstaging. ADAURA (NEJM 2023): adjuvant osimertinib after resection of EGFR-mutant stage IB–IIIA disease improved 5-year overall survival (88% vs 78%, HR 0.49).

ask.question: Why did she need EBUS when the PET showed no nodal uptake?

choices.text: A tumour over 3 cm carries a significant risk of occult mediastinal nodes; guidelines advise invasive staging for tumours over 3 cm, central tumours or cN1
choices.why: PET misses small nodal deposits. ESTS 2014 recommends invasive staging for central tumours, tumours over 3 cm, or suspected N1 even when PET is negative.

choices.text: EBUS is required before every lobectomy
Because she had been treated for TB

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body:
Right lateral decubitus, table flexed to open the intercostal spaces, right lung ventilated through a double-lumen tube.

Three ports: a 4–5 cm utility incision anteriorly, directly over the hilum and the superior vein, no rib spreading; a low anterior camera port at the level of the top of the diaphragm; and a working port at the same level further back.

The utility incision sits over the structures you will staple first.

steps.title: Open the pleura over the front of the hilum
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe posteriorly. With the peanut, sweep the mediastinal pleura off the front of the hilum, behind the phrenic nerve, from the top of the hilum down to the inferior vein.

The superior pulmonary vein comes into view as the most anterior structure. Keep the phrenic nerve and its vessels on the pericardium.

ask.question: Where does the left phrenic nerve run relative to the hilum?

choices.text: Anterior to it, on the pericardium
choices.why: The phrenic nerve descends on the pericardium anterior to the hilum; the vagus passes behind it.

choices.text: Posterior to it, with the vagus

steps.title: Superior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body:
Encircle the superior vein. Before any stapler goes round it, see the inferior pulmonary vein as a separate structure draining the lower lobe: a common trunk taken here drains the whole lung.

The artery lies directly behind and above. Pass the vascular stapler from the working port, anvil tip in view, and fire.

ask.question: Before stapling the superior vein, what must you confirm?

choices.text: That the inferior pulmonary vein is separate and drains the lower lobe
choices.why: A common pulmonary vein (a variant) taken as the "superior vein" drains the whole lung.

choices.text: That the lingular artery is already divided

steps.pearl: Staple far enough from the pericardium to leave a cuff, close enough to catch all the upper lobe tributaries.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: staple
steps.body:
With the vein gone, the pulmonary artery comes into view behind it. Its first branch, the truncus anterior, leaves the anterosuperior surface for the apicoposterior and anterior segments. It is short, wide and thin-walled.

Clear the station 5 and 10 nodes to open the angle, then staple (or ligate) it. The recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the arch just above.

ask.question: Clearing station 5 above the truncus, which nerve is at risk?

choices.why: It leaves the vagus at the arch and hooks under it beside the ligamentum arteriosum, in the AP window.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
The upper lobe bronchus now lies exposed behind the divided vein and below the artery. Sweep the station 10 and 11 nodes toward the specimen so the stapler sits on bronchus only.

Close the stapler (thick-tissue reload) and ask for the lung to be inflated: the lower lobe must ventilate. Then fire, close to the origin.

ask.question: Before firing on the upper lobe bronchus, how do you know it is not the lower lobe bronchus?

choices.text: Clamp, then inflate: the lower lobe must expand
choices.why: A test inflation with the stapler closed shows which lobe you have isolated.

choices.text: It is always the more anterior bronchus

steps.title: Posterior segmental and lingular arteries
steps.body:
Lift the bronchial stump forward: the artery runs down into the fissure. The remaining upper lobe branches leave it here, the posterior segmental above and the lingular lower down.

Opposite the lingular artery, the superior segmental artery of the lower lobe (A6) leaves the back of the artery; the basal trunk continues below. Identify both before dividing anything.

ask.question: Which lower-lobe branch arises near the lingular artery and must be kept?

choices.why: A6 leaves the posterior aspect of the interlobar artery, often opposite the lingular artery.

steps.title: Staple the fissure last, front to back
steps.body: Every hilar structure of the upper lobe is divided. Only parenchyma joins the lobes now. Staple the fissure with thick-tissue reloads from front to back, keeping the lower lobe artery below and behind the staple line.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body:
Bag the lobe and remove it through the utility incision. Complete the nodal dissection: stations 5 and 6 in the AP window and along the aorta, 7 below the carina, 10 and 11 at the hilum.

Fill the chest with saline and ventilate to test the bronchial stump and the fissure staple line.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after right upper lobectomy: the middle lobe has opacified and the patient is febrile. Most important diagnosis to exclude?

choices.why: Torsion is rare but causes infarction; bronchoscopy and return to theatre if suspected.

steps.title: The hilum from behind and in the fissure
steps.body:
Seen from behind and from the fissure, the pulmonary artery is the key: it arches over the left main bronchus, then descends in the fissure, giving off its upper lobe branches one by one.

In the fissure: the posterior segmental artery up and back, the lingular artery forward, the superior segmental (A6) to the lower lobe behind, the basal trunk continuing down. The truncus anterior is the first branch, high on the anterosuperior surface.

Order of division from behind: fissure → posterior segmental → truncus → bronchus → vein.

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, right lung ventilated. For a fissure-first approach the ports sit further back: a utility incision in the 5th intercostal space in line with the fissure, a camera port low and posterior, and a posterior working port. Port sites vary between units.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut, sweeping along the line of the artery.

The interlobar pulmonary artery appears in its sheath. Get onto the sheath: everything that follows is dissected on the artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: First segmental arteries in the fissure
steps.body:
Follow the artery up and back. The posterior segmental artery (A1+2c, sometimes two) is the first upper lobe branch you meet from the fissure, leaving the posterosuperior surface as the artery arches over the bronchus. The lingular artery runs forward into the lingula.

Map the lower lobe branches first: A6 behind, often opposite the lingular artery, and the basal trunk below. Then divide the upper lobe branches.

ask.question: In the fissure, which lower-lobe branch arises posteriorly, often opposite the lingular artery?

choices.why: A6 is the first lower-lobe branch and leaves the posterior aspect of the artery; take it by mistake and the superior segment is devascularised.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: ligate and divide
steps.body:
Follow the artery up to its first branch. Open the mediastinal pleura over the top of the hilum, in front of the vagus, and dissect the truncus anterior circumferentially.

Ligate it: two ties on the pulmonary artery side, one on the lobe side, then divide between. The truncus is short: leave enough stump for the ties.

The aortic arch, the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the station 5 nodes are just above.

ask.question: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve leave the vagus?

choices.text: At the aortic arch, hooking under it beside the ligamentum arteriosum
choices.why: On the left the nerve loops under the arch; on the right it loops under the subclavian artery.

choices.text: At the level of the inferior pulmonary vein

steps.pearl: A short, wide truncus that will not take three ties is stapled instead.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
With the upper lobe arteries divided, the upper lobe bronchus lies free beneath where the artery arched over it. Clear station 11 at the secondary carina.

Pass the endostapler (thick-tissue reload), close it, and inflate: the lower lobe must ventilate before firing.

steps.title: Pulmonary veins: superior vein last
steps.body:
Roll the lobe back to show the front of the hilum. Two veins: the superior pulmonary vein from the upper lobe, and below it the inferior pulmonary vein from the lower lobe, which stays.

Keep the phrenic nerve on the pericardium, pass the vascular stapler round the superior vein and fire. The lobe is now free except for any fused fissure.

ask.question: Taking the vein last, what is the argument for doing it this way?

choices.text: Arterial inflow is stopped before venous outflow
choices.why: Dividing arteries first avoids congesting the lobe; in cancer surgery the vein-first argument (less tumour-cell shedding) is debated.

choices.text: The vein is easier to reach from behind

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Staple any remaining fused fissure anteriorly, bag and remove the lobe, and complete the nodal dissection: stations 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11. Leak-test the stump under saline.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: congenital lobar emphysema versus CPAM
steps.body:
Congenital lobar emphysema (CLE)Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM)
What it isA normal-structured lobe that over-distends: deficient bronchial cartilage (or compression) makes a ball valve; air enters, cannot leaveA hamartomatous lesion of cysts and abnormal airways, usually one lobe; blood supply from the pulmonary artery
WhereLeft upper lobe (about 43%), middle lobe (32%), right upper (21%); lower lobes rareAny lobe; lower lobes often
WhenNeonatal respiratory distress; half at birth, most by 6 monthsMost found on antenatal ultrasound; some present with infection later
ImagingA hyperlucent lobe with vascular markings, the other lobes compressed, the mediastinum shiftedAir-filled cysts of varying size; solid in microcystic types
RisksProgressive compression, tension physiologyInfection; hydrops in the fetus (CVR over 1.6); malignancy (mucinous adenocarcinoma with type 1; type 4 now regarded as cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma)
Deficient bronchial cartilage→Airway collapses in expiration (ball valve)→Air trapping, lobe over-distends→Compresses the other lobes, shifts the mediastinum→Respiratory distress, falling venous return

The trap: CLE looks like a tension pneumothorax. A chest drain into an emphysematous lobe makes a large air leak and can kill; look for lung markings in the lucent area before inserting one.

Anaesthesia for CLE: avoid nitrous oxide (it expands the lobe) and high positive-pressure ventilation before the chest is open (spontaneous breathing or gentle ventilation); the surgeon scrubbed at induction, ready to open the chest and deliver the lobe.

Stocker types of CPAM: 0 (acinar dysplasia, lethal), 1 (large cysts over 2 cm, 50–70%), 2 (small cysts, associated anomalies), 3 (solid-appearing, alveolar), 4 (peripheral cysts; now considered cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma).

Evidence: CLE: StatPearls 2024 (lobe distribution, presentation, pneumothorax pitfall) and OpenAnesthesia 2025 (anaesthetic management). CPAM: CPAM volume ratio over 1.6 predicted hydrops in 75% (Crombleholme et al., J Pediatr Surg 2002); resection of asymptomatic lesions at 6–12 months versus surveillance remains debated (StatPearls). Pathology update: Dehner et al., Pediatr Dev Pathol 2023.

ask.question: A 3-week-old with tachypnoea has a hyperlucent left upper zone and mediastinal shift. Vascular markings are visible in the lucent area. What must you avoid?

choices.text: Inserting a chest drain for a presumed pneumothorax
choices.why: Vascular markings mean over-distended lung, not free air: this is CLE. A drain would enter the lobe and cause a large air leak. The treatment is lobectomy.

steps.title: The hilum from behind and in the fissure
steps.body:
Seen from behind and from the fissure, the pulmonary artery is the key: it arches over the left main bronchus, then descends in the fissure, giving off its upper lobe branches one by one.

In the fissure: the posterior segmental artery up and back, the lingular artery forward, the superior segmental (A6) to the lower lobe behind, the basal trunk continuing down. The truncus anterior is the first branch, high on the anterosuperior surface.

Order of division from behind: fissure → posterior segmental → truncus → bronchus → vein.

steps.title: Case: a neonate with congenital lobar emphysema
steps.lead: A 5-week-old boy, increasing tachypnoea and feeding difficulty; SpO₂ 90% in air. Chest X-ray: a hyperlucent left upper zone with faint vascular markings, the left lower lobe compressed, the mediastinum pushed to the right. CT: an over-distended left upper lobe; no mass or vascular sling compressing the bronchus.
steps.body:
Symptomatic CLE: left upper lobectomy (in a neonate by thoracotomy through the 4th or 5th space, or thoracoscopy in experienced hands). Mild, stable cases can be observed.

In theatre: gentle or spontaneous ventilation until the chest is open; no nitrous oxide. Once the chest is open the lobe herniates out of the incision and the child improves at once. Then the hilum as in the adult: the lingular and upper lobe arteries, the superior pulmonary vein, the upper lobe bronchus.

The model shows an adult chest; the neonatal anatomy is the same in arrangement, much smaller in scale.

Evidence: StatPearls 2024: lobectomy for symptomatic CLE; conservative follow-up for mild cases. OpenAnesthesia 2025: avoid N₂O, minimise positive pressure, surgeon ready at induction.

ask.question: At induction the child desaturates and becomes hypotensive with bag ventilation. Best immediate action?

choices.text: Open the chest quickly and let the lobe decompress out of the wound
choices.why: Positive pressure inflates the trapped lobe further (tension physiology). Opening the chest decompresses it at once; this is why the surgeon is scrubbed at induction.

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body:
Right lateral decubitus, table flexed, the arm forward. The incision curves from the anterior axillary line to a point midway between the tip of the scapula and the spine.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: Case: an EGFR-positive adenocarcinoma in a never-smoker
steps.lead: A 58-year-old woman, never a smoker, cooked over a wood fire for 30 years. Six months of cough; given anti-TB treatment twice at a health centre without a positive sputum test. CT: a 3.4 cm mass in the left upper lobe, no enlarged nodes; biopsy: adenocarcinoma, EGFR exon 19 deletion. PET: no nodal or distant uptake. EBUS: stations 4L, 7 and 10L negative. FEV1 78%, DLCO 72% predicted.
steps.body:
Stage: T2a (3–4 cm) N0 M0 = IB. Why EBUS with a negative PET? A tumour over 3 cm (or central, or cN1) carries enough risk of occult N2 to justify invasive staging. Fitness: the left upper lobe (with the lingula) has 5 of the 19 segments: ppoFEV1 = 78 × 14/19 ≈ 57%, ppoDLCO = 72 × 14/19 ≈ 53%; both are in the 30–60% band, and she climbs three flights (over 22 m) without stopping: fit for lobectomy.

Plan: VATS left upper lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection, then adjuvant osimertinib for the EGFR mutation.

choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Uniportal incision
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, table broken. One 3–4 cm incision in the 4th space between the anterior and mid-axillary lines, wound protector in. Camera at the back of the wound; staplers and instruments below and in front of it.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut, sweeping along the line of the artery.

The interlobar pulmonary artery appears in its sheath. Get onto the sheath: everything that follows is dissected on the artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: First segmental arteries in the fissure
steps.body:
Follow the artery up and back. The posterior segmental artery (A1+2c, sometimes two) is the first upper lobe branch you meet from the fissure, leaving the posterosuperior surface as the artery arches over the bronchus. The lingular artery runs forward into the lingula.

Map the lower lobe branches first: A6 behind, often opposite the lingular artery, and the basal trunk below. Then divide the upper lobe branches.

ask.question: In the fissure, which lower-lobe branch arises posteriorly, often opposite the lingular artery?

choices.why: A6 is the first lower-lobe branch and leaves the posterior aspect of the artery; take it by mistake and the superior segment is devascularised.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: ligate and divide
steps.body:
Follow the artery up to its first branch. Open the mediastinal pleura over the top of the hilum, in front of the vagus, and dissect the truncus anterior circumferentially.

Ligate it: two ties on the pulmonary artery side, one on the lobe side, then divide between. The truncus is short: leave enough stump for the ties.

The aortic arch, the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the station 5 nodes are just above.

ask.question: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve leave the vagus?

choices.text: At the aortic arch, hooking under it beside the ligamentum arteriosum
choices.why: On the left the nerve loops under the arch; on the right it loops under the subclavian artery.

choices.text: At the level of the inferior pulmonary vein

steps.pearl: A short, wide truncus that will not take three ties is stapled instead.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
With the upper lobe arteries divided, the upper lobe bronchus lies free beneath where the artery arched over it. Clear station 11 at the secondary carina.

Pass the endostapler (thick-tissue reload), close it, and inflate: the lower lobe must ventilate before firing.

steps.title: Pulmonary veins: superior vein last
steps.body:
Roll the lobe back to show the front of the hilum. Two veins: the superior pulmonary vein from the upper lobe, and below it the inferior pulmonary vein from the lower lobe, which stays.

Keep the phrenic nerve on the pericardium, pass the vascular stapler round the superior vein and fire. The lobe is now free except for any fused fissure.

ask.question: Taking the vein last, what is the argument for doing it this way?

choices.text: Arterial inflow is stopped before venous outflow
choices.why: Dividing arteries first avoids congesting the lobe; in cancer surgery the vein-first argument (less tumour-cell shedding) is debated.

choices.text: The vein is easier to reach from behind

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Staple any remaining fused fissure anteriorly, bag and remove the lobe, and complete the nodal dissection: stations 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11. Leak-test the stump under saline.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The hilum from behind and in the fissure
steps.body:
Seen from behind and from the fissure, the pulmonary artery is the key: it arches over the left main bronchus, then descends in the fissure, giving off its upper lobe branches one by one.

In the fissure: the posterior segmental artery up and back, the lingular artery forward, the superior segmental (A6) to the lower lobe behind, the basal trunk continuing down. The truncus anterior is the first branch, high on the anterosuperior surface.

Order of division from behind: fissure → posterior segmental → truncus → bronchus → vein.

steps.title: Case: an EGFR-positive adenocarcinoma in a never-smoker
steps.lead: A 58-year-old woman, never a smoker, cooked over a wood fire for 30 years. Six months of cough; given anti-TB treatment twice at a health centre without a positive sputum test. CT: a 3.4 cm mass in the left upper lobe, no enlarged nodes; biopsy: adenocarcinoma, EGFR exon 19 deletion. PET: no nodal or distant uptake. EBUS: stations 4L, 7 and 10L negative. FEV1 78%, DLCO 72% predicted.
steps.body:
Stage: T2a (3–4 cm) N0 M0 = IB. Why EBUS with a negative PET? A tumour over 3 cm (or central, or cN1) carries enough risk of occult N2 to justify invasive staging. Fitness: the left upper lobe (with the lingula) has 5 of the 19 segments: ppoFEV1 = 78 × 14/19 ≈ 57%, ppoDLCO = 72 × 14/19 ≈ 53%; both are in the 30–60% band, and she climbs three flights (over 22 m) without stopping: fit for lobectomy.

Plan: VATS left upper lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection, then adjuvant osimertinib for the EGFR mutation.

Evidence: VIOLET (HTA 2022; 503 patients): VATS lobectomy gave better physical function at 5 weeks and fewer in-hospital complications than open lobectomy, with no loss of nodal upstaging. ADAURA (NEJM 2023): adjuvant osimertinib after resection of EGFR-mutant stage IB–IIIA disease improved 5-year overall survival (88% vs 78%, HR 0.49).

ask.question: Why did she need EBUS when the PET showed no nodal uptake?

choices.text: A tumour over 3 cm carries a significant risk of occult mediastinal nodes; guidelines advise invasive staging for tumours over 3 cm, central tumours or cN1
choices.why: PET misses small nodal deposits. ESTS 2014 recommends invasive staging for central tumours, tumours over 3 cm, or suspected N1 even when PET is negative.

choices.text: EBUS is required before every lobectomy
Because she had been treated for TB

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

steps.title: The lower lobe hilum
steps.body:
Three structures leave the lower lobe, each lower and more posterior than its upper lobe counterpart. The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure of the hilum, with the inferior pulmonary ligament running down from its lower border to the diaphragm.

In the fissure the artery gives the superior segmental artery (A6) posteriorly, often opposite the lingular artery, and continues as the basal trunk. The lower lobe bronchus lies behind and between the artery and the vein; its superior segmental branch (B6) leaves early and posteriorly.

Keep in view what stays: the lingular artery, the posterior segmental arteries and the upper lobe bronchus.

steps.title: Case: a squamous carcinoma with a hilar node
steps.lead: A 66-year-old man, smoker (45 pack-years). A 4.6 cm squamous cell carcinoma in the left lower lobe; PET: uptake in an interlobar node (station 11L), mediastinum clear; EBUS of stations 4L and 7 negative; no distant disease. FEV1 70%, DLCO 64%.
steps.body:
Stage: T2b (4–5 cm) N1 M0 = IIB. Resectable by lobectomy (a sleeve if the node is fused to the lower lobe bronchus origin).

Sequence: for stage II–IIIA disease, neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy (platinum doublet plus nivolumab, three cycles) before surgery is now an evidence-based option where available; otherwise surgery then adjuvant chemotherapy.

Evidence: CheckMate 816 (NEJM 2022; 358 patients, stage IB–IIIA): three cycles of nivolumab plus chemotherapy before surgery gave a pathological complete response in 24% vs 2.2% with chemotherapy alone, and longer event-free survival (median 31.6 vs 20.8 months).

ask.question: What stage is a 4.6 cm tumour with an interlobar (station 11) node and a negative mediastinum?

choices.why: T2b is over 4 up to 5 cm; station 11 is N1 (intrapulmonary/hilar). T2 N1 is stage IIB.

steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, right lung ventilated. For a fissure-first approach the ports sit further back: a utility incision in the 5th intercostal space in line with the fissure, a camera port low and posterior, and a posterior working port. Port sites vary between units.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body:
Retract the lower lobe up and forward. Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the diathermy hook from the diaphragm upward, close to the lung, taking the station 9 nodes with the specimen.

Stop at the lower border of the inferior pulmonary vein. The esophagus and the descending aorta are just medial: keep the hook on the lung side.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Open the visceral pleura where the fissure is deepest and dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery.

Identify the A6 branch behind, the basal trunk continuing down and the lingular artery in front, before dividing anything.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: Superior segmental artery (A6) and basal trunk
steps.body:
In the open fissure the artery is followed down. A6 leaves its posterior surface first; the basal trunk continues below. Opposite A6, on the anterior surface, is the lingular artery, which stays.

Divide A6 and the basal trunk separately with the vascular stapler.

ask.question: Which upper lobe artery often arises opposite A6 and must be protected?

choices.why: The lingular artery leaves the anterior aspect of the interlobar artery, often at the level of A6; stapling the basal trunk too high can take it.

steps.pearl: If A6 arises high and the basal trunk is short, staple them separately; one stapler across both risks the lingular artery.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body:
With the ligament divided the inferior pulmonary vein lies free at the bottom of the hilum. Clear it circumferentially.

Before stapling, see the superior pulmonary vein as a separate structure: a common venous trunk, a recognised variant on the left, taken here would drain the whole lung.

choices.text: That the superior pulmonary vein is separate and drains the upper lobe
choices.why: A common pulmonary vein taken as the "inferior vein" drains the whole lung.

steps.title: Lower lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Sweep the station 11 nodes up into the specimen and expose the lower lobe bronchus down to the secondary carina. Staple proximal to the superior segmental bronchus (B6), which leaves early and posteriorly.

Close the stapler (thick-tissue reload) and inflate: the upper lobe must ventilate. Then fire.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the lower lobe bronchus: what must happen when the lung is inflated?

choices.why: If the upper lobe does not ventilate, the stapler is across the left main or upper lobe bronchus.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body:
Bag the lobe and remove it. Complete the nodal dissection: station 7 below the carina, 9 in the ligament, 10 and 11 at the hilum; for lower lobe tumours the subcarinal nodes matter most.

Leak-test the bronchial stump under saline and check that the upper lobe fills the chest; an upper lobe that does not reach the apex may need an apical drain.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The lower lobe hilum
steps.body:
Three structures leave the lower lobe, each lower and more posterior than its upper lobe counterpart. The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure of the hilum, with the inferior pulmonary ligament running down from its lower border to the diaphragm.

In the fissure the artery gives the superior segmental artery (A6) posteriorly, often opposite the lingular artery, and continues as the basal trunk. The lower lobe bronchus lies behind and between the artery and the vein; its superior segmental branch (B6) leaves early and posteriorly.

Keep in view what stays: the lingular artery, the posterior segmental arteries and the upper lobe bronchus.

steps.title: Case: a squamous carcinoma with a hilar node
steps.lead: A 66-year-old man, smoker (45 pack-years). A 4.6 cm squamous cell carcinoma in the left lower lobe; PET: uptake in an interlobar node (station 11L), mediastinum clear; EBUS of stations 4L and 7 negative; no distant disease. FEV1 70%, DLCO 64%.
steps.body:
Stage: T2b (4–5 cm) N1 M0 = IIB. Resectable by lobectomy (a sleeve if the node is fused to the lower lobe bronchus origin).

Sequence: for stage II–IIIA disease, neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy (platinum doublet plus nivolumab, three cycles) before surgery is now an evidence-based option where available; otherwise surgery then adjuvant chemotherapy.

Evidence: CheckMate 816 (NEJM 2022; 358 patients, stage IB–IIIA): three cycles of nivolumab plus chemotherapy before surgery gave a pathological complete response in 24% vs 2.2% with chemotherapy alone, and longer event-free survival (median 31.6 vs 20.8 months).

ask.question: What stage is a 4.6 cm tumour with an interlobar (station 11) node and a negative mediastinum?

choices.why: T2b is over 4 up to 5 cm; station 11 is N1 (intrapulmonary/hilar). T2 N1 is stage IIB.

2. Common

3. Serious

4. Specific to this operation

5. Alternatives

6. Recovery

steps.title: Pathophysiology: congenital lobar emphysema versus CPAM
steps.body:
Congenital lobar emphysema (CLE)Congenital pulmonary airway malformation (CPAM)
What it isA normal-structured lobe that over-distends: deficient bronchial cartilage (or compression) makes a ball valve; air enters, cannot leaveA hamartomatous lesion of cysts and abnormal airways, usually one lobe; blood supply from the pulmonary artery
WhereLeft upper lobe (about 43%), middle lobe (32%), right upper (21%); lower lobes rareAny lobe; lower lobes often
WhenNeonatal respiratory distress; half at birth, most by 6 monthsMost found on antenatal ultrasound; some present with infection later
ImagingA hyperlucent lobe with vascular markings, the other lobes compressed, the mediastinum shiftedAir-filled cysts of varying size; solid in microcystic types
RisksProgressive compression, tension physiologyInfection; hydrops in the fetus (CVR over 1.6); malignancy (mucinous adenocarcinoma with type 1; type 4 now regarded as cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma)
Deficient bronchial cartilage→Airway collapses in expiration (ball valve)→Air trapping, lobe over-distends→Compresses the other lobes, shifts the mediastinum→Respiratory distress, falling venous return

The trap: CLE looks like a tension pneumothorax. A chest drain into an emphysematous lobe makes a large air leak and can kill; look for lung markings in the lucent area before inserting one.

Anaesthesia for CLE: avoid nitrous oxide (it expands the lobe) and high positive-pressure ventilation before the chest is open (spontaneous breathing or gentle ventilation); the surgeon scrubbed at induction, ready to open the chest and deliver the lobe.

Stocker types of CPAM: 0 (acinar dysplasia, lethal), 1 (large cysts over 2 cm, 50–70%), 2 (small cysts, associated anomalies), 3 (solid-appearing, alveolar), 4 (peripheral cysts; now considered cystic pleuropulmonary blastoma).

Evidence: CLE: StatPearls 2024 (lobe distribution, presentation, pneumothorax pitfall) and OpenAnesthesia 2025 (anaesthetic management). CPAM: CPAM volume ratio over 1.6 predicted hydrops in 75% (Crombleholme et al., J Pediatr Surg 2002); resection of asymptomatic lesions at 6–12 months versus surveillance remains debated (StatPearls). Pathology update: Dehner et al., Pediatr Dev Pathol 2023.

choices.why: Vascular markings mean over-distended lung, not free air: this is CLE. A drain would enter the lobe and cause a large air leak. The treatment is lobectomy.

steps.title: Case: an infected CPAM in a child
steps.lead: A 6-year-old girl, three admissions for "left lower lobe pneumonia" in a year. Antenatal scans were not done. CT after treatment: multiple air-filled cysts up to 3 cm in the left lower lobe, the cyst walls thick; the arterial supply from the pulmonary artery (no systemic feeder).
steps.body:
A symptomatic, recurrently infected type 1 CPAM: left lower lobectomy once the infection has settled (a segmentectomy only if the lesion is small and clearly confined). Complete excision matters: type 1 lesions carry a risk of mucinous adenocarcinoma, especially if incompletely removed. Check the CT for a systemic artery (a hybrid lesion with sequestration): an unseen feeder from the aorta in the inferior ligament bleeds.

Evidence: StatPearls (CPAM): resection is indicated for symptomatic lesions; for asymptomatic ones, elective resection at 6–12 months versus surveillance is debated. Malignancy association: Dehner et al., Pediatr Dev Pathol 2023.

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body:

Divide latissimus dorsi, spare and retract serratus anterior, count the ribs from above under the scapula, and enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib so the neurovascular bundle under the 5th is spared. Open the space with the rib spreader, slowly.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The lower lobe hilum
steps.body:
Three structures leave the lower lobe, each lower and more posterior than its upper lobe counterpart. The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure of the hilum, with the inferior pulmonary ligament running down from its lower border to the diaphragm.

In the fissure the artery gives the superior segmental artery (A6) posteriorly, often opposite the lingular artery, and continues as the basal trunk. The lower lobe bronchus lies behind and between the artery and the vein; its superior segmental branch (B6) leaves early and posteriorly.

Keep in view what stays: the lingular artery, the posterior segmental arteries and the upper lobe bronchus.

steps.title: Case: a squamous carcinoma with a hilar node
steps.lead: A 66-year-old man, smoker (45 pack-years). A 4.6 cm squamous cell carcinoma in the left lower lobe; PET: uptake in an interlobar node (station 11L), mediastinum clear; EBUS of stations 4L and 7 negative; no distant disease. FEV1 70%, DLCO 64%.
steps.body:
Stage: T2b (4–5 cm) N1 M0 = IIB. Resectable by lobectomy (a sleeve if the node is fused to the lower lobe bronchus origin).

Sequence: for stage II–IIIA disease, neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy (platinum doublet plus nivolumab, three cycles) before surgery is now an evidence-based option where available; otherwise surgery then adjuvant chemotherapy.

Evidence: CheckMate 816 (NEJM 2022; 358 patients, stage IB–IIIA): three cycles of nivolumab plus chemotherapy before surgery gave a pathological complete response in 24% vs 2.2% with chemotherapy alone, and longer event-free survival (median 31.6 vs 20.8 months).

ask.question: What stage is a 4.6 cm tumour with an interlobar (station 11) node and a negative mediastinum?

choices.why: T2b is over 4 up to 5 cm; station 11 is N1 (intrapulmonary/hilar). T2 N1 is stage IIB.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Uniportal incision
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, table broken. One 3–4 cm incision in the 5th space between the anterior and mid-axillary lines, wound protector in. Camera at the back of the wound; staplers and instruments below and in front of it.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body:
Retract the lower lobe up and forward. Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the diathermy hook from the diaphragm upward, close to the lung, taking the station 9 nodes with the specimen.

Stop at the lower border of the inferior pulmonary vein. The esophagus and the descending aorta are just medial: keep the hook on the lung side.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Open the visceral pleura where the fissure is deepest and dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery.

Identify the A6 branch behind, the basal trunk continuing down and the lingular artery in front, before dividing anything.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: Superior segmental artery (A6) and basal trunk
steps.body:
In the open fissure the artery is followed down. A6 leaves its posterior surface first; the basal trunk continues below. Opposite A6, on the anterior surface, is the lingular artery, which stays.

Divide A6 and the basal trunk separately with the vascular stapler.

ask.question: Which upper lobe artery often arises opposite A6 and must be protected?

choices.why: The lingular artery leaves the anterior aspect of the interlobar artery, often at the level of A6; stapling the basal trunk too high can take it.

steps.pearl: If A6 arises high and the basal trunk is short, staple them separately; one stapler across both risks the lingular artery.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body:
With the ligament divided the inferior pulmonary vein lies free at the bottom of the hilum. Clear it circumferentially.

Before stapling, see the superior pulmonary vein as a separate structure: a common venous trunk, a recognised variant on the left, taken here would drain the whole lung.

ask.question: Before stapling the inferior pulmonary vein, what must you confirm?

choices.text: That the superior pulmonary vein is separate and drains the upper lobe
choices.why: A common pulmonary vein taken as the "inferior vein" drains the whole lung.

steps.title: Lower lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Sweep the station 11 nodes up into the specimen and expose the lower lobe bronchus down to the secondary carina. Staple proximal to the superior segmental bronchus (B6), which leaves early and posteriorly.

Close the stapler (thick-tissue reload) and inflate: the upper lobe must ventilate. Then fire.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the lower lobe bronchus: what must happen when the lung is inflated?

choices.why: If the upper lobe does not ventilate, the stapler is across the left main or upper lobe bronchus.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The right hilum from the front
steps.body:
From the front, the superior pulmonary vein is the most anterior structure. Its upper tributaries drain the upper lobe; its lowest tributary, the middle lobe vein, must be kept. Above and behind the vein, the truncus anterior leaves the right pulmonary artery as its first branch, just below the azygos arch and behind the SVC.

Order from the front: upper lobe veins → truncus → bronchus → ascending arteries → fissures.

steps.title: Case: a small peripheral adenocarcinoma: segment or lobe?
steps.lead: A 54-year-old woman. An incidental 1.8 cm part-solid nodule in the right upper lobe (consolidation-to-tumour ratio 0.8), growing over 6 months; PET: mild uptake, nodes clear. It lies across the plane between the apical (S1) and anterior (S3) segments, 12 mm from it. FEV1 92%.
steps.body:
Stage: cT1b N0 = IA2. For a peripheral tumour of 2 cm or less with confirmed node-negative disease, an anatomical segmentectomy is now equivalent or better than lobectomy for survival. But it needs a margin at least as wide as the tumour (2 cm, or the tumour diameter). Straddling the S1/S3 plane, a single segment would not give that margin: a bisegmentectomy or, as here, a lobectomy.

Evidence: JCOG0802/WJOG4607L (Lancet 2022; tumours ≤2 cm, C/T ratio >0.5): 5-year overall survival 94.3% after segmentectomy vs 91.1% after lobectomy (HR 0.66), with more local recurrence (10.5% vs 5.4%). CALGB 140503 (NEJM 2023; ≤2 cm, node-negative on frozen section): sublobar resection was non-inferior for disease-free survival (63.6% vs 64.1%).

ask.question: Which trial showed better overall survival with segmentectomy than lobectomy for peripheral tumours of 2 cm or less?

choices.why: 5-year OS 94.3% vs 91.1%, attributed to preserved lung function and fewer deaths from other causes, despite more local recurrence.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment
