ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body:
Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, left lung ventilated through a double-lumen tube.

Utility incision anteriorly in the 4th intercostal space over the hilum; camera low and anterior; working port at the same level further back.

steps.title: Open the pleura over the front of the hilum
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe back. With the peanut, sweep the mediastinal pleura off the front of the hilum behind the phrenic nerve, from the azygos arch down to the middle lobe vein.

Identify all the tributaries of the superior vein, including the middle lobe vein at its lower border.

steps.title: Upper lobe veins: staple, keep the middle lobe vein
steps.body:
Encircle the upper lobe tributaries of the superior vein and pass the vascular stapler from the working port.

Before firing, trace the middle lobe vein into the middle lobe and keep it out of the jaws.

ask.question: Stapling the upper lobe veins, which tributary of the superior pulmonary vein must be kept?

choices.why: The middle lobe vein is the lowest tributary of the right superior vein; taking it with the upper lobe veins leaves the middle lobe congested and may force a bilobectomy.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: staple
steps.body:
The truncus anterior is the first branch of the right pulmonary artery, leaving its upper surface for the apical and anterior segments. It is short and wide, just below the azygos arch and behind the SVC.

Clear the station 10R node from the angle between the truncus and the artery; that exposes the length you need. Pass the vascular stapler and fire.

ask.question: What lies immediately above the right truncus anterior as you clear it?

choices.why: The azygos arches forward over the right main bronchus into the SVC just above the truncus; it can be divided for exposure if needed.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Sweep stations 10R and 11R toward the specimen. The upper lobe bronchus leaves the right main bronchus high; below it the bronchus intermedius must stay intact.

Close the stapler (thick-tissue reload) on the upper lobe bronchus and inflate: the middle and lower lobes must ventilate. Then fire.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the right upper lobe bronchus: which lobes must inflate?

choices.why: If the middle and lower lobes do not ventilate, the stapler is across the bronchus intermedius or the main bronchus.

steps.title: Ascending arteries to the upper lobe
steps.body:
Lift the bronchial stump: the remaining upper lobe arteries rise from the interlobar artery below it. The ascending posterior artery (A2) and any ascending anterior branch go up into the upper lobe.

The middle lobe artery runs forward and A6 back at the same level: keep both.

ask.question: Dividing the ascending posterior artery in the fissure, which branch arises close by and must be kept?

choices.text: The superior segmental artery of the lower lobe (A6)
choices.why: A2 leaves the interlobar artery at about the level of A6 and the middle lobe artery; identify all three before dividing.

steps.title: Horizontal fissure, front to back
steps.body: Only the fissures hold the upper lobe now. Staple the horizontal fissure from the front back to where the fissures meet, keeping the middle lobe below the staple line.

steps.title: Posterior oblique fissure
steps.body: Finish with the posterior part of the oblique fissure, from the junction up and back, keeping A6 and the lower lobe below the line.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body:
Bag the lobe and remove it. Complete the nodal dissection: stations 2R and 4R (between the SVC, trachea and azygos), 7 below the carina, 10R and 11R at the hilum.

Leak-test the stump under saline. Check that the middle lobe is pink, ventilating and not twisted; if it is mobile on a complete fissure, fix it to the lower lobe to prevent torsion.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after right upper lobectomy: the middle lobe has opacified and the patient is febrile. Most important diagnosis to exclude?

choices.why: Torsion is rare but causes infarction; bronchoscopy and return to theatre if suspected.

rul-open.summary: Posterolateral thoracotomy, then fissure junction, ascending arteries, bronchus, truncus, upper lobe veins.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: post-tuberculous lung and aspergilloma
steps.body:
Cured is not healed. Up to half of people who complete TB treatment are left with lung damage (post-TB lung disease): cavities, bronchiectasis, fibrosis and pleural thickening, with obstruction, restriction or both.

Caseous necrosis in the upper lobe→Liquefaction, discharged through a bronchus→Cavity→Healing by fibrosis: thick wall, traction bronchiectasis
Cavity + bronchial and non-bronchial systemic arteries hypertrophy→Haemoptysis (from the systemic circulation, at systemic pressure)
Cavity colonised by Aspergillus→Fungal ball (aspergilloma)→Erosion of the vascular wall → haemoptysis→Chronic cavitary aspergillosis if it progresses

Simple aspergilloma: a single cavity with a fungal ball, few symptoms, no progression over 3 months. Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis: one or more cavities that enlarge or multiply over months, with symptoms and a positive Aspergillus IgG; treated with long-term oral azoles. Surgery is for simple aspergilloma, and for complex disease with haemoptysis once medically optimised.

Massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxia, not blood loss. First: lie the patient bleeding side down, secure the airway (a large tube, selective intubation of the good side or a bronchial blocker), then bronchial artery embolisation as a bridge; operate once the bleeding has settled and the patient is optimised.

Evidence: post-TB lung disease: Migliori et al. clinical standards (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis 2021): up to 50% have problems after treatment; a meta-analysis (Ivanova et al., Eur Respir Rev 2023; 14,621 people) found mean FEV1 77% predicted with obstruction in 22% and restriction in 23%. ESCMID/ERS guideline (Denning et al., Eur Respir J 2016): excise simple aspergilloma if technically possible. Bronchial artery embolisation stops haemoptysis in 70–99%, but it recurs in 10–57% (Panda et al., 2017).

ask.question: Where does the blood come from in haemoptysis from a post-TB cavity?

choices.text: Hypertrophied bronchial and non-bronchial systemic arteries, at systemic pressure
choices.why: That is why it can be massive, and why bronchial (and intercostal, phrenic) artery embolisation controls it; the pulmonary artery is the source in a minority (Rasmussen aneurysm).

choices.text: Capillaries in the cavity wall only

steps.title: The right hilum from behind
steps.body:
From behind, the upper lobe bronchus leaves the right main bronchus high, above the artery (the eparterial bronchus), with the bronchus intermedius continuing below. The azygos arch crosses above it into the SVC; the vagus runs down behind the hilum.

Where the fissures meet, the interlobar artery gives the ascending posterior artery (A2) up to the upper lobe, the middle lobe artery forward and A6 back.

Order from behind: fissure → ascending arteries → bronchus → truncus → upper lobe veins.

steps.title: Case: aspergilloma with haemoptysis
steps.lead: A 42-year-old man, treated for pulmonary TB 8 years ago (cured). Three episodes of haemoptysis in 2 months, the last about 300 mL, controlled by bronchial artery embolisation 10 days ago. CT: a thick-walled right apical cavity with a mobile fungal ball (air crescent), the rest of the lung nearly normal; Aspergillus IgG positive. FEV1 72%. Sputum smear and GeneXpert negative.
steps.body:
Simple aspergilloma in a fit patient with recurrent haemoptysis: resection (right upper lobectomy). Embolisation bought time; bleeding recurs in a large proportion. Exclude active TB first.

Why open (or experienced VATS only): dense, vascular apical adhesions; an extrapleural plane may be needed; bleeding from the chest wall collaterals; the cavity must not be entered (spillage). An antifungal (voriconazole) around surgery is reasonable if spillage is likely. Plan a muscle flap (serratus or intercostal) if a residual space is expected.

Evidence: surgical series: Akbari et al. (Mayo, 2005): no deaths or major complications after resection of simple aspergilloma vs 4.3% mortality and 26% major complications for complex disease; Kim et al. (Korea, 2005): mortality 1.1%, morbidity 27%. ESCMID/ERS 2016: excise simple aspergilloma if technically possible.

ask.question: After successful bronchial artery embolisation, why operate on this simple aspergilloma?

choices.text: Haemoptysis often recurs after embolisation, and resection of a simple aspergilloma is curative with low risk
choices.why: Recurrence after embolisation ranges from 10% to over 50%; a simple aspergilloma in a fit patient is best removed, electively, once bleeding has settled.

choices.text: Embolisation is curative; surgery is not needed
To obtain tissue for TB culture only
Only if itraconazole fails for 2 years

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body:
Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, the arm forward. The incision curves from the anterior axillary line to a point midway between the tip of the scapula and the spine.

Divide latissimus dorsi, spare and retract serratus anterior, count the ribs from above under the scapula, and enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib so the neurovascular bundle under the 5th is spared. Open the space with the rib spreader, slowly.

steps.title: Open the fissure junction with a peanut
steps.body:
Where the horizontal and oblique fissures meet, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery.

Map its branches before dividing anything: A2 up into the upper lobe, the middle lobe artery forward, A6 back, the basal trunk down.

steps.title: Ascending arteries to the upper lobe
steps.body:
In the open fissure, follow the interlobar artery up: the ascending posterior artery (A2) is the first upper lobe branch you meet from here, and any ascending anterior branch lies just in front.

Keep the middle lobe artery and A6, which leave at about the same level. Divide the ascending branches.

ask.question: Dividing the ascending posterior artery in the fissure, which branch arises close by and must be kept?

choices.text: The superior segmental artery of the lower lobe (A6)
choices.why: A2 leaves the interlobar artery at about the level of A6 and the middle lobe artery; identify all three before dividing.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Sweep stations 10R and 11R toward the specimen. The upper lobe bronchus leaves the right main bronchus high; below it the bronchus intermedius must stay intact.

Close the stapler (thick-tissue reload) on the upper lobe bronchus and inflate: the middle and lower lobes must ventilate. Then fire.

From behind, the bronchus is reached by opening the posterior mediastinal pleura below the azygos arch, in front of the vagus.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the right upper lobe bronchus: which lobes must inflate?

choices.why: If the middle and lower lobes do not ventilate, the stapler is across the bronchus intermedius or the main bronchus.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: ligate and divide
steps.body:
The truncus anterior is the first branch of the right pulmonary artery, leaving its upper surface for the apical and anterior segments. It is short and wide, just below the azygos arch and behind the SVC.

Clear the station 10R node from the angle between the truncus and the artery; that exposes the length you need. Two ties on the artery side, one on the lobe side, then divide.

ask.question: What lies immediately above the right truncus anterior as you clear it?

choices.why: The azygos arches forward over the right main bronchus into the SVC just above the truncus; it can be divided for exposure if needed.

steps.title: Upper lobe veins: staple, keep the middle lobe vein
steps.body: Roll the lobe back to show the front of the hilum. Only the upper lobe veins remain. Keep the phrenic nerve on the pericardium and the middle lobe vein out of the jaws, then fire.

ask.question: Stapling the upper lobe veins, which tributary of the superior pulmonary vein must be kept?

choices.why: The middle lobe vein is the lowest tributary of the right superior vein; taking it with the upper lobe veins leaves the middle lobe congested and may force a bilobectomy.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body:
Bag the lobe and remove it. Complete the nodal dissection: stations 2R and 4R (between the SVC, trachea and azygos), 7 below the carina, 10R and 11R at the hilum.

Leak-test the stump under saline. Check that the middle lobe is pink, ventilating and not twisted; if it is mobile on a complete fissure, fix it to the lower lobe to prevent torsion.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after right upper lobectomy: the middle lobe has opacified and the patient is febrile. Most important diagnosis to exclude?

choices.why: Torsion is rare but causes infarction; bronchoscopy and return to theatre if suspected.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: Case: a small peripheral adenocarcinoma: segment or lobe?
steps.lead: A 54-year-old woman. An incidental 1.8 cm part-solid nodule in the right upper lobe (consolidation-to-tumour ratio 0.8), growing over 6 months; PET: mild uptake, nodes clear. It lies across the plane between the apical (S1) and anterior (S3) segments, 12 mm from it. FEV1 92%.
steps.body:
Stage: cT1b N0 = IA2. For a peripheral tumour of 2 cm or less with confirmed node-negative disease, an anatomical segmentectomy is now equivalent or better than lobectomy for survival. But it needs a margin at least as wide as the tumour (2 cm, or the tumour diameter). Straddling the S1/S3 plane, a single segment would not give that margin: a bisegmentectomy or, as here, a lobectomy.

Evidence: JCOG0802/WJOG4607L (Lancet 2022; tumours ≤2 cm, C/T ratio >0.5): 5-year overall survival 94.3% after segmentectomy vs 91.1% after lobectomy (HR 0.66), with more local recurrence (10.5% vs 5.4%). CALGB 140503 (NEJM 2023; ≤2 cm, node-negative on frozen section): sublobar resection was non-inferior for disease-free survival (63.6% vs 64.1%).

choices.why: 5-year OS 94.3% vs 91.1%, attributed to preserved lung function and fewer deaths from other causes, despite more local recurrence.

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

steps.title: The right hilum from behind
steps.body:
From behind, the upper lobe bronchus leaves the right main bronchus high, above the artery (the eparterial bronchus), with the bronchus intermedius continuing below. The azygos arch crosses above it into the SVC; the vagus runs down behind the hilum.

Where the fissures meet, the interlobar artery gives the ascending posterior artery (A2) up to the upper lobe, the middle lobe artery forward and A6 back.

Order from behind: fissure → ascending arteries → bronchus → truncus → upper lobe veins.

steps.title: Case: a small peripheral adenocarcinoma: segment or lobe?
steps.lead: A 54-year-old woman. An incidental 1.8 cm part-solid nodule in the right upper lobe (consolidation-to-tumour ratio 0.8), growing over 6 months; PET: mild uptake, nodes clear. It lies across the plane between the apical (S1) and anterior (S3) segments, 12 mm from it. FEV1 92%.
steps.body:
Stage: cT1b N0 = IA2. For a peripheral tumour of 2 cm or less with confirmed node-negative disease, an anatomical segmentectomy is now equivalent or better than lobectomy for survival. But it needs a margin at least as wide as the tumour (2 cm, or the tumour diameter). Straddling the S1/S3 plane, a single segment would not give that margin: a bisegmentectomy or, as here, a lobectomy.

Evidence: JCOG0802/WJOG4607L (Lancet 2022; tumours ≤2 cm, C/T ratio >0.5): 5-year overall survival 94.3% after segmentectomy vs 91.1% after lobectomy (HR 0.66), with more local recurrence (10.5% vs 5.4%). CALGB 140503 (NEJM 2023; ≤2 cm, node-negative on frozen section): sublobar resection was non-inferior for disease-free survival (63.6% vs 64.1%).

ask.question: Which trial showed better overall survival with segmentectomy than lobectomy for peripheral tumours of 2 cm or less?

choices.why: 5-year OS 94.3% vs 91.1%, attributed to preserved lung function and fewer deaths from other causes, despite more local recurrence.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Two ports
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, table broken. A 3–4 cm utility incision in the 4th space at the anterior axillary line and a 1 cm camera port in the 7th–8th space, mid- to posterior axillary line. Every instrument and stapler goes through the utility incision.

steps.title: Open the fissure junction with a peanut
steps.body:
Where the horizontal and oblique fissures meet, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery.

Map its branches before dividing anything: A2 up into the upper lobe, the middle lobe artery forward, A6 back, the basal trunk down.

steps.title: Ascending arteries to the upper lobe
steps.body:
In the open fissure, follow the interlobar artery up: the ascending posterior artery (A2) is the first upper lobe branch you meet from here, and any ascending anterior branch lies just in front.

Keep the middle lobe artery and A6, which leave at about the same level. Divide the ascending branches.

ask.question: Dividing the ascending posterior artery in the fissure, which branch arises close by and must be kept?

choices.text: The superior segmental artery of the lower lobe (A6)
choices.why: A2 leaves the interlobar artery at about the level of A6 and the middle lobe artery; identify all three before dividing.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Sweep stations 10R and 11R toward the specimen. The upper lobe bronchus leaves the right main bronchus high; below it the bronchus intermedius must stay intact.

Close the stapler (thick-tissue reload) on the upper lobe bronchus and inflate: the middle and lower lobes must ventilate. Then fire.

From behind, the bronchus is reached by opening the posterior mediastinal pleura below the azygos arch, in front of the vagus.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the right upper lobe bronchus: which lobes must inflate?

choices.why: If the middle and lower lobes do not ventilate, the stapler is across the bronchus intermedius or the main bronchus.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: ligate and divide
steps.body:
The truncus anterior is the first branch of the right pulmonary artery, leaving its upper surface for the apical and anterior segments. It is short and wide, just below the azygos arch and behind the SVC.

Clear the station 10R node from the angle between the truncus and the artery; that exposes the length you need. Two ties on the artery side, one on the lobe side, then divide.

ask.question: What lies immediately above the right truncus anterior as you clear it?

choices.why: The azygos arches forward over the right main bronchus into the SVC just above the truncus; it can be divided for exposure if needed.

steps.title: Upper lobe veins: staple, keep the middle lobe vein
steps.body: Roll the lobe back to show the front of the hilum. Only the upper lobe veins remain. Keep the phrenic nerve on the pericardium and the middle lobe vein out of the jaws, then fire.

ask.question: Stapling the upper lobe veins, which tributary of the superior pulmonary vein must be kept?

choices.why: The middle lobe vein is the lowest tributary of the right superior vein; taking it with the upper lobe veins leaves the middle lobe congested and may force a bilobectomy.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body:
Bag the lobe and remove it. Complete the nodal dissection: stations 2R and 4R (between the SVC, trachea and azygos), 7 below the carina, 10R and 11R at the hilum.

Leak-test the stump under saline. Check that the middle lobe is pink, ventilating and not twisted; if it is mobile on a complete fissure, fix it to the lower lobe to prevent torsion.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after right upper lobectomy: the middle lobe has opacified and the patient is febrile. Most important diagnosis to exclude?

choices.why: Torsion is rare but causes infarction; bronchoscopy and return to theatre if suspected.

rml-anterior.summary: Middle lobe vein, bronchus, artery, fissures last.

Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe

N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular

steps.title: The middle lobe hilum
steps.body:
The middle lobe has three small hilar structures, all at the front. The middle lobe vein is the lowest tributary of the superior vein. Directly behind it lies the middle lobe bronchus, leaving the front of the intermedius, and behind and lateral to that, in the fissure, the middle lobe artery (often two branches) leaves the front of the interlobar artery opposite A6.

Order from the front: vein → bronchus → artery → fissures.

steps.title: Case: is he fit? Predicting lung function
steps.lead: A 71-year-old man, ex-smoker with COPD, a 2.6 cm adenocarcinoma in the middle lobe, cT1c N0 (EBUS negative). FEV1 55%, DLCO 50% predicted. He walks 2 km a day.
steps.body:
Predicted postoperative values: the middle lobe has 2 of the 19 segments. ppoFEV1 = 55 × (19 − 2)/19 ≈ 49%; ppoDLCO = 50 × 17/19 ≈ 45%. Both lie between 30 and 60%: a low-technology exercise test decides. He climbs 25 m of stairs without stopping: proceed (middle lobectomy, VATS).

ask.question: FEV1 55% and DLCO 50%; a middle lobectomy removes 2 of 19 segments. What next?

choices.text: Both ppo values are 30–60%: do a stair climb or shuttle walk test
choices.why: ppoFEV1 ≈ 49% and ppoDLCO ≈ 45%. In the 30–60% band, a simple exercise test (stairs >22 m, shuttle >400 m) separates those who can proceed from those who need CPET.

choices.text: He is inoperable: DLCO is under 60%

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, left lung ventilated through a double-lumen tube.

steps.title: Middle lobe vein: staple or ligate
steps.body:
Retract the middle lobe back. Open the pleura over the front of the hilum behind the phrenic nerve and find the lowest tributary of the superior vein running into the middle lobe.

Keep the upper lobe veins above it. Divide the middle lobe vein.

ask.question: Which vein must be kept when dividing the middle lobe vein?

choices.text: The upper lobe tributaries of the superior vein
choices.why: The middle lobe vein joins the superior vein; the upper lobe veins join it just above.

steps.title: Middle lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Directly behind the divided vein is the middle lobe bronchus. Sweep the station 11R node away and pass the stapler.

The interlobar artery lies immediately behind and lateral to this bronchus: keep the anvil tip in view. Close and inflate: upper and lower lobes must ventilate.

ask.question: Passing the stapler behind the middle lobe bronchus, what lies immediately behind it?

choices.why: The artery runs just behind and lateral to the middle lobe bronchus; a blind anvil tip can injure it.

steps.title: Middle lobe artery (A4+5)
steps.body: Lift the bronchial stump: the middle lobe artery (often two branches) leaves the front of the interlobar artery. A6 leaves the back at the same level and the ascending posterior artery goes up: keep both.

steps.title: Horizontal fissure
steps.body: Staple the horizontal fissure between the middle and upper lobes, from the front back to the fissure junction.

steps.title: Anterior oblique fissure
steps.body: Finish with the anterior part of the oblique fissure, between the middle and lower lobes, keeping the basal trunk below the line.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Remove the lobe and complete the nodal dissection: stations 4R, 7, 10R and 11R. Leak-test the stump; check the upper and lower lobes expand to fill the space.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The middle lobe hilum
steps.body:
The middle lobe has three small hilar structures, all at the front. The middle lobe vein is the lowest tributary of the superior vein. Directly behind it lies the middle lobe bronchus, leaving the front of the intermedius, and behind and lateral to that, in the fissure, the middle lobe artery (often two branches) leaves the front of the interlobar artery opposite A6.

Order from the front: vein → bronchus → artery → fissures.

steps.title: Case: is he fit? Predicting lung function
steps.lead: A 71-year-old man, ex-smoker with COPD, a 2.6 cm adenocarcinoma in the middle lobe, cT1c N0 (EBUS negative). FEV1 55%, DLCO 50% predicted. He walks 2 km a day.
steps.body:
Predicted postoperative values: the middle lobe has 2 of the 19 segments. ppoFEV1 = 55 × (19 − 2)/19 ≈ 49%; ppoDLCO = 50 × 17/19 ≈ 45%. Both lie between 30 and 60%: a low-technology exercise test decides. He climbs 25 m of stairs without stopping: proceed (middle lobectomy, VATS).

Evidence: ACCP 2013: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO >60% low risk; either 30–60%: stair climb >22 m or shuttle walk >400 m is satisfactory, otherwise CPET; either <30%: CPET, with VO2max <10 mL/kg/min (or <35% predicted) high risk.

ask.question: FEV1 55% and DLCO 50%; a middle lobectomy removes 2 of 19 segments. What next?

choices.text: Both ppo values are 30–60%: do a stair climb or shuttle walk test
choices.why: ppoFEV1 ≈ 49% and ppoDLCO ≈ 45%. In the 30–60% band, a simple exercise test (stairs >22 m, shuttle >400 m) separates those who can proceed from those who need CPET.

choices.text: He is inoperable: DLCO is under 60%

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Two ports
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, table broken. A 3–4 cm utility incision in the 4th space at the anterior axillary line and a 1 cm camera port in the 7th–8th space, mid- to posterior axillary line. Every instrument and stapler goes through the utility incision.

steps.title: Open the fissure junction with a peanut
steps.body: Where the horizontal and oblique fissures meet, dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery. The middle lobe artery leaves its front; A6 its back.

steps.title: Middle lobe artery (A4+5)
steps.body: Lift the bronchial stump: the middle lobe artery (often two branches) leaves the front of the interlobar artery. A6 leaves the back at the same level and the ascending posterior artery goes up: keep both.

steps.title: Middle lobe vein: staple or ligate
steps.body:
Retract the middle lobe back. Open the pleura over the front of the hilum behind the phrenic nerve and find the lowest tributary of the superior vein running into the middle lobe.

Keep the upper lobe veins above it. Divide the middle lobe vein.

ask.question: Which vein must be kept when dividing the middle lobe vein?

choices.text: The upper lobe tributaries of the superior vein
choices.why: The middle lobe vein joins the superior vein; the upper lobe veins join it just above.

steps.title: Middle lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Directly behind the divided vein is the middle lobe bronchus. Sweep the station 11R node away and pass the stapler.

The interlobar artery lies immediately behind and lateral to this bronchus: keep the anvil tip in view. Close and inflate: upper and lower lobes must ventilate.

ask.question: Passing the stapler behind the middle lobe bronchus, what lies immediately behind it?

choices.why: The artery runs just behind and lateral to the middle lobe bronchus; a blind anvil tip can injure it.

steps.body: Staple the horizontal fissure between the middle and upper lobes, from the front back to the fissure junction.

steps.title: The right lower lobe hilum
steps.body:
The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure of the hilum, with the inferior pulmonary ligament below it. In the fissure the artery gives A6 posteriorly and continues as the basal trunk; at the same level the middle lobe artery leaves anteriorly and must be kept.

The lower lobe bronchus continues the bronchus intermedius; the middle lobe bronchus leaves its front just above, and B6 its back at about the same level.

steps.title: Case: single-station N2 disease
steps.lead: A 60-year-old man, smoker. A 5.8 cm squamous carcinoma in the right lower lobe; PET: uptake in the subcarinal node (station 7) only; EBUS: station 7 positive, 4R and 4L negative; brain MRI clear. FEV1 80%.
steps.body:
Stage: T3 (5–7 cm) N2a (one mediastinal station) M0 = IIIA. N2 disease is treated with multimodality therapy: neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, then restaging and lobectomy with nodal dissection if the disease responds and a lobectomy suffices; or definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by durvalumab. Multi-station (N2b) or bulky N2 favours the non-surgical route. The Tumour Board decides.

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, left lung ventilated through a double-lumen tube.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body: Retract the lower lobe up. Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the hook from the diaphragm up to the lower border of the inferior vein, taking station 9R with the specimen. The esophagus lies just medial.

steps.title: Open the oblique fissure with a peanut
steps.body: Retract the upper and middle lobes forward, the lower lobe back. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery and map A6, the basal trunk and the middle lobe artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first right lower lobectomy works best when…

choices.text: The oblique fissure is complete over the artery
choices.why: With a fused fissure the hilum-first order avoids tearing parenchyma over the artery.

steps.title: Superior segmental artery (A6) and basal trunk
steps.body:
In the open fissure, A6 leaves the back of the artery and the basal trunk continues down; the middle lobe artery leaves the front at about the same level and stays.

Staple A6 and the basal trunk separately.

ask.question: Stapling the right basal trunk, which artery arising at the same level must be protected?

choices.why: The middle lobe artery leaves the front of the interlobar artery opposite A6; a stapler placed too high on the basal trunk takes it.

steps.pearl: If A6 arises opposite the middle lobe artery, staple A6 and the basal trunk separately.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: With the ligament divided the inferior pulmonary vein lies free at the bottom of the hilum. See the superior vein and its middle lobe tributary as separate before stapling.

ask.question: Before stapling the right inferior vein, which vein must you see separately?

choices.text: The superior pulmonary vein with its middle lobe tributary
choices.why: Taking a common trunk, or catching the middle lobe vein, drains lung you mean to keep.

steps.title: Lower lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Clear station 11R and expose the lower lobe bronchus. The middle lobe bronchus leaves the front of the intermedius just above: angle the stapler so it does not narrow it, or take B6 and the basal bronchus separately.

Close the stapler and inflate: the upper and middle lobes must ventilate. Then fire.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the right lower lobe bronchus: what must you check before firing?

choices.text: The upper and middle lobes ventilate and the middle lobe bronchus is not narrowed
choices.why: The middle lobe bronchus arises just above; a stapler across the intermedius takes both lobes.

choices.text: Only that the lower lobe collapses

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Remove the lobe and complete the nodal dissection: station 7, 9R, 10R and 11R, and the paratracheal stations. Leak-test the stump and check that the middle lobe is ventilating and not rotated.

rll-hilum.name: VATS right lower lobectomy
rll-hilum.summary: Ligament, inferior vein, bronchus, A6 and basal trunk, fissure last.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The right lower lobe hilum
steps.body:
The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure of the hilum, with the inferior pulmonary ligament below it. In the fissure the artery gives A6 posteriorly and continues as the basal trunk; at the same level the middle lobe artery leaves anteriorly and must be kept.

The lower lobe bronchus continues the bronchus intermedius; the middle lobe bronchus leaves its front just above, and B6 its back at about the same level.

steps.title: Case: single-station N2 disease
steps.lead: A 60-year-old man, smoker. A 5.8 cm squamous carcinoma in the right lower lobe; PET: uptake in the subcarinal node (station 7) only; EBUS: station 7 positive, 4R and 4L negative; brain MRI clear. FEV1 80%.
steps.body:
Stage: T3 (5–7 cm) N2a (one mediastinal station) M0 = IIIA. N2 disease is treated with multimodality therapy: neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy, then restaging and lobectomy with nodal dissection if the disease responds and a lobectomy suffices; or definitive chemoradiotherapy followed by durvalumab. Multi-station (N2b) or bulky N2 favours the non-surgical route. The Tumour Board decides.

Evidence: 9th-edition staging (IASLC 2024): T3 N2a is IIIA; T3 N2b is IIIB. CheckMate 816: neoadjuvant nivolumab plus chemotherapy improved pCR (24% vs 2.2%) and event-free survival in resectable IB–IIIA disease; about two-thirds of patients were stage IIIA.

ask.question: What distinguishes N2a from N2b in the 9th edition?

choices.text: The number of mediastinal stations involved: one (N2a) or several (N2b)
choices.why: The count is by station, not by the number of nodes, and it carries prognostic weight: T3 N2a is IIIA, T3 N2b IIIB.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Conversion from VATS to open
  • Final staging on the specimen may change the plan (adjuvant therapy)
  • Recurrence

5. Alternatives

  • Segmentectomy for small peripheral tumours
  • Stereotactic radiotherapy (SBRT) if unfit
  • Surveillance for indeterminate nodules
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, left lung ventilated through a double-lumen tube.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body: Retract the lower lobe up. Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the hook from the diaphragm up to the lower border of the inferior vein, taking station 9R with the specimen. The esophagus lies just medial.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: With the ligament divided the inferior pulmonary vein lies free at the bottom of the hilum. See the superior vein and its middle lobe tributary as separate before stapling.

ask.question: Before stapling the right inferior vein, which vein must you see separately?

choices.text: The superior pulmonary vein with its middle lobe tributary
choices.why: Taking a common trunk, or catching the middle lobe vein, drains lung you mean to keep.

steps.title: Lower lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Clear station 11R and expose the lower lobe bronchus. The middle lobe bronchus leaves the front of the intermedius just above: angle the stapler so it does not narrow it, or take B6 and the basal bronchus separately.

Close the stapler and inflate: the upper and middle lobes must ventilate. Then fire.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the right lower lobe bronchus: what must you check before firing?

choices.text: The upper and middle lobes ventilate and the middle lobe bronchus is not narrowed
choices.why: The middle lobe bronchus arises just above; a stapler across the intermedius takes both lobes.

choices.text: Only that the lower lobe collapses

steps.title: Superior segmental artery (A6) and basal trunk
steps.body: With the vein and bronchus divided, lift the bronchial stump: A6 and the basal trunk lie above and behind it. Identify the middle lobe artery in front first.

ask.question: Stapling the right basal trunk, which artery arising at the same level must be protected?

choices.why: The middle lobe artery leaves the front of the interlobar artery opposite A6; a stapler placed too high on the basal trunk takes it.

steps.pearl: If A6 arises opposite the middle lobe artery, staple A6 and the basal trunk separately.

steps.title: Staple the oblique fissure last
steps.body: Only the oblique fissure joins the lower lobe now. Staple it front to back, keeping the middle lobe and its artery above the line.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Remove the lobe and complete the nodal dissection: station 7, 9R, 10R and 11R, and the paratracheal stations. Leak-test the stump and check that the middle lobe is ventilating and not rotated.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after right upper lobectomy: the middle lobe has opacified and the patient is febrile. Most important diagnosis to exclude?

choices.why: Torsion is rare but causes infarction; bronchoscopy and return to theatre if suspected.

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body:
Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, the arm forward. The incision curves from the anterior axillary line to a point midway between the tip of the scapula and the spine.

Divide latissimus dorsi, spare and retract serratus anterior, count the ribs from above under the scapula, and enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib so the neurovascular bundle under the 5th is spared. Open the space with the rib spreader, slowly.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body: Retract the lower lobe up. Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the hook from the diaphragm up to the lower border of the inferior vein, taking station 9R with the specimen. The esophagus lies just medial.

steps.title: Open the oblique fissure with a peanut
steps.body: Retract the upper and middle lobes forward, the lower lobe back. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery and map A6, the basal trunk and the middle lobe artery.

choices.text: The oblique fissure is complete over the artery
choices.why: With a fused fissure the hilum-first order avoids tearing parenchyma over the artery.

steps.title: Superior segmental artery (A6) and basal trunk
steps.body:
In the open fissure, A6 leaves the back of the artery and the basal trunk continues down; the middle lobe artery leaves the front at about the same level and stays.

Staple A6 and the basal trunk separately.

steps.body:
The inferior pulmonary vein is the lowest structure of the hilum, with the inferior pulmonary ligament below it. In the fissure the artery gives A6 posteriorly and continues as the basal trunk; at the same level the middle lobe artery leaves anteriorly and must be kept.

The lower lobe bronchus continues the bronchus intermedius; the middle lobe bronchus leaves its front just above, and B6 its back at about the same level.

ask.question: Which of these belongs in consent for a VATS lobectomy in a patient with healed TB?

choices.text: A higher chance of conversion to open and of bleeding from adhesions and calcified nodes
choices.why: Post-TB pleural and nodal changes make VATS dissection harder; the conversion risk is a material risk.

steps.title: Uniportal incision
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, table broken. One 3–4 cm incision in the 5th space between the anterior and mid-axillary lines, wound protector in. Camera at the back of the wound; staplers and instruments below and in front of it.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body: Retract the lower lobe up. Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the hook from the diaphragm up to the lower border of the inferior vein, taking station 9R with the specimen. The esophagus lies just medial.

steps.title: Open the oblique fissure with a peanut
steps.body: Retract the upper and middle lobes forward, the lower lobe back. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, dissect bluntly with the peanut onto the interlobar artery and map A6, the basal trunk and the middle lobe artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first right lower lobectomy works best when…

choices.text: The oblique fissure is complete over the artery
choices.why: With a fused fissure the hilum-first order avoids tearing parenchyma over the artery.

steps.title: Superior segmental artery (A6) and basal trunk
steps.body:
In the open fissure, A6 leaves the back of the artery and the basal trunk continues down; the middle lobe artery leaves the front at about the same level and stays.

Staple A6 and the basal trunk separately.

ask.question: Stapling the right basal trunk, which artery arising at the same level must be protected?

choices.why: The middle lobe artery leaves the front of the interlobar artery opposite A6; a stapler placed too high on the basal trunk takes it.

steps.pearl: If A6 arises opposite the middle lobe artery, staple A6 and the basal trunk separately.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: With the ligament divided the inferior pulmonary vein lies free at the bottom of the hilum. See the superior vein and its middle lobe tributary as separate before stapling.

ask.question: Before stapling the right inferior vein, which vein must you see separately?

choices.text: The superior pulmonary vein with its middle lobe tributary
choices.why: Taking a common trunk, or catching the middle lobe vein, drains lung you mean to keep.

steps.title: Lower lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
Clear station 11R and expose the lower lobe bronchus. The middle lobe bronchus leaves the front of the intermedius just above: angle the stapler so it does not narrow it, or take B6 and the basal bronchus separately.

Close the stapler and inflate: the upper and middle lobes must ventilate. Then fire.

ask.question: Stapler closed on the right lower lobe bronchus: what must you check before firing?

choices.text: The upper and middle lobes ventilate and the middle lobe bronchus is not narrowed
choices.why: The middle lobe bronchus arises just above; a stapler across the intermedius takes both lobes.

choices.text: Only that the lower lobe collapses

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Remove the lobe and complete the nodal dissection: station 7, 9R, 10R and 11R, and the paratracheal stations. Leak-test the stump and check that the middle lobe is ventilating and not rotated.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak: record every shift; prolonged beyond 5 days
  • Lobar torsion (especially the middle lobe): a lobe that opacifies on X-ray
  • Sputum retention

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after right upper lobectomy: the middle lobe has opacified and the patient is febrile. Most important diagnosis to exclude?

choices.why: Torsion is rare but causes infarction; bronchoscopy and return to theatre if suspected.

steps.body:
A pneumonectomy divides four structures: the main pulmonary artery, the superior and inferior pulmonary veins, and the main bronchus. On the left the artery arches over the bronchus under the aortic arch, tethered by the ligamentum arteriosum, with the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking round it. The left main bronchus is long and runs under the arch to the carina.

Before committing, assess the fissure and hilum for a lobectomy option, and trial-clamp the artery to see that the right heart tolerates it.

steps.lead: A 63-year-old man, smoker, haemoptysis. Bronchoscopy: a squamous carcinoma at the origin of the left upper and lower lobe bronchi, extending into the left main bronchus; CT: a 5 cm hilar mass encasing the left pulmonary artery. steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, table flexed, right lung ventilated through a double-lumen tube (the tube must not sit in the bronchus you will divide). Anterior utility incision over the hilum, low camera port, posterior working port.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body: Retract the lower lobe up and divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the hook up to the inferior vein, taking station 9. The esophagus lies just medial.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: Clear the inferior pulmonary vein circumferentially down to the pericardium and staple it with a vascular load. For a central tumour it can be taken inside the pericardium.

steps.title: Superior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: Retract the lung back, open the pleura over the front of the hilum behind the phrenic nerve, and staple the superior pulmonary vein as a trunk, close to the pericardium.

steps.title: Main pulmonary artery: clamp test, staple
steps.body:
The main pulmonary artery now lies free above the bronchus. Clear it proximal to its first branch, staying below the aortic arch and clear of the recurrent laryngeal nerve at the ligamentum.

Trial-clamp it for a few minutes: watch blood pressure, heart rate and the right ventricle on echo. If tolerated, staple with a vascular load.

ask.question: Why trial-clamp the main pulmonary artery before dividing it?

choices.text: To see whether the right ventricle tolerates the whole cardiac output going to one lung
choices.why: Acute right heart strain or a fall in pressure on clamping warns that pneumonectomy may not be tolerated.

choices.text: To check for bleeding from the bronchial arteries

steps.title: Main bronchus: staple flush with the carina
steps.body:
Clear the subcarinal nodes (station 7) and follow the main bronchus to the carina. Staple it flush with the carina with a thick-tissue load: a long stump pools secretions and leaks.

On the left the bronchus runs under the aortic arch: pull the lung down and out to reach the carina.

ask.question: Why staple the main bronchus flush with the carina?

choices.text: A long stump pools secretions and is prone to breakdown (bronchopleural fistula)
choices.why: The shorter the stump, the less dead space for infection and dehiscence.

choices.text: To make the specimen easier to remove

steps.title: Specimen out, cover the stump, leak test
steps.body:
Remove the lung in a bag through an enlarged incision. Leak-test the stump under saline at 20–25 cmH2O. Cover it with a vascularised flap (pericardial fat, pleura or intercostal muscle), especially after induction therapy.

Complete the nodal dissection. Leave a balanced drain or none, and keep the mediastinum central; restrict fluids.

steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • No suction on the pneumonectomy drain; daily chest X-ray for mediastinal shift
  • Strict fluid limits

  • BPF (days 7–14): fever, serosanguinous sputum, falling fluid level: lie operated side down

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

choices.text: Lie the patient operated side down, then drain the space and arrange bronchoscopy

steps.title: Pathophysiology: post-tuberculous lung destruction
steps.body:
Cured is not healed. Up to half of people who complete TB treatment are left with lung damage (post-TB lung disease): cavities, bronchiectasis, fibrosis and pleural thickening, with obstruction, restriction or both.

Caseous necrosis in the upper lobe→Liquefaction, discharged through a bronchus→Cavity→Healing by fibrosis: thick wall, traction bronchiectasis
Cavity + bronchial and non-bronchial systemic arteries hypertrophy→Haemoptysis (from the systemic circulation, at systemic pressure)
Cavity colonised by Aspergillus→Fungal ball (aspergilloma)→Erosion of the vascular wall → haemoptysis→Chronic cavitary aspergillosis if it progresses

The destroyed lung: a whole lung reduced to cavities, bronchiectasis and fibrosis, contracted, with the pleura fused to the chest wall. It is a reservoir of infection (TB, non-tuberculous mycobacteria, Aspergillus, bacteria), a source of recurrent haemoptysis, and it contributes no gas exchange, often only shunt.

Simple aspergilloma: a single cavity with a fungal ball, few symptoms, no progression over 3 months. Chronic cavitary pulmonary aspergillosis: one or more cavities that enlarge or multiply over months, with symptoms and a positive Aspergillus IgG; treated with long-term oral azoles. Surgery is for simple aspergilloma, and for complex disease with haemoptysis once medically optimised.

Massive haemoptysis kills by asphyxia, not blood loss. First: lie the patient bleeding side down, secure the airway (a large tube, selective intubation of the good side or a bronchial blocker), then bronchial artery embolisation as a bridge; operate once the bleeding has settled and the patient is optimised.

Evidence: post-TB lung disease: Migliori et al. clinical standards (Int J Tuberc Lung Dis 2021): up to 50% have problems after treatment; a meta-analysis (Ivanova et al., Eur Respir Rev 2023; 14,621 people) found mean FEV1 77% predicted with obstruction in 22% and restriction in 23%. ESCMID/ERS guideline (Denning et al., Eur Respir J 2016): excise simple aspergilloma if technically possible. Bronchial artery embolisation stops haemoptysis in 70–99%, but it recurs in 10–57% (Panda et al., 2017).

choices.text: Hypertrophied bronchial and non-bronchial systemic arteries, at systemic pressure
choices.why: That is why it can be massive, and why bronchial (and intercostal, phrenic) artery embolisation controls it; the pulmonary artery is the source in a minority (Rasmussen aneurysm).

steps.title: Case: a TB-destroyed left lung
steps.lead: A 29-year-old woman, treated twice for TB (the second time for multidrug-resistant TB, now culture-negative after treatment). Recurrent haemoptysis and purulent sputum; CT: the left lung destroyed (cavities, bronchiectasis, volume loss, pleural thickening), the right lung clear. Perfusion scan: left lung 8% of total. FEV1 1.4 L (48%).
steps.body:
Pneumonectomy removes a lung that adds almost nothing to gas exchange (ppoFEV1 ≈ 1.4 × 0.92 ≈ 1.3 L) and is the source of her symptoms. Plan: nutrition first, culture conversion, a short bronchial stump covered with a flap.

choices.text: It shows how little the destroyed lung contributes, so the predicted postoperative function is close to the current function
choices.why: ppoFEV1 is calculated from the fraction of perfusion to the lung left behind; here 92% of perfusion goes to the right lung.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

choices.why: Acute right heart strain or a fall in pressure on clamping warns that pneumonectomy may not be tolerated.

choices.text: To check for bleeding from the bronchial arteries

steps.title: Main bronchus: staple flush with the carina
steps.body:
Clear the subcarinal nodes (station 7) and follow the main bronchus to the carina. Staple it flush with the carina with a thick-tissue load: a long stump pools secretions and leaks.

On the right the stump has no aortic arch to cover it and leaks more often: plan to cover it.

ask.question: Why staple the main bronchus flush with the carina?

choices.text: A long stump pools secretions and is prone to breakdown (bronchopleural fistula)
choices.why: The shorter the stump, the less dead space for infection and dehiscence.

choices.text: To make the specimen easier to remove

steps.title: Specimen out, cover the stump, leak test
steps.body:
Remove the lung in a bag through an enlarged incision. Leak-test the stump under saline at 20–25 cmH2O. Cover the right stump with a vascularised flap (intercostal muscle, pericardial fat or azygos-pleura).

Complete the nodal dissection. Leave a balanced drain or none, and keep the mediastinum central; restrict fluids.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • No suction on the pneumonectomy drain; daily chest X-ray for mediastinal shift
  • Strict fluid limits
  • Sudden collapse after an intrapericardial resection: cardiac herniation: operated side up, back to theatre
  • BPF (days 7–14): fever, serosanguinous sputum, falling fluid level: lie operated side down

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 9 after right pneumonectomy: coughing serosanguinous fluid, fluid level has fallen. First action?

choices.text: Lie the patient operated side down, then drain the space and arrange bronchoscopy
choices.why: Bronchopleural fistula: protect the remaining lung from spill-over first.
