pnr-open.name: Right pneumonectomy, open
pnr-open.summary: Posterolateral thoracotomy; artery first: main PA, superior vein, inferior vein, bronchus.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: The right hilum as a whole
steps.body:
A pneumonectomy divides four structures: the main pulmonary artery, the superior and inferior pulmonary veins, and the main bronchus. On the right the artery runs behind the SVC, below the azygos arch; the right main bronchus is short, with the upper lobe bronchus leaving it close to the carina.

Before committing, assess the fissure and hilum for a lobectomy option, and trial-clamp the artery to see that the right heart tolerates it.

steps.title: Case: a central squamous carcinoma needing pneumonectomy
steps.lead: A 63-year-old man, smoker, haemoptysis. Bronchoscopy: a squamous carcinoma at the origin of the right upper lobe bronchus, extending to the bronchus intermedius and the right main bronchus; CT: a 5 cm hilar mass encasing the right pulmonary artery. EBUS: 4R and 7 negative, 10R positive (N1). PET: no distant disease. FEV1 2.4 L (82%), DLCO 75%; perfusion to the right lung 45%.
steps.body:
Stage: T3 (5 cm) N1 = IIIA. A sleeve lobectomy cannot clear the artery and both lobar bronchi: pneumonectomy. ppoFEV1 = 2.4 × 0.55 ≈ 1.3 L (≈45%): exercise testing and CPET before committing. Neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy is an option. Right pneumonectomy carries the highest mortality of any lung resection and the highest risk of bronchopleural fistula (a poorly covered stump with a single bronchial artery): keep the stump short and cover it (intercostal muscle, pericardial fat, pleura), avoid fluid overload (post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema). See the post-pneumonectomy empyema and BPF module.

Evidence: BPF after pneumonectomy: 0–6.3% after left and 1.1–22.9% after right pneumonectomy across series (Wali and Billè, Shanghai Chest 2021); Deschamps et al. (Mayo, 713 pneumonectomies): empyema 7.5%, fistula 4.5%.

ask.question: Why is bronchopleural fistula commoner after right than left pneumonectomy?

choices.text: The right main bronchial stump has little mediastinal cover and usually a single bronchial artery
choices.why: The left stump retracts under the aortic arch into the mediastinum and usually has two bronchial arteries; the exposed, less well perfused right stump breaks down more often.

choices.text: It is not: left is commoner

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Higher mortality than lobectomy (right more than left)
  • Permanent reduction in exercise tolerance
  • Post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema
  • Cardiac herniation (intrapericardial)

5. Alternatives

  • Sleeve lobectomy where anatomy allows
  • Chemoradiation
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: Why is sleeve lobectomy offered, where possible, instead of pneumonectomy?

choices.text: Similar cancer control with lower mortality and better lung function
choices.why: Parenchyma-sparing: pneumonectomy carries higher mortality and permanent loss of function.

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body:
Left lateral decubitus, table flexed, the arm forward. The incision curves from the anterior axillary line to a point midway between the tip of the scapula and the spine.

Divide latissimus dorsi, spare and retract serratus anterior, count the ribs from above under the scapula, and enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib so the neurovascular bundle under the 5th is spared. Open the space with the rib spreader, slowly.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament
steps.body: Retract the lower lobe up and divide the inferior pulmonary ligament with the hook up to the inferior vein, taking station 9. The esophagus lies just medial.

steps.title: Main pulmonary artery: clamp test, staple
steps.body:
The main pulmonary artery now lies free above the bronchus. Clear it proximal to its first branch, behind the SVC and below the azygos.

Trial-clamp it for a few minutes: watch blood pressure, heart rate and the right ventricle on echo. If tolerated, staple with a vascular load.

choices.text: To check for bleeding from the bronchial arteries

steps.title: Superior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: Retract the lung back, open the pleura over the front of the hilum behind the phrenic nerve, and staple the superior pulmonary vein as a trunk, close to the pericardium.

steps.title: Inferior pulmonary vein: staple
steps.body: Clear the inferior pulmonary vein circumferentially down to the pericardium and staple it with a vascular load. For a central tumour it can be taken inside the pericardium.

bx-lul.name: Left upper lobectomy for bronchiectasis
bx-lul.summary: Post-tuberculous bronchiectasis: indications, embolisation, extrapleural dissection, a frozen hilum, protecting the stump.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: post-tuberculous bronchiectasis and the destroyed lobe
steps.body:
Tuberculosis heals with fibrosis, cavities and traction bronchiectasis, most often in the upper lobes. Dilated, thick-walled bronchi pool secretions: a vicious cycle of infection, inflammation and further damage. Chronic inflammation enlarges the bronchial arteries (systemic pressure), which bleed: haemoptysis, sometimes massive. Cavities may host an aspergilloma. The pleura fuses to the chest wall.

Healed TB: fibrosis, cavities→Traction bronchiectasis→Pooling, infection, inflammation→Recurrent infection, haemoptysis, destroyed lobe

Treat medically first: exclude active TB (sputum GeneXpert and culture) and non-tuberculous mycobacteria; airway clearance, treatment of exacerbations. Surgery for localised disease with failed medical therapy, recurrent or massive haemoptysis (after bronchial artery embolisation, or when it fails), a destroyed lobe or lung as a septic focus, or an aspergilloma.

Evidence: Surgery for bronchiectasis-destroyed lung (Interdiscip Cardiovasc Thorac Surg 2024; 143 patients): no 30- or 90-day deaths; major complications 19.6% overall, 50% after pneumonectomy versus 13.4% after lobectomy; 76.2% asymptomatic at a median of 79 months; VATS feasible in selected patients (14% converted for adhesions or a frozen hilum). Breathe (ERS) review on surgery in bronchiectasis and TB.

ask.question: What is the first treatment for massive haemoptysis from post-TB bronchiectasis?

choices.text: Protect the airway (bleeding side down), resuscitate, and bronchial artery embolisation; surgery if it fails or recurs
choices.why: Embolisation controls most bleeding; resection removes the source in localised disease.

steps.title: The hilum from behind and in the fissure
steps.body:
Seen from behind and from the fissure, the pulmonary artery is the key: it arches over the left main bronchus, then descends in the fissure, giving off its upper lobe branches one by one.

In the fissure: the posterior segmental artery up and back, the lingular artery forward, the superior segmental (A6) to the lower lobe behind, the basal trunk continuing down. The truncus anterior is the first branch, high on the anterosuperior surface.

Order of division from behind: fissure → posterior segmental → truncus → bronchus → vein.

steps.title: Case: recurrent haemoptysis from a destroyed left upper lobe
steps.body:
Localised, symptomatic disease in a fit patient with a healthy remaining lung, bleeding again after embolisation: left upper lobectomy. Open thoracotomy is safer than VATS with dense adhesions and calcified hilar nodes.

Before surgery: sputum negative for TB; treat infection; physiotherapy; nutrition; spirometry and a perfusion scan if borderline; bronchoscopy to exclude an endobronchial lesion and to see the left lower lobe bronchus is clean.

ask.question: Which finding makes her a good candidate for resection?

choices.text: Disease confined to one lobe with healthy remaining lung
choices.why: Localised disease with adequate reserve; diffuse bronchiectasis is managed medically.

steps.lead: A 32-year-old woman, TB treated 6 years ago. Two years of daily purulent sputum and three episodes of haemoptysis (the last 300 mL), recurring 4 months after bronchial artery embolisation. CT: a shrunken left upper lobe with cystic bronchiectasis and a small cavity; left lower lobe and right lung clear. Sputum GeneXpert negative twice. FEV1 72% predicted.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1, ppoDLCO; nutrition; sputum TB status. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Air leak
  • Bleeding (adhesions, collaterals)
  • Chest infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain

3. Serious

  • Bronchopleural fistula and empyema
  • Major bleeding
  • Death

4. Specific to this operation

  • Open surgery likely (adhesions); conversion if VATS
  • Symptoms may persist if disease remains elsewhere

5. Alternatives

  • Medical therapy and airway clearance
  • Bronchial artery embolisation for haemoptysis
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Exclude and treat active TB; HIV testing

ask.question: Which risk is higher after resection for post-TB bronchiectasis than after lobectomy for a small cancer?

choices.text: Bleeding from adhesions and collaterals, and bronchopleural fistula
choices.why: Inflamed, adherent fields bleed and heal poorly.

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body:
Right lateral decubitus, table flexed, the arm forward. The incision curves from the anterior axillary line to a point midway between the tip of the scapula and the spine.

Divide latissimus dorsi, spare and retract serratus anterior, count the ribs from above under the scapula, and enter the chest over the upper border of the 6th rib so the neurovascular bundle under the 5th is spared. Open the space with the rib spreader, slowly.

steps.title: Through the adhesions: the extrapleural plane
steps.body: After TB the lung is often fused to the chest wall. Where the adhesions are filmy, divide them with cautery close to the chest wall. Where the pleura is thick and symphysed, the extrapleural plane (outside the parietal pleura, against the endothoracic fascia) is often bloodless and quicker; at the apex beware the subclavian vessels, and over the spine the sympathetic chain. Expect bleeding from hypertrophied bronchial and intercostal collaterals: control them as you go.

ask.question: With a densely symphysed apex, which plane is often safest?

choices.text: The extrapleural plane, outside the parietal pleura
choices.why: It avoids tearing into the lung and its cavities; watch the subclavian vessels at the apex.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut, sweeping along the line of the artery.

The interlobar pulmonary artery appears in its sheath. Get onto the sheath: everything that follows is dissected on the artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: First segmental arteries in the fissure
steps.body:
Follow the artery up and back. The posterior segmental artery (A1+2c, sometimes two) is the first upper lobe branch you meet from the fissure, leaving the posterosuperior surface as the artery arches over the bronchus. The lingular artery runs forward into the lingula.

Map the lower lobe branches first: A6 behind, often opposite the lingular artery, and the basal trunk below. Then divide the upper lobe branches.

ask.question: In the fissure, which lower-lobe branch arises posteriorly, often opposite the lingular artery?

choices.why: A6 is the first lower-lobe branch and leaves the posterior aspect of the artery; take it by mistake and the superior segment is devascularised.

steps.title: Truncus anterior: ligate and divide
steps.body:
Follow the artery up to its first branch. Open the mediastinal pleura over the top of the hilum, in front of the vagus, and dissect the truncus anterior circumferentially.

Ligate it: two ties on the pulmonary artery side, one on the lobe side, then divide between. The truncus is short: leave enough stump for the ties.

The aortic arch, the recurrent laryngeal nerve and the station 5 nodes are just above.

ask.question: Where does the left recurrent laryngeal nerve leave the vagus?

choices.text: At the aortic arch, hooking under it beside the ligamentum arteriosum
choices.why: On the left the nerve loops under the arch; on the right it loops under the subclavian artery.

choices.text: At the level of the inferior pulmonary vein

steps.pearl: A short, wide truncus that will not take three ties is stapled instead.

steps.title: Upper lobe bronchus: clamp, inflate, staple
steps.body:
With the upper lobe arteries divided, the upper lobe bronchus lies free beneath where the artery arched over it. Clear station 11 at the secondary carina.

Pass the endostapler (thick-tissue reload), close it, and inflate: the lower lobe must ventilate before firing.

In bronchiectasis: hilar nodes are often calcified and stuck to the arteries; consider proximal control of the pulmonary artery before dissecting a frozen hilum. Close the bronchus carefully; in a heavily infected field, cover the stump with a pedicled flap (intercostal muscle or pericardial fat).

steps.title: Pulmonary veins: superior vein last
steps.body:
Roll the lobe back to show the front of the hilum. Two veins: the superior pulmonary vein from the upper lobe, and below it the inferior pulmonary vein from the lower lobe, which stays.

Keep the phrenic nerve on the pericardium, pass the vascular stapler round the superior vein and fire. The lobe is now free except for any fused fissure.

ask.question: Taking the vein last, what is the argument for doing it this way?

choices.text: Arterial inflow is stopped before venous outflow
choices.why: Dividing arteries first avoids congesting the lobe; in cancer surgery the vein-first argument (less tumour-cell shedding) is debated.

choices.text: The vein is easier to reach from behind

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, leak test
steps.body: Staple any remaining fused fissure anteriorly, bag and remove the lobe, and complete the nodal dissection: stations 5, 6, 7, 10 and 11. Leak-test the stump under saline.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Bleeding from adhesion beds: drain output closely
  • Air leak and residual space
  • Physiotherapy; culture-directed antibiotics
  • Stump: BPF risk in an infected field

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 1 after lobectomy for bronchiectasis: 250 mL/h of blood for 3 hours. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant: re-exploration for bleeding
choices.why: Adhesion beds and bronchial collaterals bleed; sustained output above the thresholds needs theatre.

seg-lingula.summary: Fissure, segmental artery, vein, bronchus, inflation–deflation line, intersegmental plane.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: lung cancer
steps.body:
In Kenya and across Africa lung cancer usually presents late: in series from Ghana and West Africa three-quarters or more are stage III–IV at diagnosis. A cough, weight loss and a shadow are often treated first as tuberculosis, frequently without bacteriological confirmation; a smear- or GeneXpert-negative "TB" that does not improve needs a CT and a tissue diagnosis.

How it arises. Carcinogens (tobacco above all; also biomass smoke, occupational exposures, radon) cause accumulating mutations in the airway epithelium. Adenocarcinoma (commonest, peripheral, and in never-smokers often driven by EGFR or ALK alterations) and squamous cell carcinoma (central, smokers) make up most non-small-cell cancer. Small-cell cancer is rarely surgical.

How it spreads decides the stage and the operation:

Primary tumour (T: size, invasion)→Intrapulmonary and hilar nodes (N1)→Mediastinal nodes (N2)→Contralateral or supraclavicular (N3)
Primary tumour→Blood: brain, bone, adrenal, liver (M1)
TTumour (9th edition keeps the 8th-edition T)
T1≤3 cm, surrounded by lung (T1a ≤1, T1b >1–2, T1c >2–3 cm)
T2>3–5 cm (T2a >3–4, T2b >4–5), or main bronchus (not carina), visceral pleura, collapse to the hilum
T3>5–7 cm, or chest wall, phrenic nerve, parietal pericardium, a separate nodule in the same lobe
T4>7 cm, or mediastinum, heart, great vessels, trachea, carina, esophagus, diaphragm, vertebra, a nodule in another ipsilateral lobe
NNodes
N1ipsilateral hilar or intrapulmonary (stations 10–14)
N2a / N2bipsilateral mediastinal or subcarinal: one station (N2a) or several stations (N2b), new in the 9th edition
N3contralateral mediastinal or hilar, or any scalene or supraclavicular
MMetastasis
M1a–cM1a pleural or pericardial spread, contralateral nodules; M1b one extrathoracic metastasis; M1c1 several in one organ system, M1c2 several organ systems (new)

Before an operation: CT and PET-CT; invasive mediastinal staging (EBUS/EUS needle aspiration, or mediastinoscopy) when the tumour is central, over 3 cm, or the nodes are enlarged or PET-positive; brain imaging for stage II and above. Then fitness: FEV1 and DLCO, and the predicted postoperative values (ppo = preoperative value × segments remaining / 19; by lobe: RUL 3, RML 2, RLL 5, LUL 5 with the lingula, LLL 4).

Evidence: 9th-edition TNM from the IASLC (Rami-Porta et al., J Thorac Oncol 2024): N2 split into N2a (single station) and N2b (multiple stations); M1c into M1c1 and M1c2; T1N1 moves to stage IIA, T1N2a is IIB. ACCP 2013 physiological evaluation (Brunelli et al.): ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO both over 60% is low risk; 30–60% needs a stair climb (over 22 m) or shuttle walk (over 400 m); under 30%, or a poor walk test, needs CPET (VO2max over 20 mL/kg/min low risk, under 10 high risk). ESTS 2014 guideline for invasive mediastinal staging (De Leyn et al.).

ask.question: Under the 9th edition, a 2.6 cm tumour (T1c) with metastasis in a single mediastinal station (subcarinal, station 7) and no distant spread is stage…

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: Lingular segmentectomy (S4+5)
steps.body:
The lingula is the upper lobe's lower division, supplied by its own three structures: the lingular artery from the front of the artery in the fissure, the lingular vein as the lowest tributary of the superior vein, and the lingular bronchus, the lower branch of the upper lobe bronchus.

What stays: the upper division above, A6 and the basal trunk in the fissure.

steps.title: Case: a small peripheral tumour: lingula
steps.lead: A 63-year-old woman with a 1.6 cm solid-predominant adenocarcinoma in the lingula, well inside the segment (margin to the intersegmental plane over 2 cm). PET: nodes clear; FEV1 62% (COPD).
steps.body:
Stage: cT1b N0 = IA2. An anatomical segmentectomy with sampling of hilar and mediastinal nodes (frozen section: if a node is positive, convert to lobectomy). It saves lung she needs, and in JCOG0802 it gave better overall survival than lobectomy.

The margin must be at least 2 cm or the tumour's diameter; the intersegmental plane is found by inflation–deflation or indocyanine green after the segmental artery is divided.

Evidence: JCOG0802 (Lancet 2022): 5-year OS 94.3% segmentectomy vs 91.1% lobectomy; local recurrence 10.5% vs 5.4%. CALGB 140503 (NEJM 2023): sublobar resection non-inferior for DFS and OS; FEV1 about 2 percentage points better at 6 months.

ask.question: During segmentectomy the frozen section of a hilar node (station 12) is positive. What now?

choices.text: Convert to lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection
choices.why: Both trials required node-negative disease; N1 disease needs a lobectomy (and adjuvant or perioperative systemic therapy).

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Local recurrence somewhat higher than lobectomy, survival not worse for small peripheral tumours (JCOG0802)
  • Conversion to lobectomy if margins or nodes demand it

5. Alternatives

  • Lobectomy
  • SBRT if unfit
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: For a 1.8 cm peripheral NSCLC, what does JCOG0802 let you tell the patient about segmentectomy versus lobectomy?

choices.text: Overall survival was better with segmentectomy, although local recurrence was higher
choices.why: JCOG0802 (Lancet 2022): 5-year OS 94.3% vs 91.1%; local recurrence 10.5% vs 5.4%.

choices.text: They are identical in every respect

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, right lung ventilated. For a fissure-first approach the ports sit further back: a utility incision in the 5th intercostal space in line with the fissure, a camera port low and posterior, and a posterior working port. Port sites vary between units.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut, sweeping along the line of the artery.

The interlobar pulmonary artery appears in its sheath. Get onto the sheath: everything that follows is dissected on the artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: Segmental artery
steps.body: In the open fissure, the lingular artery leaves the front of the interlobar artery toward the lingula, often opposite A6. Staple it clear of the basal trunk.

steps.title: Segmental vein
steps.body: Roll the lobe back. The lingular vein is the lowest tributary of the superior pulmonary vein; the upper division veins join above it and must be kept.

steps.title: Segmental bronchus, then inflate: the plane appears
steps.body: Behind the vein, the lingular bronchus leaves the lower side of the upper lobe bronchus. Clamp it and inflate: the upper division must still ventilate. Fire.

ask.question: After the segmental bronchus is divided, how is the intersegmental plane shown with the inflation–deflation method?

choices.text: Inflate the whole lung, then let it deflate: the target segment stays inflated
choices.why: Air trapped behind the divided bronchus keeps the segment inflated while the rest deflates, drawing the boundary; intravenous ICG after dividing the artery is the alternative.

steps.title: Divide the intersegmental plane
steps.body:
Lift the divided bronchus and vessels with the specimen and staple along the inflation–deflation line, from the hilum outward, keeping the intersegmental veins on the side that stays.

A margin of at least the tumour diameter (and 2 cm) is the aim for cancer.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, margins
steps.body: Remove the segment in a bag. Sample stations 10, 11 and 12/13 at its root: a positive intersegmental node means converting to lobectomy. Check the margin, then leak-test the stapled plane under saline.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak along the intersegmental plane is common
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 3 after segmentectomy: small continuous air leak, lung up, patient well. Next?

choices.text: Keep the drain, no suction, reassess daily; consider a portable valve if it persists
choices.why: Intersegmental-plane leaks usually seal; prolonged leak is defined beyond 5 days.

choices.why: The 9th edition splits N2: a single station (N2a) with a T1 tumour is IIB; several stations (N2b) make it IIIA. Many single-station N2 patients are now treated with neoadjuvant chemo-immunotherapy and surgery.

steps.title: Superior segmentectomy (S6)
steps.body:
The superior segment is the top of the lower lobe, supplied by A6 from the back of the artery in the fissure, drained by V6, the highest tributary of the inferior vein, and aerated by B6, the first posterior branch of the lower lobe bronchus.

What stays: the basal trunk, basal veins and basal bronchus.

steps.title: Case: a small peripheral tumour: superior segment (S6) of the left lower lobe
steps.lead: A 63-year-old woman with a 1.6 cm solid-predominant adenocarcinoma in the superior segment (S6) of the left lower lobe, well inside the segment (margin to the intersegmental plane over 2 cm). PET: nodes clear; FEV1 62% (COPD).
steps.body:
Stage: cT1b N0 = IA2. An anatomical segmentectomy with sampling of hilar and mediastinal nodes (frozen section: if a node is positive, convert to lobectomy). It saves lung she needs, and in JCOG0802 it gave better overall survival than lobectomy.

The margin must be at least 2 cm or the tumour's diameter; the intersegmental plane is found by inflation–deflation or indocyanine green after the segmental artery is divided.

Evidence: JCOG0802 (Lancet 2022): 5-year OS 94.3% segmentectomy vs 91.1% lobectomy; local recurrence 10.5% vs 5.4%. CALGB 140503 (NEJM 2023): sublobar resection non-inferior for DFS and OS; FEV1 about 2 percentage points better at 6 months.

ask.question: During segmentectomy the frozen section of a hilar node (station 12) is positive. What now?

choices.text: Convert to lobectomy with systematic nodal dissection
choices.why: Both trials required node-negative disease; N1 disease needs a lobectomy (and adjuvant or perioperative systemic therapy).

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: ppoFEV1 and ppoDLCO (stair climb or CPET if low); Thoracoscore. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Prolonged air leak
  • AF
  • Pneumonia and sputum retention
  • Bleeding
  • Wound infection
  • Chronic chest wall pain (more after thoracotomy)

3. Serious

  • Death
  • Respiratory failure and ventilation
  • Bronchopleural fistula
  • Return to theatre

4. Specific to this operation

  • Local recurrence somewhat higher than lobectomy, survival not worse for small peripheral tumours (JCOG0802)
  • Conversion to lobectomy if margins or nodes demand it

5. Alternatives

  • Lobectomy
  • SBRT if unfit
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-TB adhesions and calcified nodes raise bleeding and conversion risk
  • Exclude TB before calling a mass cancer
  • Cost and access to adjuvant treatment

ask.question: For a 1.8 cm peripheral NSCLC, what does JCOG0802 let you tell the patient about segmentectomy versus lobectomy?

choices.text: Overall survival was better with segmentectomy, although local recurrence was higher
choices.why: JCOG0802 (Lancet 2022): 5-year OS 94.3% vs 91.1%; local recurrence 10.5% vs 5.4%.

choices.text: They are identical in every respect

steps.title: Position and ports
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus, right lung ventilated. For a fissure-first approach the ports sit further back: a utility incision in the 5th intercostal space in line with the fissure, a camera port low and posterior, and a posterior working port. Port sites vary between units.

steps.title: Open the fissure bluntly with a peanut
steps.body:
Retract the upper lobe forward and up, the lower lobe back and down. Where the oblique fissure is deepest, open the visceral pleura and dissect bluntly with the peanut, sweeping along the line of the artery.

The interlobar pulmonary artery appears in its sheath. Get onto the sheath: everything that follows is dissected on the artery.

ask.question: A fissure-first approach works best when…

choices.text: The fissure is complete and the artery is visible in it
choices.why: In a complete fissure the interlobar artery lies just under the visceral pleura where the fissures meet.

steps.title: Segmental artery
steps.body: In the fissure, A6 leaves the back of the interlobar artery; the basal trunk continues below and the lingular artery leaves the front opposite. Staple A6 only.

steps.title: Segmental vein
steps.body: From behind, with the lower lobe lifted, V6 is the highest tributary of the inferior pulmonary vein. Divide it, keeping the basal veins.

steps.title: Segmental bronchus, then inflate: the plane appears
steps.body: B6 leaves the back of the lower lobe bronchus just below the secondary carina. Clamp it and inflate: the basal segments must ventilate. Fire.

ask.question: After the segmental bronchus is divided, how is the intersegmental plane shown with the inflation–deflation method?

choices.text: Inflate the whole lung, then let it deflate: the target segment stays inflated
choices.why: Air trapped behind the divided bronchus keeps the segment inflated while the rest deflates, drawing the boundary; intravenous ICG after dividing the artery is the alternative.

steps.title: Divide the intersegmental plane
steps.body:
Lift the divided bronchus and vessels with the specimen and staple along the inflation–deflation line, from the hilum outward, keeping the intersegmental veins on the side that stays.

A margin of at least the tumour diameter (and 2 cm) is the aim for cancer.

steps.title: Specimen out, nodes, margins
steps.body: Remove the segment in a bag. Sample stations 10, 11 and 12/13 at its root: a positive intersegmental node means converting to lobectomy. Check the margin, then leak-test the stapled plane under saline.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Air leak along the intersegmental plane is common
  • Sputum retention

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 3 after segmentectomy: small continuous air leak, lung up, patient well. Next?

choices.text: Keep the drain, no suction, reassess daily; consider a portable valve if it persists
choices.why: Intersegmental-plane leaks usually seal; prolonged leak is defined beyond 5 days.

trachea-cervical.name: Tracheal resection and reconstruction
trachea-cervical.summary: Collar incision, subplatysmal flaps, stricture freed on the wall, resected, end-to-end 4-0 PDS anastomosis.

steps.title: The cervical trachea and its nerves
steps.body:
About 11 cm long in an adult, 18–22 C-shaped rings; roughly half lies in the neck with the neck extended. The thyroid isthmus crosses rings 2–4; the innominate artery crosses the front low in the neck.

Blood supply is segmental and lateral (mostly the inferior thyroid artery): free the trachea circumferentially only for about 1 cm beyond each cut.

The recurrent laryngeal nerves run up in the tracheo-esophageal grooves and enter the larynx behind the cricothyroid joints; the right loops under the subclavian and runs more obliquely. The external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery near the upper pole down to cricothyroid; the internal branch pierces the thyrohyoid membrane.

ask.question: How do you protect the recurrent laryngeal nerves during tracheal resection?

choices.text: Keep the dissection on the tracheal wall; do not look for the nerves
choices.why: They run in the tracheo-esophageal grooves just beside the trachea; staying on the wall (especially laterally and behind) keeps them out of harm. Searching for them in scar injures them.

choices.text: Identify and sling both nerves first

steps.title: Before you resect
steps.body:
Rigid and flexible bronchoscopy: the length of the stricture, its distance below the cords and the cricoid, the state of the mucosa; CT for length and extrinsic disease. Dilate to buy time if needed.

Operate when the inflammation has settled, the patient is off steroids and off the ventilator, and any tracheostomy can be closed at the same time. Up to about half the adult trachea (4–5 cm) can be resected with mobilisation and release; less in children. Subglottic disease involving the cricoid needs a cricotracheal (Pearson) resection instead.

ask.question: Roughly how much adult trachea can be resected with primary anastomosis?

choices.text: About half (4–5 cm), with mobilisation and release manoeuvres
choices.why: Beyond that, tension rises steeply and dehiscence and restenosis follow.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Airway assessment, fitness, prior tracheostomy or steroid use. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Sore throat, hoarseness
  • Wound infection
  • Swallowing difficulty for a few days

3. Serious

  • Anastomotic dehiscence (airway emergency)
  • Restenosis
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
  • Need for tracheostomy
  • Death

4. Specific to this operation

  • Chin-to-chest guardian stitch for 7 days
  • Check bronchoscopy before discharge

5. Alternatives

  • Dilatation, stent
  • Tracheostomy or T-tube
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Post-intubation stenosis is common: ICU follow-up of the cause
  • Access to repeat bronchoscopy

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which instruction must the patient understand before tracheal resection?

choices.text: The neck will be held flexed by a chin-to-chest stitch for about a week
choices.why: It protects the anastomosis from tension; understanding it prevents the patient fighting it.

steps.title: Position and collar incision
steps.body:
Supine, a shoulder roll, the neck extended, the head on a ring. Anaesthesia: a small tube passed through or above the stricture (after dilatation if needed), or spontaneous ventilation.

A low collar incision two fingerbreadths above the sternal notch; include an old stoma. A partial upper sternal split is added only for low lesions.

steps.title: Subplatysmal flaps; straps apart; isthmus divided
steps.body: Raise subplatysmal flaps up to the thyroid cartilage and down to the notch (the anterior jugular veins stay down on the straps). Separate the strap muscles in the midline and retract them laterally. Divide the thyroid isthmus and oversew it; roll the lobes off the front of the trachea.

steps.title: The front of the trachea, and the stricture
steps.body:
Clear the anterior wall from the cricoid down past the stricture: this plane is avascular. Find the stricture from outside (scarred, narrowed; a needle through the wall seen with the bronchoscope marks its limits exactly).

Low in the field the innominate artery crosses in front: keep off it.

steps.title: Circumferential dissection, on the wall
steps.body: Encircle the trachea only at the stricture, staying on the tracheal wall laterally and behind (the plane between trachea and esophagus). Do not look for the recurrent nerves: they lie in the grooves just outside this plane. Preserve the lateral vessels beyond the segment.

steps.title: Divide below; cross-field ventilation
steps.body: Place lateral stay sutures (2-0) through the full wall a ring below the stricture. Divide the trachea just below it; pass a sterile armoured tube into the distal trachea across the field and ventilate through it.

steps.title: Divide above; the segment out
steps.body: Stay sutures above, then divide at healthy airway above the stricture (bevel it if the stricture is higher in front). Send the margins. The oral tube is pulled back above the field.

steps.title: Test the tension; release if needed
steps.body:
Flex the neck and draw the ends together on the crossed stay sutures: they should meet without strain. Mobilise the front of the distal trachea into the mediastinum by finger (pretracheal plane, avascular).

If the ends will not meet: a suprahyoid laryngeal release (Montgomery) gives 1–2 cm; a thyrohyoid release risks the internal branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (aspiration). Low lesions: hilar and pericardial release through the chest.

steps.title: The anastomosis: 4-0 PDS
steps.body:
Membranous wall first, behind: a running 4-0 PDS (or interrupted), bites about 3–4 mm from the edge and 3–4 mm apart. Cartilaginous wall in front: interrupted 4-0 PDS (or 4-0 Vicryl), each round a ring on both sides, all placed before any is tied, knots outside the lumen.

Take the cross-field tube out and advance the oral tube past the anastomosis. Flex the neck, cross and hold the stay sutures, then tie the anterior sutures (from the sides to the front). Leak test under saline to 20–30 cmH2O. Cover with the strap muscles or thyroid; put tissue between the suture line and the innominate artery if they touch.

ask.question: When are the anterior (cartilaginous) sutures tied?

choices.text: After all are placed, the neck flexed and the stay sutures crossed
choices.why: Placing every suture first keeps the view open; flexion and the stay sutures take the tension off while they are tied.

choices.text: One by one as each is placed

steps.title: Guardian stitch, extubation, bronchoscopy
steps.body:
A heavy guardian (chin-to-chest) suture keeps the neck flexed for about 7 days. Extubate in theatre where possible. Bronchoscopy before discharge (around day 7).

Watch for: stridor (oedema: steroids, racemic adrenaline, a small tube; dehiscence must be excluded), air or wound infection (a leak), voice change or aspiration (nerve injury). In large series about 95% have a good airway; restenosis around 4–5%, and dehiscence is the complication that kills.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Extubate in theatre if possible
  • Guardian stitch 7 days; neck flexed, no hyperextension
  • Stridor or neck emphysema: dehiscence: urgent bronchoscopy

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 2 after tracheal resection: new stridor and neck surgical emphysema. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant and prepare urgent bronchoscopy in theatre
choices.why: Suspect anastomotic dehiscence; secure the airway under direct vision.

b4-thymectomy-sternotomy.name: Thymectomy
b4-thymectomy-sternotomy.summary: Extended thymectomy: phrenic to phrenic, diaphragm to thyroid, the thymic veins tied.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: myasthenia gravis and the thymus
steps.body:
An antibody attack on the neuromuscular junction. In about 85% of generalised myasthenia, IgG1/IgG3 antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) bind the endplate, fix complement and destroy the postsynaptic folds; fewer receptors means a smaller endplate potential, which fails with repeated firing: fatigable weakness. Other subtypes: anti-MuSK (IgG4, no complement; the thymus is normal), anti-LRP4, and seronegative.

Thymus: myoid cells express AChR→Germinal centres: autoreactive B cells (thymic follicular hyperplasia)→Anti-AChR antibodies→Complement destroys the endplate→Fatigable weakness: eyes, bulbar, limbs, breathing

Why remove the thymus: in early-onset AChR-positive disease, about 70% of thymuses show germinal-centre hyperplasia, a factory for the antibodies. Removing it (all of it, including ectopic thymic fat) lowers the drive. Thymoma occurs in about 10–20% of patients with myasthenia, and roughly 20–25% of thymoma patients have myasthenia: every thymoma is removed.

Crisis: respiratory or bulbar failure (MGFA class V: intubation). Triggers: infection, surgery, certain drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, some anaesthetic agents), steroid initiation. A falling vital capacity warns before the gases change.

MGFA classes: I ocular only; II mild, III moderate, IV severe generalised (a: limb and axial, b: oropharyngeal and respiratory); V intubated.

Evidence: mechanisms and subtypes: Gilhus, NEJM 2016 and Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019; Fichtner et al., Front Immunol 2020 (germinal centres in about 70% of early-onset AChR MG). MG in thymoma: Lucchi et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2009.

ask.question: Why is thymectomy not recommended for anti-MuSK myasthenia?

choices.text: The thymus is usually normal in MuSK disease, and the antibodies (IgG4) are not driven by thymic germinal centres
choices.why: Thymic hyperplasia is a feature of AChR-positive, early-onset disease; guidance (2020) finds no evidence of benefit in MuSK MG.

choices.text: MuSK patients are too weak for surgery
It is recommended for all subtypes
The thymus is always malignant in MuSK MG

steps.title: The thymus and its boundaries
steps.body:
In an adult the thymus is a fatty, bilobed organ in the anterior mediastinum, on the pericardium and the great vessels. Its limits: the phrenic nerves laterally, the thyroid above (the two upper horns), the diaphragm below. Its veins drain into the back of the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein; its arteries come from the internal mammary and inferior thyroid arteries.

Indications: thymoma (stage by Masaoka-Koga) and myasthenia gravis (the MGTX trial favoured extended thymectomy in AChR-antibody-positive, non-thymomatous disease). For myasthenia, remove all the anterior mediastinal fat between the phrenic nerves: ectopic thymic tissue lies throughout it.

ask.question: What are the lateral limits of an extended thymectomy?

choices.why: Everything anterior between the phrenic nerves, from the diaphragm to the thyroid, comes out; a phrenic palsy in a myasthenic is disastrous.

choices.text: The lateral borders of the sternum

steps.title: Case: myasthenia gravis with a thymoma
steps.lead: A 47-year-old man: ptosis, diplopia, then dysarthria and difficulty swallowing over 4 months; AChR antibodies positive. CT: a 5 cm smooth, lobulated anterior mediastinal mass, abutting but with a fat plane to the pericardium and left brachiocephalic vein. On pyridostigmine; vital capacity 2.6 L.
steps.body:
Resect the thymoma with the whole thymus and surrounding fat (extended thymectomy), en bloc and without breaching the capsule: complete (R0) resection is the strongest prognostic factor. A median sternotomy gives the safest R0 resection for a 5 cm tumour, with the phrenic nerves in view and the option to take pericardium, lung or the innominate vein if invaded (send frozen sections).

Prepare the myasthenia first: bulbar weakness is a risk for postoperative crisis, so give IVIG or plasma exchange before surgery; avoid long-acting relaxants.

Staging: Masaoka-Koga (I encapsulated; IIa microscopic, IIb macroscopic capsular invasion into fat; III neighbouring organs; IVa pleural or pericardial, IVb distant) and the 9th-edition TNM (T1a ≤5 cm and T1b >5 cm confined to thymus or fat; T2 pericardium, lung or phrenic; T3 innominate vein, SVC, chest wall; T4 aorta, pulmonary artery, myocardium, trachea, esophagus).

Evidence: International consensus (Sanders et al., Neurology 2016): IVIG or plasma exchange before surgery in patients with significant bulbar dysfunction. Leuzzi et al. (2014): postoperative crisis in 12.4%; generalised, bulbar-predominant disease raised the risk. Staging: Masaoka-Koga (Detterbeck et al., J Thorac Oncol 2011) and the 9th-edition TNM (CAP protocol).

ask.question: Before thymectomy, this patient with bulbar weakness should receive…

choices.text: IVIG or plasma exchange to optimise him and reduce the risk of postoperative crisis
choices.why: Bulbar and respiratory weakness predict crisis; preoperative immunomodulation is recommended. Operate when stable.

choices.text: A high loading dose of steroids the day before

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Myasthenia severity and control; FVC. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pain
  • Wound problems
  • Pneumothorax (VATS)

3. Serious

  • Myasthenic crisis needing ventilation
  • Phrenic nerve injury
  • Bleeding
  • Deep sternal wound infection (sternotomy)

4. Specific to this operation

  • Benefit accrues over months to years; fewer steroids (MGTX)
  • Medicines continue around surgery

5. Alternatives

  • Medical therapy alone
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Access to IVIG or plasma exchange if crisis occurs
  • Pyridostigmine supply

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: What benefit can a patient with generalised MG expect from thymectomy (MGTX)?

choices.text: Better clinical scores and less prednisone over 3 years
choices.why: MGTX (NEJM 2016): improved Quantitative MG score and lower prednisone dose at 3 years; benefit is gradual.

choices.text: Stopping all medicines the next day

steps.title: Median sternotomy
steps.body:
Supine, a roll between the shoulders. Midline incision from the sternal notch to below the xiphoid. Divide the interclavicular ligament above and free the xiphoid below; sweep a finger behind the manubrium and the lower sternum.

Ask for the lungs to be deflated, then saw exactly in the midline. Wax the marrow, seat the retractor, open slowly.

steps.title: Lower poles off the pericardium
steps.body: Start low: lift the lower poles and the pericardial fat off the pericardium with diathermy and blunt dissection, working up toward the great vessels. Take the pericardiophrenic fat pads with the specimen.

steps.title: Along each phrenic nerve
steps.body: Open the mediastinal pleura 1 cm in front of each phrenic nerve and take the fat off it, never the nerve itself: no diathermy on the nerve, no traction on it. On the left the nerve crosses the aortic arch and is easily hidden in fat.

steps.title: Thymic veins into the innominate vein
steps.body: Lift the gland forward off the left brachiocephalic vein. One to three thymic veins enter its back: clip or tie each and divide it. Traction tears them flush with the innominate vein: control that with a finger and a side-biting clamp, not blind clips.

ask.question: A thymic vein tears flush with the innominate vein. First move?

choices.text: Finger pressure, then a side-biting clamp and a fine suture
choices.why: Blind clips or diathermy on a torn innominate vein make it bigger.

steps.title: The upper horns from the thyroid
steps.body: Follow each upper horn into the neck with gentle traction until it narrows to a thin band ending on the thyroid; tie or clip its tip (small inferior thyroid branches). The horns lie on the brachiocephalic veins and the innominate artery.

steps.title: En bloc, then check the fat that is left
steps.body:
The gland comes out in one piece with its fat, in a bag. Look again at the places where ectopic thymus hides: the aortopulmonary window, the aortocaval groove, the pericardiophrenic fat on both sides and the neck.

One drain; close the sternum with wires (sternotomy).

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Continue pyridostigmine and steroids
  • Avoid aggravating drugs: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium boluses, excess neuromuscular blockers
  • Myasthenic crisis: 20/30/40 rule (FVC under 20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30, PEF under 40): intubate; IVIG or plasma exchange
  • Diaphragm on chest X-ray: phrenic injury

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After thymectomy for MG: FVC falls to 15 mL/kg with a weak cough. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant; prepare to intubate and start IVIG or plasma exchange
choices.why: Myasthenic crisis: the 20/30/40 rule; do not wait for hypercapnia.

b4-thymectomy-rvats.name: Thymectomy
b4-thymectomy-rvats.summary: Extended thymectomy: phrenic to phrenic, diaphragm to thyroid, the thymic veins tied.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: myasthenia gravis and the thymus
steps.body:
An antibody attack on the neuromuscular junction. In about 85% of generalised myasthenia, IgG1/IgG3 antibodies against the acetylcholine receptor (AChR) bind the endplate, fix complement and destroy the postsynaptic folds; fewer receptors means a smaller endplate potential, which fails with repeated firing: fatigable weakness. Other subtypes: anti-MuSK (IgG4, no complement; the thymus is normal), anti-LRP4, and seronegative.

Thymus: myoid cells express AChR→Germinal centres: autoreactive B cells (thymic follicular hyperplasia)→Anti-AChR antibodies→Complement destroys the endplate→Fatigable weakness: eyes, bulbar, limbs, breathing

Why remove the thymus: in early-onset AChR-positive disease, about 70% of thymuses show germinal-centre hyperplasia, a factory for the antibodies. Removing it (all of it, including ectopic thymic fat) lowers the drive. Thymoma occurs in about 10–20% of patients with myasthenia, and roughly 20–25% of thymoma patients have myasthenia: every thymoma is removed.

Crisis: respiratory or bulbar failure (MGFA class V: intubation). Triggers: infection, surgery, certain drugs (aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, some anaesthetic agents), steroid initiation. A falling vital capacity warns before the gases change.

MGFA classes: I ocular only; II mild, III moderate, IV severe generalised (a: limb and axial, b: oropharyngeal and respiratory); V intubated.

Evidence: mechanisms and subtypes: Gilhus, NEJM 2016 and Nat Rev Dis Primers 2019; Fichtner et al., Front Immunol 2020 (germinal centres in about 70% of early-onset AChR MG). MG in thymoma: Lucchi et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2009.

choices.text: The thymus is usually normal in MuSK disease, and the antibodies (IgG4) are not driven by thymic germinal centres
choices.why: Thymic hyperplasia is a feature of AChR-positive, early-onset disease; guidance (2020) finds no evidence of benefit in MuSK MG.

steps.title: The thymus and its boundaries
steps.body:
In an adult the thymus is a fatty, bilobed organ in the anterior mediastinum, on the pericardium and the great vessels. Its limits: the phrenic nerves laterally, the thyroid above (the two upper horns), the diaphragm below. Its veins drain into the back of the left brachiocephalic (innominate) vein; its arteries come from the internal mammary and inferior thyroid arteries.

Indications: thymoma (stage by Masaoka-Koga) and myasthenia gravis (the MGTX trial favoured extended thymectomy in AChR-antibody-positive, non-thymomatous disease). For myasthenia, remove all the anterior mediastinal fat between the phrenic nerves: ectopic thymic tissue lies throughout it.

ask.question: What are the lateral limits of an extended thymectomy?

choices.why: Everything anterior between the phrenic nerves, from the diaphragm to the thyroid, comes out; a phrenic palsy in a myasthenic is disastrous.

choices.text: The lateral borders of the sternum

steps.title: Case: generalised AChR-positive myasthenia, no thymoma
steps.lead: A 28-year-old teacher, generalised myasthenia for 14 months (MGFA IIa: ptosis, arm and leg fatigue, no bulbar symptoms), AChR antibodies positive; CT: normal-sized thymus, no thymoma. On pyridostigmine and prednisolone 30 mg; weakness recurs when the steroid is tapered.
steps.body:
Thymectomy: early in the disease, for AChR-positive generalised non-thymomatous myasthenia in adults up to about 50 (MGTX included 18 to 65). The aim is less steroid, fewer relapses and admissions, and a chance of remission; benefit accrues over months to years. A minimally invasive extended thymectomy (right VATS, subxiphoid or robotic) removes the whole thymus and the fat from phrenic to phrenic, from the thyroid to the diaphragm.

Evidence: MGTX (Wolfe et al., NEJM 2016; 126 patients): at 3 years, thymectomy lowered the time-weighted QMG score (6.15 vs 8.99), the prednisone requirement (44 vs 60 mg alternate days) and admissions for exacerbation (9% vs 37%). The benefit persisted at 5 years (Lancet Neurol 2019). 2020 international guidance: thymectomy should be considered early for AChR-positive generalised MG aged 18–50; minimally invasive thymectomy has a good safety record in experienced centres. Meta-analysis (Lee et al., Surg Endosc 2023): no difference in remission between minimally invasive and open thymectomy.

ask.question: In MGTX, which outcome improved with thymectomy plus prednisone versus prednisone alone?

choices.text: Clinical score, prednisone dose and admissions for exacerbation, all at 3 years
choices.why: QMG 6.15 vs 8.99; alternate-day prednisone 44 vs 60 mg; hospitalisation 9% vs 37%. The effect lasted to 5 years.

choices.text: Better clinical scores and less prednisone over 3 years
choices.why: MGTX (NEJM 2016): improved Quantitative MG score and lower prednisone dose at 3 years; benefit is gradual.

choices.text: Stopping all medicines the next day

steps.title: Right VATS: position and ports
steps.body:
Supine with the right side raised 30°, right arm down or on an arm rest. Three ports on the right: 5th space mid-axillary (camera), 3rd space anterior axillary and 5th space mid-clavicular. CO2 at 6–8 mmHg pushes the mediastinum and lung away.

Start at the right pericardiophrenic angle, anterior to the right phrenic nerve, and work up.

steps.title: Lower poles off the pericardium
steps.body: Start low: lift the lower poles and the pericardial fat off the pericardium with diathermy and blunt dissection, working up toward the great vessels. Take the pericardiophrenic fat pads with the specimen.

steps.title: Along each phrenic nerve
steps.body: Open the mediastinal pleura 1 cm in front of each phrenic nerve and take the fat off it, never the nerve itself: no diathermy on the nerve, no traction on it. On the left the nerve crosses the aortic arch and is easily hidden in fat.

steps.title: Thymic veins into the innominate vein
steps.body: Lift the gland forward off the left brachiocephalic vein. One to three thymic veins enter its back: clip or tie each and divide it. Traction tears them flush with the innominate vein: control that with a finger and a side-biting clamp, not blind clips.

ask.question: A thymic vein tears flush with the innominate vein. First move?

choices.text: Finger pressure, then a side-biting clamp and a fine suture
choices.why: Blind clips or diathermy on a torn innominate vein make it bigger.

steps.title: The upper horns from the thyroid
steps.body: Follow each upper horn into the neck with gentle traction until it narrows to a thin band ending on the thyroid; tie or clip its tip (small inferior thyroid branches). The horns lie on the brachiocephalic veins and the innominate artery.

steps.title: En bloc, then check the fat that is left
steps.body:
The gland comes out in one piece with its fat, in a bag. Look again at the places where ectopic thymus hides: the aortopulmonary window, the aortocaval groove, the pericardiophrenic fat on both sides and the neck.

One drain; close the sternum with wires (sternotomy).

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Continue pyridostigmine and steroids
  • Avoid aggravating drugs: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium boluses, excess neuromuscular blockers
  • Myasthenic crisis: 20/30/40 rule (FVC under 20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than −30, PEF under 40): intubate; IVIG or plasma exchange
  • Diaphragm on chest X-ray: phrenic injury

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After thymectomy for MG: FVC falls to 15 mL/kg with a weak cough. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant; prepare to intubate and start IVIG or plasma exchange
choices.why: Myasthenic crisis: the 20/30/40 rule; do not wait for hypercapnia.

steps.title: Case: a young woman with bulbar myasthenia
steps.lead: A 19-year-old student, 8 months of generalised myasthenia with nasal speech and choking on fluids (MGFA IIIb), AChR antibodies positive; CT: thymic hyperplasia. Vital capacity 2.1 L (55% predicted).
steps.body:
Thymectomy is indicated (young, AChR-positive, generalised). Not yet: bulbar weakness and a reduced vital capacity mean a high risk of postoperative crisis. Optimise first: plasma exchange or IVIG, pyridostigmine adjusted, infections treated, then operate when stable. A subxiphoid approach avoids an intercostal incision and gives a symmetric view of both phrenic nerves and both cervical horns.

Evidence: International consensus (2016): IVIG or plasma exchange before surgery with significant bulbar dysfunction. Leuzzi et al. (Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2014; 177 patients): postoperative crisis in 12.4%, higher with Osserman IIB and III–IV disease.

ask.question: Which feature most raises her risk of myasthenic crisis after thymectomy?

choices.text: Bulbar weakness with a reduced vital capacity
choices.why: Bulbar-predominant, more severe disease predicts crisis; optimise with IVIG or plasma exchange, and extubate only when strength allows.

steps.title: Subxiphoid approach
steps.body:
Supine, legs apart (the surgeon stands between them). A 3 cm incision below the xiphoid; detach the rectus from the xiphoid (or excise it); develop the plane behind the sternum with a finger. Wound protector, CO2 at 8 mmHg, and a sternal lifting hook if needed. Two 5 mm subcostal ports are optional.

Both pleurae and both phrenic nerves are seen from the midline: the best view of the left side and of the neck.

b4-eso-ivor.name: Esophagectomy
b4-eso-ivor.summary: Abdomen, then right chest: anastomosis in the chest above the azygos.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: esophageal cancer
steps.body:
East Africa carries one of the world's highest rates of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, along a corridor from Ethiopia and Kenya to Malawi. About nine in ten cases here are squamous, and patients are young: in Bomet (Tenwek) 11% were 30 or younger. Risk factors studied in Kenya: very hot tea, alcohol (especially home-brewed spirits), tobacco, household smoke, and poor oral health. In high-income countries adenocarcinoma of the lower third and junction (from reflux and Barrett's esophagus) predominates.

Chronic thermal and chemical injury to the squamous mucosa→Dysplasia→Invasive squamous carcinoma→Circumferential growth→Progressive dysphagia (solids, then liquids), weight loss
No serosa: early spread→Lymphatics along the length of the esophagus (neck to coeliac)→Airway (mid third): tracheo-esophageal fistula
T (AJCC 8th)
T1a / T1blamina propria or muscularis mucosae / submucosa
T2muscularis propria
T3adventitia
T4a / T4bpleura, pericardium, azygos, diaphragm, peritoneum (resectable) / aorta, vertebra, trachea (unresectable)
Nby number of nodes: N1 1–2, N2 3–6, N3 7 or more

Separate clinical, pathological and post-neoadjuvant (yp) stage groups; squamous and adenocarcinoma are grouped differently. Work-up: endoscopy and biopsy, CT chest and abdomen, PET-CT for curative candidates, EUS for T and N, bronchoscopy for tumours at or above the carina, staging laparoscopy for junctional adenocarcinoma.

Most patients here present with advanced disease: palliation of dysphagia (a self-expanding metal stent works fastest; brachytherapy lasts longer) is the commonest intervention.

Evidence: ESCCAPE Kenya/Tanzania/Malawi (Middleton et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022): alcohol accounted for 65% of cases in Kenyan men; very hot drinks OR 3.7 in western Kenya (Int J Cancer 2019). Young patients: Lancet 2002 (Bomet). Staging: Rice et al., Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2017. SIREC (Lancet 2004): stents relieved dysphagia faster, brachytherapy gave more dysphagia-free days (115 vs 82) with fewer complications.

ask.question: A squamous carcinoma of the middle third lies at the level of the carina. Which test must precede resection?

choices.text: Bronchoscopy, to exclude invasion of the trachea or left main bronchus (T4b)
choices.why: Mid-third tumours sit against the membranous trachea and left main bronchus; airway invasion makes the tumour unresectable and changes the plan.

steps.title: The esophagus and its neighbours
steps.body:
Neck: behind the trachea, the recurrent laryngeal nerves in the grooves either side. Upper chest: behind the trachea, the azygos arch on its right, the aortic arch on its left. Mid chest: behind the left main bronchus and the left atrium. Lower chest: in front of and to the right of the descending aorta, through the hiatus at T10.

Behind it on the right: the thoracic duct between the aorta and the azygos, crossing to the left at T4–T6. The vagi form the esophageal plexus on its wall.

steps.title: Case: lower-third squamous carcinoma after chemoradiotherapy
steps.lead: A 52-year-old farmer from Bomet, 3 months of dysphagia to solids, 6 kg weight loss. Endoscopy: a lower-third ulcerated tumour at 36–40 cm, biopsy squamous cell carcinoma; CT/EUS: cT3 N1; no distant disease; bronchoscopy normal. After CROSS chemoradiotherapy (carboplatin/paclitaxel with 41.4 Gy), restaging shows a good response. Fit, BMI 19.
steps.body:
Esophagectomy after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy: Ivor Lewis (abdomen, then right thoracotomy or thoracoscopy, anastomosis in the chest) suits a lower-third tumour with a good proximal margin. Nutrition before surgery (a feeding jejunostomy is often placed). Minimally invasive or hybrid access lowers pulmonary complications.

If there is residual disease in the specimen, adjuvant nivolumab is an option.

Evidence: CROSS (NEJM 2012; Lancet Oncol 2015): chemoradiotherapy then surgery improved R0 resection (92% vs 69%) and survival; pCR 49% in squamous vs 23% in adenocarcinoma; median OS for squamous 81.6 vs 21.1 months. TIME (Lancet 2012): minimally invasive esophagectomy cut 2-week pulmonary infection (9% vs 29%). MIRO (NEJM 2019): hybrid access halved major complications (36% vs 64%). CheckMate 577 (NEJM 2021): adjuvant nivolumab doubled DFS (22.4 vs 11.0 months) with residual disease after CRT.

ask.question: In CROSS, which histology responded best to chemoradiotherapy?

choices.text: Squamous cell carcinoma (pCR 49% vs 23% in adenocarcinoma)
choices.why: Squamous tumours are more radiosensitive; the survival gain was largest in squamous carcinoma (median OS 81.6 vs 21.1 months).

ask.question: Which long-term effect must be discussed before esophagectomy?

choices.text: Reflux, early satiety, dumping and possible anastomotic stricture
choices.why: These shape life after surgery and are part of informed consent.

steps.title: Abdomen: mobilise the stomach
steps.body: Upper midline laparotomy (or laparoscopy). Divide the gastrocolic omentum well away from the right gastroepiploic arcade, which the conduit will live on, then the short gastric vessels up to the left crus. Open the lesser omentum. Kocherise the duodenum so the pylorus reaches the hiatus; a pyloric drainage procedure or none, by unit policy.

steps.title: Left gastric artery at its origin
steps.body: Lift the stomach up; the left gastric pedicle is taut in the lesser sac. Clear the coeliac nodes into the specimen and staple or tie the left gastric artery and vein at their origin. Check the common hepatic and splenic arteries first.

steps.title: Right thoracotomy (or right VATS)
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus. Right posterolateral thoracotomy through the 5th space (or four-port VATS / prone thoracoscopy). The right lung is isolated and retracted forward.

steps.title: Divide the azygos arch
steps.body: Open the mediastinal pleura along the front of the azygos arch and behind it. Staple the arch (vascular load): it opens the upper mediastinum and the space for the conduit.

steps.title: Mobilise the esophagus en bloc
steps.body:
Open the pleura in front of the aorta and along the pericardium. Take the esophagus with its periesophageal fat and nodes, including the subcarinal (station 7) packet, from the hiatus to above the azygos arch.

Clip the aortic esophageal branches. Watch the membranous trachea and left main bronchus in front, and the thoracic duct behind.

steps.title: Ligate the thoracic duct (low, above the hiatus)
steps.body: Many units ligate the duct routinely: mass-ligate all the tissue between the aorta and the azygos just above the hiatus, on the front of the spine. A missed duct injury declares itself as a milky drain output once feeding starts.

steps.title: Divide the esophagus above the azygos
steps.body: With the stomach already mobilised from below, divide the esophagus above the azygos arch (tissue load, or open for a purse-string for the anvil). Pull the specimen with the lesser curvature and its nodes into the chest.

steps.title: Make the conduit and bring it up
steps.body:
Staple the lesser curvature from below the cardia to make a 4–5 cm tube of greater curvature on the right gastroepiploic artery. Pull it up through the hiatus into the right chest, without twisting (staple line to the right).

Check the colour of the tip: poor perfusion there is what leaks.

steps.title: The anastomosis
steps.body:
Intrathoracic, at or above the azygos level: circular stapler (25–28 mm) with the anvil in the esophagus and the gun through the conduit, or linear side-to-side. Close the conduit tip, wrap the anastomosis with omentum. A leak here is a mediastinitis: prevention is everything.

Nasogastric tube past the anastomosis; feeding jejunostomy by unit policy.

steps.title: What goes wrong
steps.body: Anastomotic leak and conduit necrosis (fever, arrhythmia, effluent in the drain: contrast study or endoscopy). Chylothorax (milky drain output once fed). Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness, aspiration), mostly after neck dissection. Pneumonia above all: early mobilisation, physiotherapy, sitting up.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Labs day 1 and day 3: FBC, UEC/LFT, CRP, Ca, Mg, PCT (trend) KNH practice

  • Oral sips day 6–7 with a clean drain, falling CRP and a well patient KNH practice
  • NG on free drainage, never re-passed blind; head up 30°
  • New AF, fever, rising CRP or PCT, turbid or salivary drain: CT with oral contrast, then endoscopy

Labs

b4-eso-mckeown.name: Esophagectomy
b4-eso-mckeown.summary: Right chest, abdomen, then left neck: anastomosis in the neck.

steps.title: Pathophysiology and staging: esophageal cancer
steps.body:
East Africa carries one of the world's highest rates of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, along a corridor from Ethiopia and Kenya to Malawi. About nine in ten cases here are squamous, and patients are young: in Bomet (Tenwek) 11% were 30 or younger. Risk factors studied in Kenya: very hot tea, alcohol (especially home-brewed spirits), tobacco, household smoke, and poor oral health. In high-income countries adenocarcinoma of the lower third and junction (from reflux and Barrett's esophagus) predominates.

Chronic thermal and chemical injury to the squamous mucosa→Dysplasia→Invasive squamous carcinoma→Circumferential growth→Progressive dysphagia (solids, then liquids), weight loss
No serosa: early spread→Lymphatics along the length of the esophagus (neck to coeliac)→Airway (mid third): tracheo-esophageal fistula
T (AJCC 8th)
T1a / T1blamina propria or muscularis mucosae / submucosa
T2muscularis propria
T3adventitia
T4a / T4bpleura, pericardium, azygos, diaphragm, peritoneum (resectable) / aorta, vertebra, trachea (unresectable)
Nby number of nodes: N1 1–2, N2 3–6, N3 7 or more

Separate clinical, pathological and post-neoadjuvant (yp) stage groups; squamous and adenocarcinoma are grouped differently. Work-up: endoscopy and biopsy, CT chest and abdomen, PET-CT for curative candidates, EUS for T and N, bronchoscopy for tumours at or above the carina, staging laparoscopy for junctional adenocarcinoma.

Most patients here present with advanced disease: palliation of dysphagia (a self-expanding metal stent works fastest; brachytherapy lasts longer) is the commonest intervention.

Evidence: ESCCAPE Kenya/Tanzania/Malawi (Middleton et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022): alcohol accounted for 65% of cases in Kenyan men; very hot drinks OR 3.7 in western Kenya (Int J Cancer 2019). Young patients: Lancet 2002 (Bomet). Staging: Rice et al., Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2017. SIREC (Lancet 2004): stents relieved dysphagia faster, brachytherapy gave more dysphagia-free days (115 vs 82) with fewer complications.

ask.question: A squamous carcinoma of the middle third lies at the level of the carina. Which test must precede resection?

choices.text: Bronchoscopy, to exclude invasion of the trachea or left main bronchus (T4b)
choices.why: Mid-third tumours sit against the membranous trachea and left main bronchus; airway invasion makes the tumour unresectable and changes the plan.

steps.title: The esophagus and its neighbours
steps.body:
Neck: behind the trachea, the recurrent laryngeal nerves in the grooves either side. Upper chest: behind the trachea, the azygos arch on its right, the aortic arch on its left. Mid chest: behind the left main bronchus and the left atrium. Lower chest: in front of and to the right of the descending aorta, through the hiatus at T10.

Behind it on the right: the thoracic duct between the aorta and the azygos, crossing to the left at T4–T6. The vagi form the esophageal plexus on its wall.

steps.title: Case: a young man with mid-esophageal squamous carcinoma
steps.lead: A 27-year-old man from western Kenya, dysphagia for 4 months. Endoscopy: a tumour at 25–30 cm (mid third, at the carina), squamous; CT/EUS cT3 N1; bronchoscopy: no airway invasion; PET: no distant disease. Good performance status.
steps.body:
Mid-third tumours need a long proximal margin: a McKeown (three-stage) esophagectomy with a neck anastomosis, after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (CROSS). The thoracic dissection is close to the membranous trachea and the left main bronchus: injury there is a disaster.

Definitive chemoradiotherapy is an alternative for squamous carcinoma: surgery adds local control but not clearly survival, at higher treatment mortality; it suits patients who respond clinically, the frail, or those declining surgery, with salvage surgery for residual disease.

Evidence: Stahl et al. (J Clin Oncol 2005; 172 patients, squamous): adding surgery after chemoradiotherapy improved 2-year local control (64% vs 41%) but not overall survival (40% vs 35%); treatment mortality 12.8% vs 3.5%. CROSS long-term (Lancet Oncol 2015).

ask.question: Why a neck anastomosis (McKeown) for this tumour?

choices.text: A mid-third tumour needs a long proximal margin that a chest anastomosis may not give
choices.why: Taking the esophagus into the neck gives a longer margin above the tumour and a complete thoracic lymphadenectomy; a cervical leak is also easier to manage than an intrathoracic one.

choices.text: It is always required for squamous carcinoma
Because the stomach is too short

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Fitness, nutrition (weight loss, albumin), cardiorespiratory reserve. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pneumonia
  • AF
  • Wound infection
  • Hoarse voice (neck anastomosis)

3. Serious

  • Anastomotic leak
  • Conduit necrosis
  • Chylothorax
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy
  • Death

4. Specific to this operation

  • Long-term: reflux (sleep head-up), early satiety, dumping, stricture needing dilatation, weight loss
  • Feeding jejunostomy for weeks

5. Alternatives

  • Definitive chemoradiation
  • Palliation: stent, radiotherapy
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Most present late and malnourished: pre-operative nutrition
  • The realistic chance of cure, and palliation as an option
