steps.title: Right thoracotomy (or right VATS)
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus. Right posterolateral thoracotomy through the 5th space (or four-port VATS / prone thoracoscopy). The right lung is isolated and retracted forward.

steps.title: Divide the azygos arch
steps.body: Open the mediastinal pleura along the front of the azygos arch and behind it. Staple the arch (vascular load): it opens the upper mediastinum and the space for the conduit.

steps.title: Mobilise the esophagus en bloc
steps.body:
Open the pleura in front of the aorta and along the pericardium. Take the esophagus with its periesophageal fat and nodes, including the subcarinal (station 7) packet, from the hiatus to the thoracic inlet, keeping close to the esophagus near the trachea to spare the recurrent nerves.

Clip the aortic esophageal branches. Watch the membranous trachea and left main bronchus in front, and the thoracic duct behind.

steps.title: Ligate the thoracic duct (low, above the hiatus)
steps.body: Many units ligate the duct routinely: mass-ligate all the tissue between the aorta and the azygos just above the hiatus, on the front of the spine. A missed duct injury declares itself as a milky drain output once feeding starts.

steps.title: Abdomen: mobilise the stomach
steps.body: Upper midline laparotomy (or laparoscopy). Divide the gastrocolic omentum well away from the right gastroepiploic arcade, which the conduit will live on, then the short gastric vessels up to the left crus. Open the lesser omentum. Kocherise the duodenum so the pylorus reaches the hiatus; a pyloric drainage procedure or none, by unit policy.

steps.title: Left gastric artery at its origin
steps.body: Lift the stomach up; the left gastric pedicle is taut in the lesser sac. Clear the coeliac nodes into the specimen and staple or tie the left gastric artery and vein at their origin. Check the common hepatic and splenic arteries first.

steps.title: Left neck: find the cervical esophagus
steps.body:
Head turned to the right. Incision along the anterior border of the left sternocleidomastoid. Retract the carotid sheath laterally, divide the omohyoid and the middle thyroid vein, and reach the esophagus on the prevertebral fascia.

The left recurrent laryngeal nerve lies in the tracheo-esophageal groove: no metal retractor against it, finger dissection only.

steps.title: Divide the esophagus in the neck
steps.body: Encircle the cervical esophagus with a finger from the neck, meeting the thoracic dissection. Divide it low in the neck and deliver the specimen through the abdomen.

action.label: Divide the esophagus in the neck

steps.title: Make the conduit and bring it up
steps.body:
Staple the lesser curvature from below the cardia to make a 4–5 cm tube of greater curvature on the right gastroepiploic artery. Pass it through the posterior mediastinum (the esophageal bed) to the neck in a plastic sleeve, without twisting.

Check the colour of the tip: poor perfusion there is what leaks.

steps.title: The anastomosis
steps.body:
Cervical: hand-sewn single layer or a linear-stapled side-to-side (Orringer). More leaks than in the chest, but a neck leak usually drains through the wound and heals.

Nasogastric tube past the anastomosis; feeding jejunostomy by unit policy.

b4-duct.name: Thoracic duct ligation
b4-duct.summary: Mass ligation between the aorta and the azygos above the right hemidiaphragm.

steps.title: The course of the thoracic duct
steps.body:
From the cisterna chyli (L1–L2, behind and right of the aorta) through the aortic hiatus, up on the right front of the vertebral bodies between the aorta and the azygos, behind the esophagus. At T4–T6 it crosses to the left and climbs on the left of the esophagus to end in the left venous angle (internal jugular and subclavian).

So an injury below T5 gives a right chylothorax, above it a left one. Doubled and plexiform ducts are common.

ask.question: After a left upper lobectomy, a patient has a milky left pleural effusion. At what level is the duct most likely injured?

choices.text: Above T5, where it runs on the left
choices.why: The duct crosses from right to left at T4-T6: upper injuries leak into the left chest, lower ones into the right.

steps.title: Chylothorax: when to operate
steps.body:
Milky fluid; confirm with triglycerides above 1.24 mmol/L (110 mg/dL) or chylomicrons. Start with drainage, nil by mouth or a fat-free / medium-chain diet, parenteral nutrition, octreotide.

Operate (or embolise) for high output (commonly more than 1 L a day, or more than 10 mL/kg/day in a child), failure after about 5–7 days, or nutritional and immune depletion. Thoracic duct embolisation by interventional radiology is the alternative where available.

Give cream or olive oil 2–4 hours before surgery: the leak turns white and shows itself.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Nutritional and immune state after chyle loss. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pain
  • Wound infection

3. Serious

  • Persistent chyle leak
  • Bleeding

4. Specific to this operation

  • Output should fall within 24–48 h

5. Alternatives

  • Conservative: fat-free diet or TPN (± octreotide)
  • Thoracic duct embolisation where available
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Access to TPN and embolisation

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: When is thoracic duct ligation offered?

choices.text: When a chylothorax persists or has a high output despite conservative treatment
choices.why: Surgery follows a failed trial of fat-free feeding or TPN, especially with high output.

steps.title: Right VATS, whichever side the effusion is
steps.body: Left lateral decubitus, right VATS (three ports, low). The duct is ligated on the right, just above the diaphragm, where it is a single trunk in most patients, even for a left chylothorax.

steps.title: Divide the inferior pulmonary ligament, lift the lung
steps.body: Retract the right lower lobe up and forward and divide the ligament. Open the pleura over the triangle formed by the aorta, the azygos vein and the vertebral bodies, just above the diaphragm.

steps.title: Mass ligation above the diaphragm
steps.body:
Pass a right-angle clamp round all the tissue between the aorta and the azygos, on the front of the spine, 2–5 cm above the hiatus. Tie it with non-absorbable ligatures (two) or clip it. You do not need to see the duct itself.

Watch the intercostal arteries behind, the esophagus in front, and the azygos on the right.

steps.title: Check, glue, drain
steps.body: Look for any white leak above the ligature (cream helps); clip or oversew it. Fibrin glue and a mechanical or talc pleurodesis by preference. One drain; record the output after feeding restarts.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Chest drain output should fall within 24–48 h
  • Replace protein, fluid and lymphocyte losses; nutrition

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: 24 h after duct ligation, output is unchanged at 1.5 L of milky fluid. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant: ligation may have failed
choices.why: Output should fall within 24–48 h; persistence suggests a missed or accessory duct.

b4-emp-vats.name: Empyema and decortication
b4-emp-vats.summary: Stage II: break the loculations, evacuate, strip an early peel.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: parapneumonic effusion to empyema
steps.body:
From pneumonia to peel. Inflammation next to the pleura makes the pleural capillaries leak: a sterile exudate. If bacteria cross, neutrophils and bacteria consume glucose and produce lactate and CO₂ (pH falls, LDH rises), fibrin is laid down and the fluid loculates. Fibroblasts then organise the fibrin into a peel that traps the lung.

I exudative (days): free-flowing, sterile→II fibrinopurulent (1–2 weeks): infected, pH and glucose fall, septations→III organising (3–6 weeks): fibrous peel, trapped lung

Drain when: pus, organisms on Gram stain or culture, pH 7.2 or less, or (if pH unavailable) glucose under 3.3 mmol/L; loculation on ultrasound supports it. A pH of 7.2–7.4 is intermediate (LDH over 900 IU/L supports drainage).

Treatment follows the stage: antibiotics and a small-bore drain; intrapleural tPA plus DNase for a residual collection; surgery (VATS debridement, or decortication) when sepsis and collection persist, or the lung is trapped. Tuberculous empyema is chronic from the start, with a thick peel, often a trapped lung, and needs TB treatment before and after decortication.

Risk at presentation: the RAPID score (renal: urea; age; purulence; infection source; dietary: albumin) sorts patients into low, medium and high risk of death at 3 months (about 2%, 9% and 29%).

Evidence: BTS 2023 guideline (Roberts et al., Thorax 2023): small-bore drains, tPA 10 mg + DNase 5 mg twice daily for 3 days for residual collections, not streptokinase or either drug alone; VATS preferred when surgery is needed. MIST1 (NEJM 2005): streptokinase gave no benefit. MIST2 (NEJM 2011): tPA+DNase improved drainage and cut surgical referral (4% vs 16%). RAPID validated in PILOT (Eur Respir J 2020). Uganda (Mwesige et al., BMC Pulm Med 2025; 200 adults): 6.5% of empyemas were tuberculous; in-hospital mortality 10.5%.

ask.question: After 5 days of a small-bore drain and antibiotics a loculated collection remains and the patient is still febrile. Next step?

choices.text: Intrapleural tPA plus DNase, or surgical referral (VATS) if unsuitable or it fails
choices.why: MIST2: the combination (not either drug alone, nor streptokinase) improves drainage and reduces surgery; persistent sepsis despite drainage is the trigger for surgery.

steps.title: Empyema: three stages
steps.body:
I, exudative (days): thin fluid, the lung still expands: a chest drain and antibiotics. II, fibrinopurulent (1–2 weeks): fibrin septa and loculations: drain plus intrapleural tPA and DNase (MIST2), or early VATS debridement. III, organising (after 3–6 weeks): a thick peel on the visceral pleura traps the lung: decortication.

Here the left lung is shown trapped, smaller than the chest, under its peel, with pus in the posterior costophrenic gutter.

ask.question: A patient with a parapneumonic effusion has septated fluid on ultrasound and a pleural fluid pH of 7.0. Stage?

choices.why: Septations and a low pH or glucose mean a complicated effusion or empyema in the fibrinopurulent stage: drain it, and add fibrinolytics or VATS if it does not clear.

steps.title: Case: a fibrinopurulent empyema that did not drain
steps.lead: A 38-year-old man, 10 days of community-acquired pneumonia; febrile, CRP 280. Ultrasound: a septated left effusion; pleural fluid pH 7.0, glucose 1.8 mmol/L, turbid; Streptococcus on culture. A 12F drain and 5 days of antibiotics, then tPA/DNase for 3 days: a posterior basal collection persists and he is still febrile. HIV-negative; GeneXpert on the fluid negative. RAPID score 2 (low risk).
steps.body:
Stage II (fibrinopurulent) not controlled by drainage and fibrinolytics: VATS debridement, breaking the loculations, evacuating the pus and stripping the early peel so the lung re-expands.

Evidence: VATS vs open decortication meta-analysis (Pan et al., J Thorac Dis 2017; 918 patients, retrospective): lower mortality (4.1% vs 6.2%) and morbidity, shorter stay, no difference in relapse. BTS 2023: prefer VATS when surgery is needed.

ask.question: What finding on pleural fluid most clearly mandated chest drainage here?

choices.text: pH 7.0 (with positive culture and turbid fluid)
choices.why: A pleural pH of 7.2 or less indicates complicated parapneumonic effusion or empyema; culture positivity and pus are independent indications.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Sepsis, nutrition, lung trapped or not. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Air leak
  • Bleeding from the decorticated surface
  • Pain

3. Serious

  • Persistent space or recurrence
  • Sepsis
  • Conversion to open

4. Specific to this operation

  • Antibiotics continue for weeks

5. Alternatives

  • Chest drain with intrapleural tPA and DNase (MIST2)
  • Open drainage
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Test for TB (GeneXpert) and treat
  • HIV testing

ask.question: Before decortication for empyema, which alternative should the patient hear about?

choices.text: A chest drain with intrapleural tPA and DNase
choices.why: MIST2 (NEJM 2011): improved drainage and fewer surgical referrals.

steps.title: Ports over the collection
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus. Place the first port where the collection is largest on ultrasound or CT (often low and posterior), by open finger dissection: the lung may be stuck to the wall. Two more ports under vision.

steps.title: Break the loculations, evacuate the pus
steps.body: With a sucker, a sponge on a holder and the camera, break every septum so the space becomes one cavity; take the fibrin off the lung and the diaphragm. Send pus and pleura for culture. Irrigate with warm saline.

steps.title: Early peel: strip it thoracoscopically
steps.body: A young peel strips with a peanut: find the plane between the peel and the visceral pleura, then ask the anaesthetist to inflate the lung as you go: it helps the peel lift. A thick, old peel is a conversion to thoracotomy.

steps.title: Re-expansion and drains
steps.body: The lung should fill the chest. Two large drains, apical and basal-posterior. Air leak from small tears is expected; persistent space or leak means the peel was left.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Expect air leak and ooze
  • Ongoing sepsis: undrained collection: CT
  • Culture-directed antibiotics; TB screen

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 3 after decortication: persistent fever, new loculated collection on CT. Next?

choices.text: Drain the collection and review cultures, including TB
choices.why: Undrained pus is the usual cause of persistent sepsis.

steps.title: Case: a chronic tuberculous empyema with a trapped lung
steps.lead: A 24-year-old woman, HIV-positive (on ART, CD4 380), 3 months of cough and weight loss; a left pleural collection drained 6 weeks ago grew nothing on routine culture, but GeneXpert: M. tuberculosis, rifampicin-sensitive. On TB treatment for 5 weeks. CT: a thick, enhancing pleural peel, a residual posterior collection, the left lung trapped, ribs crowded.
steps.body:
Stage III (organising), tuberculous: continue TB treatment, and decortication through a thoracotomy (a thick, old peel rarely comes off thoracoscopically) once she is on treatment and nutritionally supported. The goal: free the lung so it fills the chest and the space is gone.

If the lung is destroyed underneath, decortication will not re-expand it: plan for space-filling (muscle flap, limited thoracoplasty) or an open window.

ask.question: Why continue TB treatment before and after decortication?

choices.text: Surgery removes the peel and the space, but only drugs treat the mycobacterial infection
choices.why: Operating on a patient already established on effective TB treatment lowers the risk of bronchopleural fistula and recurrent infection; treatment completes the course afterwards.

choices.text: It is not needed after decortication

steps.title: Posterolateral thoracotomy, 5th intercostal space
steps.body: Right lateral decubitus. Posterolateral thoracotomy, often through the 6th space for a basal cavity; a rib may be resected. The ribs are often crowded by the contracted hemithorax: spread slowly.

steps.title: Open the cavity, evacuate
steps.body: Enter the cavity through the parietal peel, suck out pus and debris, and send it for culture.

steps.title: Decorticate the lung
steps.body:
Incise the visceral peel with a knife until the glistening visceral pleura bulges into the cut (inflation helps); then separate the peel with a peanut and scissors, lobe by lobe, and in the fissure. Stay on the peel, not in the lung: tears leak air for days.

Free the diaphragm too, so it moves. Decorticate the parietal side only as needed for the lung to meet the wall.

ask.question: The lung does not re-expand after decortication and the space persists. Options?

choices.text: Muscle flap or thoracoplasty to fill the space, or an open window (Eloesser) in the frail
choices.why: A residual space re-infects: fill it (serratus or latissimus flap, limited thoracoplasty) or leave it open to drain.

steps.title: Re-expansion, drains, close
steps.body: Two large drains. For the frail patient who cannot stand a decortication, an open thoracostomy window (Eloesser flap) drains a chronic cavity instead.

ppe-window.name: Post-pneumonectomy empyema and bronchopleural fistula
ppe-window.summary: The infected post-pneumonectomy space and a stump fistula: protect the other lung, drain, then open window and Clagett closure, or stump re-closure with a muscle flap.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: the post-pneumonectomy space, empyema and fistula
steps.body:
The empty hemithorax. After pneumonectomy the space fills with serous fluid over days to weeks, while the mediastinum shifts across, the diaphragm rises and the ribs crowd in. The fluid is an ideal culture medium: seeded at operation, from the blood, or through a bronchopleural fistula (BPF), it becomes post-pneumonectomy empyema (PPE), reported in 2–16%.

Stump ischaemia (stripped bronchial arteries), tension, a long stump, residual tumour, radiation, infection→Stump dehiscence: BPF→Air enters the space; fluid drains into the airway→Aspiration into the only lung: pneumonia, ARDS, death
Infected fluid in a rigid space→Sepsis→Erodes the stump from outside: late BPF

Early BPF (first days to about 2 weeks) is usually technical; late BPF follows infection or ischaemia and can appear months later. Right pneumonectomy is worst: the right stump lies uncovered in the pleural space, usually on a single bronchial artery, while the left retracts under the aortic arch and has two.

Signs: fever, coughing up large volumes of serous or brownish fluid (the pleural fluid), a falling fluid level or a new air-fluid level on the X-ray, subcutaneous emphysema, contralateral aspiration pneumonia.

First move: sit up or lie operated side down (so the fluid cannot run into the good lung), then a chest drain into the space, antibiotics, and bronchoscopy.

Evidence: incidence: Deschamps et al. (Mayo, 713 pneumonectomies, Ann Thorac Surg 2001): empyema 7.5%, BPF 4.5%; BPF 0–6.3% after left vs 1.1–22.9% after right pneumonectomy, mortality 18–71% (Wali and Billè, 2021; Gritsiuta et al., 2025). Anatomy of right-sided risk: Wali and Billè 2021.

ask.question: Ten days after right pneumonectomy, a patient suddenly coughs up 300 mL of thin brown fluid and becomes breathless. How should he be positioned?

choices.text: Operated (right) side down, or sitting up, so the space fluid cannot flood the left lung
choices.why: This is a bronchopleural fistula: the pneumonectomy space is draining into the airway. Positioning protects the remaining lung until a drain is in.

steps.title: The right stump and its neighbours
steps.body:
The right main bronchial stump sits at the carina, behind the SVC and the stump of the right pulmonary artery, under the azygos arch, with the esophagus behind and medial. Re-exposing it through the infected space means dense, friable tissue; the transsternal, transpericardial route reaches the carina through clean tissue, between the SVC and the aorta, when the pleural route is hostile.

The space itself is bounded by the mediastinum, the raised diaphragm and the chest wall; its lowest point laterally (about the 6th–8th ribs) is where an open window drains it.

steps.title: Case: fever and a falling fluid level after right pneumonectomy
steps.lead: A 61-year-old man, right pneumonectomy 11 days ago for a central squamous carcinoma after neoadjuvant chemotherapy; the stump was stapled and not covered. Now: fever 38.9 °C, WCC 21, and he coughs up thin brown fluid. X-ray: the fluid level in the right hemithorax has fallen by 4 cm since yesterday; a patchy shadow in the left lower zone. Bronchoscopy: a 5 mm dehiscence at the stump; the pleural fluid is turbid.
steps.body:
Early BPF with post-pneumonectomy empyema. Immediate: operated side down, a chest drain into the space, broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU. Then two paths:

  • Fit, early fistula, clean enough: re-operate early: debride the space, re-amputate and close the stump, cover it with a vascularised flap (latissimus, serratus, intercostal muscle or omentum), then sterilise and close the space (Clagett-type fill, or repeated debridement with negative pressure and closure).
  • Unfit, or late, established infection: open window thoracostomy (Eloesser) to drain the space for weeks, dressing changes, then a later closure (Clagett) once the cavity is clean, with or without muscle transposition.

Small fistulas (under 3–5 mm) in unfit patients can sometimes be closed endoscopically (glue, occluder devices, stents), usually as a bridge.

Evidence: Clagett and Geraci (1963): open window drainage then filling the cavity with antibiotic solution and closing it; Zaheer et al. (Mayo 2006): success 81% after the first attempt. Pairolero et al. (JTCVS 1990): muscle transposition to close the fistula and fill the space, success 84%. Accelerated treatment (Schneiter et al., JTCVS 2008; 75 patients, 59% with BPF): repeated debridement, negative pressure and antibiotic-filled closure healed 97% with 4% 90-day mortality. Stump coverage (Di Maio et al., meta-analysis 2015): coverage was selective in most series; the one trial, in diabetics, favoured coverage.

ask.question: What is the first priority when this patient starts coughing up space fluid?

choices.text: Protect the left lung: position operated side down and drain the space
choices.why: Death in BPF comes from aspiration of the infected space fluid into the remaining lung; positioning and a chest drain stop it, before bronchoscopy or definitive surgery.

ask.question: What must a patient know before an open window thoracostomy?

choices.text: The chest stays open for weeks to months, with regular dressings, before closure
choices.why: Expectations about a long course prevent distress and non-attendance.

steps.title: Position, drain the space, bronchoscopy
steps.body:
Sit him up, operated side down. A large-bore drain into the space in the mid-axillary line, above the diaphragm (which has risen: check the level on ultrasound), connected to an underwater seal without suction (suction pulls the mediastinum across). Send the fluid for culture, including TB.

Bronchoscopy: the size and site of the defect, and the viability of the stump; clear aspirated secretions from the left lung.

steps.title: Open window thoracostomy (Eloesser)
steps.body:
Over the lowest part of the cavity, laterally (confirm with CT or a needle), make a U-shaped or inverted-U skin flap with its base at the dependent edge. Resect segments of two ribs (about 8–10 cm each) under the flap, open the thickened parietal pleura, and suture the skin to the pleura all round so the window lines itself and stays open.

The cavity now drains by gravity and can be packed and inspected; the mediastinum is already fixed, so an open chest is tolerated.

ask.question: Where should the open window be placed?

choices.text: Over the most dependent part of the cavity, laterally
choices.why: Gravity drainage needs the lowest point; too high and pus pools below it.

steps.title: Debride, pack or apply negative pressure
steps.body:
Debride the fibrin and necrotic tissue; irrigate. Pack with gauze soaked in dilute povidone-iodine or antibiotic solution, changed daily or every 2 days, or apply negative-pressure therapy (a sponge in the cavity) if there is no open fistula or it has been closed and covered. The fistula often closes as the space granulates; if not, it is closed and covered with muscle later.

Evidence: accelerated treatment (Schneiter et al., JTCVS 2008): repeated debridement in theatre every 48 hours, povidone-iodine packing and negative pressure, then closure with the cavity filled with antibiotic solution: 97% healed, chest closed within 8 days in 95%.

steps.title: Clagett closure: fill the clean cavity and close
steps.body:
When the cavity is clean and granulating, and the fistula closed (weeks to months later, typically 6–8 weeks), fill the space with antibiotic solution (for example DAB: neomycin, polymyxin B and gentamicin per litre), and close the window in layers, watertight. The sterile fluid then obliterates slowly, like a normal post-pneumonectomy space.

A persistent fistula must first be closed and covered with muscle (latissimus or serratus through the window), or the Clagett fails.

Evidence: Clagett and Geraci (JTCVS 1963); success 81% at first attempt and 88% after a second (Zaheer et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2006).

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Window dressings; nutrition
  • Watch for fistula closure or reopening
  • Plan the Clagett or flap

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ppe-flap.name: Post-pneumonectomy empyema and bronchopleural fistula
ppe-flap.approach: Stump closure with a muscle flap
ppe-flap.summary: The infected post-pneumonectomy space and a stump fistula: protect the other lung, drain, then open window and Clagett closure, or stump re-closure with a muscle flap.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: the post-pneumonectomy space, empyema and fistula
steps.body:
The empty hemithorax. After pneumonectomy the space fills with serous fluid over days to weeks, while the mediastinum shifts across, the diaphragm rises and the ribs crowd in. The fluid is an ideal culture medium: seeded at operation, from the blood, or through a bronchopleural fistula (BPF), it becomes post-pneumonectomy empyema (PPE), reported in 2–16%.

Stump ischaemia (stripped bronchial arteries), tension, a long stump, residual tumour, radiation, infection→Stump dehiscence: BPF→Air enters the space; fluid drains into the airway→Aspiration into the only lung: pneumonia, ARDS, death
Infected fluid in a rigid space→Sepsis→Erodes the stump from outside: late BPF

Early BPF (first days to about 2 weeks) is usually technical; late BPF follows infection or ischaemia and can appear months later. Right pneumonectomy is worst: the right stump lies uncovered in the pleural space, usually on a single bronchial artery, while the left retracts under the aortic arch and has two.

Signs: fever, coughing up large volumes of serous or brownish fluid (the pleural fluid), a falling fluid level or a new air-fluid level on the X-ray, subcutaneous emphysema, contralateral aspiration pneumonia.

First move: sit up or lie operated side down (so the fluid cannot run into the good lung), then a chest drain into the space, antibiotics, and bronchoscopy.

Evidence: incidence: Deschamps et al. (Mayo, 713 pneumonectomies, Ann Thorac Surg 2001): empyema 7.5%, BPF 4.5%; BPF 0–6.3% after left vs 1.1–22.9% after right pneumonectomy, mortality 18–71% (Wali and Billè, 2021; Gritsiuta et al., 2025). Anatomy of right-sided risk: Wali and Billè 2021.

ask.question: Ten days after right pneumonectomy, a patient suddenly coughs up 300 mL of thin brown fluid and becomes breathless. How should he be positioned?

choices.text: Operated (right) side down, or sitting up, so the space fluid cannot flood the left lung
choices.why: This is a bronchopleural fistula: the pneumonectomy space is draining into the airway. Positioning protects the remaining lung until a drain is in.

steps.title: The right stump and its neighbours
steps.body:
The right main bronchial stump sits at the carina, behind the SVC and the stump of the right pulmonary artery, under the azygos arch, with the esophagus behind and medial. Re-exposing it through the infected space means dense, friable tissue; the transsternal, transpericardial route reaches the carina through clean tissue, between the SVC and the aorta, when the pleural route is hostile.

The space itself is bounded by the mediastinum, the raised diaphragm and the chest wall; its lowest point laterally (about the 6th–8th ribs) is where an open window drains it.

steps.title: Case: fever and a falling fluid level after right pneumonectomy
steps.lead: A 61-year-old man, right pneumonectomy 11 days ago for a central squamous carcinoma after neoadjuvant chemotherapy; the stump was stapled and not covered. Now: fever 38.9 °C, WCC 21, and he coughs up thin brown fluid. X-ray: the fluid level in the right hemithorax has fallen by 4 cm since yesterday; a patchy shadow in the left lower zone. Bronchoscopy: a 5 mm dehiscence at the stump; the pleural fluid is turbid.
steps.body:
Early BPF with post-pneumonectomy empyema. Immediate: operated side down, a chest drain into the space, broad-spectrum antibiotics, ICU. Then two paths:

  • Fit, early fistula, clean enough: re-operate early: debride the space, re-amputate and close the stump, cover it with a vascularised flap (latissimus, serratus, intercostal muscle or omentum), then sterilise and close the space (Clagett-type fill, or repeated debridement with negative pressure and closure).
  • Unfit, or late, established infection: open window thoracostomy (Eloesser) to drain the space for weeks, dressing changes, then a later closure (Clagett) once the cavity is clean, with or without muscle transposition.

Small fistulas (under 3–5 mm) in unfit patients can sometimes be closed endoscopically (glue, occluder devices, stents), usually as a bridge.

Evidence: Clagett and Geraci (1963): open window drainage then filling the cavity with antibiotic solution and closing it; Zaheer et al. (Mayo 2006): success 81% after the first attempt. Pairolero et al. (JTCVS 1990): muscle transposition to close the fistula and fill the space, success 84%. Accelerated treatment (Schneiter et al., JTCVS 2008; 75 patients, 59% with BPF): repeated debridement, negative pressure and antibiotic-filled closure healed 97% with 4% 90-day mortality. Stump coverage (Di Maio et al., meta-analysis 2015): coverage was selective in most series; the one trial, in diabetics, favoured coverage.

choices.text: The chest stays open for weeks to months, with regular dressings, before closure
choices.why: Expectations about a long course prevent distress and non-attendance.

steps.title: Position, drain the space, bronchoscopy
steps.body:
Sit him up, operated side down. A large-bore drain into the space in the mid-axillary line, above the diaphragm (which has risen: check the level on ultrasound), connected to an underwater seal without suction (suction pulls the mediastinum across). Send the fluid for culture, including TB.

Bronchoscopy: the size and site of the defect, and the viability of the stump; clear aspirated secretions from the left lung.

steps.title: Re-thoracotomy: evacuate and debride the space
steps.body: Through the old incision (or a fresh one through the rib bed), evacuate the infected fluid and fibrin; debride the parietal pleura; irrigate generously. Send tissue for culture. The mediastinum is fixed and the heart lies close under the fibrin: take care over the pericardium and the SVC.

steps.title: Re-amputate and close the stump
steps.body:
Free the stump from the fibrin without stripping its remaining blood supply. Trim back to healthy, bleeding cartilage, flush with the carina, and close it again: interrupted absorbable (or polypropylene) sutures, membranous to cartilaginous wall, or a stapler if there is length. Test under saline at 25–30 cmH₂O.

If the pleural field is too hostile, the stump can be reached and re-amputated transsternally and transpericardially, between the SVC and the aorta, in clean tissue.

ask.question: Why must a re-closed stump in an infected field be covered?

choices.text: A sutured stump in an infected space breaks down again unless a vascularised flap brings blood supply and seals it
choices.why: Muscle (latissimus, serratus, intercostal), omentum or pericardial fat buttresses the closure and helps clear infection; it is the key step in Pairolero's approach.

steps.title: Latissimus dorsi flap onto the stump
steps.body: Raise the latissimus dorsi on its thoracodorsal pedicle (if it was divided at the first thoracotomy, use serratus anterior, an intercostal muscle, or omentum through the diaphragm instead). Bring it into the chest through a window made by resecting a 5–6 cm segment of the 2nd or 3rd rib, and suture it over the closed stump so it seals and supplies it; the bulk fills part of the space.

steps.title: Fill the space and close; or open window
steps.body:
If the space is clean after debridement: fill it with antibiotic solution and close (a Clagett-type closure), or use the accelerated approach (repeat debridement every 48 hours with negative pressure, then antibiotic-filled closure). If it is not clean: leave an open window and close later.

Evidence: Pairolero et al. (JTCVS 1990): muscle transposition closed the fistula and controlled the empyema in 84%. Schneiter et al. (JTCVS 2008): accelerated treatment healed 97%.

rt.name: Resuscitative thoracotomy
rt.summary: Anterolateral thoracotomy, pericardiotomy, cardiorrhaphy, aortic cross-clamp, massage.

steps.title: Who gets a resuscitative thoracotomy
steps.body:
The goals: release tamponade, control bleeding from the heart or lung, cross-clamp the descending aorta, internal cardiac massage, and stop air embolism.

Best results after a penetrating chest wound with signs of life, poorest after blunt injury. Commonly used cut-offs: thoracotomy is futile after about 15 minutes of CPR for penetrating injury, and after about 10 minutes for blunt injury, without a response. Follow your unit's protocol.

ask.question: A man with a stab wound to the left chest loses his pulse on arrival; CPR for 6 minutes. What now?

choices.text: Left anterolateral thoracotomy in the resuscitation room
choices.why: Penetrating chest injury, pulseless, CPR well under 15 minutes: the best indication there is (EAST: strong recommendation).

choices.text: Keep up CPR and give blood only

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
Life-saving emergency surgery: when the patient cannot consent and delay risks life, proceed on necessity, document why, and inform the next of kin as soon as possible. If the patient can talk, a short explanation still matters.

Discuss with the family afterwards

  • Survival after resuscitative thoracotomy is low overall; best for penetrating cardiac injury with signs of life
  • Re-operation, bleeding, infection
  • Missed injuries
  • Long ICU stay

ask.question: An unconscious patient needs a resuscitative thoracotomy. How is consent handled?

choices.text: Proceed on necessity to save life, document it, and inform the next of kin as soon as possible
choices.why: Emergency treatment without consent is justified when the patient cannot consent and delay risks life.

steps.title: Left anterolateral thoracotomy, 5th space
steps.body:
Supine, the left arm up above the head. Incise along the 5th intercostal space from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line: below the nipple in a man, in the inframammary fold in a woman (lift the breast). Curve slightly upward toward the axilla, following the rib.

Cut through the pectoralis and serratus in one pass, then divide the intercostal muscles on the upper border of the 6th rib with scissors (heavy Mayo), pushing the lung away. Place the rib spreader with its handle toward the axilla, so it does not block an extension across the sternum.

Medially the internal mammary artery runs 1–2 cm from the sternal edge: it is cut if the incision goes onto the sternum, and bleeds once there is a pressure.

steps.title: Pericardiotomy, anterior to the phrenic nerve
steps.body:
Push the collapsed lung back. The phrenic nerve runs down the side of the pericardium. Pick up the pericardium with toothed forceps anterior to the nerve, nick it with scissors, and open it longitudinally, parallel to the nerve, from the apex to the root of the aorta.

A tense, blue, non-pulsatile pericardium is tamponade: scoop out the clot and deliver the heart into the wound.

ask.question: Where do you open the pericardium?

choices.text: Anterior to the phrenic nerve, parallel to it
choices.why: The nerve runs on the lateral pericardium; a longitudinal cut in front of it spares it. A transverse cut divides it.

steps.title: Cardiorrhaphy: right ventricular stab wound
steps.body:
Put a finger on the hole first. The right ventricle is the chamber most often hit, as it lies under the sternum.

Close with 3-0 or 4-0 polypropylene, pledgeted horizontal mattress sutures, sliding the finger along as each stitch goes in. Tie gently: ventricular muscle tears.

Bridges while you get ready: a Foley catheter through the hole, balloon inflated and pulled up gently; or a skin stapler across a clean wound.
steps.pearl: Near a coronary artery, pass the mattress stitch beneath the artery so it is not tied off. Atrial wounds: a side-biting clamp, then a running suture.

steps.title: Cross-clamp the descending aorta
steps.body:
Lift the left lung up and forward. Just above the diaphragm, open the mediastinal pleura over the aorta and separate it from the esophagus with the fingers: the aorta is the firm tube on the spine; a nasogastric tube makes the esophagus easy to feel.

Place a vascular clamp across the aorta. It diverts what cardiac output there is to the heart and brain and cuts bleeding below the diaphragm. Note the time: visceral and spinal ischaemia build after about 30 minutes.

ask.question: Where does the esophagus lie relative to the lower descending aorta?

choices.text: Anterior and to its right, closely applied
choices.why: Low in the chest the esophagus lies in front of and to the right of the aorta; a blind clamp can take both.

choices.text: Lateral to it, under the lung

steps.title: Internal massage and defibrillation
steps.body:
Two-handed massage: the heart between the flat palms, compressing from the apex toward the base. Not the fingertips: they go through the ventricle.

Fill the heart first: an empty heart gains nothing from massage. For VF, internal paddles on either side of the ventricles, starting at about 10–20 J.

steps.title: Extend, or go to theatre
steps.body:
Cannot reach the right side of the heart, the right lung or the great vessels? Extend across the sternum into a clamshell (next operation in the menu).

With a circulation back: go to theatre; release the aortic clamp slowly with the anaesthetist ready; ligate both internal mammary arteries; look for bleeding you could not see at a pressure of zero.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the thoracic core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Damage control: correct the lethal triad (hypothermia, acidosis, coagulopathy)
  • 1:1:1 transfusion; TXA within 3 h of injury (CRASH-2) guideline
  • Repeat and tertiary survey: missed injuries
  • After hilar twist or pneumonectomy for trauma: RV failure: avoid overload, inodilator
  • Air embolism after lung injury
  • Cardiorrhaphy: echo for residual VSD, valve injury, effusion

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: CRASH-2 (Lancet 2010): TXA within 3 h reduces death from bleeding. Damage-control resuscitation principles (ATLS 10th edition).

ask.question: After a clamshell for penetrating trauma: temperature 34 °C, pH 7.1, oozing. Priority?

choices.text: Correct the lethal triad: warm, transfuse 1:1:1, give TXA if within 3 h
choices.why: Damage-control resuscitation before further surgery.

choices.text: Return to theatre immediately for definitive repair

clamshell.name: Clamshell thoracotomy
clamshell.summary: Both 5th-space thoracotomies, transverse sternotomy, mammaries ligated, lid lifted.

steps.title: Clamshell: when and what it opens
steps.body:
Both 5th-space anterolateral incisions, joined by a transverse sternotomy. The chest wall above lifts like a lid, opening both pleural cavities, the whole anterior heart, the pulmonary hila and, with traction, the arch and its branches.

Use it for a wound to the right chest, a precordial wound in an arrested patient, or when a left anterolateral thoracotomy cannot reach the injury. Many trauma teams start with a clamshell in the arrested patient.

steps.title: Right anterolateral thoracotomy, 5th space
steps.body:
The same incision on the right: 5th space, sternal edge to mid-axillary line, intercostals divided on the upper border of the 6th rib. A second spreader goes in with its handle toward the right axilla.

The right internal mammary artery crosses the line of the sternal cut 1–2 cm from the edge.

steps.title: Divide the sternum transversely
steps.body:
Join the two incisions across the sternum at the same level. Divide the bone with a Gigli saw passed behind it, a Lebsche knife struck with a mallet, or heavy trauma shears.

Stay in the same intercostal level on both sides so the lid lifts evenly.

steps.title: Internal mammary arteries: ligate both ends
steps.body:
Both internal mammary arteries are divided with the sternum. In arrest they do not bleed; once there is a pressure they bleed briskly, from both ends.

Find each end 1–2 cm from the sternal edge on the cut surface and ligate or clip all four. A missed mammary is a common cause of return to theatre.

ask.question: After a clamshell, the heart restarts and the chest fills with blood from the wound edges. First suspect?

choices.why: Both are cut with the sternum and do not bleed until there is a pressure.

steps.title: Lift the lid
steps.body: With both spreaders open, lift the upper chest wall and sternum up toward the head. The whole anterior mediastinum, both lungs and both hila come into view.

steps.title: What you can reach
steps.body:
Open the pericardium in the midline (an inverted T), clear of both phrenic nerves. You now reach the whole anterior heart, both hila for a clamp or twist, the descending aorta through the left chest, and the SVC and right atrium through the right.

For the arch branches, add a vertical upper sternotomy from the midpoint of the transverse cut.

cardio.name: Cardiorrhaphy
cardio.summary: Cardiac box, anterolateral thoracotomy, pericardiotomy, pledgeted repair.

steps.title: The cardiac box
steps.body:
A wound between the clavicles, the mid-clavicular lines and the costal margins is a heart wound until proved otherwise.

The right ventricle is the most anterior chamber and the most often hit, then the left ventricle; atrial wounds are rarer and bleed less. Beck's triad (hypotension, raised venous pressure, muffled heart sounds) is often incomplete: scan the pericardium (FAST).

steps.body:
Supine, the left arm up above the head. Incise along the 5th intercostal space from the sternal edge to the mid-axillary line: below the nipple in a man, in the inframammary fold in a woman (lift the breast). Curve slightly upward toward the axilla, following the rib.

steps.title: Pericardiotomy, anterior to the phrenic nerve
steps.body:
Push the collapsed lung back. The phrenic nerve runs down the side of the pericardium. Pick up the pericardium with toothed forceps anterior to the nerve, nick it with scissors, and open it longitudinally, parallel to the nerve, from the apex to the root of the aorta.

A tense, blue, non-pulsatile pericardium is tamponade: scoop out the clot and deliver the heart into the wound.

ask.question: Where do you open the pericardium?

choices.text: Anterior to the phrenic nerve, parallel to it
choices.why: The nerve runs on the lateral pericardium; a longitudinal cut in front of it spares it. A transverse cut divides it.

steps.title: Cardiorrhaphy: right ventricular stab wound
steps.body:
Put a finger on the hole first. The right ventricle is the chamber most often hit, as it lies under the sternum.

Close with 3-0 or 4-0 polypropylene, pledgeted horizontal mattress sutures, sliding the finger along as each stitch goes in. Tie gently: ventricular muscle tears.

Bridges while you get ready: a Foley catheter through the hole, balloon inflated and pulled up gently; or a skin stapler across a clean wound.
steps.pearl: Near a coronary artery, pass the mattress stitch beneath the artery so it is not tied off. Atrial wounds: a side-biting clamp, then a running suture.

steps.title: After the repair
steps.body:
Check the back of the heart for an exit wound: lift the apex gently (the pressure falls while you do). Leave the pericardium open or loosely closed so it cannot tamponade again.

Get an echo before discharge: septal and valve injuries are easily missed.

tract.summary: Find the tract, staple through it, ligate each vessel and bronchus, leave it open.

steps.title: The bleeding lung: what to do
steps.body:
Most lung wounds need only a chest drain. Operate for continuing bleeding: commonly about 1500 mL at insertion, or 200 mL an hour for several hours, or shock.

Choose the least lung resection that controls it: suture (pneumonorrhaphy) for a superficial wound, tractotomy for a through-and-through tract, a stapled wedge at the periphery; lobectomy or pneumonectomy only for hilar injury. Mortality climbs steeply with each step up.

choices.why: It opens the tract, controls the bleeding vessels and air leaks individually, and saves the lobe.

steps.title: Find the entry and exit wounds
steps.body:
Deliver the lobe into the wound. Compress it in the hand to hold the bleeding; find both holes. Pass a finger or the jaw of a clamp along the tract to check it is a single straight path, well away from the hilum.

A tract through the hilum is not for tractotomy: control the hilum instead.

steps.title: Tractotomy: staple through the tract
steps.body: Pass one jaw of a linear stapler (or two long clamps) through the tract, the other over the thin bridge of lung above it, and fire. The tract lies open as a trough.

steps.title: Selective ligation in the tract
steps.body: In the open tract, find each bleeding vessel and each leaking bronchus and tie or suture it individually (4-0 polypropylene). Leave the tract open: closing it over traps blood and risks air embolism.

ask.question: Why not simply oversew the entry and exit holes of a deep tract?

choices.text: Bleeding continues inside, and air can enter the pulmonary veins
choices.why: An oversewn tract becomes a haematoma and a route for systemic air embolism.

steps.title: Test and close
steps.body: Fill the chest with warm saline and inflate the lung: no bubbles, no bleeding. Two drains (apical and basal). Close the ribs with pericostal sutures.

steps.title: When to control the whole hilum
steps.body:
Hilar control is for massive bleeding from the hilum or deep lung that a hand cannot hold, or for systemic air embolism from a lung wound (air in the coronary arteries, sudden arrest when ventilated).

Two ways: a clamp across the whole hilum, or the hilar twist. Both need the inferior pulmonary ligament divided first. The right ventricle then pumps into one lung: expect acute right heart strain.

Slide a large Satinsky clamp round the hilum from above, the jaws taking the pulmonary artery, both veins and the bronchus together, as close to the mediastinum as you can. A hand round the hilum holds it while you position the clamp.

Watch the right heart: if it dilates, release partially.

steps.title: After the clamp
steps.body:
The clamp buys time. Repair the injured vessel if it is proximal and simple; otherwise a stapled pneumonectomy (one fire across the hilum) may be all the patient can stand.

Trauma pneumonectomy carries a very high mortality, largely from right heart failure: give fluids carefully and consider inotropes early.

choices.why: The ligament tethers the lower lobe to the mediastinum; the lung cannot turn until it is cut.

mvr-std.name: Mitral valve replacement
mvr-std.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the decision, then the operation (access, bypass, left atrium, excision, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: rheumatic mitral stenosis
steps.body:
In Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa most mitral stenosis, and most aortic regurgitation in the young, is rheumatic. Patients present in their 20s and 30s, often late, with atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension or in pregnancy. In the REMEDY registry (14 low- and middle-income countries, median age 28 years) about 17% had died within two years.

From sore throat to scarred valve.

  1. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (skin infection may also contribute) in a susceptible child.
  2. Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein and its carbohydrate (GlcNAc) cross-react with cardiac myosin and with laminin on the valve shown in human rheumatic tissue.
  3. The valve endothelium is activated (VCAM-1), T cells home into the valve along the closure line and drive a valvulitis (Th1/Th17) shown in human rheumatic tissue. This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis.
  4. Each recurrence re-injures the valve. Over years, valve interstitial cells lay down scar (TGF-β-driven fibrosis) and calcium: the commissures fuse, the leaflets thicken, the chordae shorten and fuse inferred (much of this signalling is from calcific aortic valve disease).
Acute carditisChronic rheumatic heart disease
LesionMitral regurgitation: annular dilatation, elongated chordae, anterior leaflet prolapse (Carpentier I, II)Mitral stenosis (often with regurgitation): commissural fusion, thick leaflets, fused short chordae (Carpentier IIIa)
The valve…cannot closecannot open
Reversible?partly, if carditis settles and recurrences are preventedno: scar and calcium, treated mechanically (balloon or surgery)

The haemodynamics. A normal mitral orifice is 4–6 cm²; stenosis becomes clinically significant at 1.5 cm² or less. The LV is protected (it is under-filled); the load falls on everything behind the valve:

Small orifice→LA→LV gradient→LA pressure ↑, LA dilates→Atrial fibrillation→LA appendage thrombus → stroke
LA pressure ↑→Pulmonary venous pressure ↑ (breathless, oedema)→Pulmonary hypertension→RV pressure overload→RV dilates → TR → right heart failure

Why a fast heart rate decompensates MS. The gradient depends on flow and on the time available for the LA to empty: diastole. Tachycardia (AF with a fast ventricular rate, exercise, fever, anaemia, pregnancy) shortens diastole, so the gradient and LA pressure climb and pulmonary oedema follows. Hence rate control (a β-blocker) and why MS often declares itself in pregnancy. AF also removes the atrial kick and adds stasis: rheumatic AF carries a high embolic risk, and it is treated with warfarin, not a direct oral anticoagulant.

Evidence: the immunology (mimicry, valvular endothelial activation, T-cell infiltration) rests on studies of human rheumatic valves and valve-derived T-cell clones (Guilherme et al., Circulation 1995; Cunningham, Clin Microbiol Rev 2000); the later fibrocalcific steps are largely extrapolated from calcific aortic valve disease. Clinical picture: Carapetis et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016; Chandrashekhar, Westaby and Narula, Lancet 2009. Prevention works: in GOAL (NEJM 2022; 818 Ugandan children with latent RHD) monthly benzathine penicillin cut progression over 2 years from 8.3% to 0.8%. INVICTUS (NEJM 2022; 4,531 patients with rheumatic AF) found more vascular deaths and ischaemic strokes with rivaroxaban than with a vitamin K antagonist; ESC/EACTS 2025 advise against DOACs in AF with rheumatic MS and a valve area of 2.0 cm² or less.

ask.question: A 26-year-old woman with moderate rheumatic MS, comfortable at rest, goes into AF at 150 beats per minute and within hours is in pulmonary oedema. Why?

choices.text: The short diastole leaves too little time to empty the LA through the narrow valve, so the gradient and LA pressure rise
choices.why: In MS the transmitral gradient rises steeply with heart rate. Slowing the rate (and cardioversion, with anticoagulation) often relieves the oedema before anything is done to the valve.

choices.text: The valve has suddenly narrowed further
AF has caused acute mitral regurgitation

steps.title: The mitral valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
The mitral annulus is D-shaped and saddle-shaped. The anterior leaflet hangs from the fibrous aortomitral curtain, in continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; the posterior leaflet takes the rest of the circumference. Chordae run from both leaflets to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles.

Round the posterior annulus, in the AV groove: the circumflex artery (close near the anterolateral commissure, closer in left dominance) and the coronary sinus. At the posteromedial commissure, next to the right trigone: the AV node and His bundle. These are what deep annular sutures injure.

ask.question: A deep suture at the posterior annulus near the anterolateral commissure is most likely to injure…

choices.why: It runs in the AV groove close to the annulus there, especially in a left-dominant circulation.

steps.title: Case: rheumatic mitral stenosis, AF and an appendage thrombus
steps.lead: A 32-year-old woman from western Kenya, NYHA III, on monthly benzathine penicillin since a teenage episode of rheumatic fever. Atrial fibrillation, rate controlled. Echo: MVA 0.9 cm² (planimetry), mean gradient 14 mmHg at 90/min, Wilkins score 11 (thick, calcified commissures, fused chordae), mild MR; PA systolic pressure 60 mmHg; aortic and tricuspid valves normal. TOE: a thrombus in the left atrial appendage. She has two children and does not plan more; the INR clinic is at the county hospital.
steps.body:
Why not a balloon? Percutaneous mitral commissurotomy (PMC) is the first choice for symptomatic MS with favourable anatomy. Here there are three reasons against it: an LA thrombus (a contraindication: the catheter crosses the LA), unfavourable morphology (Wilkins over 8, commissural calcium) and a poor predicted result. So: surgery.

Which operation? Heavily calcified, fused rheumatic valves rarely repair durably: replacement, with removal of the thrombus, closure of the appendage and, where available, surgical ablation of the AF.

Which valve? At 32 with reliable INR access: a mechanical valve (mitral INR target about 3.0, range 2.5–3.5). She needs warfarin for rheumatic AF anyway, so a tissue valve would not spare her anticoagulation, and it would degenerate early (sooner after rheumatic disease) and need a redo.

Access: median sternotomy and a left atriotomy (the default; any concomitant surgery). Transseptal for a small LA, tricuspid surgery or a redo; a right mini-thoracotomy for isolated mitral surgery in selected patients.

Evidence: Wilkins score (Br Heart J 1988): leaflet mobility, thickening, calcification and subvalvular disease, each 1–4; 8 or less favours PMC; commissural calcium is the strongest single predictor of a poor result (Nunes et al., Circulation 2014). ESC/EACTS 2025 list LA thrombus, more than mild MR, severe or bicommissural calcification and severe concomitant aortic or tricuspid disease as contraindications to PMC.

ask.question: What makes surgery, not a balloon, the right choice here?

choices.text: The left atrial appendage thrombus together with a calcified, unfavourable valve (Wilkins 11)
choices.why: An LA thrombus contraindicates PMC, and the morphology predicts a poor balloon result. A tissue valve would not spare her warfarin, as rheumatic AF needs it anyway.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding and return to theatre
  • AF
  • Chest and wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Deep sternal wound infection
  • Heart block needing a pacemaker

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical: lifelong warfarin, INR checks, bleeding, valve thrombosis if INR lapses
  • Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy and valve thrombosis; plan before conception
  • Tissue: degenerates faster in the young; reoperation likely
  • Repair where possible

5. Alternatives

  • Balloon mitral valvotomy for pliable MS without LA thrombus or significant MR
  • Medical therapy
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR testing near home
  • Continue benzathine penicillin prophylaxis
  • Blood availability
  • Cost of follow-up

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: A 24-year-old woman planning children needs MVR. Which topic must her consent cover that a 65-year-old's would not?

choices.text: Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy, valve thrombosis, and a plan before conception
choices.why: Valve choice in young women is decided with pregnancy in mind (ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline).

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin (about 300–400 U/kg; ACT above 480 s). Two purse-strings on the distal ascending aorta for the arterial cannula. Bicaval venous drainage: two separate cannulas: an angled SVC cannula directly into the SVC (or through the appendage), and an IVC cannula through a purse-string low on the right atrium, its tip passed into the IVC; snares are needed if the right atrium is to be opened.

An antegrade cardioplegia and root vent line in the ascending aorta; a retrograde cannula into the coronary sinus if wanted; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body: On full bypass, cool as planned. Cross-clamp the ascending aorta between the arterial cannula and the cardioplegia line; arrest with cold blood cardioplegia antegrade, then retrograde through the coronary sinus, repeated every 15–20 minutes.

steps.title: Sondergaard's groove and the left atriotomy
steps.body: Develop Sondergaard's plane: the fat between the right atrium and the right pulmonary veins, back toward the septum, for 1–2 cm. Open the left atrium there, in front of the right pulmonary veins, extending up behind the SVC and down behind the IVC as needed. A self-retaining atrial retractor lifts the septum toward you.

steps.title: Remove the thrombus; close the appendage
steps.body:
Before touching the valve, look into the appendage. Lift the thrombus out whole with a spoon or forceps, without fragmenting it; wash and suck out the appendage and the LA. Keep the aortic cross-clamp on until the atrium is cleared.

Close the appendage from inside: a double layer of running 4-0 or 5-0 polypropylene across its orifice (or excise it and close, or an external clip). Check for a residual stump: a leak into an incompletely closed appendage is itself a source of emboli.

With AF, add a surgical ablation (a left atrial lesion set or a full Cox-Maze) where the equipment and experience exist; in a very large rheumatic LA sinus rhythm is less often restored.

Evidence: LAAOS III (NEJM 2021; 4,770 patients with AF having cardiac surgery): closing the appendage reduced ischaemic stroke or systemic embolism (4.8% vs 7.0% over 3.8 years), on top of continued anticoagulation. The 2024 ESC AF guideline recommends appendage closure at cardiac surgery in AF (class I) and concomitant surgical ablation at mitral surgery (class I). Warfarin continues after surgery.

ask.question: Why is the appendage closed even though the patient will stay on warfarin?

choices.text: Closure adds protection against stroke on top of anticoagulation
choices.why: In LAAOS III most patients stayed on anticoagulation, and closure still cut stroke and systemic embolism by about a third.

choices.text: It is not: warfarin makes closure unnecessary

steps.title: Excise the anterior leaflet; keep the posterior chordae
steps.body:
Inspect the valve. For replacement, excise the anterior leaflet (detach it 2–3 mm from the annulus, divide its chordae; some reattach anterior chordae to the annulus), preserve the posterior leaflet and its chordae: chordal sparing keeps left ventricular function and guards against rupture of the ventricle.

Debride calcium off the annulus carefully: deep debridement posteriorly risks AV groove disruption. Size the annulus with the valve sizers.

In this rheumatic valve the leaflets are fused into a thick funnel. Split the fused commissures to see the subvalvular apparatus; keep the posterior leaflet and its chordae only if they are pliable (a thick, fused posterior apparatus can obstruct the prosthesis or trap a disc: excise it and, if you wish, resuspend a few chordae). Remove calcium from the annulus piece by piece, catching every fragment.

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
2-0 braided polyester horizontal mattress sutures, 12–16 of them. Where the pledgets sit decides where the valve sits, and the choice follows the quality of the annulus.

Ventricular pledgets (non-everting: needle from the LV side up through the annulus; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the strongest hold in friable, calcified, rheumatic or infected tissue, so fewer paravalvular leaks and dehiscences; the pledget spreads the load; supra-annular seating often takes one size larger.
Against: deeper, blinder bites (circumflex and AV groove posteriorly, AV node at the posteromedial commissure, aortic cusps anteriorly); pledgets and preserved chordae under the ring can trap a leaflet or seed pannus and thrombus; anterior pledgets can narrow the LVOT; awkward through a small LA or a MICS port.

Annulus-only (everting, with atrial pledgets, or unpledgeted; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: shallow bites you can see; nothing below the ring to catch a leaflet; LVOT clear; quicker; suits a healthy annulus and MICS.
Against: sutures can cut through poor tissue; the prosthesis is often a size smaller; unpledgeted sutures are the weakest.

A common compromise: ventricular pledgets posteriorly and at the commissures (where the tissue is worst and leaks happen), atrial pledgets anteriorly (to protect the aortic valve and LVOT).

Whatever the technique, bite in the annulus, not beyond it.

Evidence: no randomised trial compares everting and non-everting sutures in MVR. In the AVERT trial cohort, pledgeted sutures were associated with fewer major paravalvular leaks than unpledgeted ones (Englberger et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2005). The ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guidelines make no recommendation on suture technique, but support preserving the subvalvular apparatus in MVR (for LV function), and that is one more reason to keep pledgets clear of preserved chordae.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a heavily calcified, small posterior annulus. Which suture technique gives the most secure seat and the largest valve?

choices.text: Pledgeted mattress sutures with ventricular pledgets (non-everting, supra-annular), at least posteriorly
choices.why: Ventricular pledgets hold best in poor tissue and seat the ring above the annulus, which usually allows a larger size. Keep bites in the annulus to spare the circumflex and AV groove, and check that no pledget traps a leaflet.

choices.text: Everting sutures with atrial pledgets all round, one size smaller

steps.title: Size the mitral prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
The sizer tells you what the annulus takes; the patient's body size tells you what orifice they need. Too small a valve for the body is prosthesis–patient mismatch (PPM): persistent gradients, pulmonary hypertension and worse survival.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 2.3 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 1.2 cm²/m² to avoid PPM (severe if the indexed EOA is ≤0.9)
  3. Choose the smallest size whose reference EOA on the manufacturer's chart reaches it
ProblemOptions
Small annulus, small rheumatic womanA valve with a larger EOA for its size; preserve the posterior chordae and seat it well; avoid forcing an oversized valve
ChildCheck size / weight: a high ratio predicts early death (LVOT obstruction, circumflex and conduction injury). Supra-annular placement of a too-large valve worsens survival. Small 15–17 mm valves will need replacing as the child grows

Evidence: Magne et al., Circulation 2007: mitral PPM (indexed EOA ≤1.2 cm²/m²; severe ≤0.9) reduced survival after MVR. ICVTS 2024 (children): median prosthesis size/weight about 1.7 mm/kg; oversizing and supra-annular placement linked to death; 44–65% of 15–17 mm mechanical valves replaced within years.

ask.question: A 1.40 m² rheumatic patient: what reference EOA must a mitral prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the prosthesis and tie
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring in order, lower the valve down the sutures onto the annulus and tie. For a bileaflet mechanical valve, the usual orientation is anti-anatomical (hinges perpendicular to the natural commissures).

Check that both leaflets open and close fully: nothing trapped (preserved chordae, a long suture tail, pledget).

ask.question: After seating a mechanical mitral valve, the most important check before closing the atrium is…

choices.why: Preserved chordae, suture tails or pledgets can trap a leaflet; fix it now, not after the clamp is off.

choices.text: That the LA appendage is closed
That the sutures are cut short

steps.title: Close the atrium, de-air, clamp off
steps.body:
Close the left atriotomy with 3-0/4-0 polypropylene, leaving the LV vent across until the last suture.

De-air: CO₂ in the field, head down, fill the heart as the last sutures go in, ventilate the lungs to push air out of the pulmonary veins, aortic root vent on suction; release the clamp; rewarm. Consider closing the left atrial appendage if the patient is in AF.

De-air early and come off (most de-airing done in the arrested heart before the clamp is released; vent out and wean soon after)
For: the flaccid, arrested heart can be balloted and needle-vented; a shorter bypass and clamp time.
Against: air stays trapped in the pulmonary veins, LA appendage and LV trabeculae until the heart beats and the lungs are ventilated. It then comes out when the root vent is already out: into the RCA (the most anterior ostium, uppermost with the patient supine), giving inferior ST elevation, RV failure and VF, or into the brain. Mitral surgery opens the left heart widely, so it carries more air than CABG.

Keep de-airing during reperfusion (the beating, ejecting heart on partial bypass, root vent still on, until TOE is clear)
For: contraction and ventilation release the trapped air while the vent can still catch it; if air does reach the RCA, the heart is still supported, so raise the perfusion pressure and let it pass. It overlaps with the rest the heart needs anyway.
Against: longer bypass; strong root-vent suction with a low root pressure can draw air in through the purse-string; handling the beating heart can cause arrhythmia.

The end-point is TOE, not the clock: no bubbles in the LA, LV or pulmonary veins at near-normal filling, then vent out.

Evidence: no trial compares early with late de-airing; practice rests on physiology and TOE studies. CO₂ field flooding cut microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004) and reduced neurocognitive impairment in another (Martens et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2008); a benefit for stroke has not been shown. Intraoperative TOE in valve surgery, including to guide de-airing, is standard practice (ASE/SCA guidelines, Hahn et al., J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013).

TOE before leaving theatre: no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving, no LVOT obstruction. Pacing wires, drains.

Serious complications: AV groove disruption (catastrophic), circumflex injury, heart block, paravalvular leak, stroke.

ask.question: Ten minutes after the clamp is released and the root vent is removed, the inferior leads show ST elevation and the RV dilates. The likely cause and the move?

choices.text: Air in the right coronary: stay on (or go back on) bypass, raise the perfusion pressure, and let the heart beat unloaded until it clears
choices.why: The RCA ostium is uppermost with the patient supine and catches retained left-heart air. Supported, higher-pressure perfusion usually clears it in minutes; weaning onto a failing RV does not. Keeping the root vent on until TOE is clear prevents it.

choices.text: Circumflex injury from an annular suture: re-arrest and inspect
Prosthetic leaflet stuck: re-open the atrium

steps.title: Reperfuse on bypass, or separate early?
steps.body:
With the clamp off the heart is reperfused while bypass still carries the circulation. How long to rest it before weaning is a judgement, not a fixed rule. A common rule of thumb is about a third of the cross-clamp time (roughly 10 minutes for each 30 of ischaemia).

Waiting for myocardial recovery (a longer supported reperfusion): it washes out cardioplegia and potassium, restores energy stores, lets the rhythm settle and rewarming finish, and needs fewer inotropes. Worth it after a long clamp, with a poor LV or RV, a hypertrophied ventricle, doubtful protection, or pulmonary hypertension (common in rheumatic mitral stenosis: the RV fails first).

Separating early: every extra minute of bypass adds haemodilution, platelet damage, inflammation and bleeding. After a short clamp, a good ventricle, sound protection and a stable rhythm, wean as soon as the conditions are met.

Before either: temperature 36–37 °C, sinus rhythm or pacing, potassium and haemoglobin corrected, lungs ventilated, de-airing confirmed on TOE, and the valve checked (no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving). The cost of weaning too early is a low-output state and a return to bypass; that is still easy while the cannulas are in and protamine has not been given.

ask.question: After MVR for rheumatic stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension (clamp time 95 min), the heart is sluggish on first weaning attempt. Best move?

choices.text: Go back to full bypass, rest the heart longer, start RV support (inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator), then wean again
choices.why: The RV is failing against a high pulmonary pressure; more supported reperfusion and RV-directed support usually rescue it. Pushing on off bypass drives the RV into failure.

choices.text: Give protamine and push inotropes off bypass
Decannulate and accept the low output

steps.title: Separate, then decannulate in order
steps.body:
Wean slowly, watching the pressures and the TOE. Then the order that keeps a way back:

  1. Venous cannula(s) out first (IVC, then SVC); tie the purse-strings.
  2. Protamine started slowly (watch for pulmonary hypertension and hypotension); stop the pump suckers once it runs.
  3. Arterial cannula out last, after part of the protamine and a stable pressure: while it is in, blood can be given from the pump and bypass restarted quickly.

A fast decannulation saves pump time only if the heart is ready; a return to bypass after full protamine means re-heparinising and re-cannulating a heart that is already struggling.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure: avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inodilator if the RV fails
  • AF: rate or rhythm control
  • Anticoagulation: enoxaparin day 1, bridge to warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guideline; ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline; INVICTUS (NEJM 2022).

ask.question: Day 1 after mechanical MVR, drains dry. When is the first INR checked?

choices.text: 72 h after the first warfarin dose, while enoxaparin continues
choices.why: Warfarin takes 2–3 days to move the INR; enoxaparin bridges until the INR is in range.

choices.text: Two hours after the first dose
