steps.title: Pathophysiology: rheumatic mitral stenosis and functional TR
steps.body:
In Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa most mitral stenosis, and most aortic regurgitation in the young, is rheumatic. Patients present in their 20s and 30s, often late, with atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension or in pregnancy. In the REMEDY registry (14 low- and middle-income countries, median age 28 years) about 17% had died within two years.

From sore throat to scarred valve.

  1. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (skin infection may also contribute) in a susceptible child.
  2. Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein and its carbohydrate (GlcNAc) cross-react with cardiac myosin and with laminin on the valve shown in human rheumatic tissue.
  3. The valve endothelium is activated (VCAM-1), T cells home into the valve along the closure line and drive a valvulitis (Th1/Th17) shown in human rheumatic tissue. This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis.
  4. Each recurrence re-injures the valve. Over years, valve interstitial cells lay down scar (TGF-β-driven fibrosis) and calcium: the commissures fuse, the leaflets thicken, the chordae shorten and fuse inferred (much of this signalling is from calcific aortic valve disease).
Acute carditisChronic rheumatic heart disease
LesionMitral regurgitation: annular dilatation, elongated chordae, anterior leaflet prolapse (Carpentier I, II)Mitral stenosis (often with regurgitation): commissural fusion, thick leaflets, fused short chordae (Carpentier IIIa)
The valve…cannot closecannot open
Reversible?partly, if carditis settles and recurrences are preventedno: scar and calcium, treated mechanically (balloon or surgery)

The haemodynamics. A normal mitral orifice is 4–6 cm²; stenosis becomes clinically significant at 1.5 cm² or less. The LV is protected (it is under-filled); the load falls on everything behind the valve:

Small orifice→LA→LV gradient→LA pressure ↑, LA dilates→Atrial fibrillation→LA appendage thrombus → stroke
LA pressure ↑→Pulmonary venous pressure ↑ (breathless, oedema)→Pulmonary hypertension→RV pressure overload→RV dilates → TR → right heart failure

Why a fast heart rate decompensates MS. The gradient depends on flow and on the time available for the LA to empty: diastole. Tachycardia (AF with a fast ventricular rate, exercise, fever, anaemia, pregnancy) shortens diastole, so the gradient and LA pressure climb and pulmonary oedema follows. Hence rate control (a β-blocker) and why MS often declares itself in pregnancy. AF also removes the atrial kick and adds stasis: rheumatic AF carries a high embolic risk, and it is treated with warfarin, not a direct oral anticoagulant.

Functional tricuspid regurgitation. Pulmonary hypertension dilates the RV; the tricuspid annulus stretches along its anterior and posterior segments (the septal segment is fixed), the leaflets are pulled apart, and TR appears on an anatomically normal valve. It may persist or progress after the mitral valve is fixed. Rheumatic (organic) tricuspid disease also occurs, in perhaps 10–15% of advanced cases.

Evidence: the immunology (mimicry, valvular endothelial activation, T-cell infiltration) rests on studies of human rheumatic valves and valve-derived T-cell clones (Guilherme et al., Circulation 1995; Cunningham, Clin Microbiol Rev 2000); the later fibrocalcific steps are largely extrapolated from calcific aortic valve disease. Clinical picture: Carapetis et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016; Chandrashekhar, Westaby and Narula, Lancet 2009. Prevention works: in GOAL (NEJM 2022; 818 Ugandan children with latent RHD) monthly benzathine penicillin cut progression over 2 years from 8.3% to 0.8%. INVICTUS (NEJM 2022; 4,531 patients with rheumatic AF) found more vascular deaths and ischaemic strokes with rivaroxaban than with a vitamin K antagonist; ESC/EACTS 2025 advise against DOACs in AF with rheumatic MS and a valve area of 2.0 cm² or less.

ask.question: A 26-year-old woman with moderate rheumatic MS, comfortable at rest, goes into AF at 150 beats per minute and within hours is in pulmonary oedema. Why?

choices.text: The short diastole leaves too little time to empty the LA through the narrow valve, so the gradient and LA pressure rise
choices.why: In MS the transmitral gradient rises steeply with heart rate. Slowing the rate (and cardioversion, with anticoagulation) often relieves the oedema before anything is done to the valve.

choices.text: The valve has suddenly narrowed further
AF has caused acute mitral regurgitation

steps.title: The mitral valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
The mitral annulus is D-shaped and saddle-shaped. The anterior leaflet hangs from the fibrous aortomitral curtain, in continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; the posterior leaflet takes the rest of the circumference. Chordae run from both leaflets to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles.

Round the posterior annulus, in the AV groove: the circumflex artery (close near the anterolateral commissure, closer in left dominance) and the coronary sinus. At the posteromedial commissure, next to the right trigone: the AV node and His bundle. These are what deep annular sutures injure.

ask.question: A deep suture at the posterior annulus near the anterolateral commissure is most likely to injure…

choices.why: It runs in the AV groove close to the annulus there, especially in a left-dominant circulation.

steps.title: Case: mitral stenosis with pulmonary hypertension and severe TR
steps.lead: A 38-year-old man with rheumatic MS: MVA 1.0 cm², Wilkins 10, moderate MR. PA systolic pressure 75 mmHg, a dilated RV, severe functional TR with a tricuspid annulus of 44 mm; ankle oedema and a large liver. Sinus rhythm; LA 52 mm; no thrombus.
steps.body:
Mitral: unfavourable for PMC (calcium, more than mild MR): replace. Tricuspid: severe TR at left-sided surgery is repaired at the same operation. Pulmonary pressure usually falls after the mitral valve is fixed, but the dilated annulus does not shrink back, and untreated TR often progresses.

Access: the transseptal route suits two-valve surgery from the right side: bicaval cannulation with snares, one right atriotomy, the mitral through the septum and the tricuspid in the same field.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020: tricuspid repair for severe TR at left-sided valve surgery (class I); for less than severe TR with annular dilatation it should be considered. The rheumatic tricuspid valve can be organic (thickened, fused) too: look at it, not only the echo.

ask.question: Why repair the tricuspid now, when pulmonary pressure may fall after MVR?

choices.text: The dilated annulus does not recover, and TR left at left-sided surgery often progresses; a redo for TR carries high risk
choices.why: Functional TR is an annular problem; lowering the afterload helps but does not reverse annular dilatation. Isolated tricuspid reoperation later carries a high mortality.

choices.text: It is not needed: TR always resolves
Because the transseptal route requires it

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin (about 300–400 U/kg; ACT above 480 s). Two purse-strings on the distal ascending aorta for the arterial cannula. Bicaval venous drainage: two separate cannulas: an angled SVC cannula directly into the SVC (or through the appendage), and an IVC cannula through a purse-string low on the right atrium, its tip passed into the IVC, with snares round both cavae: the right atrium will be opened.

An antegrade cardioplegia and root vent line in the ascending aorta; a retrograde cannula into the coronary sinus if wanted; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body: On full bypass, cool as planned. Cross-clamp the ascending aorta between the arterial cannula and the cardioplegia line; arrest with cold blood cardioplegia antegrade, then retrograde through the coronary sinus, repeated every 15–20 minutes.

steps.title: Right atriotomy
steps.body: Snare both cavae. Open the right atrium obliquely, from the base of the appendage toward the IVC, parallel to the AV groove and away from the sinus node at the SVC junction.

steps.title: Through the fossa ovalis
steps.body:
Incise the fossa ovalis vertically and extend it up (toward the dome) or down as needed; the mitral valve lies straight behind. Stay off the coronary sinus orifice and Koch's triangle below and in front (AV node), and off the aortic root in front of the septum.

The superior septal (Guiraudon) extension carries the incision across the roof of the left atrium: widest view, but it divides the sinus node artery.

steps.title: Excise the anterior leaflet; keep the posterior chordae
steps.body:
Inspect the valve. For replacement, excise the anterior leaflet (detach it 2–3 mm from the annulus, divide its chordae; some reattach anterior chordae to the annulus), preserve the posterior leaflet and its chordae: chordal sparing keeps left ventricular function and guards against rupture of the ventricle.

Debride calcium off the annulus carefully: deep debridement posteriorly risks AV groove disruption. Size the annulus with the valve sizers.

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
2-0 braided polyester horizontal mattress sutures, 12–16 of them. Where the pledgets sit decides where the valve sits, and the choice follows the quality of the annulus.

Ventricular pledgets (non-everting: needle from the LV side up through the annulus; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the strongest hold in friable, calcified, rheumatic or infected tissue, so fewer paravalvular leaks and dehiscences; the pledget spreads the load; supra-annular seating often takes one size larger.
Against: deeper, blinder bites (circumflex and AV groove posteriorly, AV node at the posteromedial commissure, aortic cusps anteriorly); pledgets and preserved chordae under the ring can trap a leaflet or seed pannus and thrombus; anterior pledgets can narrow the LVOT; awkward through a small LA or a MICS port.

Annulus-only (everting, with atrial pledgets, or unpledgeted; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: shallow bites you can see; nothing below the ring to catch a leaflet; LVOT clear; quicker; suits a healthy annulus and MICS.
Against: sutures can cut through poor tissue; the prosthesis is often a size smaller; unpledgeted sutures are the weakest.

A common compromise: ventricular pledgets posteriorly and at the commissures (where the tissue is worst and leaks happen), atrial pledgets anteriorly (to protect the aortic valve and LVOT).

Whatever the technique, bite in the annulus, not beyond it.

Evidence: no randomised trial compares everting and non-everting sutures in MVR. In the AVERT trial cohort, pledgeted sutures were associated with fewer major paravalvular leaks than unpledgeted ones (Englberger et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2005). The ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guidelines make no recommendation on suture technique, but support preserving the subvalvular apparatus in MVR (for LV function), and that is one more reason to keep pledgets clear of preserved chordae.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a heavily calcified, small posterior annulus. Which suture technique gives the most secure seat and the largest valve?

choices.text: Pledgeted mattress sutures with ventricular pledgets (non-everting, supra-annular), at least posteriorly
choices.why: Ventricular pledgets hold best in poor tissue and seat the ring above the annulus, which usually allows a larger size. Keep bites in the annulus to spare the circumflex and AV groove, and check that no pledget traps a leaflet.

choices.text: Everting sutures with atrial pledgets all round, one size smaller

steps.title: Size the mitral prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
The sizer tells you what the annulus takes; the patient's body size tells you what orifice they need. Too small a valve for the body is prosthesis–patient mismatch (PPM): persistent gradients, pulmonary hypertension and worse survival.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 2.3 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 1.2 cm²/m² to avoid PPM (severe if the indexed EOA is ≤0.9)
  3. Choose the smallest size whose reference EOA on the manufacturer's chart reaches it
ProblemOptions
Small annulus, small rheumatic womanA valve with a larger EOA for its size; preserve the posterior chordae and seat it well; avoid forcing an oversized valve
ChildCheck size / weight: a high ratio predicts early death (LVOT obstruction, circumflex and conduction injury). Supra-annular placement of a too-large valve worsens survival. Small 15–17 mm valves will need replacing as the child grows

Evidence: Magne et al., Circulation 2007: mitral PPM (indexed EOA ≤1.2 cm²/m²; severe ≤0.9) reduced survival after MVR. ICVTS 2024 (children): median prosthesis size/weight about 1.7 mm/kg; oversizing and supra-annular placement linked to death; 44–65% of 15–17 mm mechanical valves replaced within years.

ask.question: A 1.40 m² rheumatic patient: what reference EOA must a mitral prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the prosthesis and tie
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring in order, lower the valve down the sutures onto the annulus and tie. For a bileaflet mechanical valve, the usual orientation is anti-anatomical (hinges perpendicular to the natural commissures).

Check that both leaflets open and close fully: nothing trapped (preserved chordae, a long suture tail, pledget).

ask.question: After seating a mechanical mitral valve, the most important check before closing the atrium is…

choices.why: Preserved chordae, suture tails or pledgets can trap a leaflet; fix it now, not after the clamp is off.

choices.text: That the LA appendage is closed
That the sutures are cut short

steps.title: Tricuspid annuloplasty (after the mitral)
steps.body:
With the mitral prosthesis in, close the septum. The tricuspid ring can then go in with the cross-clamp off and the heart beating (caval snares still tight), which shortens ischaemic time and shows at once if a suture has caught the conduction tissue.

An incomplete ring sized to the anterior leaflet, the sutures along the anterior and posterior annulus; leave the septal annulus near Koch's triangle (AV node) without sutures, or stay very shallow. A De Vega suture annuloplasty is the cheaper alternative. (The Tricuspid module covers this step by step.)

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020: repair severe TR at left-sided surgery (class I); consider it for milder TR with a dilated annulus (≥40 mm or 21 mm/m² on echo). Dreyfus et al. (Ann Thorac Surg 2005) showed that annuloplasty guided by annular dilatation rather than TR grade improved function over years.

steps.title: Close the atrium, de-air, clamp off
steps.body:
Close the septum and the right atrium (3-0/4-0 polypropylene); release the caval snares.

De-air: CO₂ in the field, head down, fill the heart as the last sutures go in, ventilate the lungs to push air out of the pulmonary veins, aortic root vent on suction; release the clamp; rewarm. Consider closing the left atrial appendage if the patient is in AF.

De-air early and come off (most de-airing done in the arrested heart before the clamp is released; vent out and wean soon after)
For: the flaccid, arrested heart can be balloted and needle-vented; a shorter bypass and clamp time.
Against: air stays trapped in the pulmonary veins, LA appendage and LV trabeculae until the heart beats and the lungs are ventilated. It then comes out when the root vent is already out: into the RCA (the most anterior ostium, uppermost with the patient supine), giving inferior ST elevation, RV failure and VF, or into the brain. Mitral surgery opens the left heart widely, so it carries more air than CABG.

Keep de-airing during reperfusion (the beating, ejecting heart on partial bypass, root vent still on, until TOE is clear)
For: contraction and ventilation release the trapped air while the vent can still catch it; if air does reach the RCA, the heart is still supported, so raise the perfusion pressure and let it pass. It overlaps with the rest the heart needs anyway.
Against: longer bypass; strong root-vent suction with a low root pressure can draw air in through the purse-string; handling the beating heart can cause arrhythmia.

The end-point is TOE, not the clock: no bubbles in the LA, LV or pulmonary veins at near-normal filling, then vent out.

Evidence: no trial compares early with late de-airing; practice rests on physiology and TOE studies. CO₂ field flooding cut microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004) and reduced neurocognitive impairment in another (Martens et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2008); a benefit for stroke has not been shown. Intraoperative TOE in valve surgery, including to guide de-airing, is standard practice (ASE/SCA guidelines, Hahn et al., J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013).

TOE before leaving theatre: no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving, no LVOT obstruction. Pacing wires, drains.

Serious complications: AV groove disruption (catastrophic), circumflex injury, heart block, paravalvular leak, stroke.

ask.question: Ten minutes after the clamp is released and the root vent is removed, the inferior leads show ST elevation and the RV dilates. The likely cause and the move?

choices.text: Air in the right coronary: stay on (or go back on) bypass, raise the perfusion pressure, and let the heart beat unloaded until it clears
choices.why: The RCA ostium is uppermost with the patient supine and catches retained left-heart air. Supported, higher-pressure perfusion usually clears it in minutes; weaning onto a failing RV does not. Keeping the root vent on until TOE is clear prevents it.

choices.text: Circumflex injury from an annular suture: re-arrest and inspect
Prosthetic leaflet stuck: re-open the atrium

steps.title: Reperfuse on bypass, or separate early?
steps.body:
With the clamp off the heart is reperfused while bypass still carries the circulation. How long to rest it before weaning is a judgement, not a fixed rule. A common rule of thumb is about a third of the cross-clamp time (roughly 10 minutes for each 30 of ischaemia).

Waiting for myocardial recovery (a longer supported reperfusion): it washes out cardioplegia and potassium, restores energy stores, lets the rhythm settle and rewarming finish, and needs fewer inotropes. Worth it after a long clamp, with a poor LV or RV, a hypertrophied ventricle, doubtful protection, or pulmonary hypertension (common in rheumatic mitral stenosis: the RV fails first).

Separating early: every extra minute of bypass adds haemodilution, platelet damage, inflammation and bleeding. After a short clamp, a good ventricle, sound protection and a stable rhythm, wean as soon as the conditions are met.

Before either: temperature 36–37 °C, sinus rhythm or pacing, potassium and haemoglobin corrected, lungs ventilated, de-airing confirmed on TOE, and the valve checked (no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving). The cost of weaning too early is a low-output state and a return to bypass; that is still easy while the cannulas are in and protamine has not been given.

ask.question: After MVR for rheumatic stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension (clamp time 95 min), the heart is sluggish on first weaning attempt. Best move?

choices.text: Go back to full bypass, rest the heart longer, start RV support (inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator), then wean again
choices.why: The RV is failing against a high pulmonary pressure; more supported reperfusion and RV-directed support usually rescue it. Pushing on off bypass drives the RV into failure.

choices.text: Give protamine and push inotropes off bypass
Decannulate and accept the low output

steps.title: Separate, then decannulate in order
steps.body:
Wean slowly, watching the pressures and the TOE. Then the order that keeps a way back:

  1. Venous cannula(s) out first (IVC, then SVC); tie the purse-strings.
  2. Protamine started slowly (watch for pulmonary hypertension and hypotension); stop the pump suckers once it runs.
  3. Arterial cannula out last, after part of the protamine and a stable pressure: while it is in, blood can be given from the pump and bypass restarted quickly.

A fast decannulation saves pump time only if the heart is ready; a return to bypass after full protamine means re-heparinising and re-cannulating a heart that is already struggling.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure: avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inodilator if the RV fails
  • AF: rate or rhythm control
  • Anticoagulation: enoxaparin day 1, bridge to warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guideline; ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline; INVICTUS (NEJM 2022).

ask.question: Day 1 after mechanical MVR, drains dry. When is the first INR checked?

choices.text: 72 h after the first warfarin dose, while enoxaparin continues
choices.why: Warfarin takes 2–3 days to move the INR; enoxaparin bridges until the INR is in range.

choices.text: Two hours after the first dose

mvr-repair.name: Mitral valve replacement
mvr-repair.approach: Teenager with rheumatic MR: repair or replace
mvr-repair.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the decision, then the operation (access, bypass, left atrium, excision, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: rheumatic mitral regurgitation
steps.body:
In Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa most mitral stenosis, and most aortic regurgitation in the young, is rheumatic. Patients present in their 20s and 30s, often late, with atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension or in pregnancy. In the REMEDY registry (14 low- and middle-income countries, median age 28 years) about 17% had died within two years.

From sore throat to scarred valve.

  1. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (skin infection may also contribute) in a susceptible child.
  2. Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein and its carbohydrate (GlcNAc) cross-react with cardiac myosin and with laminin on the valve shown in human rheumatic tissue.
  3. The valve endothelium is activated (VCAM-1), T cells home into the valve along the closure line and drive a valvulitis (Th1/Th17) shown in human rheumatic tissue. This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis.
  4. Each recurrence re-injures the valve. Over years, valve interstitial cells lay down scar (TGF-β-driven fibrosis) and calcium: the commissures fuse, the leaflets thicken, the chordae shorten and fuse inferred (much of this signalling is from calcific aortic valve disease).
Acute carditisChronic rheumatic heart disease
LesionMitral regurgitation: annular dilatation, elongated chordae, anterior leaflet prolapse (Carpentier I, II)Mitral stenosis (often with regurgitation): commissural fusion, thick leaflets, fused short chordae (Carpentier IIIa)
The valve…cannot closecannot open
Reversible?partly, if carditis settles and recurrences are preventedno: scar and calcium, treated mechanically (balloon or surgery)

How carditis makes the valve leak. Rheumatic carditis is a pancarditis: the leaflets are oedematous and friable, the chordae elongate so the anterior leaflet prolapses (Carpentier II), the inflamed ventricle and atrium dilate and stretch the annulus (Carpentier I), and displaced papillary muscles tether the leaflets. The jet points away from the prolapsing leaflet: posteriorly. With time, fibrosis retracts the posterior leaflet and the lesion becomes restrictive (IIIa), often with some stenosis.

Regurgitant volume into the LA→LA and LV volume overload→LV dilates (eccentric hypertrophy)→Contractility falls while the EF still looks normal→Irreversible LV dysfunction
LA pressure ↑→Pulmonary congestion→Pulmonary hypertension→AF

Why the EF misleads. In MR the LV empties partly into the low-pressure LA, so the ejection fraction overstates how well the muscle works. Guidelines therefore operate in symptomatic severe MR, and in asymptomatic patients once the EF falls to 60% or less or the LV end-systolic diameter reaches 40 mm, before damage is permanent.

Repair or replace? Repair keeps the native valve and avoids warfarin, which matters for young women and where INR monitoring is hard, but rheumatic repair is less durable than repair of degenerative valves: the fibrotic process goes on, and recurrences re-injure the valve, so penicillin prophylaxis continues after surgery.

Evidence: mechanisms from human pathology and the Carpentier functional classification; see Carapetis et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016. Intervention thresholds from the ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021/2025 guidelines. A meta-analysis of 16 retrospective studies (Jiang et al., Ann Transl Med 2021; 8,659 patients) found lower early mortality (OR 0.58) and better long-term survival with repair than replacement for rheumatic mitral disease, but about twice the risk of reoperation (HR 1.96); the studies are observational and repaired valves were selected. The AHA 2020 statement notes repair is feasible in most patients in expert hands, while many endemic-region centres favour replacement to avoid redo surgery.

ask.question: A 16-year-old has severe rheumatic MR, mild breathlessness, EF 62% and LV end-systolic diameter 43 mm. Why not wait until the EF falls?

choices.text: In MR the EF overstates LV function; an end-systolic diameter of 40 mm or more already signals damage, and waiting risks permanent dysfunction
choices.why: Because the LV unloads into the low-pressure LA, a "normal" EF can hide falling contractility. Guidelines use EF ≤60% or LVESD ≥40 mm as triggers for surgery.

choices.text: The EF is normal, so surgery can safely wait
Surgery is only for mitral stenosis
Medical therapy reverses chronic rheumatic MR

steps.title: The mitral valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
The mitral annulus is D-shaped and saddle-shaped. The anterior leaflet hangs from the fibrous aortomitral curtain, in continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; the posterior leaflet takes the rest of the circumference. Chordae run from both leaflets to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles.

Round the posterior annulus, in the AV groove: the circumflex artery (close near the anterolateral commissure, closer in left dominance) and the coronary sinus. At the posteromedial commissure, next to the right trigone: the AV node and His bundle. These are what deep annular sutures injure.

ask.question: A deep suture at the posterior annulus near the anterolateral commissure is most likely to injure…

choices.why: It runs in the AV groove close to the annulus there, especially in a left-dominant circulation.

steps.title: Case: a teenager with severe rheumatic mitral regurgitation
steps.lead: A 17-year-old girl, two admissions with acute rheumatic fever, now NYHA II–III. Echo: severe MR with a posteriorly directed jet from anterior leaflet prolapse; the posterior leaflet is thick and restricted; LV end-diastolic diameter 64 mm, end-systolic 43 mm, EF 60%. Mitral valve area normal. No active carditis (ESR, CRP normal). She lives 80 km from the nearest INR clinic and hopes to have children.
steps.body:
Operate now: symptoms, and an LV end-systolic diameter over 40 mm.

Repair first, if the valve allows: in a young woman, repair avoids warfarin (teratogenic, and hard to monitor far from a clinic) and keeps the native valve for pregnancy. Its weakness in rheumatic disease is durability.

If it must be replaced, the choice is hard. A mechanical valve lasts but needs warfarin: a high-risk pregnancy (valve thrombosis, embryopathy, bleeding). A tissue valve avoids warfarin and is favoured for women planning pregnancy, but in a 17-year-old it may fail within about 10 years and needs a redo (mitral valve-in-valve is possible later). Decide with her and her family, before theatre.

Access: median sternotomy and a left atriotomy (the default; any concomitant surgery). Transseptal for a small LA, tricuspid surgery or a redo; a right mini-thoracotomy for isolated mitral surgery in selected patients.

Evidence: ESC 2025 pregnancy guideline: when valve replacement is needed in a woman contemplating pregnancy, a bioprosthesis is recommended (class I, upgraded from IIa). Pregnancy with a mechanical valve is high risk (modified WHO class III); in the ESC ROPAC registry only about 58% of such pregnancies were free of serious adverse events (van Hagen et al., Circulation 2015). Continue secondary prophylaxis after surgery (AHA 2020 statement).

ask.question: The valve is unrepairable. For this 17-year-old who wants children and lives far from an INR clinic, which valve do current guidelines favour?

choices.text: A bioprosthesis, accepting a likely reoperation, after a shared decision
choices.why: The ESC 2025 pregnancy guideline recommends a bioprosthesis in women contemplating pregnancy; poor access to INR monitoring adds to the case. The cost is early degeneration and a redo, which she must understand.

choices.text: A mechanical valve: durability matters most
No valve: continue medical therapy until after pregnancy
A Ross-type pulmonary autograft in the mitral position

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding and return to theatre
  • AF
  • Chest and wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Deep sternal wound infection
  • Heart block needing a pacemaker

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical: lifelong warfarin, INR checks, bleeding, valve thrombosis if INR lapses
  • Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy and valve thrombosis; plan before conception
  • Tissue: degenerates faster in the young; reoperation likely
  • Repair where possible

5. Alternatives

  • Balloon mitral valvotomy for pliable MS without LA thrombus or significant MR
  • Medical therapy
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR testing near home
  • Continue benzathine penicillin prophylaxis
  • Blood availability
  • Cost of follow-up

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: A 24-year-old woman planning children needs MVR. Which topic must her consent cover that a 65-year-old's would not?

choices.text: Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy, valve thrombosis, and a plan before conception
choices.why: Valve choice in young women is decided with pregnancy in mind (ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline).

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin (about 300–400 U/kg; ACT above 480 s). Two purse-strings on the distal ascending aorta for the arterial cannula. Bicaval venous drainage: two separate cannulas: an angled SVC cannula directly into the SVC (or through the appendage), and an IVC cannula through a purse-string low on the right atrium, its tip passed into the IVC; snares are needed if the right atrium is to be opened.

An antegrade cardioplegia and root vent line in the ascending aorta; a retrograde cannula into the coronary sinus if wanted; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body: On full bypass, cool as planned. Cross-clamp the ascending aorta between the arterial cannula and the cardioplegia line; arrest with cold blood cardioplegia antegrade, then retrograde through the coronary sinus, repeated every 15–20 minutes.

steps.title: Sondergaard's groove and the left atriotomy
steps.body: Develop Sondergaard's plane: the fat between the right atrium and the right pulmonary veins, back toward the septum, for 1–2 cm. Open the left atrium there, in front of the right pulmonary veins, extending up behind the SVC and down behind the IVC as needed. A self-retaining atrial retractor lifts the septum toward you.

steps.title: Valve analysis: repair or replace?
steps.body:
Analyse the valve systematically before deciding (Carpentier): the annulus (dilated?), each leaflet segment (pliable, thickened, retracted, calcified?), the commissures (fused?), the chordae (elongated, ruptured, fused?) and the papillary muscles. Test with saline under pressure.

Rheumatic repair, when the tissue allows: commissurotomy, thinning (peeling) of thickened leaflets, fenestration of fused chordae, augmenting a retracted leaflet with a pericardial patch, chordal shortening, transfer or artificial chordae for prolapse, and a complete ring annuloplasty. Replace when the leaflets are thick, retracted and calcified, the subvalvular apparatus is fused, or a durable repair is unlikely: a failed repair in a young patient means another sternotomy.

Evidence: repair versus replacement in rheumatic disease has no randomised trial; observational data and meta-analysis favour repair for survival with more reoperations (Jiang et al., 2021). Intraoperative TOE after repair (residual MR, gradient, systolic anterior motion) is standard.

ask.question: The anterior leaflet prolapses on long chordae, but the posterior leaflet is thick, retracted and calcified with fused chordae. The most likely durable option in this 17-year-old?

choices.text: Replacement: a retracted, calcified posterior leaflet leaves no coaptation surface a repair can rely on
choices.why: Prolapse alone can be repaired, but repair needs a pliable posterior leaflet to coapt against. Patch augmentation is possible in selected cases; in a heavily diseased valve, replacement is more durable.

choices.text: Close the chest and treat medically

steps.title: Excise the anterior leaflet; keep the posterior chordae
steps.body:
Inspect the valve. For replacement, excise the anterior leaflet (detach it 2–3 mm from the annulus, divide its chordae; some reattach anterior chordae to the annulus), preserve the posterior leaflet and its chordae: chordal sparing keeps left ventricular function and guards against rupture of the ventricle.

Debride calcium off the annulus carefully: deep debridement posteriorly risks AV groove disruption. Size the annulus with the valve sizers.

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
2-0 braided polyester horizontal mattress sutures, 12–16 of them. Where the pledgets sit decides where the valve sits, and the choice follows the quality of the annulus.

Ventricular pledgets (non-everting: needle from the LV side up through the annulus; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the strongest hold in friable, calcified, rheumatic or infected tissue, so fewer paravalvular leaks and dehiscences; the pledget spreads the load; supra-annular seating often takes one size larger.
Against: deeper, blinder bites (circumflex and AV groove posteriorly, AV node at the posteromedial commissure, aortic cusps anteriorly); pledgets and preserved chordae under the ring can trap a leaflet or seed pannus and thrombus; anterior pledgets can narrow the LVOT; awkward through a small LA or a MICS port.

Annulus-only (everting, with atrial pledgets, or unpledgeted; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: shallow bites you can see; nothing below the ring to catch a leaflet; LVOT clear; quicker; suits a healthy annulus and MICS.
Against: sutures can cut through poor tissue; the prosthesis is often a size smaller; unpledgeted sutures are the weakest.

A common compromise: ventricular pledgets posteriorly and at the commissures (where the tissue is worst and leaks happen), atrial pledgets anteriorly (to protect the aortic valve and LVOT).

Whatever the technique, bite in the annulus, not beyond it.

Evidence: no randomised trial compares everting and non-everting sutures in MVR. In the AVERT trial cohort, pledgeted sutures were associated with fewer major paravalvular leaks than unpledgeted ones (Englberger et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2005). The ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guidelines make no recommendation on suture technique, but support preserving the subvalvular apparatus in MVR (for LV function), and that is one more reason to keep pledgets clear of preserved chordae.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a heavily calcified, small posterior annulus. Which suture technique gives the most secure seat and the largest valve?

choices.text: Pledgeted mattress sutures with ventricular pledgets (non-everting, supra-annular), at least posteriorly
choices.why: Ventricular pledgets hold best in poor tissue and seat the ring above the annulus, which usually allows a larger size. Keep bites in the annulus to spare the circumflex and AV groove, and check that no pledget traps a leaflet.

choices.text: Everting sutures with atrial pledgets all round, one size smaller

steps.title: Size the mitral prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
The sizer tells you what the annulus takes; the patient's body size tells you what orifice they need. Too small a valve for the body is prosthesis–patient mismatch (PPM): persistent gradients, pulmonary hypertension and worse survival.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 2.3 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 1.2 cm²/m² to avoid PPM (severe if the indexed EOA is ≤0.9)
  3. Choose the smallest size whose reference EOA on the manufacturer's chart reaches it
ProblemOptions
Small annulus, small rheumatic womanA valve with a larger EOA for its size; preserve the posterior chordae and seat it well; avoid forcing an oversized valve
ChildCheck size / weight: a high ratio predicts early death (LVOT obstruction, circumflex and conduction injury). Supra-annular placement of a too-large valve worsens survival. Small 15–17 mm valves will need replacing as the child grows

Evidence: Magne et al., Circulation 2007: mitral PPM (indexed EOA ≤1.2 cm²/m²; severe ≤0.9) reduced survival after MVR. ICVTS 2024 (children): median prosthesis size/weight about 1.7 mm/kg; oversizing and supra-annular placement linked to death; 44–65% of 15–17 mm mechanical valves replaced within years.

ask.question: A 1.40 m² rheumatic patient: what reference EOA must a mitral prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the prosthesis and tie
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring in order, lower the valve down the sutures onto the annulus and tie. For a bioprosthesis (this patient), orient the struts so that none sits in the LV outflow tract. For a bileaflet mechanical valve, the usual orientation is anti-anatomical.

Check that both leaflets open and close fully: nothing trapped (preserved chordae, a long suture tail, pledget).

ask.question: After seating a mechanical mitral valve, the most important check before closing the atrium is…

choices.why: Preserved chordae, suture tails or pledgets can trap a leaflet; fix it now, not after the clamp is off.

choices.text: That the LA appendage is closed
That the sutures are cut short

steps.title: Close the atrium, de-air, clamp off
steps.body:
Close the left atriotomy with 3-0/4-0 polypropylene, leaving the LV vent across until the last suture.

De-air: CO₂ in the field, head down, fill the heart as the last sutures go in, ventilate the lungs to push air out of the pulmonary veins, aortic root vent on suction; release the clamp; rewarm. Consider closing the left atrial appendage if the patient is in AF.

De-air early and come off (most de-airing done in the arrested heart before the clamp is released; vent out and wean soon after)
For: the flaccid, arrested heart can be balloted and needle-vented; a shorter bypass and clamp time.
Against: air stays trapped in the pulmonary veins, LA appendage and LV trabeculae until the heart beats and the lungs are ventilated. It then comes out when the root vent is already out: into the RCA (the most anterior ostium, uppermost with the patient supine), giving inferior ST elevation, RV failure and VF, or into the brain. Mitral surgery opens the left heart widely, so it carries more air than CABG.

Keep de-airing during reperfusion (the beating, ejecting heart on partial bypass, root vent still on, until TOE is clear)
For: contraction and ventilation release the trapped air while the vent can still catch it; if air does reach the RCA, the heart is still supported, so raise the perfusion pressure and let it pass. It overlaps with the rest the heart needs anyway.
Against: longer bypass; strong root-vent suction with a low root pressure can draw air in through the purse-string; handling the beating heart can cause arrhythmia.

The end-point is TOE, not the clock: no bubbles in the LA, LV or pulmonary veins at near-normal filling, then vent out.

Evidence: no trial compares early with late de-airing; practice rests on physiology and TOE studies. CO₂ field flooding cut microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004) and reduced neurocognitive impairment in another (Martens et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2008); a benefit for stroke has not been shown. Intraoperative TOE in valve surgery, including to guide de-airing, is standard practice (ASE/SCA guidelines, Hahn et al., J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013).

TOE before leaving theatre: no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving, no LVOT obstruction. Pacing wires, drains.

Serious complications: AV groove disruption (catastrophic), circumflex injury, heart block, paravalvular leak, stroke.

ask.question: Ten minutes after the clamp is released and the root vent is removed, the inferior leads show ST elevation and the RV dilates. The likely cause and the move?

choices.text: Air in the right coronary: stay on (or go back on) bypass, raise the perfusion pressure, and let the heart beat unloaded until it clears
choices.why: The RCA ostium is uppermost with the patient supine and catches retained left-heart air. Supported, higher-pressure perfusion usually clears it in minutes; weaning onto a failing RV does not. Keeping the root vent on until TOE is clear prevents it.

choices.text: Circumflex injury from an annular suture: re-arrest and inspect
Prosthetic leaflet stuck: re-open the atrium

steps.title: Reperfuse on bypass, or separate early?
steps.body:
With the clamp off the heart is reperfused while bypass still carries the circulation. How long to rest it before weaning is a judgement, not a fixed rule. A common rule of thumb is about a third of the cross-clamp time (roughly 10 minutes for each 30 of ischaemia).

Waiting for myocardial recovery (a longer supported reperfusion): it washes out cardioplegia and potassium, restores energy stores, lets the rhythm settle and rewarming finish, and needs fewer inotropes. Worth it after a long clamp, with a poor LV or RV, a hypertrophied ventricle, doubtful protection, or pulmonary hypertension (common in rheumatic mitral stenosis: the RV fails first).

Separating early: every extra minute of bypass adds haemodilution, platelet damage, inflammation and bleeding. After a short clamp, a good ventricle, sound protection and a stable rhythm, wean as soon as the conditions are met.

Before either: temperature 36–37 °C, sinus rhythm or pacing, potassium and haemoglobin corrected, lungs ventilated, de-airing confirmed on TOE, and the valve checked (no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving). The cost of weaning too early is a low-output state and a return to bypass; that is still easy while the cannulas are in and protamine has not been given.

ask.question: After MVR for rheumatic stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension (clamp time 95 min), the heart is sluggish on first weaning attempt. Best move?

choices.text: Go back to full bypass, rest the heart longer, start RV support (inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator), then wean again
choices.why: The RV is failing against a high pulmonary pressure; more supported reperfusion and RV-directed support usually rescue it. Pushing on off bypass drives the RV into failure.

choices.text: Give protamine and push inotropes off bypass
Decannulate and accept the low output

steps.title: Separate, then decannulate in order
steps.body:
Wean slowly, watching the pressures and the TOE. Then the order that keeps a way back:

  1. Venous cannula(s) out first (IVC, then SVC); tie the purse-strings.
  2. Protamine started slowly (watch for pulmonary hypertension and hypotension); stop the pump suckers once it runs.
  3. Arterial cannula out last, after part of the protamine and a stable pressure: while it is in, blood can be given from the pump and bypass restarted quickly.

A fast decannulation saves pump time only if the heart is ready; a return to bypass after full protamine means re-heparinising and re-cannulating a heart that is already struggling.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure: avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inodilator if the RV fails
  • AF: rate or rhythm control
  • Anticoagulation: enoxaparin day 1, bridge to warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guideline; ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline; INVICTUS (NEJM 2022).

ask.question: Day 1 after mechanical MVR, drains dry. When is the first INR checked?

choices.text: 72 h after the first warfarin dose, while enoxaparin continues
choices.why: Warfarin takes 2–3 days to move the INR; enoxaparin bridges until the INR is in range.

choices.text: Two hours after the first dose

mvr-ie.name: Mitral valve replacement
mvr-ie.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the decision, then the operation (access, bypass, left atrium, excision, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: endocarditis on a rheumatic valve
steps.body:
Why rheumatic valves get infected. Rheumatic heart disease is the commonest substrate for endocarditis in African adults. A regurgitant jet and a scarred valve damage the endothelium on the low-pressure side (the atrial face of the mitral leaflets); platelets and fibrin settle there (a sterile thrombus). A transient bacteraemia (dental sepsis, skin infection, an intravenous line, injecting) seeds it, and the organisms multiply inside the growing vegetation, shielded from white cells and antibiotics. This is why bactericidal antibiotics are given intravenously for weeks.

What the infection does:

Vegetation→Destruction: leaflet perforation, chordal rupture→Acute severe MR→Pulmonary oedema, shock
Vegetation→Embolism: brain, spleen, kidneys, limbs→Risk highest with mobile vegetations ≥10 mm on the anterior mitral leaflet
Vegetation→Local spread: annular abscess (commoner at the aortic valve)→Uncontrolled infection

An acute leak gives the LA no time to dilate: the pressure rises at once and the lungs flood, unlike the slow volume overload of chronic MR.

Evidence: in a meta-analysis of 42 African studies (Noubiap et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022), rheumatic heart disease was the underlying condition in 52% of adults; staphylococci (41%) and streptococci (34%) dominated; only about half of blood cultures were positive (often after antibiotics); in-hospital mortality was 23%. Surgical indications and timing: ESC 2023 endocarditis guidelines (Delgado et al.).

ask.question: Which vegetation carries the highest risk of embolism?

choices.text: A mobile vegetation of 10 mm or more on the anterior mitral leaflet
choices.why: Size (≥10 mm), mobility and the mitral (especially anterior leaflet) position predict embolism; the risk is highest in the first days to weeks of treatment, which is the case for early surgery.

choices.text: A small, sessile vegetation on the aortic valve
Any vegetation after two weeks of antibiotics
A vegetation on the tricuspid valve

steps.title: The mitral valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
The mitral annulus is D-shaped and saddle-shaped. The anterior leaflet hangs from the fibrous aortomitral curtain, in continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; the posterior leaflet takes the rest of the circumference. Chordae run from both leaflets to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles.

Round the posterior annulus, in the AV groove: the circumflex artery (close near the anterolateral commissure, closer in left dominance) and the coronary sinus. At the posteromedial commissure, next to the right trigone: the AV node and His bundle. These are what deep annular sutures injure.

ask.question: A deep suture at the posterior annulus near the anterolateral commissure is most likely to injure…

choices.why: It runs in the AV groove close to the annulus there, especially in a left-dominant circulation.

steps.title: Case: endocarditis on a rheumatic mitral valve
steps.lead: A 24-year-old man with known rheumatic MR, three weeks of fever after a dental abscess. Two blood cultures grow Streptococcus. Today: sudden left arm weakness; CT head: a small ischaemic infarct, no haemorrhage. TOE: a 14 mm mobile vegetation on the anterior leaflet, a leaflet perforation, severe MR; breathless on minimal exertion.
steps.body:
Indications (ESC 2023): severe MR with heart failure; a vegetation of 10 mm or more after an embolic event. Both point to urgent surgery, within days, on antibiotics.

The stroke: after a transient ischaemic attack or an ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage or coma, surgery should not be delayed when it is indicated for heart failure, uncontrolled infection or a high embolic risk. After an intracranial haemorrhage, surgery is generally deferred (often about 4 weeks) unless the patient is unstable.

Evidence: EASE (NEJM 2012; 76 patients with left-sided endocarditis, severe valve disease and vegetations over 10 mm): surgery within 48 hours reduced in-hospital death or embolism at 6 weeks from 23% to 3%, mainly by preventing embolism. ESC 2023 endocarditis guidelines (Delgado et al.) define emergency (within 24 h), urgent (3–5 days) and non-urgent timing.

ask.question: Small ischaemic stroke without haemorrhage, a 14 mm mobile vegetation, severe MR with heart failure. When should he have surgery?

choices.text: Urgently, within days, without waiting for the stroke to recover
choices.why: A non-haemorrhagic stroke without coma is not a reason to delay when surgery is indicated; waiting risks a second embolus and worsening heart failure (EASE; ESC 2023).

choices.text: After 4 weeks, to let the stroke settle
Only if a second embolus occurs

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding and return to theatre
  • AF
  • Chest and wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Deep sternal wound infection
  • Heart block needing a pacemaker

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical: lifelong warfarin, INR checks, bleeding, valve thrombosis if INR lapses
  • Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy and valve thrombosis; plan before conception
  • Tissue: degenerates faster in the young; reoperation likely
  • Repair where possible

5. Alternatives

  • Balloon mitral valvotomy for pliable MS without LA thrombus or significant MR
  • Medical therapy
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR testing near home
  • Continue benzathine penicillin prophylaxis
  • Blood availability
  • Cost of follow-up

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: A 24-year-old woman planning children needs MVR. Which topic must her consent cover that a 65-year-old's would not?

choices.text: Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy, valve thrombosis, and a plan before conception
choices.why: Valve choice in young women is decided with pregnancy in mind (ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline).

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin (about 300–400 U/kg; ACT above 480 s). Two purse-strings on the distal ascending aorta for the arterial cannula. Bicaval venous drainage: two separate cannulas: an angled SVC cannula directly into the SVC (or through the appendage), and an IVC cannula through a purse-string low on the right atrium, its tip passed into the IVC; snares are needed if the right atrium is to be opened.

An antegrade cardioplegia and root vent line in the ascending aorta; a retrograde cannula into the coronary sinus if wanted; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body: On full bypass, cool as planned. Cross-clamp the ascending aorta between the arterial cannula and the cardioplegia line; arrest with cold blood cardioplegia antegrade, then retrograde through the coronary sinus, repeated every 15–20 minutes.

steps.title: Sondergaard's groove and the left atriotomy
steps.body: Develop Sondergaard's plane: the fat between the right atrium and the right pulmonary veins, back toward the septum, for 1–2 cm. Open the left atrium there, in front of the right pulmonary veins, extending up behind the SVC and down behind the IVC as needed. A self-retaining atrial retractor lifts the septum toward you.

steps.title: Radical debridement of the infected valve
steps.body:
Remove the vegetation whole, without fragmenting it into the LV, and send it for culture, Gram stain, histology and (if cultures were negative) 16S PCR. Excise all infected and necrotic tissue back to healthy tissue; inspect the annulus for an abscess. Irrigate; change gloves and instruments before implanting.

A limited lesion (a perforation, one ruptured chord) in a young patient may be repaired (autologous pericardial patch, chordal repair). With extensive destruction, or a rheumatic valve that would not repair anyway, replace it. A posterior annular abscess is debrided and the defect closed with a pericardial patch before the sutures go in.

Evidence: ESC 2023: mitral repair is preferred when a durable result is likely, especially in the young; mechanical and biological prostheses have similar reinfection risk, so the choice follows age and anticoagulation, not the infection.

choices.text: Culture, histology and 16S PCR of the excised valve and vegetation
choices.why: Molecular diagnosis on valve tissue identifies the organism in many culture-negative cases, and it guides the length and choice of antibiotics.

Evidence: Magne et al., Circulation 2007: mitral PPM (indexed EOA ≤1.2 cm²/m²; severe ≤0.9) reduced survival after MVR. ICVTS 2024 (children): median prosthesis size/weight about 1.7 mm/kg; oversizing and supra-annular placement linked to death; 44–65% of 15–17 mm mechanical valves replaced within years.

ask.question: A 1.40 m² rheumatic patient: what reference EOA must a mitral prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the prosthesis and tie
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring in order, lower the valve down the sutures onto the annulus and tie. For a bileaflet mechanical valve, the usual orientation is anti-anatomical (hinges perpendicular to the natural commissures).

Check that both leaflets open and close fully: nothing trapped (preserved chordae, a long suture tail, pledget).

ask.question: After seating a mechanical mitral valve, the most important check before closing the atrium is…

choices.why: Preserved chordae, suture tails or pledgets can trap a leaflet; fix it now, not after the clamp is off.

choices.text: That the LA appendage is closed
That the sutures are cut short

steps.title: Close the atrium, de-air, clamp off
steps.body:
Close the left atriotomy with 3-0/4-0 polypropylene, leaving the LV vent across until the last suture.

De-air: CO₂ in the field, head down, fill the heart as the last sutures go in, ventilate the lungs to push air out of the pulmonary veins, aortic root vent on suction; release the clamp; rewarm. Consider closing the left atrial appendage if the patient is in AF.

De-air early and come off (most de-airing done in the arrested heart before the clamp is released; vent out and wean soon after)
For: the flaccid, arrested heart can be balloted and needle-vented; a shorter bypass and clamp time.
Against: air stays trapped in the pulmonary veins, LA appendage and LV trabeculae until the heart beats and the lungs are ventilated. It then comes out when the root vent is already out: into the RCA (the most anterior ostium, uppermost with the patient supine), giving inferior ST elevation, RV failure and VF, or into the brain. Mitral surgery opens the left heart widely, so it carries more air than CABG.

Keep de-airing during reperfusion (the beating, ejecting heart on partial bypass, root vent still on, until TOE is clear)
For: contraction and ventilation release the trapped air while the vent can still catch it; if air does reach the RCA, the heart is still supported, so raise the perfusion pressure and let it pass. It overlaps with the rest the heart needs anyway.
Against: longer bypass; strong root-vent suction with a low root pressure can draw air in through the purse-string; handling the beating heart can cause arrhythmia.

The end-point is TOE, not the clock: no bubbles in the LA, LV or pulmonary veins at near-normal filling, then vent out.

Evidence: no trial compares early with late de-airing; practice rests on physiology and TOE studies. CO₂ field flooding cut microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004) and reduced neurocognitive impairment in another (Martens et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2008); a benefit for stroke has not been shown. Intraoperative TOE in valve surgery, including to guide de-airing, is standard practice (ASE/SCA guidelines, Hahn et al., J Am Soc Echocardiogr 2013).

TOE before leaving theatre: no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving, no LVOT obstruction. Pacing wires, drains.

Serious complications: AV groove disruption (catastrophic), circumflex injury, heart block, paravalvular leak, stroke.

ask.question: Ten minutes after the clamp is released and the root vent is removed, the inferior leads show ST elevation and the RV dilates. The likely cause and the move?

choices.text: Air in the right coronary: stay on (or go back on) bypass, raise the perfusion pressure, and let the heart beat unloaded until it clears
choices.why: The RCA ostium is uppermost with the patient supine and catches retained left-heart air. Supported, higher-pressure perfusion usually clears it in minutes; weaning onto a failing RV does not. Keeping the root vent on until TOE is clear prevents it.

choices.text: Circumflex injury from an annular suture: re-arrest and inspect
Prosthetic leaflet stuck: re-open the atrium

steps.title: Reperfuse on bypass, or separate early?
steps.body:
With the clamp off the heart is reperfused while bypass still carries the circulation. How long to rest it before weaning is a judgement, not a fixed rule. A common rule of thumb is about a third of the cross-clamp time (roughly 10 minutes for each 30 of ischaemia).

Waiting for myocardial recovery (a longer supported reperfusion): it washes out cardioplegia and potassium, restores energy stores, lets the rhythm settle and rewarming finish, and needs fewer inotropes. Worth it after a long clamp, with a poor LV or RV, a hypertrophied ventricle, doubtful protection, or pulmonary hypertension (common in rheumatic mitral stenosis: the RV fails first).

Separating early: every extra minute of bypass adds haemodilution, platelet damage, inflammation and bleeding. After a short clamp, a good ventricle, sound protection and a stable rhythm, wean as soon as the conditions are met.

Before either: temperature 36–37 °C, sinus rhythm or pacing, potassium and haemoglobin corrected, lungs ventilated, de-airing confirmed on TOE, and the valve checked (no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving). The cost of weaning too early is a low-output state and a return to bypass; that is still easy while the cannulas are in and protamine has not been given.

ask.question: After MVR for rheumatic stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension (clamp time 95 min), the heart is sluggish on first weaning attempt. Best move?

choices.text: Go back to full bypass, rest the heart longer, start RV support (inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator), then wean again
choices.why: The RV is failing against a high pulmonary pressure; more supported reperfusion and RV-directed support usually rescue it. Pushing on off bypass drives the RV into failure.

choices.text: Give protamine and push inotropes off bypass
Decannulate and accept the low output

steps.title: Separate, then decannulate in order
steps.body:
Wean slowly, watching the pressures and the TOE. Then the order that keeps a way back:

  1. Venous cannula(s) out first (IVC, then SVC); tie the purse-strings.
  2. Protamine started slowly (watch for pulmonary hypertension and hypotension); stop the pump suckers once it runs.
  3. Arterial cannula out last, after part of the protamine and a stable pressure: while it is in, blood can be given from the pump and bypass restarted quickly.

A fast decannulation saves pump time only if the heart is ready; a return to bypass after full protamine means re-heparinising and re-cannulating a heart that is already struggling.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure: avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inodilator if the RV fails
  • AF: rate or rhythm control
  • Anticoagulation: enoxaparin day 1, bridge to warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guideline; ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline; INVICTUS (NEJM 2022).

ask.question: Day 1 after mechanical MVR, drains dry. When is the first INR checked?

choices.text: 72 h after the first warfarin dose, while enoxaparin continues
choices.why: Warfarin takes 2–3 days to move the INR; enoxaparin bridges until the INR is in range.

choices.text: Two hours after the first dose

mvr-mics.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the decision, then the operation (access, bypass, left atrium, excision, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: rheumatic mitral stenosis
steps.body:
In Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa most mitral stenosis, and most aortic regurgitation in the young, is rheumatic. Patients present in their 20s and 30s, often late, with atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension or in pregnancy. In the REMEDY registry (14 low- and middle-income countries, median age 28 years) about 17% had died within two years.

From sore throat to scarred valve.

  1. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (skin infection may also contribute) in a susceptible child.
  2. Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein and its carbohydrate (GlcNAc) cross-react with cardiac myosin and with laminin on the valve shown in human rheumatic tissue.
  3. The valve endothelium is activated (VCAM-1), T cells home into the valve along the closure line and drive a valvulitis (Th1/Th17) shown in human rheumatic tissue. This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis.
  4. Each recurrence re-injures the valve. Over years, valve interstitial cells lay down scar (TGF-β-driven fibrosis) and calcium: the commissures fuse, the leaflets thicken, the chordae shorten and fuse inferred (much of this signalling is from calcific aortic valve disease).
Acute carditisChronic rheumatic heart disease
LesionMitral regurgitation: annular dilatation, elongated chordae, anterior leaflet prolapse (Carpentier I, II)Mitral stenosis (often with regurgitation): commissural fusion, thick leaflets, fused short chordae (Carpentier IIIa)
The valve…cannot closecannot open
Reversible?partly, if carditis settles and recurrences are preventedno: scar and calcium, treated mechanically (balloon or surgery)

The haemodynamics. A normal mitral orifice is 4–6 cm²; stenosis becomes clinically significant at 1.5 cm² or less. The LV is protected (it is under-filled); the load falls on everything behind the valve:

Small orifice→LA→LV gradient→LA pressure ↑, LA dilates→Atrial fibrillation→LA appendage thrombus → stroke
LA pressure ↑→Pulmonary venous pressure ↑ (breathless, oedema)→Pulmonary hypertension→RV pressure overload→RV dilates → TR → right heart failure

Why a fast heart rate decompensates MS. The gradient depends on flow and on the time available for the LA to empty: diastole. Tachycardia (AF with a fast ventricular rate, exercise, fever, anaemia, pregnancy) shortens diastole, so the gradient and LA pressure climb and pulmonary oedema follows. Hence rate control (a β-blocker) and why MS often declares itself in pregnancy. AF also removes the atrial kick and adds stasis: rheumatic AF carries a high embolic risk, and it is treated with warfarin, not a direct oral anticoagulant.

Evidence: the immunology (mimicry, valvular endothelial activation, T-cell infiltration) rests on studies of human rheumatic valves and valve-derived T-cell clones (Guilherme et al., Circulation 1995; Cunningham, Clin Microbiol Rev 2000); the later fibrocalcific steps are largely extrapolated from calcific aortic valve disease. Clinical picture: Carapetis et al., Nat Rev Dis Primers 2016; Chandrashekhar, Westaby and Narula, Lancet 2009. Prevention works: in GOAL (NEJM 2022; 818 Ugandan children with latent RHD) monthly benzathine penicillin cut progression over 2 years from 8.3% to 0.8%. INVICTUS (NEJM 2022; 4,531 patients with rheumatic AF) found more vascular deaths and ischaemic strokes with rivaroxaban than with a vitamin K antagonist; ESC/EACTS 2025 advise against DOACs in AF with rheumatic MS and a valve area of 2.0 cm² or less.

ask.question: A 26-year-old woman with moderate rheumatic MS, comfortable at rest, goes into AF at 150 beats per minute and within hours is in pulmonary oedema. Why?

choices.text: The short diastole leaves too little time to empty the LA through the narrow valve, so the gradient and LA pressure rise
choices.why: In MS the transmitral gradient rises steeply with heart rate. Slowing the rate (and cardioversion, with anticoagulation) often relieves the oedema before anything is done to the valve.

choices.text: The valve has suddenly narrowed further
AF has caused acute mitral regurgitation

steps.title: The mitral valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
The mitral annulus is D-shaped and saddle-shaped. The anterior leaflet hangs from the fibrous aortomitral curtain, in continuity with the left and non-coronary cusps of the aortic valve; the posterior leaflet takes the rest of the circumference. Chordae run from both leaflets to the anterolateral and posteromedial papillary muscles.

Round the posterior annulus, in the AV groove: the circumflex artery (close near the anterolateral commissure, closer in left dominance) and the coronary sinus. At the posteromedial commissure, next to the right trigone: the AV node and His bundle. These are what deep annular sutures injure.

ask.question: A deep suture at the posterior annulus near the anterolateral commissure is most likely to injure…

choices.why: It runs in the AV groove close to the annulus there, especially in a left-dominant circulation.

steps.title: Case: restenosis after balloon commissurotomy
steps.lead: A 41-year-old teacher, balloon mitral commissurotomy 9 years ago, now breathless again. Echo: MVA 1.0 cm², mean gradient 11 mmHg, bicommissural calcium, Wilkins 10, mild MR; sinus rhythm, no LA thrombus; aortic and tricuspid valves normal. CT: good femoral and iliac vessels, no aortic atheroma. She wants to return to work quickly.
steps.body:
A second balloon? Repeat PMC works for restenosis caused by commissural refusion when the anatomy is still favourable. Bicommissural calcium makes a good result unlikely, so: surgery.

Access: isolated mitral disease, no aortic regurgitation, good femoral vessels and no pleural adhesions: a right mini-thoracotomy is reasonable in a centre that does it regularly. A sternotomy would be equally correct.

Evidence: UK Mini Mitral (Akowuah et al., JAMA 2023; 330 patients, degenerative MR repair): the minithoracotomy did not improve physical function at 12 weeks over sternotomy, but was as safe, with a shorter stay and faster early recovery. Evidence for rheumatic valves is observational, from experienced centres.

ask.question: What makes a second balloon commissurotomy unlikely to succeed here?

choices.why: Balloon commissurotomy works by splitting fused commissures; calcified commissures do not split cleanly, and the balloon then tears the leaflets (severe MR).

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding and return to theatre
  • AF
  • Chest and wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Deep sternal wound infection
  • Heart block needing a pacemaker

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical: lifelong warfarin, INR checks, bleeding, valve thrombosis if INR lapses
  • Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy and valve thrombosis; plan before conception
  • Tissue: degenerates faster in the young; reoperation likely
  • Repair where possible

5. Alternatives

  • Balloon mitral valvotomy for pliable MS without LA thrombus or significant MR
  • Medical therapy
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR testing near home
  • Continue benzathine penicillin prophylaxis
  • Blood availability
  • Cost of follow-up

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: A 24-year-old woman planning children needs MVR. Which topic must her consent cover that a 65-year-old's would not?

choices.text: Pregnancy on warfarin: embryopathy, valve thrombosis, and a plan before conception
choices.why: Valve choice in young women is decided with pregnancy in mind (ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline).

steps.title: Position, femoral cannulation, the incision
steps.body:
Supine with the right chest raised about 30°, the right arm by the side. Double-lumen tube (right lung down), external defibrillator pads, TOE.

Femoral cannulation (open or percutaneous): the venous cannula guided up into the SVC under TOE, the arterial cannula into the femoral artery (check iliofemoral atheroma on CT first). A 4–6 cm incision in the right 4th space, in the inframammary fold; a soft-tissue retractor; camera through the incision or a port above it; CO2 flooding the field.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body: A transthoracic (Chitwood) clamp through a stab in the 3rd space, mid-axillary line, across the ascending aorta behind the pulmonary artery (avoiding the left atrial appendage and the right PA); or an endoballoon occlusion. Antegrade cardioplegia through a root needle placed through the incision.

steps.title: Sondergaard's groove and the left atriotomy
steps.body: Develop Sondergaard's plane: the fat between the right atrium and the right pulmonary veins, back toward the septum, for 1–2 cm. Open the left atrium there, in front of the right pulmonary veins, extending up behind the SVC and down behind the IVC as needed. A self-retaining atrial retractor lifts the septum toward you.

steps.title: Excise the anterior leaflet; keep the posterior chordae
steps.body:
Inspect the valve. For replacement, excise the anterior leaflet (detach it 2–3 mm from the annulus, divide its chordae; some reattach anterior chordae to the annulus), preserve the posterior leaflet and its chordae: chordal sparing keeps left ventricular function and guards against rupture of the ventricle.

Debride calcium off the annulus carefully: deep debridement posteriorly risks AV groove disruption. Size the annulus with the valve sizers.

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
2-0 braided polyester horizontal mattress sutures, 12–16 of them. Where the pledgets sit decides where the valve sits, and the choice follows the quality of the annulus.

Ventricular pledgets (non-everting: needle from the LV side up through the annulus; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the strongest hold in friable, calcified, rheumatic or infected tissue, so fewer paravalvular leaks and dehiscences; the pledget spreads the load; supra-annular seating often takes one size larger.
Against: deeper, blinder bites (circumflex and AV groove posteriorly, AV node at the posteromedial commissure, aortic cusps anteriorly); pledgets and preserved chordae under the ring can trap a leaflet or seed pannus and thrombus; anterior pledgets can narrow the LVOT; awkward through a small LA or a MICS port.

Annulus-only (everting, with atrial pledgets, or unpledgeted; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: shallow bites you can see; nothing below the ring to catch a leaflet; LVOT clear; quicker; suits a healthy annulus and MICS.
Against: sutures can cut through poor tissue; the prosthesis is often a size smaller; unpledgeted sutures are the weakest.

A common compromise: ventricular pledgets posteriorly and at the commissures (where the tissue is worst and leaks happen), atrial pledgets anteriorly (to protect the aortic valve and LVOT).

Whatever the technique, bite in the annulus, not beyond it.

Evidence: no randomised trial compares everting and non-everting sutures in MVR. In the AVERT trial cohort, pledgeted sutures were associated with fewer major paravalvular leaks than unpledgeted ones (Englberger et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2005). The ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guidelines make no recommendation on suture technique, but support preserving the subvalvular apparatus in MVR (for LV function), and that is one more reason to keep pledgets clear of preserved chordae.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a heavily calcified, small posterior annulus. Which suture technique gives the most secure seat and the largest valve?

choices.text: Pledgeted mattress sutures with ventricular pledgets (non-everting, supra-annular), at least posteriorly
choices.why: Ventricular pledgets hold best in poor tissue and seat the ring above the annulus, which usually allows a larger size. Keep bites in the annulus to spare the circumflex and AV groove, and check that no pledget traps a leaflet.

choices.text: Everting sutures with atrial pledgets all round, one size smaller

steps.title: Size the mitral prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
The sizer tells you what the annulus takes; the patient's body size tells you what orifice they need. Too small a valve for the body is prosthesis–patient mismatch (PPM): persistent gradients, pulmonary hypertension and worse survival.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 2.3 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 1.2 cm²/m² to avoid PPM (severe if the indexed EOA is ≤0.9)
  3. Choose the smallest size whose reference EOA on the manufacturer's chart reaches it
ProblemOptions
Small annulus, small rheumatic womanA valve with a larger EOA for its size; preserve the posterior chordae and seat it well; avoid forcing an oversized valve
ChildCheck size / weight: a high ratio predicts early death (LVOT obstruction, circumflex and conduction injury). Supra-annular placement of a too-large valve worsens survival. Small 15–17 mm valves will need replacing as the child grows

Evidence: Magne et al., Circulation 2007: mitral PPM (indexed EOA ≤1.2 cm²/m²; severe ≤0.9) reduced survival after MVR. ICVTS 2024 (children): median prosthesis size/weight about 1.7 mm/kg; oversizing and supra-annular placement linked to death; 44–65% of 15–17 mm mechanical valves replaced within years.

Decannulate the femoral vessels and repair them; check the right lung re-expands.
