Prosthetic leaflet stuck: re-open the atrium

steps.title: Reperfuse on bypass, or separate early?
steps.body:
With the clamp off the heart is reperfused while bypass still carries the circulation. How long to rest it before weaning is a judgement, not a fixed rule. A common rule of thumb is about a third of the cross-clamp time (roughly 10 minutes for each 30 of ischaemia).

Waiting for myocardial recovery (a longer supported reperfusion): it washes out cardioplegia and potassium, restores energy stores, lets the rhythm settle and rewarming finish, and needs fewer inotropes. Worth it after a long clamp, with a poor LV or RV, a hypertrophied ventricle, doubtful protection, or pulmonary hypertension (common in rheumatic mitral stenosis: the RV fails first).

Separating early: every extra minute of bypass adds haemodilution, platelet damage, inflammation and bleeding. After a short clamp, a good ventricle, sound protection and a stable rhythm, wean as soon as the conditions are met.

Before either: temperature 36–37 °C, sinus rhythm or pacing, potassium and haemoglobin corrected, lungs ventilated, de-airing confirmed on TOE, and the valve checked (no paravalvular leak, leaflets moving). The cost of weaning too early is a low-output state and a return to bypass; that is still easy while the cannulas are in and protamine has not been given.

ask.question: After MVR for rheumatic stenosis with severe pulmonary hypertension (clamp time 95 min), the heart is sluggish on first weaning attempt. Best move?

choices.text: Go back to full bypass, rest the heart longer, start RV support (inotrope, pulmonary vasodilator), then wean again
choices.why: The RV is failing against a high pulmonary pressure; more supported reperfusion and RV-directed support usually rescue it. Pushing on off bypass drives the RV into failure.

choices.text: Give protamine and push inotropes off bypass
Decannulate and accept the low output

steps.title: Separate, then decannulate in order
steps.body:
Wean slowly, watching the pressures and the TOE. Then the order that keeps a way back:

  1. Venous cannula(s) out first (the femoral venous cannula).
  2. Protamine started slowly (watch for pulmonary hypertension and hypotension); stop the pump suckers once it runs.
  3. Arterial cannula out last, after part of the protamine and a stable pressure (repair the femoral artery): while it is in, blood can be given from the pump and bypass restarted quickly.

A fast decannulation saves pump time only if the heart is ready; a return to bypass after full protamine means re-heparinising and re-cannulating a heart that is already struggling.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Pulmonary hypertension and RV failure: avoid hypoxia, hypercapnia, acidosis; inodilator if the RV fails
  • AF: rate or rhythm control
  • Anticoagulation: enoxaparin day 1, bridge to warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guideline; ESC 2018 pregnancy guideline; INVICTUS (NEJM 2022).

ask.question: Day 1 after mechanical MVR, drains dry. When is the first INR checked?

choices.text: 72 h after the first warfarin dose, while enoxaparin continues
choices.why: Warfarin takes 2–3 days to move the INR; enoxaparin bridges until the INR is in range.

choices.text: Two hours after the first dose

avr-std.name: Aortic valve replacement
avr-std.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the Heart Team decision, then the operation (access, bypass and protection, aortotomy, debridement, sizing, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing, TOE).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: rheumatic aortic regurgitation
steps.body:
In Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa most mitral stenosis, and most aortic regurgitation in the young, is rheumatic. Patients present in their 20s and 30s, often late, with atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension or in pregnancy. In the REMEDY registry (14 low- and middle-income countries, median age 28 years) about 17% had died within two years.

From sore throat to scarred valve.

  1. Group A streptococcal pharyngitis (skin infection may also contribute) in a susceptible child.
  2. Molecular mimicry: antibodies and T cells raised against the streptococcal M protein and its carbohydrate (GlcNAc) cross-react with cardiac myosin and with laminin on the valve shown in human rheumatic tissue.
  3. The valve endothelium is activated (VCAM-1), T cells home into the valve along the closure line and drive a valvulitis (Th1/Th17) shown in human rheumatic tissue. This is acute rheumatic fever with carditis.
  4. Each recurrence re-injures the valve. Over years, valve interstitial cells lay down scar (TGF-β-driven fibrosis) and calcium: the commissures fuse, the leaflets thicken, the chordae shorten and fuse inferred (much of this signalling is from calcific aortic valve disease).
Acute carditisChronic rheumatic heart disease
LesionMitral regurgitation: annular dilatation, elongated chordae, anterior leaflet prolapse (Carpentier I, II)Mitral stenosis (often with regurgitation): commissural fusion, thick leaflets, fused short chordae (Carpentier IIIa)
The valve…cannot closecannot open
Reversible?partly, if carditis settles and recurrences are preventedno: scar and calcium, treated mechanically (balloon or surgery)

The pattern of rheumatic valve disease. The mitral valve is involved, alone or with others, in about 85%; mitral plus aortic disease in roughly a fifth; isolated aortic disease is uncommon (under 5%) and is then nearly always regurgitation. Rheumatic aortic stenosis comes late, as fusion and calcium accumulate, and almost never without regurgitation or mitral disease. One explanation (a hypothesis) is load: the mitral valve closes against full LV systolic pressure every beat, the aortic cusps against the lower diastolic pressure.

The rheumatic aortic valve: fibrosis retracts the cusps so they no longer meet in the centre (a central leak), the free edges thicken and roll, and the commissures fuse. Contrast degenerative calcific stenosis, where calcium in the cusp bodies stiffens a valve whose commissures are open.

Regurgitant volume back into the LV→LV volume and pressure overload→Eccentric hypertrophy, dilatation (years compensated)→End-systolic size ↑, EF ↓→Irreversible LV dysfunction
Low aortic diastolic pressure→Wide pulse pressure→Less coronary perfusion (diastole)→Angina, breathlessness

Acute aortic regurgitation (endocarditis, dissection) is different: a normal-sized LV cannot take the sudden volume, the diastolic pressure rises steeply, and pulmonary oedema and shock follow.

Evidence: distribution of rheumatic valve involvement: Kumar et al., AHA scientific statement 2020; Afifi, Hosny and Yacoub, Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2019. Haemodynamics and intervention thresholds: ACC/AHA 2020, ESC/EACTS 2021 and 2025 guidelines.

ask.question: Chronic severe AR: which finding shows the LV is beginning to fail and surgery should not wait?

choices.text: LV end-systolic diameter over 50 mm (or 25 mm/m²) or an EF of 50% or less
choices.why: The end-systolic size tracks contractility. Guidelines (class I) operate at these thresholds even without symptoms, because beyond them LV function may not recover.

choices.text: An end-diastolic diameter of 60 mm alone

steps.title: The aortic root and what lies around it
steps.body:
The cusps do not hinge on a flat ring but on a three-pronged crown: low at each nadir (the virtual basal ring, which is what echo and CT call the annulus) and high at the three commissures, just below the sinotubular junction.

What the sutures and the debridement can injure:

  • Coronary ostia: the left main in the left sinus, the right coronary in the right sinus, usually 1–1.5 cm above the annulus. Keep prosthesis posts and pledgets clear of them.
  • Membranous septum and His bundle: below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Deep bites or aggressive decalcification here cause complete heart block.
  • Anterior mitral leaflet: below the left and non-coronary cusps, through the fibrous aortomitral curtain. Deep bites there distort the mitral valve.

Evidence: the crown-shaped annulus and its relations are from anatomical and CT studies of the root; conduction injury is the main cause of the permanent pacemakers needed after surgical AVR.

ask.question: A deep annular suture below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps is most likely to cause…

choices.why: The His bundle runs in the membranous septum just below that commissure.

steps.title: Case: a young man with rheumatic aortic regurgitation
steps.lead: A 22-year-old matatu driver, breathless on climbing stairs for 6 months. On benzathine penicillin since age 14. Collapsing pulse, BP 140/40. Echo: severe AR (central jet from retracted, thickened cusps), LV end-diastolic 72 mm, end-systolic 54 mm, EF 48%; the mitral valve is thickened with mild MR and no stenosis; tricuspid normal. Coronary angiography not needed at his age.
steps.body:
Operate: he is symptomatic, and the LV is already failing (end-systolic diameter over 50 mm, EF 50% or less). Each alone is a class I indication.

The options. Repair: rarely durable in rheumatic AR (retracted, fibrotic cusps; the disease goes on). Ross: attractive in the young (no warfarin, growth, near-normal survival in non-rheumatic series), but in rheumatic patients, particularly the young and those with mitral disease, the autograft fails more often. Tissue valve: degenerates fast in a 22-year-old. Mechanical AVR with warfarin (aortic INR target about 2.5): the usual choice, with an INR plan agreed before surgery.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 and 2025: surgery for symptomatic severe AR, and for asymptomatic severe AR with LVESD over 50 mm, LVESDi over 25 mm/m² or LVEF 50% or less (class I). A best-evidence review (Interact CardioVasc Thorac Surg 2010) found poorer autograft durability after the Ross in young rheumatic patients, more so with mitral disease. Rheumatic aortic repair: Afifi, Hosny and Yacoub, Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2019.

ask.question: Which valve suits this 22-year-old man with rheumatic AR and some mitral involvement, who can attend an INR clinic?

choices.why: Durable, and the Ross is less reliable in young rheumatic patients with mitral involvement. A tissue valve would fail early. Warfarin is manageable with a reliable INR plan.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding
  • AF
  • Wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
  • Paravalvular leak

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical versus tissue valve: warfarin against durability
  • Patient–prosthesis mismatch with a small annulus

5. Alternatives

  • TAVI where available and suitable
  • Balloon valvotomy as a bridge
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR access
  • Penicillin prophylaxis if rheumatic
  • Cost

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which AVR risk is specific to the valve's position next to the conduction system?

choices.text: Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The His bundle runs beneath the non-coronary/right-coronary commissure.

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body:
Median sternotomy; open the pericardium and hitch it up. Look at the ascending aorta (size, calcification by palpation or epiaortic scan) before choosing the cannulation and clamp sites.

Evidence: epiaortic scanning finds atheroma that palpation misses; it changes cannulation or clamp site in a proportion of patients.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta, two-stage venous cannula (RA to IVC), LV vent
steps.body:
Heparin (ACT above 480 s). Arterial cannula in the distal ascending aorta, high enough to leave room for the clamp and an aortotomy below it. For isolated AVR the right atrium is not opened, so venous drainage is by a single two-stage (cavoatrial) cannula: in through a purse-string on the right atrial appendage, its tip passed down into the IVC. The tip drains the IVC, the side holes (the second stage) sit in the right atrium and drain the SVC return. It cannot be snared, so it is not used when the right atrium must be opened (mitral, tricuspid, septal defects: use two caval cannulas).

Root cardioplegia and vent line; a retrograde cannula in the coronary sinus; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein, placed before the heart slows if there is aortic regurgitation, so the ventricle never distends.

Evidence: this is standard practice (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes). A regurgitant valve lets cardioplegia and bypass return fill the arrested LV; distension damages the myocardium, which is why the vent goes in early.

steps.title: Cross-clamp; cardioplegia depends on the valve
steps.body:
On full bypass, clamp the ascending aorta below the arterial cannula.

  • Aortic stenosis, competent valve: antegrade into the root arrests the heart.
  • Aortic regurgitation: antegrade into the root runs into the LV and distends it instead of perfusing the coronaries. Give it retrograde, and/or open the aorta and give it directly into each ostium with hand-held cannulas.

Repeat every 15–20 minutes (retrograde, or down the ostia), or as the solution in use requires.

Evidence: the choice follows the physiology rather than trials; retrograde perfusion reaches the right ventricle less well, which is one reason many combine retrograde with direct ostial doses.

ask.question: Severe aortic regurgitation. After the cross-clamp, antegrade root cardioplegia is started and the LV swells while the heart keeps beating. Next?

choices.text: Stop the root infusion, vent the LV, open the aorta and give cardioplegia directly into the ostia (and/or retrograde)
choices.why: Root cardioplegia is going through the incompetent valve into the LV, not down the coronaries. Distension injures the myocardium.

choices.text: Cool further and wait for arrest

steps.title: Oblique aortotomy into the non-coronary sinus
steps.body:
Find the right coronary origin first. Open the aorta 1–1.5 cm above it, across the front, and carry the incision obliquely down into the non-coronary sinus toward its nadir ("hockey stick"). A transverse aortotomy above the STJ is the alternative, and is easier to close for a later root operation.

Stay above the right coronary and away from the left main on the other side. Stay sutures open the aorta; give ostial cardioplegia now if needed.

Evidence: the placement is technique by consensus (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes); the risks it avoids are right coronary injury and distortion of the sinuses and STJ when closing.

steps.title: Excise the cusps, debride the annulus, catch every fragment
steps.body:
Protect the LV: a moist sponge or gauze through the valve into the outflow tract, and the vent on. Excise the cusps 1–2 mm from their hinge, one cusp at a time.

Debride the calcium back to a pliable annulus so the sewing ring can sit flat, without leaks. The danger zones:

  • under the right and non-coronary commissure: the membranous septum and His bundle (heart block; a VSD if you go through);
  • under the left and non-coronary cusps: the aortomitral curtain (a hole into the left atrium; mitral damage);
  • the ostia: calcium near them is lifted out, not avulsed.

Remove the sponge, irrigate the LV and root with saline and suction, and look for loose fragments before sizing.

Evidence: stroke after SAVR is mostly embolic, and calcific debris is one source; catching and irrigating it is standard practice. Aggressive debridement near the membranous septum raises the risk of heart block and of annular disruption.

In this rheumatic valve the cusps are thick, retracted and fused at one commissure, with little calcium: excision is easier than in calcific AS, but check the anterior mitral leaflet through the valve and the aortomitral curtain.

ask.question: While debriding, you take calcium from beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps and see the septum bulge. What is at risk?

choices.text: The His bundle (heart block) and the membranous septum (a VSD)
choices.why: That area is the membranous septum carrying the His bundle. Take less calcium there; a little residual calcium is safer than a VSD or heart block.

steps.title: Size, and avoid patient–prosthesis mismatch
steps.body:
Measure the annulus with the sizers made for the chosen valve (sizes differ between makers). The question is not only "what fits" but whether the valve's effective orifice area indexed to body surface area (EOAi) will be big enough for this patient.

Patient–prosthesis mismatch (VARC-3), BMI under 30: moderate at EOAi 0.85–0.66, severe at 0.65 cm²/m² or less. BMI 30 or more: moderate 0.70–0.56, severe 0.55 or less. Look up the valve's expected EOA before choosing.

If the annulus is too small:

  • a valve with a better orifice for its size (supra-annular, thin-sewing-ring, or stentless);
  • annular enlargement: Nicks (through the non-coronary sinus toward the aortomitral curtain), Manouguian (through the left–non-coronary commissure into the curtain and the anterior mitral leaflet), Y-incision (Yang: through the left–non-coronary commissure with a Y into both trigones, allowing about 3–4 sizes larger). The Konno operation (into the septum) is mainly for children.

Evidence: VARC-3 (Généreux et al., JACC 2021) sets the definitions. In a meta-analysis of about 123,000 patients (J Am Heart Assoc 2024), mismatch after SAVR was associated with higher late mortality and earlier failure of tissue valves. The Y-incision series (Yang et al., JTCVS) reported enlargement by 3–4 sizes with low early mortality; these are single-centre, non-randomised data.

ask.question: A 1.9 m² patient (BMI 26). The largest valve that fits has an expected EOA of 1.2 cm². What is the predicted mismatch, and what should you consider?

choices.text: EOAi 0.63: severe mismatch; consider annular enlargement or a valve with a larger orifice
choices.why: 1.2 / 1.9 = 0.63 cm²/m², which is 0.65 or less: severe by VARC-3 (BMI under 30).

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
Usually 12–15 sutures of 2-0 braided polyester, following the crown: up to the commissures, down to the nadirs. Where they sit decides where the valve sits.

Non-everting mattress, pledgets below (on the LV side; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the usual technique for supra-annular valves; pledgets spread the load in calcified or fragile tissue; the largest valve for the annulus.
Against: pledgets sit in the outflow tract; the bites below the right–non-coronary commissure are near the His bundle.

Everting mattress, pledgets above (on the aortic side; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: nothing below the annulus; everts the tissue for a good seal.
Against: the ring sits inside the annulus, so the valve is often a size smaller: a mismatch risk in a small root.

Simple interrupted (no pledgets)
For: less material on the annulus, so the valve seats deeper and opens more. Against: no buttress in poor tissue.

Continuous polypropylene
For: fast. Against: one weak point can loosen the whole line; not for calcified or infected annuli.

Keep pledgets and sutures clear of the ostia; take shallow bites under the right–non-coronary commissure.

Evidence: no randomised trial has settled this. In the AVERT cohort (807 patients), major paravalvular leak occurred in 1.7% with pledgets and 5.8% without (Englberger et al., EJCTS 2005). A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 observational SAVR studies (4,390 patients; Boltje et al.) found no clear difference in leak, gradients or mortality, and concluded that the evidence neither supports nor opposes pledgets. In 152 patients with small (19–21 mm) supra-annular bioprostheses, simple interrupted sutures gave a larger orifice and less mismatch than mattress sutures (Tabata et al., JTCVS 2014; retrospective).

ask.question: An elderly woman with a heavily calcified 19 mm annulus, receiving a supra-annular bioprosthesis. Which suture choice best balances sealing and orifice size?

choices.text: Pledgeted non-everting mattress sutures (supra-annular), or simple interrupted where the tissue holds
choices.why: Supra-annular seating gives the largest valve. Pledgets protect calcified tissue from cutting through; simple interrupted bites (Tabata) gain orifice where the tissue is sound. Everting sutures would push the valve intra-annular and a size down.

steps.title: Size the aortic prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
A valve that fits the annulus can still be too small for the patient. Aortic prosthesis–patient mismatch leaves a gradient, less LV mass regression and worse long-term outcomes.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 1.48 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 0.85 cm²/m² (BMI 30 or more: × 0.70) to avoid PPM; severe if ≤0.65 (≤0.55 when obese)
  3. Pick the smallest size whose reference EOA reaches it on the manufacturer's chart
If the projected EOA is too smallOptions
Different prosthesisA supra-annular or stentless bioprosthesis, or a newer mechanical valve with a larger EOA for the same size
Enlarge the rootPosterior annular enlargement (Nicks, Manouguian or a Y-incision) to take one or two sizes more
Older or high-risk patientTranscatheter options where available

Evidence: Hahn & Pibarot 2024 (VARC-3 categories): moderate PPM indexed EOA 0.85–0.66, severe ≤0.65 cm²/m²; with BMI ≥30, moderate 0.70–0.56, severe ≤0.55; predicted EOAi from reference EOA ÷ BSA guides valve choice before implantation.

ask.question: A 1.70 m², BMI 24 adult: what reference EOA must an aortic prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the valve; check the ostia and the leaflets
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring and lower the valve. For a stented tissue valve, line the three posts up with the native commissures, so that no post faces a coronary ostium. Tie, with even tension, the ring seated flat.

Before closing: look into both ostia (nothing overhanging); check for gaps under the ring; check that the leaflets move freely (for a mechanical valve, rotate it to free them of the septum).

Evidence: coronary obstruction after SAVR is rare but often fatal; it is prevented by post orientation and direct inspection. Post-bypass TOE confirms leaflet motion, gradient and paravalvular leak (ASE/SCA guidance).

This patient has a mechanical bileaflet valve: check that both leaflets open and close fully and that no suture tail or pledget can catch them.

ask.question: After weaning, new ST elevation in the anterolateral leads and poor anterior wall motion on TOE. The valve looks well seated. First suspicion?

choices.text: The left main ostium is partly obstructed by a post, a pledget or the sewing ring (or has embolised air/debris)
choices.why: Coronary compromise right after SAVR is the prosthesis or embolism until proved otherwise: go back on bypass, inspect, and re-seat or graft.

steps.title: Close the aorta and de-air
steps.body:
Close the aortotomy in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene (a horizontal mattress, then over-and-over), with felt strips if the wall is thin. Before the last sutures: fill the heart, ventilate the lungs, head down; the root vent on; release the clamp.

Early vs late de-airing is the same question as in mitral surgery, with less air because the left atrium was not opened: venting only until the clamp is off is quicker, but air trapped in the pulmonary veins and LV comes out later and goes up the right coronary (uppermost) or to the brain; keeping the root vent on while the heart ejects on partial bypass catches it. Stop when TOE shows no air, not by the clock.

Evidence: no trial compares de-airing strategies; CO₂ field flooding reduced microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004); a stroke benefit has not been shown.

steps.title: Reperfuse, wean, TOE, decannulate
steps.body:
Reperfuse on bypass until the heart is ready (about a third of the clamp time is a common rule of thumb; longer after a long clamp or with a thick, hypertrophied ventricle). Pace (epicardial wires) if there is heart block: it often recovers over days.

TOE after bypass: prosthesis gradient and leaflet motion, paravalvular leak, new regional wall-motion abnormality (ostia), mitral function, and, in a small hypertrophied LV, outflow obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet (treat with volume and beta-blockade; stop inotropes).

Then venous cannula out, protamine, arterial cannula out last.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE is standard in valve surgery (ASE/SCA guidelines). A leak more than mild on TOE is usually repaired before leaving theatre, because significant paravalvular leak is associated with haemolysis, heart failure and worse survival.

ask.question: After AVR for severe AS (small, thick LV), the patient becomes hypotensive on adrenaline. TOE: hyperdynamic LV, mitral leaflet touching the septum in systole, high LVOT gradient. Treatment?

choices.text: Stop inotropes, give volume, a beta-blocker or phenylephrine
choices.why: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet, which inotropes worsen. Fill, slow and constrict.

choices.text: Go back on bypass and replace the mitral valve

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heart block (conduction tissue beside the annulus): test wires; pacemaker if block persists
  • Hypertrophied ventricle: keep filled, avoid tachycardia
  • Mechanical valve: enoxaparin, warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After AVR, complete heart block: the epicardial wires are not capturing. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant; increase output, check connections, prepare transcutaneous pacing
choices.why: Loss of capture in complete heart block is an emergency.

avr-dvr.name: Aortic valve replacement
avr-dvr.approach: Double valve: MS with mixed aortic disease
avr-dvr.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the Heart Team decision, then the operation (access, bypass and protection, aortotomy, debridement, sizing, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing, TOE).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: rheumatic multivalve disease
steps.body:
In Kenya and sub-Saharan Africa most mitral stenosis, and most aortic regurgitation in the young, is rheumatic. Patients present in their 20s and 30s, often late, with atrial fibrillation, pulmonary hypertension or in pregnancy. In the REMEDY registry (14 low- and middle-income countries, median age 28 years) about 17% had died within two years.

The pattern of rheumatic valve disease. The mitral valve is involved, alone or with others, in about 85%; mitral plus aortic disease in roughly a fifth; isolated aortic disease is uncommon (under 5%) and is then nearly always regurgitation. Rheumatic aortic stenosis comes late, as fusion and calcium accumulate, and almost never without regurgitation or mitral disease. One explanation (a hypothesis) is load: the mitral valve closes against full LV systolic pressure every beat, the aortic cusps against the lower diastolic pressure.

The rheumatic aortic valve: fibrosis retracts the cusps so they no longer meet in the centre (a central leak), the free edges thicken and roll, and the commissures fuse. Contrast degenerative calcific stenosis, where calcium in the cusp bodies stiffens a valve whose commissures are open.

Regurgitant volume back into the LV→LV volume and pressure overload→Eccentric hypertrophy, dilatation (years compensated)→End-systolic size ↑, EF ↓→Irreversible LV dysfunction
Low aortic diastolic pressure→Wide pulse pressure→Less coronary perfusion (diastole)→Angina, breathlessness

Two lesions mask each other. Mitral stenosis under-fills the LV, so aortic regurgitation seems milder and an aortic gradient is lower than the stenosis deserves (low flow). After the mitral valve is opened, the aortic lesion can be unmasked. Assess each valve on its own (valve area, regurgitant volume, LV size), and inspect them at surgery.

Acute aortic regurgitation (endocarditis, dissection) is different: a normal-sized LV cannot take the sudden volume, the diastolic pressure rises steeply, and pulmonary oedema and shock follow.

Evidence: distribution of rheumatic valve involvement: Kumar et al., AHA scientific statement 2020; Afifi, Hosny and Yacoub, Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2019. Haemodynamics and intervention thresholds: ACC/AHA 2020, ESC/EACTS 2021 and 2025 guidelines.

ask.question: Rheumatic MS and moderate aortic stenosis on echo (mean aortic gradient 25 mmHg). Why might the aortic stenosis be worse than it looks?

choices.text: The narrow mitral valve limits LV filling and output, so the aortic gradient is low for the degree of stenosis
choices.why: Gradients depend on flow. With low forward flow, a severe aortic stenosis can produce a modest gradient; valve area and direct inspection matter.

choices.text: It cannot be: rheumatic aortic disease is always pure regurgitation

steps.title: The aortic root and what lies around it
steps.body:
The cusps do not hinge on a flat ring but on a three-pronged crown: low at each nadir (the virtual basal ring, which is what echo and CT call the annulus) and high at the three commissures, just below the sinotubular junction.

What the sutures and the debridement can injure:

  • Coronary ostia: the left main in the left sinus, the right coronary in the right sinus, usually 1–1.5 cm above the annulus. Keep prosthesis posts and pledgets clear of them.
  • Membranous septum and His bundle: below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Deep bites or aggressive decalcification here cause complete heart block.
  • Anterior mitral leaflet: below the left and non-coronary cusps, through the fibrous aortomitral curtain. Deep bites there distort the mitral valve.

Evidence: the crown-shaped annulus and its relations are from anatomical and CT studies of the root; conduction injury is the main cause of the permanent pacemakers needed after surgical AVR.

ask.question: A deep annular suture below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps is most likely to cause…

choices.why: The His bundle runs in the membranous septum just below that commissure.

steps.title: Case: rheumatic mitral stenosis with mixed aortic disease
steps.lead: A 35-year-old woman, NYHA III, in AF. Echo: mitral stenosis (MVA 1.1 cm², thick, calcified commissures) and mixed aortic disease: moderate-to-severe AR and aortic valve area 1.0 cm² with a mean gradient of only 28 mmHg. PA pressure 55 mmHg; mild functional TR, annulus 36 mm.
steps.body:
Both valves: the mitral is unfavourable for a balloon, and the aortic valve is significantly diseased (a balloon would leave it). Low flow through the stenotic mitral makes the aortic gradient understate the stenosis. Double valve replacement, with the appendage closed and AF ablation where possible.

The order at surgery: open the aorta and excise the aortic valve first (it opens the view of the mitral through the LA and lets you see the aortomitral curtain), then replace the mitral, then implant the aortic prosthesis: an aortic valve already in place would block access to the anterior mitral annulus, and mitral sutures pulled against it could distort it.

Valves: she needs warfarin for AF anyway, so two mechanical valves are usual; a tissue option would mean two redos at a young age.

Evidence: technique: Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes Cardiac Surgery. The AHA 2020 statement notes that in endemic regions double-valve surgery is common and replacement is usually preferred to limit redo operations.

ask.question: In a double valve replacement, in which order are the valves dealt with?

choices.text: Excise the aortic valve, replace the mitral, then implant the aortic prosthesis
choices.why: The mitral annulus, especially anteriorly, is reached best with the aortic valve out and no aortic prosthesis in the way; the aortic prosthesis goes in last.

choices.text: Implant the aortic prosthesis, then the mitral
Mitral first, before opening the aorta at all
Either order; it makes no difference

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding
  • AF
  • Wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
  • Paravalvular leak

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical versus tissue valve: warfarin against durability
  • Patient–prosthesis mismatch with a small annulus

5. Alternatives

  • TAVI where available and suitable
  • Balloon valvotomy as a bridge
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR access
  • Penicillin prophylaxis if rheumatic
  • Cost

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which AVR risk is specific to the valve's position next to the conduction system?

choices.text: Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The His bundle runs beneath the non-coronary/right-coronary commissure.

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin (about 300–400 U/kg; ACT above 480 s). Two purse-strings on the distal ascending aorta for the arterial cannula. Bicaval venous drainage: two separate cannulas: an angled SVC cannula directly into the SVC (or through the appendage), and an IVC cannula through a purse-string low on the right atrium, its tip passed into the IVC; snares are needed if the right atrium is to be opened.

An antegrade cardioplegia and root vent line in the ascending aorta; a retrograde cannula into the coronary sinus if wanted; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein.

steps.title: Cross-clamp; cardioplegia depends on the valve
steps.body:
On full bypass, clamp the ascending aorta below the arterial cannula.

  • Aortic stenosis, competent valve: antegrade into the root arrests the heart.
  • Aortic regurgitation: antegrade into the root runs into the LV and distends it instead of perfusing the coronaries. Give it retrograde, and/or open the aorta and give it directly into each ostium with hand-held cannulas.

Repeat every 15–20 minutes (retrograde, or down the ostia), or as the solution in use requires.

Evidence: the choice follows the physiology rather than trials; retrograde perfusion reaches the right ventricle less well, which is one reason many combine retrograde with direct ostial doses.

ask.question: Severe aortic regurgitation. After the cross-clamp, antegrade root cardioplegia is started and the LV swells while the heart keeps beating. Next?

choices.text: Stop the root infusion, vent the LV, open the aorta and give cardioplegia directly into the ostia (and/or retrograde)
choices.why: Root cardioplegia is going through the incompetent valve into the LV, not down the coronaries. Distension injures the myocardium.

choices.text: Cool further and wait for arrest

steps.title: Oblique aortotomy into the non-coronary sinus
steps.body:
Find the right coronary origin first. Open the aorta 1–1.5 cm above it, across the front, and carry the incision obliquely down into the non-coronary sinus toward its nadir ("hockey stick"). A transverse aortotomy above the STJ is the alternative, and is easier to close for a later root operation.

Stay above the right coronary and away from the left main on the other side. Stay sutures open the aorta; give ostial cardioplegia now if needed.

Evidence: the placement is technique by consensus (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes); the risks it avoids are right coronary injury and distortion of the sinuses and STJ when closing.

steps.title: Excise the cusps, debride the annulus, catch every fragment
steps.body:
Protect the LV: a moist sponge or gauze through the valve into the outflow tract, and the vent on. Excise the cusps 1–2 mm from their hinge, one cusp at a time.

Debride the calcium back to a pliable annulus so the sewing ring can sit flat, without leaks. The danger zones:

  • under the right and non-coronary commissure: the membranous septum and His bundle (heart block; a VSD if you go through);
  • under the left and non-coronary cusps: the aortomitral curtain (a hole into the left atrium; mitral damage);
  • the ostia: calcium near them is lifted out, not avulsed.

Remove the sponge, irrigate the LV and root with saline and suction, and look for loose fragments before sizing.

Evidence: stroke after SAVR is mostly embolic, and calcific debris is one source; catching and irrigating it is standard practice. Aggressive debridement near the membranous septum raises the risk of heart block and of annular disruption.

ask.question: While debriding, you take calcium from beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps and see the septum bulge. What is at risk?

choices.text: The His bundle (heart block) and the membranous septum (a VSD)
choices.why: That area is the membranous septum carrying the His bundle. Take less calcium there; a little residual calcium is safer than a VSD or heart block.

steps.title: Sondergaard's groove and the left atriotomy
steps.body: Develop Sondergaard's plane: the fat between the right atrium and the right pulmonary veins, back toward the septum, for 1–2 cm. Open the left atrium there, in front of the right pulmonary veins, extending up behind the SVC and down behind the IVC as needed. A self-retaining atrial retractor lifts the septum toward you.

steps.title: Excise the anterior leaflet; keep the posterior chordae
steps.body:
Inspect the valve. For replacement, excise the anterior leaflet (detach it 2–3 mm from the annulus, divide its chordae; some reattach anterior chordae to the annulus), preserve the posterior leaflet and its chordae: chordal sparing keeps left ventricular function and guards against rupture of the ventricle.

Debride calcium off the annulus carefully: deep debridement posteriorly risks AV groove disruption. Size the annulus with the valve sizers.

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
2-0 braided polyester horizontal mattress sutures, 12–16 of them. Where the pledgets sit decides where the valve sits, and the choice follows the quality of the annulus.

Ventricular pledgets (non-everting: needle from the LV side up through the annulus; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the strongest hold in friable, calcified, rheumatic or infected tissue, so fewer paravalvular leaks and dehiscences; the pledget spreads the load; supra-annular seating often takes one size larger.
Against: deeper, blinder bites (circumflex and AV groove posteriorly, AV node at the posteromedial commissure, aortic cusps anteriorly); pledgets and preserved chordae under the ring can trap a leaflet or seed pannus and thrombus; anterior pledgets can narrow the LVOT; awkward through a small LA or a MICS port.

Annulus-only (everting, with atrial pledgets, or unpledgeted; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: shallow bites you can see; nothing below the ring to catch a leaflet; LVOT clear; quicker; suits a healthy annulus and MICS.
Against: sutures can cut through poor tissue; the prosthesis is often a size smaller; unpledgeted sutures are the weakest.

A common compromise: ventricular pledgets posteriorly and at the commissures (where the tissue is worst and leaks happen), atrial pledgets anteriorly (to protect the aortic valve and LVOT).

Whatever the technique, bite in the annulus, not beyond it.

Evidence: no randomised trial compares everting and non-everting sutures in MVR. In the AVERT trial cohort, pledgeted sutures were associated with fewer major paravalvular leaks than unpledgeted ones (Englberger et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2005). The ACC/AHA 2020 and ESC/EACTS 2021 valve guidelines make no recommendation on suture technique, but support preserving the subvalvular apparatus in MVR (for LV function), and that is one more reason to keep pledgets clear of preserved chordae.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis with a heavily calcified, small posterior annulus. Which suture technique gives the most secure seat and the largest valve?

choices.text: Pledgeted mattress sutures with ventricular pledgets (non-everting, supra-annular), at least posteriorly
choices.why: Ventricular pledgets hold best in poor tissue and seat the ring above the annulus, which usually allows a larger size. Keep bites in the annulus to spare the circumflex and AV groove, and check that no pledget traps a leaflet.

choices.text: Everting sutures with atrial pledgets all round, one size smaller

steps.title: Size the mitral prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
The sizer tells you what the annulus takes; the patient's body size tells you what orifice they need. Too small a valve for the body is prosthesis–patient mismatch (PPM): persistent gradients, pulmonary hypertension and worse survival.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 2.3 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 1.2 cm²/m² to avoid PPM (severe if the indexed EOA is ≤0.9)
  3. Choose the smallest size whose reference EOA on the manufacturer's chart reaches it
ProblemOptions
Small annulus, small rheumatic womanA valve with a larger EOA for its size; preserve the posterior chordae and seat it well; avoid forcing an oversized valve
ChildCheck size / weight: a high ratio predicts early death (LVOT obstruction, circumflex and conduction injury). Supra-annular placement of a too-large valve worsens survival. Small 15–17 mm valves will need replacing as the child grows

Evidence: Magne et al., Circulation 2007: mitral PPM (indexed EOA ≤1.2 cm²/m²; severe ≤0.9) reduced survival after MVR. ICVTS 2024 (children): median prosthesis size/weight about 1.7 mm/kg; oversizing and supra-annular placement linked to death; 44–65% of 15–17 mm mechanical valves replaced within years.

ask.question: A 1.40 m² rheumatic patient: what reference EOA must a mitral prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the prosthesis and tie
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring in order, lower the valve down the sutures onto the annulus and tie. For a bileaflet mechanical valve, the usual orientation is anti-anatomical (hinges perpendicular to the natural commissures).

Check that both leaflets open and close fully: nothing trapped (preserved chordae, a long suture tail, pledget).

ask.question: After seating a mechanical mitral valve, the most important check before closing the atrium is…

choices.why: Preserved chordae, suture tails or pledgets can trap a leaflet; fix it now, not after the clamp is off.

choices.text: That the LA appendage is closed
That the sutures are cut short

steps.title: Size, and avoid patient–prosthesis mismatch
steps.body:
Measure the annulus with the sizers made for the chosen valve (sizes differ between makers). The question is not only "what fits" but whether the valve's effective orifice area indexed to body surface area (EOAi) will be big enough for this patient.

Patient–prosthesis mismatch (VARC-3), BMI under 30: moderate at EOAi 0.85–0.66, severe at 0.65 cm²/m² or less. BMI 30 or more: moderate 0.70–0.56, severe 0.55 or less. Look up the valve's expected EOA before choosing.

If the annulus is too small:

  • a valve with a better orifice for its size (supra-annular, thin-sewing-ring, or stentless);
  • annular enlargement: Nicks (through the non-coronary sinus toward the aortomitral curtain), Manouguian (through the left–non-coronary commissure into the curtain and the anterior mitral leaflet), Y-incision (Yang: through the left–non-coronary commissure with a Y into both trigones, allowing about 3–4 sizes larger). The Konno operation (into the septum) is mainly for children.

Evidence: VARC-3 (Généreux et al., JACC 2021) sets the definitions. In a meta-analysis of about 123,000 patients (J Am Heart Assoc 2024), mismatch after SAVR was associated with higher late mortality and earlier failure of tissue valves. The Y-incision series (Yang et al., JTCVS) reported enlargement by 3–4 sizes with low early mortality; these are single-centre, non-randomised data.

ask.question: A 1.9 m² patient (BMI 26). The largest valve that fits has an expected EOA of 1.2 cm². What is the predicted mismatch, and what should you consider?

choices.text: EOAi 0.63: severe mismatch; consider annular enlargement or a valve with a larger orifice
choices.why: 1.2 / 1.9 = 0.63 cm²/m², which is 0.65 or less: severe by VARC-3 (BMI under 30).

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
Usually 12–15 sutures of 2-0 braided polyester, following the crown: up to the commissures, down to the nadirs. Where they sit decides where the valve sits.

Non-everting mattress, pledgets below (on the LV side; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the usual technique for supra-annular valves; pledgets spread the load in calcified or fragile tissue; the largest valve for the annulus.
Against: pledgets sit in the outflow tract; the bites below the right–non-coronary commissure are near the His bundle.

Everting mattress, pledgets above (on the aortic side; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: nothing below the annulus; everts the tissue for a good seal.
Against: the ring sits inside the annulus, so the valve is often a size smaller: a mismatch risk in a small root.

Simple interrupted (no pledgets)
For: less material on the annulus, so the valve seats deeper and opens more. Against: no buttress in poor tissue.

Continuous polypropylene
For: fast. Against: one weak point can loosen the whole line; not for calcified or infected annuli.

Keep pledgets and sutures clear of the ostia; take shallow bites under the right–non-coronary commissure.

Evidence: no randomised trial has settled this. In the AVERT cohort (807 patients), major paravalvular leak occurred in 1.7% with pledgets and 5.8% without (Englberger et al., EJCTS 2005). A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 observational SAVR studies (4,390 patients; Boltje et al.) found no clear difference in leak, gradients or mortality, and concluded that the evidence neither supports nor opposes pledgets. In 152 patients with small (19–21 mm) supra-annular bioprostheses, simple interrupted sutures gave a larger orifice and less mismatch than mattress sutures (Tabata et al., JTCVS 2014; retrospective).

ask.question: An elderly woman with a heavily calcified 19 mm annulus, receiving a supra-annular bioprosthesis. Which suture choice best balances sealing and orifice size?

choices.text: Pledgeted non-everting mattress sutures (supra-annular), or simple interrupted where the tissue holds
choices.why: Supra-annular seating gives the largest valve. Pledgets protect calcified tissue from cutting through; simple interrupted bites (Tabata) gain orifice where the tissue is sound. Everting sutures would push the valve intra-annular and a size down.

steps.title: Size the aortic prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
A valve that fits the annulus can still be too small for the patient. Aortic prosthesis–patient mismatch leaves a gradient, less LV mass regression and worse long-term outcomes.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 1.48 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 0.85 cm²/m² (BMI 30 or more: × 0.70) to avoid PPM; severe if ≤0.65 (≤0.55 when obese)
  3. Pick the smallest size whose reference EOA reaches it on the manufacturer's chart
If the projected EOA is too smallOptions
Different prosthesisA supra-annular or stentless bioprosthesis, or a newer mechanical valve with a larger EOA for the same size
Enlarge the rootPosterior annular enlargement (Nicks, Manouguian or a Y-incision) to take one or two sizes more
Older or high-risk patientTranscatheter options where available

Evidence: Hahn & Pibarot 2024 (VARC-3 categories): moderate PPM indexed EOA 0.85–0.66, severe ≤0.65 cm²/m²; with BMI ≥30, moderate 0.70–0.56, severe ≤0.55; predicted EOAi from reference EOA ÷ BSA guides valve choice before implantation.

ask.question: A 1.70 m², BMI 24 adult: what reference EOA must an aortic prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the valve; check the ostia and the leaflets
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring and lower the valve. For a stented tissue valve, line the three posts up with the native commissures, so that no post faces a coronary ostium. Tie, with even tension, the ring seated flat.

Before closing: look into both ostia (nothing overhanging); check for gaps under the ring; check that the leaflets move freely (for a mechanical valve, rotate it to free them of the septum).

Evidence: coronary obstruction after SAVR is rare but often fatal; it is prevented by post orientation and direct inspection. Post-bypass TOE confirms leaflet motion, gradient and paravalvular leak (ASE/SCA guidance).

ask.question: After weaning, new ST elevation in the anterolateral leads and poor anterior wall motion on TOE. The valve looks well seated. First suspicion?

choices.text: The left main ostium is partly obstructed by a post, a pledget or the sewing ring (or has embolised air/debris)
choices.why: Coronary compromise right after SAVR is the prosthesis or embolism until proved otherwise: go back on bypass, inspect, and re-seat or graft.

steps.title: Close the left atrium, then the aorta; de-air
steps.body:
Close the left atriotomy first (LV vent across the mitral prosthesis until the last suture), then the aortotomy.

Close the aortotomy in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene (a horizontal mattress, then over-and-over), with felt strips if the wall is thin. Before the last sutures: fill the heart, ventilate the lungs, head down; the root vent on; release the clamp.

Early vs late de-airing is the same question as in mitral surgery, with less air because the left atrium was not opened: venting only until the clamp is off is quicker, but air trapped in the pulmonary veins and LV comes out later and goes up the right coronary (uppermost) or to the brain; keeping the root vent on while the heart ejects on partial bypass catches it. Stop when TOE shows no air, not by the clock.

Evidence: no trial compares de-airing strategies; CO₂ field flooding reduced microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004); a stroke benefit has not been shown.

steps.title: Reperfuse, wean, TOE, decannulate
steps.body:
Reperfuse on bypass until the heart is ready (about a third of the clamp time is a common rule of thumb; longer after a long clamp or with a thick, hypertrophied ventricle). Pace (epicardial wires) if there is heart block: it often recovers over days.

TOE after bypass: prosthesis gradient and leaflet motion, paravalvular leak, new regional wall-motion abnormality (ostia), mitral function, and, in a small hypertrophied LV, outflow obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet (treat with volume and beta-blockade; stop inotropes).

Then venous cannula out, protamine, arterial cannula out last.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE is standard in valve surgery (ASE/SCA guidelines). A leak more than mild on TOE is usually repaired before leaving theatre, because significant paravalvular leak is associated with haemolysis, heart failure and worse survival.

ask.question: After AVR for severe AS (small, thick LV), the patient becomes hypotensive on adrenaline. TOE: hyperdynamic LV, mitral leaflet touching the septum in systole, high LVOT gradient. Treatment?

choices.text: Stop inotropes, give volume, a beta-blocker or phenylephrine
choices.why: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet, which inotropes worsen. Fill, slow and constrict.

choices.text: Go back on bypass and replace the mitral valve

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heart block (conduction tissue beside the annulus): test wires; pacemaker if block persists
  • Hypertrophied ventricle: keep filled, avoid tachycardia
  • Mechanical valve: enoxaparin, warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After AVR, complete heart block: the epicardial wires are not capturing. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant; increase output, check connections, prepare transcutaneous pacing
choices.why: Loss of capture in complete heart block is an emergency.

avr-hemi.name: Aortic valve replacement
avr-hemi.approach: Older patient, calcific AS, TAVI unsuitable (hemisternotomy)
avr-hemi.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the Heart Team decision, then the operation (access, bypass and protection, aortotomy, debridement, sizing, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing, TOE).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: calcific aortic stenosis
steps.body:
How the valve calcifies. Years of mechanical stress injure the endothelium on the aortic side of the cusps; lipids (LDL, lipoprotein(a)) enter and oxidise; macrophages and T cells follow; and the valve interstitial cells switch to a bone-forming programme (RUNX2), laying calcium nodules in the cusp bodies. The commissures stay open; the cusps become stiff. It is a disease of later life, sharing risk factors with atherosclerosis.

Aortic valve area ↓→LV pressure overload→Concentric hypertrophy→O₂ demand ↑, coronary reserve ↓ → angina
Fixed outflow→Exercise vasodilatation→Pressure falls → exertional syncope
Stiff, thick LV→Filling depends on the atrial kick→Diastolic, then systolic failure → breathlessness

Once symptoms appear, the clock runs fast: without valve replacement, average survival is a few years (shortest after heart failure). No drug slows the valve: lipid lowering did not change progression in trials. So the treatment of severe symptomatic AS is mechanical: SAVR or TAVI.

Severe AS: aortic valve area under 1.0 cm², mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more (with low-flow variants that need extra testing).

Evidence: natural history: Ross and Braunwald, Circulation 1968 (angina, syncope, heart failure as the turning points). SEAS (NEJM 2008): simvastatin plus ezetimibe did not reduce aortic valve events. Mechanisms from human valve studies of calcific aortic valve disease.

ask.question: Why does exertional syncope occur in severe aortic stenosis?

choices.text: Exercise dilates peripheral vessels, but the narrowed valve cannot increase output to match, so pressure falls
choices.why: Cardiac output is fixed by the valve; vasodilatation drops the blood pressure and cerebral perfusion. Arrhythmia can also contribute.

choices.text: The coronary arteries go into spasm

steps.title: The aortic root and what lies around it
steps.body:
The cusps do not hinge on a flat ring but on a three-pronged crown: low at each nadir (the virtual basal ring, which is what echo and CT call the annulus) and high at the three commissures, just below the sinotubular junction.

What the sutures and the debridement can injure:

  • Coronary ostia: the left main in the left sinus, the right coronary in the right sinus, usually 1–1.5 cm above the annulus. Keep prosthesis posts and pledgets clear of them.
  • Membranous septum and His bundle: below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Deep bites or aggressive decalcification here cause complete heart block.
  • Anterior mitral leaflet: below the left and non-coronary cusps, through the fibrous aortomitral curtain. Deep bites there distort the mitral valve.

Evidence: the crown-shaped annulus and its relations are from anatomical and CT studies of the root; conduction injury is the main cause of the permanent pacemakers needed after surgical AVR.

ask.question: A deep annular suture below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps is most likely to cause…

choices.why: The His bundle runs in the membranous septum just below that commissure.

steps.title: Case: an older patient with calcific aortic stenosis
steps.lead: A 74-year-old woman, retired nurse, exertional chest tightness and a presyncopal episode. Echo: tricuspid calcific AS, AVA 0.7 cm², mean gradient 48 mmHg, EF 60%; no other valve disease. Coronary angiography: no significant disease. CT: annulus 20 mm, left main ostium 8 mm above the annulus with shallow sinuses; small, calcified iliofemoral arteries (4.5 mm). Surgical risk low (STS 2.4%).
steps.body:
The default at 74 with tricuspid AS and suitable anatomy is TAVI (ESC/EACTS 2025, class I from 70 years). But her anatomy is not suitable: a low left main with shallow sinuses risks coronary obstruction by the displaced native cusp, and the femoral route is poor. The Heart Team recommends SAVR, which also allows the largest valve for a small annulus (avoiding mismatch).

Valve: a bioprosthesis at 74 (no warfarin; valve-in-valve possible later). Access: upper hemisternotomy, since the operation is isolated AVR.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2025: TAVI (class I) at 70 or over with tricuspid AS and suitable anatomy; SAVR (class I) under 70 at low risk. PARTNER 3 and Evolut Low Risk (NEJM 2019) enrolled patients with suitable anatomy only. Coronary obstruction after TAVI is rare but often fatal; low coronary height (under about 10–12 mm) and shallow sinuses are the main CT predictors (Ribeiro et al., JACC 2013).

ask.question: At 74 with severe tricuspid AS, what makes SAVR preferable to TAVI for this patient?

choices.text: Anatomy: a low left main ostium with shallow sinuses (coronary obstruction risk) and poor femoral access
choices.why: Age favours TAVI, but the Heart Team decides on anatomy too; when TAVI anatomy is hostile and surgical risk is low, SAVR is the safer choice.

choices.text: The aortic valve area of 0.7 cm²

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding
  • AF
  • Wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
  • Paravalvular leak

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical versus tissue valve: warfarin against durability
  • Patient–prosthesis mismatch with a small annulus

5. Alternatives

  • TAVI where available and suitable
  • Balloon valvotomy as a bridge
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR access
  • Penicillin prophylaxis if rheumatic
  • Cost

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which AVR risk is specific to the valve's position next to the conduction system?

choices.text: Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The His bundle runs beneath the non-coronary/right-coronary commissure.

steps.title: Upper hemisternotomy (J into the right 3rd or 4th space)
steps.body:
A 6–8 cm skin incision from just below the sternal notch. Saw the sternum in the midline from the notch down to the 3rd or 4th space (choose from CT: the level of the root), then turn the cut out into that space on the right ("J"). Watch the right internal thoracic vessels at the J. The lower sternum stays whole.

Central cannulation is usually possible: the aorta directly, and venous drainage either through the right atrial appendage or percutaneously from the femoral vein under TOE. Convert to full sternotomy (extend the cut) if exposure is poor or there is bleeding.

Evidence: randomised trials and meta-analyses comparing hemisternotomy with full sternotomy show similar mortality and valve results. Differences in bleeding, ventilation and stay are small and inconsistent, and cross-clamp and bypass times are slightly longer.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta, two-stage venous cannula (RA to IVC), LV vent
steps.body:
Heparin (ACT above 480 s). Arterial cannula in the distal ascending aorta, high enough to leave room for the clamp and an aortotomy below it. For isolated AVR the right atrium is not opened, so venous drainage is by a single two-stage (cavoatrial) cannula: in through a purse-string on the right atrial appendage, its tip passed down into the IVC. The tip drains the IVC, the side holes (the second stage) sit in the right atrium and drain the SVC return. It cannot be snared, so it is not used when the right atrium must be opened (mitral, tricuspid, septal defects: use two caval cannulas).

Root cardioplegia and vent line; a retrograde cannula in the coronary sinus; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein, placed before the heart slows if there is aortic regurgitation, so the ventricle never distends.

Evidence: this is standard practice (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes). A regurgitant valve lets cardioplegia and bypass return fill the arrested LV; distension damages the myocardium, which is why the vent goes in early.

steps.title: Cross-clamp; cardioplegia depends on the valve
steps.body:
On full bypass, clamp the ascending aorta below the arterial cannula.

  • Aortic stenosis, competent valve: antegrade into the root arrests the heart.
  • Aortic regurgitation: antegrade into the root runs into the LV and distends it instead of perfusing the coronaries. Give it retrograde, and/or open the aorta and give it directly into each ostium with hand-held cannulas.

Repeat every 15–20 minutes (retrograde, or down the ostia), or as the solution in use requires.

Evidence: the choice follows the physiology rather than trials; retrograde perfusion reaches the right ventricle less well, which is one reason many combine retrograde with direct ostial doses.

ask.question: Severe aortic regurgitation. After the cross-clamp, antegrade root cardioplegia is started and the LV swells while the heart keeps beating. Next?

choices.text: Stop the root infusion, vent the LV, open the aorta and give cardioplegia directly into the ostia (and/or retrograde)
choices.why: Root cardioplegia is going through the incompetent valve into the LV, not down the coronaries. Distension injures the myocardium.

choices.text: Cool further and wait for arrest

steps.title: Oblique aortotomy into the non-coronary sinus
steps.body:
Find the right coronary origin first. Open the aorta 1–1.5 cm above it, across the front, and carry the incision obliquely down into the non-coronary sinus toward its nadir ("hockey stick"). A transverse aortotomy above the STJ is the alternative, and is easier to close for a later root operation.

Stay above the right coronary and away from the left main on the other side. Stay sutures open the aorta; give ostial cardioplegia now if needed.

Evidence: the placement is technique by consensus (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes); the risks it avoids are right coronary injury and distortion of the sinuses and STJ when closing.

steps.title: Excise the cusps, debride the annulus, catch every fragment
steps.body:
Protect the LV: a moist sponge or gauze through the valve into the outflow tract, and the vent on. Excise the cusps 1–2 mm from their hinge, one cusp at a time.

Debride the calcium back to a pliable annulus so the sewing ring can sit flat, without leaks. The danger zones:

  • under the right and non-coronary commissure: the membranous septum and His bundle (heart block; a VSD if you go through);
  • under the left and non-coronary cusps: the aortomitral curtain (a hole into the left atrium; mitral damage);
  • the ostia: calcium near them is lifted out, not avulsed.

Remove the sponge, irrigate the LV and root with saline and suction, and look for loose fragments before sizing.

Evidence: stroke after SAVR is mostly embolic, and calcific debris is one source; catching and irrigating it is standard practice. Aggressive debridement near the membranous septum raises the risk of heart block and of annular disruption.

ask.question: While debriding, you take calcium from beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps and see the septum bulge. What is at risk?

choices.text: The His bundle (heart block) and the membranous septum (a VSD)
choices.why: That area is the membranous septum carrying the His bundle. Take less calcium there; a little residual calcium is safer than a VSD or heart block.

steps.title: Size, and avoid patient–prosthesis mismatch
steps.body:
Measure the annulus with the sizers made for the chosen valve (sizes differ between makers). The question is not only "what fits" but whether the valve's effective orifice area indexed to body surface area (EOAi) will be big enough for this patient.

Patient–prosthesis mismatch (VARC-3), BMI under 30: moderate at EOAi 0.85–0.66, severe at 0.65 cm²/m² or less. BMI 30 or more: moderate 0.70–0.56, severe 0.55 or less. Look up the valve's expected EOA before choosing.

If the annulus is too small:

  • a valve with a better orifice for its size (supra-annular, thin-sewing-ring, or stentless);
  • annular enlargement: Nicks (through the non-coronary sinus toward the aortomitral curtain), Manouguian (through the left–non-coronary commissure into the curtain and the anterior mitral leaflet), Y-incision (Yang: through the left–non-coronary commissure with a Y into both trigones, allowing about 3–4 sizes larger). The Konno operation (into the septum) is mainly for children.

Evidence: VARC-3 (Généreux et al., JACC 2021) sets the definitions. In a meta-analysis of about 123,000 patients (J Am Heart Assoc 2024), mismatch after SAVR was associated with higher late mortality and earlier failure of tissue valves. The Y-incision series (Yang et al., JTCVS) reported enlargement by 3–4 sizes with low early mortality; these are single-centre, non-randomised data.

ask.question: A 1.9 m² patient (BMI 26). The largest valve that fits has an expected EOA of 1.2 cm². What is the predicted mismatch, and what should you consider?

choices.text: EOAi 0.63: severe mismatch; consider annular enlargement or a valve with a larger orifice
choices.why: 1.2 / 1.9 = 0.63 cm²/m², which is 0.65 or less: severe by VARC-3 (BMI under 30).

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
Usually 12–15 sutures of 2-0 braided polyester, following the crown: up to the commissures, down to the nadirs. Where they sit decides where the valve sits.

Non-everting mattress, pledgets below (on the LV side; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the usual technique for supra-annular valves; pledgets spread the load in calcified or fragile tissue; the largest valve for the annulus.
Against: pledgets sit in the outflow tract; the bites below the right–non-coronary commissure are near the His bundle.

Everting mattress, pledgets above (on the aortic side; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: nothing below the annulus; everts the tissue for a good seal.
Against: the ring sits inside the annulus, so the valve is often a size smaller: a mismatch risk in a small root.

Simple interrupted (no pledgets)
For: less material on the annulus, so the valve seats deeper and opens more. Against: no buttress in poor tissue.

Continuous polypropylene
For: fast. Against: one weak point can loosen the whole line; not for calcified or infected annuli.

Keep pledgets and sutures clear of the ostia; take shallow bites under the right–non-coronary commissure.

Evidence: no randomised trial has settled this. In the AVERT cohort (807 patients), major paravalvular leak occurred in 1.7% with pledgets and 5.8% without (Englberger et al., EJCTS 2005). A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 observational SAVR studies (4,390 patients; Boltje et al.) found no clear difference in leak, gradients or mortality, and concluded that the evidence neither supports nor opposes pledgets. In 152 patients with small (19–21 mm) supra-annular bioprostheses, simple interrupted sutures gave a larger orifice and less mismatch than mattress sutures (Tabata et al., JTCVS 2014; retrospective).

ask.question: An elderly woman with a heavily calcified 19 mm annulus, receiving a supra-annular bioprosthesis. Which suture choice best balances sealing and orifice size?

choices.text: Pledgeted non-everting mattress sutures (supra-annular), or simple interrupted where the tissue holds
choices.why: Supra-annular seating gives the largest valve. Pledgets protect calcified tissue from cutting through; simple interrupted bites (Tabata) gain orifice where the tissue is sound. Everting sutures would push the valve intra-annular and a size down.

steps.title: Size the aortic prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
A valve that fits the annulus can still be too small for the patient. Aortic prosthesis–patient mismatch leaves a gradient, less LV mass regression and worse long-term outcomes.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 1.48 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 0.85 cm²/m² (BMI 30 or more: × 0.70) to avoid PPM; severe if ≤0.65 (≤0.55 when obese)
  3. Pick the smallest size whose reference EOA reaches it on the manufacturer's chart
If the projected EOA is too smallOptions
Different prosthesisA supra-annular or stentless bioprosthesis, or a newer mechanical valve with a larger EOA for the same size
Enlarge the rootPosterior annular enlargement (Nicks, Manouguian or a Y-incision) to take one or two sizes more
Older or high-risk patientTranscatheter options where available

Evidence: Hahn & Pibarot 2024 (VARC-3 categories): moderate PPM indexed EOA 0.85–0.66, severe ≤0.65 cm²/m²; with BMI ≥30, moderate 0.70–0.56, severe ≤0.55; predicted EOAi from reference EOA ÷ BSA guides valve choice before implantation.

ask.question: A 1.70 m², BMI 24 adult: what reference EOA must an aortic prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the valve; check the ostia and the leaflets
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring and lower the valve. For a stented tissue valve, line the three posts up with the native commissures, so that no post faces a coronary ostium. Tie, with even tension, the ring seated flat.

Before closing: look into both ostia (nothing overhanging); check for gaps under the ring; check that the leaflets move freely (for a mechanical valve, rotate it to free them of the septum).

Evidence: coronary obstruction after SAVR is rare but often fatal; it is prevented by post orientation and direct inspection. Post-bypass TOE confirms leaflet motion, gradient and paravalvular leak (ASE/SCA guidance).

ask.question: After weaning, new ST elevation in the anterolateral leads and poor anterior wall motion on TOE. The valve looks well seated. First suspicion?

choices.text: The left main ostium is partly obstructed by a post, a pledget or the sewing ring (or has embolised air/debris)
choices.why: Coronary compromise right after SAVR is the prosthesis or embolism until proved otherwise: go back on bypass, inspect, and re-seat or graft.

steps.title: Close the aorta and de-air
steps.body:
Close the aortotomy in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene (a horizontal mattress, then over-and-over), with felt strips if the wall is thin. Before the last sutures: fill the heart, ventilate the lungs, head down; the root vent on; release the clamp.

Early vs late de-airing is the same question as in mitral surgery, with less air because the left atrium was not opened: venting only until the clamp is off is quicker, but air trapped in the pulmonary veins and LV comes out later and goes up the right coronary (uppermost) or to the brain; keeping the root vent on while the heart ejects on partial bypass catches it. Stop when TOE shows no air, not by the clock.

Through a mini-thoracotomy the heart cannot be handled, so CO₂ in the field and TOE-guided venting carry more weight.

Evidence: no trial compares de-airing strategies; CO₂ field flooding reduced microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004); a stroke benefit has not been shown.

steps.title: Reperfuse, wean, TOE, decannulate
steps.body:
Reperfuse on bypass until the heart is ready (about a third of the clamp time is a common rule of thumb; longer after a long clamp or with a thick, hypertrophied ventricle). Pace (epicardial wires) if there is heart block: it often recovers over days.

Then venous cannula out, protamine, arterial cannula out last.

choices.why: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet, which inotropes worsen. Fill, slow and constrict.
