avr-ramt.name: Aortic valve replacement
avr-ramt.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the Heart Team decision, then the operation (access, bypass and protection, aortotomy, debridement, sizing, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing, TOE).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: calcific aortic stenosis (bicuspid valve)
steps.body:
How the valve calcifies. Years of mechanical stress injure the endothelium on the aortic side of the cusps; lipids (LDL, lipoprotein(a)) enter and oxidise; macrophages and T cells follow; and the valve interstitial cells switch to a bone-forming programme (RUNX2), laying calcium nodules in the cusp bodies. The commissures stay open; the cusps become stiff. A bicuspid valve (about 1–2% of people) carries more stress on its two cusps and calcifies a decade or two earlier, and it comes with a weaker ascending aorta (aortopathy).

Aortic valve area ↓→LV pressure overload→Concentric hypertrophy→O₂ demand ↑, coronary reserve ↓ → angina
Fixed outflow→Exercise vasodilatation→Pressure falls → exertional syncope
Stiff, thick LV→Filling depends on the atrial kick→Diastolic, then systolic failure → breathlessness

Once symptoms appear, the clock runs fast: without valve replacement, average survival is a few years (shortest after heart failure). No drug slows the valve: lipid lowering did not change progression in trials. So the treatment of severe symptomatic AS is mechanical: SAVR or TAVI.

Severe AS: aortic valve area under 1.0 cm², mean gradient 40 mmHg or more, peak velocity 4 m/s or more (with low-flow variants that need extra testing).

Evidence: natural history: Ross and Braunwald, Circulation 1968 (angina, syncope, heart failure as the turning points). SEAS (NEJM 2008): simvastatin plus ezetimibe did not reduce aortic valve events. Mechanisms from human valve studies of calcific aortic valve disease.

ask.question: Why does exertional syncope occur in severe aortic stenosis?

choices.text: Exercise dilates peripheral vessels, but the narrowed valve cannot increase output to match, so pressure falls
choices.why: Cardiac output is fixed by the valve; vasodilatation drops the blood pressure and cerebral perfusion. Arrhythmia can also contribute.

choices.text: The coronary arteries go into spasm

steps.title: The aortic root and what lies around it
steps.body:
The cusps do not hinge on a flat ring but on a three-pronged crown: low at each nadir (the virtual basal ring, which is what echo and CT call the annulus) and high at the three commissures, just below the sinotubular junction.

What the sutures and the debridement can injure:

  • Coronary ostia: the left main in the left sinus, the right coronary in the right sinus, usually 1–1.5 cm above the annulus. Keep prosthesis posts and pledgets clear of them.
  • Membranous septum and His bundle: below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Deep bites or aggressive decalcification here cause complete heart block.
  • Anterior mitral leaflet: below the left and non-coronary cusps, through the fibrous aortomitral curtain. Deep bites there distort the mitral valve.

Evidence: the crown-shaped annulus and its relations are from anatomical and CT studies of the root; conduction injury is the main cause of the permanent pacemakers needed after surgical AVR.

ask.question: A deep annular suture below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps is most likely to cause…

choices.why: The His bundle runs in the membranous septum just below that commissure.

steps.title: Case: bicuspid aortic stenosis at 64
steps.lead: A 64-year-old businessman, breathless on exertion. Echo: bicuspid valve (fused right and left cusps with a raphe), heavily calcified; AVA 0.8 cm², mean gradient 55 mmHg, EF 58%. Ascending aorta 42 mm. Coronaries normal. CT: the ascending aorta lies mostly to the right of the sternum, close behind it. He wants to be back at work quickly and dislikes the idea of warfarin.
steps.body:
SAVR: he is under 70 at low risk (class I), and his valve is bicuspid, the anatomy TAVI trials excluded. The aorta is 42 mm: below the threshold for replacing it at AVR (45 mm or more with a bicuspid valve), so it is left and followed.

Valve: between 60 and 65 the choice is individual; he chooses a bioprosthesis, accepting a likely valve-in-valve later. Access: CT meets the criteria for a right anterior mini-thoracotomy.

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2025: SAVR recommended under 70 at low risk; TAVI may be considered in bicuspid stenosis only at increased surgical risk (class IIb, new). ACC/AHA 2022 aortic guideline: replacing the ascending aorta at AVR is reasonable at 4.5 cm or more with a bicuspid valve.

ask.question: Why is SAVR, rather than TAVI, the standard for this 64-year-old?

choices.text: He is under 70 at low surgical risk, and the valve is bicuspid
choices.why: Both favour surgery: ESC/EACTS 2025 recommend SAVR under 70 at low risk, and bicuspid valves were excluded from the low-risk TAVI trials.

choices.text: Bioprostheses cannot be implanted by TAVI

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding
  • AF
  • Wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
  • Paravalvular leak

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical versus tissue valve: warfarin against durability
  • Patient–prosthesis mismatch with a small annulus

5. Alternatives

  • TAVI where available and suitable
  • Balloon valvotomy as a bridge
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR access
  • Penicillin prophylaxis if rheumatic
  • Cost

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which AVR risk is specific to the valve's position next to the conduction system?

choices.text: Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The His bundle runs beneath the non-coronary/right-coronary commissure.

steps.title: Right anterior mini-thoracotomy: select on CT first
steps.body:
CT selection (Glauber and colleagues): more than half of the ascending aorta lies to the right of the right sternal border; the aorta is less than 10 cm from the sternum; and the aorta's angle to the midline is over 45°. If not, choose hemisternotomy.

A 5–6 cm incision in the right 2nd space from the sternal edge. Ligate the right internal thoracic vessels (or keep them); divide the 3rd costal cartilage for more room if needed. Femoral venous cannulation percutaneously, the arterial cannula in the ascending aorta directly (or femoral). CO₂ in the field; external defibrillator pads.

Evidence: criteria and technique from Miceli, Ferrarini and Glauber (Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2015). Large series and meta-analyses report mortality similar to sternotomy with longer clamp times. The evidence is mostly observational and from experienced centres.

steps.title: Cross-clamp; cardioplegia depends on the valve
steps.body:
Femoral venous and aortic cannulation are already in. On full bypass, clamp (through the incision, or a flexible clamp) the ascending aorta below the arterial cannula.

  • Aortic stenosis, competent valve: antegrade into the root arrests the heart.
  • Aortic regurgitation: antegrade into the root runs into the LV and distends it instead of perfusing the coronaries. Give it retrograde, and/or open the aorta and give it directly into each ostium with hand-held cannulas.

Repeat every 15–20 minutes (retrograde, or down the ostia), or as the solution in use requires.

Evidence: the choice follows the physiology rather than trials; retrograde perfusion reaches the right ventricle less well, which is one reason many combine retrograde with direct ostial doses.

ask.question: Severe aortic regurgitation. After the cross-clamp, antegrade root cardioplegia is started and the LV swells while the heart keeps beating. Next?

choices.text: Stop the root infusion, vent the LV, open the aorta and give cardioplegia directly into the ostia (and/or retrograde)
choices.why: Root cardioplegia is going through the incompetent valve into the LV, not down the coronaries. Distension injures the myocardium.

choices.text: Cool further and wait for arrest

steps.title: Oblique aortotomy into the non-coronary sinus
steps.body:
Find the right coronary origin first. Open the aorta 1–1.5 cm above it, across the front, and carry the incision obliquely down into the non-coronary sinus toward its nadir ("hockey stick"). A transverse aortotomy above the STJ is the alternative, and is easier to close for a later root operation.

Stay above the right coronary and away from the left main on the other side. Stay sutures open the aorta; give ostial cardioplegia now if needed.

Evidence: the placement is technique by consensus (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes); the risks it avoids are right coronary injury and distortion of the sinuses and STJ when closing.

steps.title: Excise the cusps, debride the annulus, catch every fragment
steps.body:
Protect the LV: a moist sponge or gauze through the valve into the outflow tract, and the vent on. Excise the cusps 1–2 mm from their hinge, one cusp at a time.

Debride the calcium back to a pliable annulus so the sewing ring can sit flat, without leaks. The danger zones:

  • under the right and non-coronary commissure: the membranous septum and His bundle (heart block; a VSD if you go through);
  • under the left and non-coronary cusps: the aortomitral curtain (a hole into the left atrium; mitral damage);
  • the ostia: calcium near them is lifted out, not avulsed.

Remove the sponge, irrigate the LV and root with saline and suction, and look for loose fragments before sizing.

Evidence: stroke after SAVR is mostly embolic, and calcific debris is one source; catching and irrigating it is standard practice. Aggressive debridement near the membranous septum raises the risk of heart block and of annular disruption.

ask.question: While debriding, you take calcium from beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps and see the septum bulge. What is at risk?

choices.text: The His bundle (heart block) and the membranous septum (a VSD)
choices.why: That area is the membranous septum carrying the His bundle. Take less calcium there; a little residual calcium is safer than a VSD or heart block.

steps.title: Size, and avoid patient–prosthesis mismatch
steps.body:
Measure the annulus with the sizers made for the chosen valve (sizes differ between makers). The question is not only "what fits" but whether the valve's effective orifice area indexed to body surface area (EOAi) will be big enough for this patient.

Patient–prosthesis mismatch (VARC-3), BMI under 30: moderate at EOAi 0.85–0.66, severe at 0.65 cm²/m² or less. BMI 30 or more: moderate 0.70–0.56, severe 0.55 or less. Look up the valve's expected EOA before choosing.

If the annulus is too small:

  • a valve with a better orifice for its size (supra-annular, thin-sewing-ring, or stentless);
  • annular enlargement: Nicks (through the non-coronary sinus toward the aortomitral curtain), Manouguian (through the left–non-coronary commissure into the curtain and the anterior mitral leaflet), Y-incision (Yang: through the left–non-coronary commissure with a Y into both trigones, allowing about 3–4 sizes larger). The Konno operation (into the septum) is mainly for children.

Through a mini-thoracotomy, a sutureless or rapid-deployment valve shortens the clamp time and needs few or no annular sutures.

Evidence: VARC-3 (Généreux et al., JACC 2021) sets the definitions. In a meta-analysis of about 123,000 patients (J Am Heart Assoc 2024), mismatch after SAVR was associated with higher late mortality and earlier failure of tissue valves. The Y-incision series (Yang et al., JTCVS) reported enlargement by 3–4 sizes with low early mortality; these are single-centre, non-randomised data. PERSIST-AVR (Fischlein et al., JTCVS 2021), a randomised trial, found a sutureless valve non-inferior to a stented one for major adverse events at one year, with more permanent pacemakers.

ask.question: A 1.9 m² patient (BMI 26). The largest valve that fits has an expected EOA of 1.2 cm². What is the predicted mismatch, and what should you consider?

choices.text: EOAi 0.63: severe mismatch; consider annular enlargement or a valve with a larger orifice
choices.why: 1.2 / 1.9 = 0.63 cm²/m², which is 0.65 or less: severe by VARC-3 (BMI under 30).

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
Usually 12–15 sutures of 2-0 braided polyester, following the crown: up to the commissures, down to the nadirs. Where they sit decides where the valve sits.

Non-everting mattress, pledgets below (on the LV side; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the usual technique for supra-annular valves; pledgets spread the load in calcified or fragile tissue; the largest valve for the annulus.
Against: pledgets sit in the outflow tract; the bites below the right–non-coronary commissure are near the His bundle.

Everting mattress, pledgets above (on the aortic side; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: nothing below the annulus; everts the tissue for a good seal.
Against: the ring sits inside the annulus, so the valve is often a size smaller: a mismatch risk in a small root.

Simple interrupted (no pledgets)
For: less material on the annulus, so the valve seats deeper and opens more. Against: no buttress in poor tissue.

Continuous polypropylene
For: fast. Against: one weak point can loosen the whole line; not for calcified or infected annuli.

Keep pledgets and sutures clear of the ostia; take shallow bites under the right–non-coronary commissure.

Evidence: no randomised trial has settled this. In the AVERT cohort (807 patients), major paravalvular leak occurred in 1.7% with pledgets and 5.8% without (Englberger et al., EJCTS 2005). A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 observational SAVR studies (4,390 patients; Boltje et al.) found no clear difference in leak, gradients or mortality, and concluded that the evidence neither supports nor opposes pledgets. In 152 patients with small (19–21 mm) supra-annular bioprostheses, simple interrupted sutures gave a larger orifice and less mismatch than mattress sutures (Tabata et al., JTCVS 2014; retrospective).

ask.question: An elderly woman with a heavily calcified 19 mm annulus, receiving a supra-annular bioprosthesis. Which suture choice best balances sealing and orifice size?

choices.text: Pledgeted non-everting mattress sutures (supra-annular), or simple interrupted where the tissue holds
choices.why: Supra-annular seating gives the largest valve. Pledgets protect calcified tissue from cutting through; simple interrupted bites (Tabata) gain orifice where the tissue is sound. Everting sutures would push the valve intra-annular and a size down.

steps.title: Size the aortic prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
A valve that fits the annulus can still be too small for the patient. Aortic prosthesis–patient mismatch leaves a gradient, less LV mass regression and worse long-term outcomes.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 1.48 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 0.85 cm²/m² (BMI 30 or more: × 0.70) to avoid PPM; severe if ≤0.65 (≤0.55 when obese)
  3. Pick the smallest size whose reference EOA reaches it on the manufacturer's chart
If the projected EOA is too smallOptions
Different prosthesisA supra-annular or stentless bioprosthesis, or a newer mechanical valve with a larger EOA for the same size
Enlarge the rootPosterior annular enlargement (Nicks, Manouguian or a Y-incision) to take one or two sizes more
Older or high-risk patientTranscatheter options where available

Evidence: Hahn & Pibarot 2024 (VARC-3 categories): moderate PPM indexed EOA 0.85–0.66, severe ≤0.65 cm²/m²; with BMI ≥30, moderate 0.70–0.56, severe ≤0.55; predicted EOAi from reference EOA ÷ BSA guides valve choice before implantation.

ask.question: A 1.70 m², BMI 24 adult: what reference EOA must an aortic prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the valve; check the ostia and the leaflets
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring and lower the valve. For a stented tissue valve, line the three posts up with the native commissures, so that no post faces a coronary ostium. Tie, with even tension, the ring seated flat.

Before closing: look into both ostia (nothing overhanging); check for gaps under the ring; check that the leaflets move freely (for a mechanical valve, rotate it to free them of the septum).

Evidence: coronary obstruction after SAVR is rare but often fatal; it is prevented by post orientation and direct inspection. Post-bypass TOE confirms leaflet motion, gradient and paravalvular leak (ASE/SCA guidance).

ask.question: After weaning, new ST elevation in the anterolateral leads and poor anterior wall motion on TOE. The valve looks well seated. First suspicion?

choices.text: The left main ostium is partly obstructed by a post, a pledget or the sewing ring (or has embolised air/debris)
choices.why: Coronary compromise right after SAVR is the prosthesis or embolism until proved otherwise: go back on bypass, inspect, and re-seat or graft.

steps.title: Close the aorta and de-air
steps.body:
Close the aortotomy in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene (a horizontal mattress, then over-and-over), with felt strips if the wall is thin. Before the last sutures: fill the heart, ventilate the lungs, head down; the root vent on; release the clamp.

Early vs late de-airing is the same question as in mitral surgery, with less air because the left atrium was not opened: venting only until the clamp is off is quicker, but air trapped in the pulmonary veins and LV comes out later and goes up the right coronary (uppermost) or to the brain; keeping the root vent on while the heart ejects on partial bypass catches it. Stop when TOE shows no air, not by the clock.

Through a mini-thoracotomy the heart cannot be handled, so CO₂ in the field and TOE-guided venting carry more weight.

Evidence: no trial compares de-airing strategies; CO₂ field flooding reduced microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004); a stroke benefit has not been shown.

steps.title: Reperfuse, wean, TOE, decannulate
steps.body:
Reperfuse on bypass until the heart is ready (about a third of the clamp time is a common rule of thumb; longer after a long clamp or with a thick, hypertrophied ventricle). Pace (epicardial wires) if there is heart block: it often recovers over days.

TOE after bypass: prosthesis gradient and leaflet motion, paravalvular leak, new regional wall-motion abnormality (ostia), mitral function, and, in a small hypertrophied LV, outflow obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet (treat with volume and beta-blockade; stop inotropes).

Then venous cannula out, protamine, arterial cannula out last.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE is standard in valve surgery (ASE/SCA guidelines). A leak more than mild on TOE is usually repaired before leaving theatre, because significant paravalvular leak is associated with haemolysis, heart failure and worse survival.

ask.question: After AVR for severe AS (small, thick LV), the patient becomes hypotensive on adrenaline. TOE: hyperdynamic LV, mitral leaflet touching the septum in systole, high LVOT gradient. Treatment?

choices.text: Stop inotropes, give volume, a beta-blocker or phenylephrine
choices.why: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet, which inotropes worsen. Fill, slow and constrict.

choices.text: Go back on bypass and replace the mitral valve

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heart block (conduction tissue beside the annulus): test wires; pacemaker if block persists
  • Hypertrophied ventricle: keep filled, avoid tachycardia
  • Mechanical valve: enoxaparin, warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After AVR, complete heart block: the epicardial wires are not capturing. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant; increase output, check connections, prepare transcutaneous pacing
choices.why: Loss of capture in complete heart block is an emergency.

avr-ie.name: Aortic valve replacement
avr-ie.summary: Case-based: pathophysiology, anatomy, the patient and the Heart Team decision, then the operation (access, bypass and protection, aortotomy, debridement, sizing, sutures, prosthesis, de-airing, TOE).

steps.title: Pathophysiology: aortic endocarditis and root abscess
steps.body:
On the aortic valve the vegetation sits on the ventricular face of the cusps (the low-pressure side of the regurgitant jet). The infection perforates or tears the cusps (acute severe AR), and it can burrow into the annulus: a paravalvular abscess, typically in the aortomitral curtain and under the non-coronary sinus, next to the His bundle.

Vegetation→Cusp perforation → acute severe AR→Sudden volume load on a normal-sized LV→Pulmonary oedema, shock
Annular extension→Abscess, false aneurysm→Fistula (to the RA, LA, RV)→Heart block (the His bundle lies just below)

New PR prolongation or heart block in aortic endocarditis means the infection has reached the conduction tissue: an abscess until proved otherwise, and an indication for urgent surgery (uncontrolled infection). Staphylococcus aureus is the commonest cause of destructive, abscess-forming disease.

Evidence: ESC 2023 endocarditis guidelines (Delgado et al.): locally uncontrolled infection (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation) is an indication for urgent surgery. African data: Noubiap et al., Lancet Glob Health 2022.

ask.question: A patient with aortic endocarditis develops a PR interval of 280 ms, then complete heart block. What does it mean?

choices.text: The infection has extended into the annulus near the His bundle: a paravalvular abscess
choices.why: The conduction tissue lies just below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps; heart block signals annular extension and calls for urgent surgery.

choices.text: A vegetation on the mitral valve
Nothing specific: heart block is common in fever

steps.title: The aortic root and what lies around it
steps.body:
The cusps do not hinge on a flat ring but on a three-pronged crown: low at each nadir (the virtual basal ring, which is what echo and CT call the annulus) and high at the three commissures, just below the sinotubular junction.

What the sutures and the debridement can injure:

  • Coronary ostia: the left main in the left sinus, the right coronary in the right sinus, usually 1–1.5 cm above the annulus. Keep prosthesis posts and pledgets clear of them.
  • Membranous septum and His bundle: below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps. Deep bites or aggressive decalcification here cause complete heart block.
  • Anterior mitral leaflet: below the left and non-coronary cusps, through the fibrous aortomitral curtain. Deep bites there distort the mitral valve.

Evidence: the crown-shaped annulus and its relations are from anatomical and CT studies of the root; conduction injury is the main cause of the permanent pacemakers needed after surgical AVR.

ask.question: A deep annular suture below the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps is most likely to cause…

choices.why: The His bundle runs in the membranous septum just below that commissure.

steps.title: Case: aortic endocarditis with a root abscess
steps.lead: A 30-year-old man with known mild rheumatic AR, admitted with fever and rigors; three blood cultures grow Staphylococcus aureus despite 7 days of cloxacillin. The PR interval has lengthened from 180 to 300 ms. TOE: a 12 mm vegetation on the non-coronary cusp, a cusp perforation with severe AR, and an echolucent cavity in the aortomitral curtain. He is breathless but not in shock.
steps.body:
Indications (ESC 2023): uncontrolled infection (a paravalvular abscess; persistent bacteraemia on appropriate antibiotics) and severe AR with heart failure: urgent surgery, within days.

The operation: radical debridement of all infected tissue, closure of the abscess cavity (autologous or bovine pericardium), then valve replacement; if the root is destroyed, root replacement (homograft, or a composite graft or stentless root: see the Root module). Pacing wires: heart block may be permanent.

Evidence: ESC 2023: urgent surgery for locally uncontrolled infection (abscess, false aneurysm, fistula, enlarging vegetation) and for persistent positive cultures despite appropriate antibiotics. No prosthesis type (mechanical, biological, homograft) has been shown to reduce reinfection; complete debridement matters more than the choice of substitute.

ask.question: What makes this an urgent operation rather than completing 6 weeks of antibiotics first?

choices.text: Uncontrolled infection: a paravalvular abscess and persistent bacteraemia, with severe AR
choices.why: Abscess and persistent bacteraemia do not resolve on antibiotics alone; waiting risks fistula, complete heart block, embolism and death.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II (or STS PROM). Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding
  • AF
  • Wound infection
  • Kidney injury

3. Serious

  • Stroke
  • Death
  • Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
  • Paravalvular leak

4. Specific to this operation

  • Mechanical versus tissue valve: warfarin against durability
  • Patient–prosthesis mismatch with a small annulus

5. Alternatives

  • TAVI where available and suitable
  • Balloon valvotomy as a bridge
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR access
  • Penicillin prophylaxis if rheumatic
  • Cost

ask.question: Which AVR risk is specific to the valve's position next to the conduction system?

choices.text: Complete heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The His bundle runs beneath the non-coronary/right-coronary commissure.

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body:
Median sternotomy; open the pericardium and hitch it up. Look at the ascending aorta (size, calcification by palpation or epiaortic scan) before choosing the cannulation and clamp sites.

Evidence: epiaortic scanning finds atheroma that palpation misses; it changes cannulation or clamp site in a proportion of patients.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta, two-stage venous cannula (RA to IVC), LV vent
steps.body:
Heparin (ACT above 480 s). Arterial cannula in the distal ascending aorta, high enough to leave room for the clamp and an aortotomy below it. For isolated AVR the right atrium is not opened, so venous drainage is by a single two-stage (cavoatrial) cannula: in through a purse-string on the right atrial appendage, its tip passed down into the IVC. The tip drains the IVC, the side holes (the second stage) sit in the right atrium and drain the SVC return. It cannot be snared, so it is not used when the right atrium must be opened (mitral, tricuspid, septal defects: use two caval cannulas).

Root cardioplegia and vent line; a retrograde cannula in the coronary sinus; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein, placed before the heart slows if there is aortic regurgitation, so the ventricle never distends.

Evidence: this is standard practice (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes). A regurgitant valve lets cardioplegia and bypass return fill the arrested LV; distension damages the myocardium, which is why the vent goes in early.

steps.title: Cross-clamp; cardioplegia depends on the valve
steps.body:
On full bypass, clamp the ascending aorta below the arterial cannula.

  • Aortic stenosis, competent valve: antegrade into the root arrests the heart.
  • Aortic regurgitation: antegrade into the root runs into the LV and distends it instead of perfusing the coronaries. Give it retrograde, and/or open the aorta and give it directly into each ostium with hand-held cannulas.

Repeat every 15–20 minutes (retrograde, or down the ostia), or as the solution in use requires.

Evidence: the choice follows the physiology rather than trials; retrograde perfusion reaches the right ventricle less well, which is one reason many combine retrograde with direct ostial doses.

ask.question: Severe aortic regurgitation. After the cross-clamp, antegrade root cardioplegia is started and the LV swells while the heart keeps beating. Next?

choices.text: Stop the root infusion, vent the LV, open the aorta and give cardioplegia directly into the ostia (and/or retrograde)
choices.why: Root cardioplegia is going through the incompetent valve into the LV, not down the coronaries. Distension injures the myocardium.

choices.text: Cool further and wait for arrest

steps.title: Oblique aortotomy into the non-coronary sinus
steps.body:
Find the right coronary origin first. Open the aorta 1–1.5 cm above it, across the front, and carry the incision obliquely down into the non-coronary sinus toward its nadir ("hockey stick"). A transverse aortotomy above the STJ is the alternative, and is easier to close for a later root operation.

Stay above the right coronary and away from the left main on the other side. Stay sutures open the aorta; give ostial cardioplegia now if needed.

Evidence: the placement is technique by consensus (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes); the risks it avoids are right coronary injury and distortion of the sinuses and STJ when closing.

steps.title: Excise the cusps, debride the annulus, catch every fragment
steps.body:
Protect the LV: a moist sponge or gauze through the valve into the outflow tract, and the vent on. Excise the cusps 1–2 mm from their hinge, one cusp at a time.

Debride the calcium back to a pliable annulus so the sewing ring can sit flat, without leaks. The danger zones:

  • under the right and non-coronary commissure: the membranous septum and His bundle (heart block; a VSD if you go through);
  • under the left and non-coronary cusps: the aortomitral curtain (a hole into the left atrium; mitral damage);
  • the ostia: calcium near them is lifted out, not avulsed.

Remove the sponge, irrigate the LV and root with saline and suction, and look for loose fragments before sizing.

Evidence: stroke after SAVR is mostly embolic, and calcific debris is one source; catching and irrigating it is standard practice. Aggressive debridement near the membranous septum raises the risk of heart block and of annular disruption.

Here: lift the vegetation out whole with the non-coronary cusp and send both for culture; do not let fragments fall into the LV.

ask.question: While debriding, you take calcium from beneath the commissure between the right and non-coronary cusps and see the septum bulge. What is at risk?

choices.text: The His bundle (heart block) and the membranous septum (a VSD)
choices.why: That area is the membranous septum carrying the His bundle. Take less calcium there; a little residual calcium is safer than a VSD or heart block.

steps.title: Radical debridement of the abscess
steps.body:
With the cusps out, find the abscess: here in the aortomitral curtain under the non-coronary and left sinuses. Unroof it, then debride to healthy, bleeding tissue, removing all necrotic and infected material; send it for culture, histology and PCR. Irrigate (dilute povidone-iodine or saline); change gloves and instruments.

Respect what lies close: the His bundle below the right/non-coronary commissure, the anterior mitral leaflet below the curtain, the left main ostium above. Incomplete debridement is the main cause of recurrent infection and paravalvular leak.

Evidence: surgical principles from the ESC 2023 guideline and the 2025 EJCTS review of its surgical implications: complete debridement first; the reconstruction is chosen after the extent of destruction is seen.

ask.question: What is the commonest cause of recurrent infection after surgery for aortic root abscess?

choices.why: Residual infected tissue seeds the new prosthesis; the extent of debridement, not the choice of valve, determines reinfection.

steps.title: Close the cavity; patch or replace the root
steps.body:
A localised cavity: close it with a patch of glutaraldehyde-fixed autologous or bovine pericardium, sewn to healthy tissue with running 4-0 polypropylene, so that the new valve sits on the patch and healthy annulus rather than in infected space. Then size and implant the valve as usual, with pledgeted sutures in sound tissue.

Extensive destruction (circumferential abscess, aorto-ventricular discontinuity, fistula): replace the root (an aortic homograft, whose anterior mitral leaflet can patch the curtain, or a composite valved graft or stentless root) with coronary buttons. The Root module shows these steps.

Evidence: a homograft offers no proven advantage against reinfection over prosthetic roots (ESC 2023); it is chosen for its handling of destroyed tissue where available. Complete heart block after surgery for abscess often needs a permanent pacemaker; epicardial leads may be placed at the operation.

steps.title: Size, and avoid patient–prosthesis mismatch
steps.body:
Measure the annulus with the sizers made for the chosen valve (sizes differ between makers). The question is not only "what fits" but whether the valve's effective orifice area indexed to body surface area (EOAi) will be big enough for this patient.

Patient–prosthesis mismatch (VARC-3), BMI under 30: moderate at EOAi 0.85–0.66, severe at 0.65 cm²/m² or less. BMI 30 or more: moderate 0.70–0.56, severe 0.55 or less. Look up the valve's expected EOA before choosing.

If the annulus is too small:

  • a valve with a better orifice for its size (supra-annular, thin-sewing-ring, or stentless);
  • annular enlargement: Nicks (through the non-coronary sinus toward the aortomitral curtain), Manouguian (through the left–non-coronary commissure into the curtain and the anterior mitral leaflet), Y-incision (Yang: through the left–non-coronary commissure with a Y into both trigones, allowing about 3–4 sizes larger). The Konno operation (into the septum) is mainly for children.

Evidence: VARC-3 (Généreux et al., JACC 2021) sets the definitions. In a meta-analysis of about 123,000 patients (J Am Heart Assoc 2024), mismatch after SAVR was associated with higher late mortality and earlier failure of tissue valves. The Y-incision series (Yang et al., JTCVS) reported enlargement by 3–4 sizes with low early mortality; these are single-centre, non-randomised data.

ask.question: A 1.9 m² patient (BMI 26). The largest valve that fits has an expected EOA of 1.2 cm². What is the predicted mismatch, and what should you consider?

choices.text: EOAi 0.63: severe mismatch; consider annular enlargement or a valve with a larger orifice
choices.why: 1.2 / 1.9 = 0.63 cm²/m², which is 0.65 or less: severe by VARC-3 (BMI under 30).

steps.title: Annular sutures: which technique?
steps.body:
Usually 12–15 sutures of 2-0 braided polyester, following the crown: up to the commissures, down to the nadirs. Where they sit decides where the valve sits.

Non-everting mattress, pledgets below (on the LV side; the valve sits supra-annular)
For: the usual technique for supra-annular valves; pledgets spread the load in calcified or fragile tissue; the largest valve for the annulus.
Against: pledgets sit in the outflow tract; the bites below the right–non-coronary commissure are near the His bundle.

Everting mattress, pledgets above (on the aortic side; the valve sits intra-annular)
For: nothing below the annulus; everts the tissue for a good seal.
Against: the ring sits inside the annulus, so the valve is often a size smaller: a mismatch risk in a small root.

Simple interrupted (no pledgets)
For: less material on the annulus, so the valve seats deeper and opens more. Against: no buttress in poor tissue.

Continuous polypropylene
For: fast. Against: one weak point can loosen the whole line; not for calcified or infected annuli.

Keep pledgets and sutures clear of the ostia; take shallow bites under the right–non-coronary commissure.

Evidence: no randomised trial has settled this. In the AVERT cohort (807 patients), major paravalvular leak occurred in 1.7% with pledgets and 5.8% without (Englberger et al., EJCTS 2005). A 2024 meta-analysis of 9 observational SAVR studies (4,390 patients; Boltje et al.) found no clear difference in leak, gradients or mortality, and concluded that the evidence neither supports nor opposes pledgets. In 152 patients with small (19–21 mm) supra-annular bioprostheses, simple interrupted sutures gave a larger orifice and less mismatch than mattress sutures (Tabata et al., JTCVS 2014; retrospective).

ask.question: An elderly woman with a heavily calcified 19 mm annulus, receiving a supra-annular bioprosthesis. Which suture choice best balances sealing and orifice size?

choices.text: Pledgeted non-everting mattress sutures (supra-annular), or simple interrupted where the tissue holds
choices.why: Supra-annular seating gives the largest valve. Pledgets protect calcified tissue from cutting through; simple interrupted bites (Tabata) gain orifice where the tissue is sound. Everting sutures would push the valve intra-annular and a size down.

steps.title: Size the aortic prosthesis to the patient
steps.body:
A valve that fits the annulus can still be too small for the patient. Aortic prosthesis–patient mismatch leaves a gradient, less LV mass regression and worse long-term outcomes.

  1. Body surface area from height and weight (Haycock); the expected annulus is about 1.48 cm × √BSA (z-score norms)
  2. Minimum EOA = BSA × 0.85 cm²/m² (BMI 30 or more: × 0.70) to avoid PPM; severe if ≤0.65 (≤0.55 when obese)
  3. Pick the smallest size whose reference EOA reaches it on the manufacturer's chart
If the projected EOA is too smallOptions
Different prosthesisA supra-annular or stentless bioprosthesis, or a newer mechanical valve with a larger EOA for the same size
Enlarge the rootPosterior annular enlargement (Nicks, Manouguian or a Y-incision) to take one or two sizes more
Older or high-risk patientTranscatheter options where available

Evidence: Hahn & Pibarot 2024 (VARC-3 categories): moderate PPM indexed EOA 0.85–0.66, severe ≤0.65 cm²/m²; with BMI ≥30, moderate 0.70–0.56, severe ≤0.55; predicted EOAi from reference EOA ÷ BSA guides valve choice before implantation.

ask.question: A 1.70 m², BMI 24 adult: what reference EOA must an aortic prosthesis reach to avoid mismatch?

steps.title: Seat the valve; check the ostia and the leaflets
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the sewing ring and lower the valve. For a stented tissue valve, line the three posts up with the native commissures, so that no post faces a coronary ostium. Tie, with even tension, the ring seated flat.

Before closing: look into both ostia (nothing overhanging); check for gaps under the ring; check that the leaflets move freely (for a mechanical valve, rotate it to free them of the septum).

Evidence: coronary obstruction after SAVR is rare but often fatal; it is prevented by post orientation and direct inspection. Post-bypass TOE confirms leaflet motion, gradient and paravalvular leak (ASE/SCA guidance).

ask.question: After weaning, new ST elevation in the anterolateral leads and poor anterior wall motion on TOE. The valve looks well seated. First suspicion?

choices.text: The left main ostium is partly obstructed by a post, a pledget or the sewing ring (or has embolised air/debris)
choices.why: Coronary compromise right after SAVR is the prosthesis or embolism until proved otherwise: go back on bypass, inspect, and re-seat or graft.

steps.title: Close the aorta and de-air
steps.body:
Close the aortotomy in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene (a horizontal mattress, then over-and-over), with felt strips if the wall is thin. Before the last sutures: fill the heart, ventilate the lungs, head down; the root vent on; release the clamp.

Early vs late de-airing is the same question as in mitral surgery, with less air because the left atrium was not opened: venting only until the clamp is off is quicker, but air trapped in the pulmonary veins and LV comes out later and goes up the right coronary (uppermost) or to the brain; keeping the root vent on while the heart ejects on partial bypass catches it. Stop when TOE shows no air, not by the clock.

Evidence: no trial compares de-airing strategies; CO₂ field flooding reduced microemboli on TOE in a randomised trial (Svenarud et al., Circulation 2004); a stroke benefit has not been shown.

steps.title: Reperfuse, wean, TOE, decannulate
steps.body:
Reperfuse on bypass until the heart is ready (about a third of the clamp time is a common rule of thumb; longer after a long clamp or with a thick, hypertrophied ventricle). Pace (epicardial wires) if there is heart block: it often recovers over days.

TOE after bypass: prosthesis gradient and leaflet motion, paravalvular leak, new regional wall-motion abnormality (ostia), mitral function, and, in a small hypertrophied LV, outflow obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet (treat with volume and beta-blockade; stop inotropes).

Then venous cannula out, protamine, arterial cannula out last.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE is standard in valve surgery (ASE/SCA guidelines). A leak more than mild on TOE is usually repaired before leaving theatre, because significant paravalvular leak is associated with haemolysis, heart failure and worse survival.

This patient: atrioventricular pacing through epicardial wires from the start; if heart block persists, a permanent system once the infection is controlled.

ask.question: After AVR for severe AS (small, thick LV), the patient becomes hypotensive on adrenaline. TOE: hyperdynamic LV, mitral leaflet touching the septum in systole, high LVOT gradient. Treatment?

choices.text: Stop inotropes, give volume, a beta-blocker or phenylephrine
choices.why: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet, which inotropes worsen. Fill, slow and constrict.

choices.text: Go back on bypass and replace the mitral valve

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heart block (conduction tissue beside the annulus): test wires; pacemaker if block persists
  • Hypertrophied ventricle: keep filled, avoid tachycardia
  • Mechanical valve: enoxaparin, warfarin, INR at 72 h KNH practice

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After AVR, complete heart block: the epicardial wires are not capturing. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant; increase output, check connections, prepare transcutaneous pacing
choices.why: Loss of capture in complete heart block is an emergency.

root-bentall.name: Aortic root replacement
root-bentall.summary: Thresholds, choice of root operation, excision with coronary buttons, composite graft or pulmonary autograft, button reimplantation, distal anastomosis, homograft.

steps.title: The aortic root as a unit
steps.body:
The root runs from the ventricular attachment of the cusps (the annulus) to the sinotubular junction: the cusps, the three sinuses of Valsalva, the coronary ostia and the interleaflet triangles. In a root aneurysm the sinuses dilate and the STJ effaces, so replacing only the valve or only the tube above leaves diseased sinuses behind.

Evidence: the root as a functional unit is from Anderson's anatomical work and the Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes descriptions; the sinuses and the STJ shape how the cusps close, which is why valve-sparing operations restore them.

ask.question: Why is a Bentall (or valve-sparing root) needed for a root aneurysm rather than an AVR plus a supracoronary tube?

choices.text: The dilated sinuses would be left behind and keep enlarging
choices.why: In root disease the sinuses themselves are aneurysmal; a supracoronary graft leaves them in place to dilate or dissect.

choices.text: The coronary ostia are always too low
An AVR cannot be done in a large root

steps.title: Which root operation
steps.body:
When to replace the root (ACC/AHA 2022): sporadic aneurysm at 5.5 cm (5.0 cm is reasonable with an experienced surgeon), or with symptoms or rapid growth; bicuspid at 5.5 cm, at 5.0–5.4 cm with risk factors, and at 4.5 cm or more when the valve is being operated on anyway; Marfan at 5.0 cm (4.5 cm with a family history of dissection or rapid growth); Loeys–Dietz by variant, size and growth.

Which root operation:

  • Valve-sparing root replacement (David, Yacoub) when the cusps are good: no prosthesis, no warfarin. It needs experience.
  • Bentall (composite valved graft) when the valve is diseased: the reliable standard. Mechanical for the young with reliable INR monitoring, biological ("bio-Bentall") for the older.
  • Ross (pulmonary autograft) for selected young adults with aortic valve disease, at experienced centres.

Evidence: no randomised trial compares mechanical and biological Bentall; in a propensity-matched series of 1,112 patients (Pantaleo et al., EJCTS 2017), 5-year survival did not differ (84% vs 87%), with more reoperation after tissue valves and more bleeding after mechanical ones.

ask.question: A 45-year-old with a 5.6 cm root aneurysm and a severely stenotic bicuspid valve. What operation fits?

choices.text: A Bentall (mechanical composite graft, if INR monitoring is reliable)
choices.why: The root is past 5.5 cm and the valve is diseased, so valve-sparing is not an option; at 45 guidelines favour a mechanical valve if anticoagulation is safe.

ask.question: What should a Ross patient understand about reoperation?

choices.text: Both the autograft and the pulmonary homograft may need later intervention
choices.why: The Ross converts single-valve disease into two-valve disease.

choices.text: Only the mitral valve is at risk

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulate distally, vent, protect
steps.body:
The arterial cannula high: distal ascending aorta or arch, or the right axillary artery if the aorta is large up to the arch. A two-stage venous cannula; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein; retrograde cardioplegia in the coronary sinus.

Evidence: practice by consensus (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes): the whole root is replaced, so the cannula and clamp must sit above the diseased segment.

steps.title: Cross-clamp; cardioplegia depends on the valve
steps.body:
On full bypass, clamp the ascending aorta below the arterial cannula.

  • Aortic stenosis, competent valve: antegrade into the root arrests the heart.
  • Aortic regurgitation: antegrade into the root runs into the LV and distends it instead of perfusing the coronaries. Give it retrograde, and/or open the aorta and give it directly into each ostium with hand-held cannulas.

Repeat every 15–20 minutes (retrograde, or down the ostia), or as the solution in use requires.

Evidence: the choice follows the physiology rather than trials; retrograde perfusion reaches the right ventricle less well, which is one reason many combine retrograde with direct ostial doses.

ask.question: Severe aortic regurgitation. After the cross-clamp, antegrade root cardioplegia is started and the LV swells while the heart keeps beating. Next?

choices.text: Stop the root infusion, vent the LV, open the aorta and give cardioplegia directly into the ostia (and/or retrograde)
choices.why: Root cardioplegia is going through the incompetent valve into the LV, not down the coronaries. Distension injures the myocardium.

choices.text: Cool further and wait for arrest

steps.title: Transect, excise the sinuses, keep the coronary buttons
steps.body:
Cross-clamp high; cardioplegia retrograde and directly into the ostia once open. Transect the aorta above the STJ. Excise the valve and the sinus walls, leaving a 3–5 mm rim at the annulus and a button of sinus wall (5–8 mm) round each coronary ostium.

Mobilise each button just enough to reach the graft: the left main is short and lies behind the pulmonary trunk; the right coronary has branches (conus, RV branches) that tether it.

Evidence: the "open" button technique replaced the older inclusion and wrap methods, which were associated with pseudoaneurysms at the coronary suture lines. When buttons cannot be mobilised (redo, low ostia), a small interposition graft (Cabrol) is used.

action.label: Excise the root, keep the buttons

steps.title: Sew the composite graft to the annulus
steps.body:
Size the annulus. Place pledgeted horizontal mattress sutures round the annulus (non-everting, pledgets below, so the valve sits supra-annular), through the sewing ring of the composite graft, and tie. Shallow bites under the right–non-coronary commissure (His bundle).

The graft diameter is usually the annulus size plus a few millimetres, so the coronary buttons can be reached and the distal aorta matched.

Evidence: pledgeted interrupted sutures are the usual choice at the proximal line, where bleeding after the graft is in is hard to reach; there is no trial of techniques in root replacement.

steps.title: Reimplant the coronary buttons
steps.body:
Cut a hole in the graft (cautery) opposite each ostium. Sew each button end-to-side with running 5-0 polypropylene, often with a felt or pericardial strip on the outside. Left main first (lower, posterior). Place the right with the heart filled (release the vent briefly, or fill the root) so it is not too low, twisted or stretched.

Test each suture line (cardioplegia down the graft) before the distal anastomosis: afterwards the back of these suture lines is hard to reach.

Evidence: coronary button problems (kinking, tension, bleeding) are the main technical causes of early death and ischaemia after root replacement in series; positioning with the heart filled is standard advice.

ask.question: After a Bentall, the patient comes off bypass with inferior ST elevation and a failing RV. The left side looks fine. Most likely?

choices.text: The right coronary button is kinked or under tension
choices.why: The right button, placed too low or with the heart empty, kinks when the heart fills. Go back on bypass and redo it (or bypass the RCA).

steps.title: Distal anastomosis, de-air, check
steps.body:
Cut the graft to length and join it to the ascending aorta with running 4-0 polypropylene, often with a felt strip. De-air through the root vent in the graft, release the clamp, and check every suture line, especially the backs of the buttons.

TOE: valve function, regional wall motion in the left and right coronary territories, no leak. Bleeding is the other big risk: keep haemostatic agents and blood ready.

Evidence: bleeding and coronary problems dominate early morbidity after root replacement in large series (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes).

steps.title: Reperfuse, wean, TOE, decannulate
steps.body:
Reperfuse on bypass until the heart is ready (about a third of the clamp time is a common rule of thumb; longer after a long clamp or with a thick, hypertrophied ventricle). Pace (epicardial wires) if there is heart block: it often recovers over days.

TOE after bypass: prosthesis gradient and leaflet motion, paravalvular leak, new regional wall-motion abnormality (ostia), mitral function, and, in a small hypertrophied LV, outflow obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet (treat with volume and beta-blockade; stop inotropes).

Then venous cannula out, protamine, arterial cannula out last.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE is standard in valve surgery (ASE/SCA guidelines). A leak more than mild on TOE is usually repaired before leaving theatre, because significant paravalvular leak is associated with haemolysis, heart failure and worse survival.

choices.text: Stop inotropes, give volume, a beta-blocker or phenylephrine
choices.why: This is dynamic LVOT obstruction with systolic anterior motion of the mitral leaflet, which inotropes worsen. Fill, slow and constrict.

choices.text: Go back on bypass and replace the mitral valve

root-ross.name: Aortic root replacement
root-ross.summary: Thresholds, choice of root operation, excision with coronary buttons, composite graft or pulmonary autograft, button reimplantation, distal anastomosis, homograft.

steps.title: The aortic root as a unit and the pulmonary root beside it
steps.body:
The root runs from the ventricular attachment of the cusps (the annulus) to the sinotubular junction: the cusps, the three sinuses of Valsalva, the coronary ostia and the interleaflet triangles. In a root aneurysm the sinuses dilate and the STJ effaces, so replacing only the valve or only the tube above leaves diseased sinuses behind.

The pulmonary root lies in front and to the left, sharing a fascial plane with the aortic root. Behind it run the left main coronary and, beneath its posterior RVOT, the first septal perforator of the LAD. Both are at risk during harvest.

Evidence: the root as a functional unit is from Anderson's anatomical work and the Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes descriptions; the sinuses and the STJ shape how the cusps close, which is why valve-sparing operations restore them.

ask.question: Why is a Bentall (or valve-sparing root) needed for a root aneurysm rather than an AVR plus a supracoronary tube?

choices.text: The dilated sinuses would be left behind and keep enlarging
choices.why: In root disease the sinuses themselves are aneurysmal; a supracoronary graft leaves them in place to dilate or dissect.

choices.text: The coronary ostia are always too low
An AVR cannot be done in a large root

steps.title: Which root operation: is this patient for a Ross?
steps.body:
When to replace the root (ACC/AHA 2022): sporadic aneurysm at 5.5 cm (5.0 cm is reasonable with an experienced surgeon), or with symptoms or rapid growth; bicuspid at 5.5 cm, at 5.0–5.4 cm with risk factors, and at 4.5 cm or more when the valve is being operated on anyway; Marfan at 5.0 cm (4.5 cm with a family history of dissection or rapid growth); Loeys–Dietz by variant, size and growth.

Which root operation:

  • Valve-sparing root replacement (David, Yacoub) when the cusps are good: no prosthesis, no warfarin. It needs experience.
  • Bentall (composite valved graft) when the valve is diseased: the reliable standard. Mechanical for the young with reliable INR monitoring, biological ("bio-Bentall") for the older.
  • Ross (pulmonary autograft) for selected young adults with aortic valve disease, at experienced centres.

Ross: good candidates: young adults (typically under about 50–60) with a long life expectancy, active lives, women planning pregnancy (no warfarin). Cautions (EACTS consensus 2025): rheumatic valve disease, connective tissue disease, a dilated annulus or severe AR (dilatation risk), and a need for other valve surgery.

Rheumatic disease matters here: in 81 rheumatic Ross patients (mean age 29.5), freedom from autograft dysfunction was 65% under 30 vs 98.5% over 30, and explanted autografts showed rheumatic valvulitis.

Evidence: Ross: the one RCT (El-Hamamsy et al., Lancet 2010; 228 adults, mean age 38) found 10-year survival of 97% after the autograft vs 83% after a homograft root, and 99% vs 51% freedom from aortic valve reoperation at 13 years; survival matched the general population. ACC/AHA 2020 gives the Ross a class 2b recommendation in young adults, at experienced centres; ESC/EACTS 2025 calls it a valid alternative in well-selected young patients.

ask.question: A 24-year-old with rheumatic aortic regurgitation and mild mitral disease asks for the Ross operation. What does the evidence suggest?

choices.text: Rheumatic disease is a caution: the autograft can be affected and fail early; a mechanical valve (or a repair) is usually the better choice
choices.why: In young rheumatic patients autograft dysfunction was far more common (freedom only 65%), with rheumatic changes in the explanted autografts; EACTS 2025 lists rheumatic disease among the cautions.

choices.text: The Ross is ideal: young and wants to avoid warfarin

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Cannulate distally, vent, protect
steps.body:
The arterial cannula high: distal ascending aorta or arch, or the right axillary artery if the aorta is large up to the arch. A two-stage venous cannula; an LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein; retrograde cardioplegia in the coronary sinus.

steps.body:

action.label: Excise the root, keep the buttons

steps.title: Harvest the pulmonary autograft
steps.body:
Transect the PA trunk just below its bifurcation and look at the pulmonary valve: it must be tricuspid and competent, or the Ross is abandoned. Open the RVOT 3–5 mm below the valve (a right-angle clamp through the valve marks the level).

Free the root from the septum posteriorly and to the left, keeping the plane shallow: the first septal perforator runs just beneath, and the left main lies behind the root. Keep the muscle cuff thin but intact.

Evidence: injury to the first septal perforator (septal infarction, ventricular arrhythmia) is a recognised harvest complication; the EACTS 2025 consensus highlights preserving it.

ask.question: During harvest, dissection is carried deep into the muscle behind the pulmonary root. What is at risk?

choices.text: The first septal perforator of the LAD
choices.why: It runs just beneath the posterior RVOT; dividing it gives a septal infarct. Stay shallow and close to the root.

steps.title: Implant the autograft as a root; stabilise it
steps.body:
Sew the autograft to the aortic annulus with interrupted sutures (or a running suture with a strip), in the same plane as the annulus so the cusps do not distort. The pulmonary sinuses are thinner than aortic ones.

To limit later dilatation (the main long-term failure mode): reduce and fix the annulus if it is large, keep the STJ at the right size, and consider reinforcing the autograft (inclusion inside a polyester graft, or an external wrap), especially with pre-existing AR or a big annulus.

Evidence: the EACTS 2025 consensus recommends annular assessment and stabilisation, and considering autograft reinforcement in higher-risk roots. The full-root technique is the most widely used; the best form of reinforcement is not settled.

action.label: Move the autograft to the aortic position

steps.title: Reimplant the coronary buttons
steps.body:
Open the autograft's facing sinuses opposite each ostium. Sew each button end-to-side with running 5-0 polypropylene, often with a felt or pericardial strip on the outside. steps.body:
Cut the graft to length and join it to the ascending aorta with running 4-0 polypropylene, often with a felt strip. De-air through the root vent in the graft, release the clamp, and check every suture line, especially the backs of the buttons.

TOE: valve function, regional wall motion in the left and right coronary territories, no leak. Bleeding is the other big risk: keep haemostatic agents and blood ready.

steps.title: Rebuild the RVOT with a pulmonary homograft
steps.body:
Sew a pulmonary homograft (or another conduit if none is available) to the PA bifurcation and to the RVOT with running 4-0 polypropylene, often on the beating heart after the clamp is off. It lies in the low-pressure circuit, so it lasts longer than a homograft would in the aortic position.

steps.body:

Evidence: blood-pressure control after the Ross is recommended in expert consensus (EACTS 2025) to limit early autograft dilatation; its exact targets have not been tested in trials.

root-david.name: Aortic root replacement
root-david.summary: Thresholds, choice of root operation, excision with coronary buttons, composite graft or pulmonary autograft, button reimplantation, distal anastomosis, homograft.

steps.title: The functional aortic annulus
steps.body:
The valve works as a unit with its root: the ventriculo-aortic junction (the base), the sinuses, and the sinotubular junction. Together they are the functional aortic annulus. In a root aneurysm with thin, normal cusps, the cusps leak only because the STJ and the base have dilated and pulled the commissures apart (type I regurgitation in El Khoury's classification). Restore the root's size and shape, and the cusps meet again: keep the valve.

Evidence: the functional classification of AR (type I dilatation, type II prolapse, type III restriction) guides repair; valve-sparing works best for type I with pliable cusps.

ask.question: Root aneurysm 5.3 cm, moderate central AR, thin mobile cusps without calcium. Why does the valve leak?

choices.text: The dilated root (STJ and base) pulls the commissures apart, so the cusps no longer meet
choices.why: This is type I (functional annulus dilatation) regurgitation: the cusps are normal, which is exactly the case for keeping them.

choices.text: The cusps are calcified and restricted

steps.title: Who is right for a valve-sparing root?
steps.body:
Good candidates: a root aneurysm with normal or near-normal cusps: young patients, Marfan and other heritable aortopathies, some bicuspid valves in experienced hands, and type A dissection with a normal valve. Not suitable: calcified, thickened, retracted or badly fenestrated cusps; then a Bentall or Ross.

Reimplantation (David) puts the whole valve inside a graft and fixes the base, so it also treats a dilated annulus. Remodelling (Yacoub) replaces the sinuses with a scalloped graft but leaves the base free (often with an external ring).

Evidence: in David's 20-year series (374 patients), survival was 69% at 20 years and 97% were free of reoperation at 10 years. A 2023 meta-analysis of reimplantation (44 studies, 7,878 patients) found early mortality 1.6% and 91% freedom from reoperation at 10 years, with no difference between bicuspid and tricuspid valves. A meta-analysis of 14 cohort studies (1,672 patients) found lower late mortality and reoperation after reimplantation than after remodelling (retrospective data). No valve means no anticoagulation and very low rates of valve-related events.

ask.question: A 28-year-old with Marfan syndrome, root 5.0 cm, mild AR, normal cusps. Which operation keeps his own valve and also stabilises the annulus?

choices.why: Reimplantation fixes the base inside the graft as well as replacing the sinuses; with normal cusps it avoids a prosthesis and anticoagulation.

steps.title: Free the root down to the base; excise the sinuses
steps.body:
Transect the aorta above the STJ; inspect the cusps (thin, mobile, no fenestration or calcium: go on). Free the root outside down to the level of the ventriculo-aortic junction: off the RVOT and the roof of the left atrium, as far as the muscle beneath the right cusp allows. Excise the sinus walls leaving a 4–5 mm rim along the cusp attachments and buttons round the coronaries. Keep the cusps untouched.

Evidence: the depth of the external dissection sets how low the graft can go; the right coronary sinus is limited by the muscular septum, which is why the graft lies higher there.

action.label: Excise the sinuses, keep the cusps

steps.title: Subannular sutures in one horizontal plane
steps.body:
Twelve or so horizontal mattress sutures (2-0 polyester, often pledgeted), passed from inside the LVOT to the outside, just below the nadirs of the cusps, all in one horizontal plane. Under the right–non-coronary commissure (membranous septum, His bundle) keep them shallow, or through the fibrous tissue; under the right cusp they sit higher, on the muscular septum.

Evidence: a single horizontal plane at the base is what fixes the ventriculo-aortic junction and prevents later annular dilatation, the main reason for late failure of valve-sparing repair.

steps.title: Size the graft; lower it over the valve; tie
steps.body:
Size the graft to the valve, not to the aneurysm: several methods are used (the cusp height, the span between commissures, or the annulus plus a few millimetres); commonly 26–32 mm. Too large leaves the cusps without coaptation; too small crowds them.

Pass the subannular sutures through the base of the graft, lower it over the valve and tie them over the graft: the valve now sits inside the tube.

Evidence: no trial compares sizing methods; surgeons follow their method consistently. Residual AR after reimplantation is most often due to a mismatch between graft size and cusp size, or to unrecognised cusp prolapse.

action.label: Lower the graft over the valve

steps.title: Resuspend the commissures; sew the valve inside the graft
steps.body:
Pull each commissure up vertically inside the graft and fix it with a pledgeted suture at a height that lets the cusps meet. Then sew the rim of sinus wall to the inside of the graft with running 4-0 polypropylene, following each cusp's scalloped attachment from nadir to commissure.

Evidence: commissural height and symmetry determine coaptation; asymmetric resuspension is a common cause of residual regurgitation.

steps.title: Check the cusps: effective height and prolapse
steps.body:
Look at the valve from above. The free margins should meet at the same level, well above the base. Measure the effective height (from the base of the cusp to its free margin at the centre) with a calliper: a common target is about 9 mm. A cusp lying lower than the others is prolapsing: correct it by central plication of its free margin (a fine polypropylene suture), then re-check. A saline test into the graft (clamped above) shows central coaptation.

Evidence: effective height as a target (about 9–10 mm) and the importance of the geometric (cusp) height come from the Homburg group (Schäfers et al.) and are widely used in valve repair; they are expert practice rather than trial-based thresholds.

ask.question: After reimplantation, one cusp's free margin sits 3 mm lower than the other two, and the effective height is 6 mm. What next?

choices.text: Central plication of the prolapsing cusp, then re-measure
choices.why: A low-lying cusp is prolapsing; shortening its free margin (central plication) restores coaptation. Leaving it means residual AR and early failure.

steps.title: Reimplant the coronary buttons
steps.body:
Cut holes in the graft opposite each coronary ostium (the valve is already inside). Sew each button end-to-side with running 5-0 polypropylene, often with a felt or pericardial strip on the outside. Left main first (lower, posterior). Place the right with the heart filled (release the vent briefly, or fill the root) so it is not too low, twisted or stretched.

Test each suture line (cardioplegia down the graft) before the distal anastomosis: afterwards the back of these suture lines is hard to reach.

Evidence: coronary button problems (kinking, tension, bleeding) are the main technical causes of early death and ischaemia after root replacement in series; positioning with the heart filled is standard advice.

ask.question: After a Bentall, the patient comes off bypass with inferior ST elevation and a failing RV. The left side looks fine. Most likely?

choices.text: The right coronary button is kinked or under tension
choices.why: The right button, placed too low or with the heart empty, kinks when the heart fills. Go back on bypass and redo it (or bypass the RCA).

steps.title: Distal anastomosis; TOE of the repaired valve
steps.body:
Join the graft to the ascending aorta (running 4-0 polypropylene). After bypass, TOE: no more than trivial AR, coaptation well above the base of the root, no cusp prolapse, normal gradients, and regional wall motion (buttons). More than mild AR at this point: go back and repair, or replace the valve.

Evidence: residual AR more than mild on intraoperative TOE predicts late failure of valve-sparing repair in large series; that is why it is corrected before leaving theatre.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Strict blood pressure control to protect suture lines
  • New ST change or ventricular arrhythmia: coronary button ischaemia
  • Ross: control autograft pressure

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After a Bentall, new ST elevation in the inferior leads. Think of?

choices.text: Right coronary button kinking or ischaemia
choices.why: Coronary button problems present early with ST change or arrhythmia: echo and angiography.

tv-ring.name: Tricuspid valve surgery
tv-ring.summary: Guideline indications, bicaval snares, arrested or beating, assessment and sizing, ring vs suture repair, replacement, conduction and RCA safety.

steps.title: The tricuspid valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
Three leaflets: the large anterior, the posterior, and the septal, hinged on the septum. In functional regurgitation the annulus dilates along the anterior and posterior leaflets; the septal part is held by the fibrous skeleton and hardly stretches. That is why rings and suture annuloplasties shorten the anterior and posterior annulus.

What the sutures can injure:

  • The AV node and His bundle, at the apex of Koch's triangle (coronary sinus ostium, tendon of Todaro, septal leaflet hinge), close to the anteroseptal commissure. Deep bites here cause heart block.
  • The right coronary artery, a few millimetres outside the anterior and posterior annulus in the AV groove.
  • The non-coronary sinus of the aortic root, just beyond the anteroseptal commissure.

Evidence: heart block is the commonest serious complication of tricuspid surgery. In a national Swedish registry of 1,502 annuloplasties, 14.2% needed a permanent pacemaker within 30 days, mostly for AV block (Ragnarsson et al., JTCVS Open 2023).

ask.question: Where is the AV node relative to the tricuspid valve?

choices.text: At the apex of Koch's triangle, near the anteroseptal commissure
choices.why: Bounded by the coronary sinus ostium, the tendon of Todaro and the septal leaflet hinge; the node sits at the apex, near the anteroseptal commissure.

choices.text: In the middle of the posterior annulus

steps.title: When to operate on the tricuspid, and how
steps.body:
At left-sided valve surgery (the commonest setting, often after rheumatic mitral disease):

  • Severe TR: operate on the tricuspid too. Recommended in both ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 (class I).
  • Moderate TR, or milder TR with a dilated annulus (40 mm or more, or 21 mm/m², on echo), or previous right heart failure: annuloplasty is reasonable (ACC/AHA class 2a; ESC should be considered). It stops progression but adds a pacemaker risk, so weigh atrial fibrillation, right atrial size and pulmonary pressure.

Isolated severe TR: surgery for symptomatic primary TR; for secondary TR, consider it before the RV fails. It is not for advanced biventricular failure or severe pulmonary hypertension. For high-risk patients, transcatheter repair (TEER) or replacement (TTVR) is a class IIa option (ESC 2025).

Repair or replace. Annuloplasty for a dilated annulus with mobile leaflets. Replace when the leaflets are destroyed or tethered deep into the ventricle, or thickened and retracted (rheumatic, carcinoid, endocarditis, pacing-lead damage), or when a repair has failed.

Evidence: CTSN trial (Gammie et al., NEJM 2022; 401 patients having mitral repair for degenerative MR, with moderate TR or a dilated annulus): adding annuloplasty cut the two-year composite of reoperation, progression or severe TR from 10.2% to 3.9%. It did not change mortality, and it raised the permanent pacemaker rate to 14.1% vs 2.5%. TRILUMINATE (TEER, NEJM 2023) and TRISCEND II (TTVR, NEJM 2025) improved quality of life in severe TR; TTVR needed a new pacemaker in about a quarter of patients.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis for MVR. Mild TR, but the tricuspid annulus measures 44 mm and there has been right heart failure. What do the guidelines advise?

choices.text: Tricuspid annuloplasty at the same operation is reasonable
choices.why: An annulus of 40 mm or more, or previous right heart failure, makes concomitant annuloplasty reasonable even with less than severe TR: the annulus keeps dilating after the mitral operation, and reoperation for late TR carries high risk.

choices.text: Leave it; mild TR regresses once the mitral valve is fixed
