choices.text: Heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The AV node lies close to the septal leaflet annulus.

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Bicaval cannulation and snares
steps.body:
Heparin. The aortic cannula as usual. Separate SVC and IVC cannulas (the IVC one low on the atrium, near the IVC junction, so the atriotomy is clear), with snares round both cavae. Tightened, they isolate the right atrium, so it can be opened without the venous line taking in air.

Evidence: bicaval cannulation with snares is the standard for any right atrial opening (Kirklin/Barratt-Boyes). With vacuum-assisted drainage, some surgeons open the atrium without snaring.

steps.title: Arrested or beating heart?
steps.body:
Arrested (cross-clamp and cardioplegia): a still, bloodless field; the usual choice when the tricuspid follows a mitral or aortic procedure under the same clamp.
Beating (on bypass, clamp off, the right heart isolated by the snares): no cardioplegia or ischaemia for the left heart. The rhythm can be watched as each suture is tied near the AV node, and a stitch that causes block can be removed at once. Any left-heart opening (a patent foramen ovale) risks air embolism, so check the septum on TOE first.

After a mitral operation the tricuspid is often done after the clamp is off, during reperfusion, which also shortens the ischaemic time.

Evidence: a 2025 meta-analysis of 6 observational studies (767 isolated tricuspid operations; Caldonazo et al., Innovations) found no difference between beating and arrested hearts in permanent pacemaker rate, early or late mortality, or bypass time. The theoretical advantage in conduction safety has not been shown; randomised trials are lacking.

ask.question: Isolated tricuspid ring annuloplasty on the beating heart. While tying the sutures near the anteroseptal commissure, complete heart block appears. Best move?

choices.text: Cut and remove that suture, and place it more superficially or on the atrial side
choices.why: Watching the rhythm while tying is the point of the beating-heart technique: a block that appears with one stitch often resolves when it is removed.

choices.text: Carry on and put in a pacemaker later

steps.title: Right atriotomy
steps.body:
Tighten the snares. Open the right atrium obliquely, from the base of the appendage toward the IVC, parallel to the AV groove and well above it (the right coronary), and away from the sinus node at the SVC junction. Stay sutures; a sucker into the coronary sinus if it floods the field.

Evidence: the incision is placed by anatomy: the sinus node lies at the SVC-atrial junction (the crista terminalis), and the right coronary runs in the AV groove below.

steps.title: Assess the valve and size the annulus
steps.body:
Look at the leaflets (thickened, retracted, perforated, tethered), the chordae and the commissures. A saline test (fluid into the RV) shows where it leaks.

Size the ring by the septal leaflet length (base of the septal leaflet, commissure to commissure) or the anterior leaflet area, with the maker's sizers. The septal annulus hardly dilates, so it guides the true size.

Signs a repair will not last: severe tethering (a coaptation depth of about 8 mm or more on echo, or a large tenting area), a very dilated annulus with a failing RV, or destroyed or rheumatic leaflets. Then consider leaflet augmentation or replacement.

Evidence: tethering depth and annular size predict residual and recurrent TR after annuloplasty in observational echo series; exact thresholds vary between studies.

steps.title: Which repair: ring, De Vega, Kay, clover
steps.body:
Ring annuloplasty (incomplete or 3D ring, open at the AV node)
For: fixes the annulus in a normal shape and resists late dilatation; the most durable repair. Against: foreign material; cost; a downsized rigid ring can kink the right coronary or cause stenosis.

De Vega (double running suture, anteroseptal to posteroseptal commissure)
For: quick, cheap, no prosthesis: attractive where rings are costly or scarce. Against: the suture can cut through or the annulus re-dilate ("guitar-string" effect): more late recurrence.

Kay (bicuspidisation: obliterates the posterior leaflet annulus)
For: simple, for moderate dilatation. Against: less durable than a ring when the annulus is very large.

Clover (edge-to-edge, the three leaflets stitched at their centres, with a ring)
for complex or prolapsing leaflets.

Evidence: meta-analysis of 9 studies (2 randomised; Parolari et al., Ann Thorac Surg 2014): rings protected against early mortality and late recurrence, with freedom from moderate or worse TR at 15 years of about 79% with a ring vs 60% with suture annuloplasty; late survival did not differ.

ask.question: A young patient with functional TR (annulus 44 mm) at MVR. What does the evidence favour for durability?

choices.why: Rings reduce late recurrence compared with suture techniques (Parolari 2014). A De Vega is a reasonable fallback where rings are not available.

steps.title: Ring sutures: round the anterior and posterior annulus
steps.body:
Horizontal mattress sutures of 2-0 braided polyester in the annulus, not the leaflet. Start just beyond the anteroseptal commissure, go round the anterior and posterior annulus, and finish on the septal annulus short of the coronary sinus. No sutures at the apex of Koch's triangle: the ring's gap sits there. Bites posteriorly and anteriorly are firm but not deep (the right coronary lies just outside).

Evidence: the incomplete ring was designed to leave the conduction tissue untouched. Heart block still occurs after annuloplasty; concomitant mitral surgery, ablation and a low-volume centre raised the risk in the Swedish registry (Ragnarsson 2023).

steps.title: Seat and tie the ring; test
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the ring, lower it and tie. The ring pulls the dilated anterior and posterior annulus back to size. Saline test: fill the RV; the leaflets should meet along a good line of coaptation.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE after bypass confirms the result: residual TR more than mild, or a gradient, is usually corrected before leaving theatre.

steps.title: Close the atrium, release the snares, wean
steps.body:
Close the right atrium in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene, de-airing as the last stitches go in, and release the snares. Release the cross-clamp with the root vent on. Place atrial and ventricular pacing wires.

TOE: residual TR, gradient, RV function. The RV that has pumped against regurgitation now pumps against a competent valve (a higher afterload). With pulmonary hypertension, support it: inotropes, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators, and a slow wean.

Check the rhythm: heart block after tricuspid surgery may recover over days; persistent block needs a permanent pacemaker.

Evidence: RV dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension are the main predictors of death after tricuspid surgery, which is why guidelines advise operating before RV failure (ESC/EACTS 2025).

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heart block: test wires; permanent pacemaker if it persists
  • RV failure: inodilator, avoid overload, keep the pulmonary resistance low

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After tricuspid repair: CVP rising, low output, RV dilated on echo. Priority?

choices.text: Treat RV failure: inodilator, avoid more fluid, lower pulmonary resistance
choices.why: The RV fails with overload and high afterload.

action.label: Excise the anterior and posterior leaflets

Evidence: technique by consensus; no trial compares the suture routes. Paravalvular leak and heart block are the two complications these routes are designed to avoid.

steps.title: Seat the prosthesis: tissue or mechanical
steps.body:
Lower and tie a large prosthesis (the right heart tolerates no gradient). Orient a stented valve so that no post points into the RV outflow tract, and check the leaflets move.

Tissue or mechanical? In the low-pressure, low-flow right heart, a mechanical valve thromboses more readily, and a tissue valve can later take a valve-in-valve transcatheter valve. A transvenous pacing lead cannot pass a mechanical tricuspid valve, and will be trapped between a tissue valve and the annulus, so place an epicardial lead now if block is likely.

Evidence: meta-analysis of 37 studies (8,316 prostheses; Said et al., J Cardiothorac Surg 2024): no difference in 30-day or long-term survival or reoperation; mechanical valves had about a sixfold higher risk of valve thrombosis.

ask.question: A 30-year-old woman needs tricuspid replacement for rheumatic disease; her mitral valve was repaired. Which prosthesis does the evidence favour?

choices.why: Survival is the same either way, but mechanical tricuspid valves thrombose far more often (about sixfold); a tissue valve also allows later valve-in-valve and avoids warfarin in pregnancy.

steps.title: Close the atrium, release the snares, wean
steps.body:
Close the right atrium in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene, de-airing as the last stitches go in, and release the snares. Release the cross-clamp with the root vent on. Place atrial and ventricular pacing wires.

TOE: residual TR, gradient, RV function. The RV that has pumped against regurgitation now pumps against a competent valve (a higher afterload). With pulmonary hypertension, support it: inotropes, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators, and a slow wean.

Check the rhythm: heart block after tricuspid surgery may recover over days; persistent block needs a permanent pacemaker.

Evidence: RV dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension are the main predictors of death after tricuspid surgery, which is why guidelines advise operating before RV failure (ESC/EACTS 2025).

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heart block: test wires; permanent pacemaker if it persists
  • RV failure: inodilator, avoid overload, keep the pulmonary resistance low

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

choices.text: Treat RV failure: inodilator, avoid more fluid, lower pulmonary resistance
choices.why: The RV fails with overload and high afterload.

tv-mics.name: Tricuspid valve surgery
tv-mics.summary: Guideline indications, bicaval snares, arrested or beating, assessment and sizing, ring vs suture repair, replacement, conduction and RCA safety.

steps.title: The tricuspid valve and what lies around it
steps.body:
Three leaflets: the large anterior, the posterior, and the septal, hinged on the septum. In functional regurgitation the annulus dilates along the anterior and posterior leaflets; the septal part is held by the fibrous skeleton and hardly stretches. That is why rings and suture annuloplasties shorten the anterior and posterior annulus.

What the sutures can injure:

  • The AV node and His bundle, at the apex of Koch's triangle (coronary sinus ostium, tendon of Todaro, septal leaflet hinge), close to the anteroseptal commissure. Deep bites here cause heart block.
  • The right coronary artery, a few millimetres outside the anterior and posterior annulus in the AV groove.
  • The non-coronary sinus of the aortic root, just beyond the anteroseptal commissure.

Evidence: heart block is the commonest serious complication of tricuspid surgery. In a national Swedish registry of 1,502 annuloplasties, 14.2% needed a permanent pacemaker within 30 days, mostly for AV block (Ragnarsson et al., JTCVS Open 2023).

ask.question: Where is the AV node relative to the tricuspid valve?

choices.text: At the apex of Koch's triangle, near the anteroseptal commissure
choices.why: Bounded by the coronary sinus ostium, the tendon of Todaro and the septal leaflet hinge; the node sits at the apex, near the anteroseptal commissure.

choices.text: In the middle of the posterior annulus

steps.title: When to operate on the tricuspid, and how
steps.body:
At left-sided valve surgery (the commonest setting, often after rheumatic mitral disease):

  • Severe TR: operate on the tricuspid too. Recommended in both ESC/EACTS 2025 and ACC/AHA 2020 (class I).
  • Moderate TR, or milder TR with a dilated annulus (40 mm or more, or 21 mm/m², on echo), or previous right heart failure: annuloplasty is reasonable (ACC/AHA class 2a; ESC should be considered). It stops progression but adds a pacemaker risk, so weigh atrial fibrillation, right atrial size and pulmonary pressure.

Isolated severe TR: surgery for symptomatic primary TR; for secondary TR, consider it before the RV fails. It is not for advanced biventricular failure or severe pulmonary hypertension. For high-risk patients, transcatheter repair (TEER) or replacement (TTVR) is a class IIa option (ESC 2025).

Repair or replace. Annuloplasty for a dilated annulus with mobile leaflets. Replace when the leaflets are destroyed or tethered deep into the ventricle, or thickened and retracted (rheumatic, carcinoid, endocarditis, pacing-lead damage), or when a repair has failed.

Evidence: CTSN trial (Gammie et al., NEJM 2022; 401 patients having mitral repair for degenerative MR, with moderate TR or a dilated annulus): adding annuloplasty cut the two-year composite of reoperation, progression or severe TR from 10.2% to 3.9%. It did not change mortality, and it raised the permanent pacemaker rate to 14.1% vs 2.5%. TRILUMINATE (TEER, NEJM 2023) and TRISCEND II (TTVR, NEJM 2025) improved quality of life in severe TR; TTVR needed a new pacemaker in about a quarter of patients.

ask.question: Rheumatic mitral stenosis for MVR. Mild TR, but the tricuspid annulus measures 44 mm and there has been right heart failure. What do the guidelines advise?

choices.text: Tricuspid annuloplasty at the same operation is reasonable
choices.why: An annulus of 40 mm or more, or previous right heart failure, makes concomitant annuloplasty reasonable even with less than severe TR: the annulus keeps dilating after the mitral operation, and reoperation for late TR carries high risk.

choices.text: Leave it; mild TR regresses once the mitral valve is fixed

ask.question: Which risk is higher after tricuspid surgery than after most valve operations?

choices.text: Heart block needing a permanent pacemaker
choices.why: The AV node lies close to the septal leaflet annulus.

steps.title: Right mini-thoracotomy, peripheral cannulation, snares
steps.body:
Supine, right chest raised about 30°, external pads, TOE. Femoral venous drainage plus an SVC (right internal jugular) cannula, or a single femoral cannula with vacuum; femoral arterial return. A 4–6 cm incision in the right 4th space; CO₂ in the field; snares round both cavae (or occlusion balloons).

An attractive route for isolated or redo tricuspid surgery after sternotomy: no re-entry, and it is often done on the beating heart without a clamp.

Evidence: observational series only; outcomes depend on centre experience. For redo isolated tricuspid surgery, avoiding re-sternotomy is the main practical argument.

steps.title: Arrested or beating heart?
steps.body:
Arrested (cross-clamp and cardioplegia): a still, bloodless field; the usual choice when the tricuspid follows a mitral or aortic procedure under the same clamp.
Beating (on bypass, clamp off, the right heart isolated by the snares): no cardioplegia or ischaemia for the left heart. The rhythm can be watched as each suture is tied near the AV node, and a stitch that causes block can be removed at once. Any left-heart opening (a patent foramen ovale) risks air embolism, so check the septum on TOE first.

After a mitral operation the tricuspid is often done after the clamp is off, during reperfusion, which also shortens the ischaemic time.

Evidence: a 2025 meta-analysis of 6 observational studies (767 isolated tricuspid operations; Caldonazo et al., Innovations) found no difference between beating and arrested hearts in permanent pacemaker rate, early or late mortality, or bypass time. The theoretical advantage in conduction safety has not been shown; randomised trials are lacking.

ask.question: Isolated tricuspid ring annuloplasty on the beating heart. While tying the sutures near the anteroseptal commissure, complete heart block appears. Best move?

choices.text: Cut and remove that suture, and place it more superficially or on the atrial side
choices.why: Watching the rhythm while tying is the point of the beating-heart technique: a block that appears with one stitch often resolves when it is removed.

choices.text: Carry on and put in a pacemaker later

steps.title: Right atriotomy
steps.body:
Tighten the snares. Open the right atrium obliquely, from the base of the appendage toward the IVC, parallel to the AV groove and well above it (the right coronary), and away from the sinus node at the SVC junction. Stay sutures; a sucker into the coronary sinus if it floods the field.

Evidence: the incision is placed by anatomy: the sinus node lies at the SVC-atrial junction (the crista terminalis), and the right coronary runs in the AV groove below.

steps.title: Assess the valve and size the annulus
steps.body:
Look at the leaflets (thickened, retracted, perforated, tethered), the chordae and the commissures. A saline test (fluid into the RV) shows where it leaks.

Size the ring by the septal leaflet length (base of the septal leaflet, commissure to commissure) or the anterior leaflet area, with the maker's sizers. The septal annulus hardly dilates, so it guides the true size.

Signs a repair will not last: severe tethering (a coaptation depth of about 8 mm or more on echo, or a large tenting area), a very dilated annulus with a failing RV, or destroyed or rheumatic leaflets. Then consider leaflet augmentation or replacement.

Evidence: tethering depth and annular size predict residual and recurrent TR after annuloplasty in observational echo series; exact thresholds vary between studies.

steps.title: Ring sutures: round the anterior and posterior annulus
steps.body:
Horizontal mattress sutures of 2-0 braided polyester in the annulus, not the leaflet. Start just beyond the anteroseptal commissure, go round the anterior and posterior annulus, and finish on the septal annulus short of the coronary sinus. No sutures at the apex of Koch's triangle: the ring's gap sits there. Bites posteriorly and anteriorly are firm but not deep (the right coronary lies just outside).

Evidence: the incomplete ring was designed to leave the conduction tissue untouched. Heart block still occurs after annuloplasty; concomitant mitral surgery, ablation and a low-volume centre raised the risk in the Swedish registry (Ragnarsson 2023).

steps.title: Seat and tie the ring; test
steps.body:
Pass the sutures through the ring, lower it and tie. The ring pulls the dilated anterior and posterior annulus back to size. Saline test: fill the RV; the leaflets should meet along a good line of coaptation.

Evidence: intraoperative TOE after bypass confirms the result: residual TR more than mild, or a gradient, is usually corrected before leaving theatre.

steps.title: Close the atrium, release the snares, wean
steps.body:
Close the right atrium in two layers of 4-0 polypropylene, de-airing as the last stitches go in, and release the snares. Place atrial and ventricular pacing wires.

TOE: residual TR, gradient, RV function. The RV that has pumped against regurgitation now pumps against a competent valve (a higher afterload). With pulmonary hypertension, support it: inotropes, inhaled pulmonary vasodilators, and a slow wean.

Check the rhythm: heart block after tricuspid surgery may recover over days; persistent block needs a permanent pacemaker.

Evidence: RV dysfunction and pulmonary hypertension are the main predictors of death after tricuspid surgery, which is why guidelines advise operating before RV failure (ESC/EACTS 2025).

steps.title: Case: isolated proximal LAD disease
steps.lead: A 62-year-old man, angina (CCS III) despite full medical therapy; stress imaging shows a large anterior ischaemic area. Angiogram: a long, calcified 90% ostial–proximal LAD stenosis involving the diagonal origin; circumflex and RCA normal; EF 55%. The interventional team judge it unfavourable for PCI.
steps.body: Evidence: in stable coronary disease, revascularisation relieves angina, but ISCHEMIA (NEJM 2020, over 5,000 patients with moderate or severe ischaemia) found no reduction in death or MI with an initial invasive strategy. For isolated proximal LAD disease, the randomised Leipzig trial (Blazek et al., JACC Cardiovasc Interv 2013; 220 patients, 10 years) found MIDCAB and stenting similar for death and MI, with far fewer repeat revascularisations after MIDCAB (11% vs 34%).

ask.question: What is the main aim of revascularising this man?

choices.text: Relieving angina that persists despite medical therapy
choices.why: In stable single-vessel disease, trials have not shown a survival benefit; the indication is symptoms despite optimal medical therapy (and here an anatomy unfavourable for PCI).

ask.question: For a diabetic with three-vessel disease, what does the evidence let you say about CABG versus PCI?

choices.text: CABG reduces death and MI compared with PCI (FREEDOM)
choices.why: FREEDOM (NEJM 2012): lower all-cause mortality and MI with CABG in diabetics, with more stroke.

steps.title: MIDCAB: left anterior mini-thoracotomy
steps.body:
Double-lumen tube, left lung deflated, the left chest raised about 30°, external defibrillator pads. A 6–8 cm incision in the left 4th (or 5th) space from near the sternal edge laterally, positioned over the LAD target (check on the angiogram or CT).

No sternotomy, no bypass: the operation is off-pump, and the only graft is the LIMA to the LAD.

Evidence: MIDCAB avoids sternotomy and cardiopulmonary bypass; its results depend on centre experience, and conversion to sternotomy must always be possible.

steps.title: Harvest the LIMA
steps.body:
A special retractor lifts the upper ribs. The LIMA is harvested under direct vision (or thoracoscopically) from as high as possible down to the incision, pedicled or skeletonised, with clips on each branch. Heparin before dividing it.

Evidence: a long LIMA is essential here: the target must be reached without tension through a small incision, and the pedicle cannot be brought round other structures as at sternotomy.

steps.title: Open the pericardium over the LAD; stabilise
steps.body:
Open the pericardium over the LAD, stitch its edges up to lift the heart. Find the target beyond the lesion (and beyond the diagonal); place the stabiliser, a proximal silicone snare or an intracoronary shunt, and a CO₂ blower.

Evidence: ischaemic preconditioning (a brief trial occlusion) before the arteriotomy is practised by some surgeons; its benefit is not proven in trials.

steps.title: LIMA to LAD, off-pump
steps.body:
Bring the LIMA pedicle down lateral to the pulmonary artery, with no tension or twist and enough length for the heart to fill. On the mid LAD beyond the disease (after the second diagonal here): a 4–5 mm arteriotomy on the vessel's anterior surface; an end-to-side anastomosis with running 8-0 polypropylene, heel and toe first; tack the pedicle to the epicardium on each side.

Off-pump: the stabiliser holds the target still; an intracoronary shunt or a silicone snare proximally keeps the field bloodless; a CO₂ blower clears the view. Warn the anaesthetist before lifting the heart.

Evidence: LIMA to LAD gives the best long-term patency and survival of any graft and is the basis of the class I recommendation to use it; its patency is above 90% at 10 years in large series.

steps.title: Check the graft, close
steps.body:
Transit-time flow on the LIMA (a good mean flow and a PI below about 5), TOE for anterior wall motion. Protamine. A chest drain, the lung re-expanded, the ribs approximated, a local anaesthetic block for pain.

Evidence: TTFM thresholds come from observational series; a poor reading on the only graft calls for revision before closing.

ask.question: The LIMA reads mean flow 5 mL/min, PI 12. What next?

choices.text: Look for a kink, twist or anastomotic problem and revise the graft now
choices.why: On a single graft, a technical failure means an anterior infarct; fix it before closing.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Aspirin within 6 h once bleeding settles; statin; beta-blocker guideline
  • New ST change or ventricular arrhythmia: graft failure until proven otherwise
  • Radial graft: vasospasm prophylaxis per unit

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Four hours after CABG, bleeding has settled. What should start within 6 h?

choices.why: Early aspirin after CABG reduces death and ischaemic complications (Mangano, NEJM 2002).

steps.title: Case: two-vessel disease (LAD and OM) with diabetes
steps.lead: A 55-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, exertional angina. Angiogram: 90% proximal LAD and 85% OM1; the RCA is normal; EF 50%. Good radial pulses; a normal ulnar collateral test on the left (non-dominant) arm.
steps.body: Evidence: FREEDOM (NEJM 2012) randomised patients with diabetes and multivessel disease (two or more vessels in at least two territories) to CABG or drug-eluting stents: CABG reduced the 5-year rate of death, MI or stroke, with more strokes after surgery.

ask.question: For this diabetic patient with two-vessel disease involving the proximal LAD, which strategy has trial evidence of fewer deaths and MIs?

choices.why: FREEDOM included diabetics with two- or three-vessel disease; CABG reduced death and MI at 5 years compared with drug-eluting stents (with more strokes).

steps.title: Why surgery, which conduits
steps.body:
Surgery over PCI (Heart Team, ACC/AHA/SCAI 2021): left main disease (CABG class I; PCI class IIa if anatomy is of low or intermediate complexity); diabetes with three-vessel disease (CABG class I); three-vessel disease with a normal EF (CABG class IIb for survival). With ischaemic cardiomyopathy, CABG improves long-term survival (STICHES).

Conduits: the LIMA to the LAD is the foundation. For the second most important target, a radial artery is preferred to vein (ACC/AHA/SCAI class IIa). Saphenous vein for the rest.

Evidence: FREEDOM (NEJM 2012): in diabetes with multivessel disease, CABG reduced death, MI and stroke at 5 years compared with drug-eluting stents. STICHES (NEJM 2016): CABG reduced 10-year death in ischaemic cardiomyopathy (EF 35% or less). RADIAL (NEJM 2018, 6 trials, 1,036 patients): radial artery grafts had fewer adverse cardiac events (HR 0.67) and graft occlusions (HR 0.44) than vein at 5 years, with no difference in death. ART (NEJM 2019): bilateral ITA grafts did not reduce 10-year death on intention to treat (many crossovers; radial artery used in some single-ITA patients), and sternal wound complications were more frequent.

ask.question: A 58-year-old with diabetes and three-vessel disease, EF 50%. What do the guidelines recommend?

choices.why: In diabetes with multivessel disease, CABG reduced death, MI and stroke compared with PCI in FREEDOM; the 2021 guideline gives surgery class I.

choices.text: CABG reduces death and MI compared with PCI (FREEDOM)

steps.title: Median sternotomy, pericardial cradle
steps.body: Median sternotomy; open the pericardium in the midline and hitch it up as a cradle, more on the right, which lifts the right atrium and the interatrial groove toward you.

steps.title: Harvest the LIMA
steps.body:
A retractor lifts the left sternal half. Open the left pleura if needed. Harvest the left internal mammary artery from its origin under the subclavian vein to its bifurcation at the 6th space: as a pedicle (with its veins, fat and muscle) or skeletonised (the artery alone, with low-energy diathermy and clips on each branch).

Heparin before dividing it distally; check the free flow; spray papaverine to prevent spasm; keep it long enough to reach the LAD without tension.

Evidence: skeletonisation gives a longer conduit and preserves sternal blood supply (fewer sternal wound problems with bilateral ITA). In a post hoc analysis of ART, skeletonised grafts were associated with more adverse events in some analyses, so the choice remains debated and experience-dependent.

steps.title: Harvest the radial artery (for the OM)
steps.body:
Radial artery from the non-dominant arm, after confirming ulnar collateral flow (modified Allen test, oximetry or Doppler with the radial compressed). Harvest it as a pedicle with its veins, from the elbow crease to the wrist, avoiding the lateral antebrachial cutaneous and superficial radial nerves. Topical and systemic vasodilators against spasm. Evidence: RADIAL (NEJM 2018; 6 trials, 1,036 patients): radial artery grafts had fewer adverse cardiac events (HR 0.67) and occlusions (HR 0.44) than saphenous vein at about 5 years; the 2021 ACC/AHA/SCAI guideline prefers the radial to vein for the second most important target (class IIa).

choices.why: Arterial grafts, the radial above all, need a severe proximal stenosis; with competitive native flow they string down or occlude. Vein is more forgiving here.

steps.title: Cannulate (aorta; two-stage venous RA to IVC), arrest
steps.body:
Heparin (about 300–400 U/kg; ACT above 480 s). Arterial cannula in the distal ascending aorta. Venous drainage by one two-stage cannula: through the right atrial appendage, tip in the IVC, side holes in the atrium (the heart is not opened, so separate caval cannulas are not needed). Antegrade cardioplegia and root vent, and a retrograde cannula in the coronary sinus. Palpate or scan the aorta (epiaortic ultrasound) for calcium before cannulating or clamping.

Cross-clamp and arrest: antegrade and retrograde cardioplegia (retrograde reaches beyond the blocked arteries); after each distal anastomosis, give cardioplegia down the new graft too.

Evidence: epiaortic scanning finds atheroma missed by palpation and changes the cannulation or clamp site in some patients; stroke after CABG is mostly embolic from the aorta.

steps.body:

Evidence: arterial grafts are sewn with finer suture; the radial must not be stretched or twisted, and its spasm is prevented with vasodilators.

steps.body:
Bring the LIMA pedicle down lateral to the pulmonary artery, with no tension or twist and enough length for the heart to fill. steps.body:

steps.body:
De-air, release the clamp, reperfuse and wean. Transit-time flow measurement on each graft: mean flow, pulsatility index and diastolic filling. A low flow with a high PI means a technical problem until proved otherwise: look, and redo it now. TOE for new wall-motion abnormalities.

With a side-biting clamp at low blood pressure (systolic about 90 mmHg), or a clampless sealing device; with a porcelain aorta, no aortic touch at all: take the vein or radial off the LIMA (a composite "Y" or "T" graft). A 4–5 mm aortotomy with a punch; the vein end-to-side with running 6-0 polypropylene; lay out the grafts so they neither kink nor stretch when the heart fills.

Evidence: partial aortic clamping is a source of emboli; single-clamp and clampless techniques aim to reduce stroke; the comparative evidence is observational.

steps.title: Check every graft, then close
steps.body:
Reverse heparin with protamine once all grafts are checked. Transit-time flow measurement on each graft: mean flow, pulsatility index and diastolic filling. A low flow with a high PI means a technical problem until proved otherwise: look, and redo it now. TOE for new wall-motion abnormalities.

Before closing: the LIMA pedicle lies without tension; the veins do not kink when the lungs inflate; a drain in each opened pleura.

Evidence: the commonly used TTFM thresholds (for example PI below 5 and a mean flow above about 15–20 mL/min for a left-sided graft) come from observational series; in them, abnormal readings predict early graft failure, and correcting grafts intraoperatively is associated with better outcomes.

ask.question: After the LIMA–LAD, TTFM shows mean flow 6 mL/min and PI 9. Next?

choices.text: Inspect the anastomosis and the pedicle; revise the graft now
choices.why: Low flow with a high PI points to a technical problem (kink, twist, anastomotic narrowing). Fixing it before leaving theatre is far safer than finding it after an infarct.

choices.text: Accept it: flows improve after weaning
Add a vein graft to the LAD later if needed

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Aspirin within 6 h once bleeding settles; statin; beta-blocker guideline
  • New ST change or ventricular arrhythmia: graft failure until proven otherwise
  • Radial graft: vasospasm prophylaxis per unit

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Four hours after CABG, bleeding has settled. What should start within 6 h?

choices.why: Early aspirin after CABG reduces death and ischaemic complications (Mangano, NEJM 2002).

peri-tb.name: Pericardiectomy
peri-tb.summary: Tuberculous constriction: physiology, timing after anti-TB therapy, total pericardiectomy from phrenic to phrenic, left ventricle first.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: tuberculous constrictive pericarditis
steps.body:
In Kenya and across sub-Saharan Africa most constrictive pericarditis follows tuberculous pericarditis, often with HIV. The pericardium thickens and fibroses, then often calcifies, into a rigid shell.

TB pericardial effusion→Fibrinous, then fibrotic pericardium→Rigid shell (± calcium)→All four chambers cannot fill in late diastole

Physiology: early diastolic filling is rapid, then stops abruptly when the heart meets the shell (the dip-and-plateau or "square root" sign). Diastolic pressures equalise in all chambers. Filling of the two ventricles is interdependent: on inspiration the septum shifts left. The JVP rises on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign); there is a pericardial knock, ascites and hepatomegaly out of proportion to oedema, and a small, quiet heart.

Diagnosis: echocardiography (respiratory septal shift, preserved or raised medial e', hepatic vein expiratory flow reversal; the Mayo criteria); CT for thickness and calcium; catheter pressures when unclear. Restrictive cardiomyopathy is the main differential.

Prevention: anti-tuberculous therapy for all; adjunctive prednisolone reduced progression to constriction in IMPI (4.4% vs 7.8%) but raised HIV-associated cancers, so it is not given routinely to people living with HIV.

Evidence: IMPI (Mayosi et al., NEJM 2014): prednisolone did not reduce the combined outcome (23.8% vs 24.5%) but reduced constriction (4.4% vs 7.8%) and hospitalisation; cancers 1.05 vs 0.32 per 100 person-years. Mayo echo criteria (Welch et al., Circ Cardiovasc Imaging 2014). ESC 2015 pericardial guideline (Adler et al., Eur Heart J 2015).

ask.question: Which bedside sign points to constriction rather than tamponade?

choices.text: The JVP rises on inspiration (Kussmaul's sign)
choices.why: In constriction the rigid shell stops the right heart accepting the extra inspiratory venous return; pulsus paradoxus is the hallmark of tamponade.

choices.text: A large heart on chest X-ray

steps.title: The pericardium, the phrenic nerves and what to free
steps.body:
The fibrous pericardium is fused to the diaphragm below and the great vessels above. The phrenic nerves run on its lateral surfaces, in front of the hila, with the pericardiophrenic vessels: they mark the lateral limits of a total (radical) pericardiectomy, which frees the anterior surface from phrenic nerve to phrenic nerve, the diaphragmatic surface, and the bands around the cavae.

The coronary arteries run under the epicardium in the atrioventricular and interventricular grooves, where calcium is often densest: peel around them, not through them. The right atrium and the cavae are thin-walled and tear easily.

steps.title: Case: constriction after 8 weeks of anti-TB treatment
steps.body:
Constrictive pericarditis persisting after 8 weeks of anti-tuberculous therapy: refer for pericardiectomy. She is NYHA class III; with class IV, cachexia and liver dysfunction, risk rises sharply, so do not wait for her to deteriorate.

Evidence: Africa meta-analysis (Oluwajuyigbe et al., The Cardiothoracic Surgeon 2026; 11 studies, 604 patients): perioperative mortality 10.0% (East Africa 12.9%); low cardiac output the commonest cause of death; NYHA IV the most consistent predictor.

ask.question: She has completed 8 weeks of anti-TB therapy and is not improving. What next?

choices.text: Pericardiectomy, before she reaches NYHA class IV
choices.why: Pericardiectomy is indicated when constriction persists or worsens after several weeks of anti-TB therapy; advanced functional class is the strongest predictor of death.

steps.lead: A 28-year-old woman, HIV-positive on antiretrovirals, treated for tuberculous pericardial effusion 3 months ago. Now: abdominal swelling, breathlessness on walking 100 m. JVP 12 cm, rising on inspiration, ascites, hepatomegaly, mild ankle oedema. Echo: septal bounce, respiratory variation in mitral inflow, dilated IVC. CT: pericardium 6 mm with calcium over the AV grooves.

steps.title: Timing, extent and approach
steps.body:
QuestionAnswer
When?Constriction that persists or worsens after about 4–8 weeks of anti-TB therapy; early, before NYHA IV, cachexia and liver failure
How much?Total: phrenic to phrenic, the diaphragmatic surface, the cavae. Better long-term results than partial (anterior) resection
Approach?Median sternotomy (access to both sides and the cavae, bypass if needed); a left anterolateral thoracotomy is an alternative when the disease is left-sided or for a redo
Bypass?Off-pump; bypass on standby (groin prepped) for bleeding or a torn chamber

Before surgery: optimise with diuretics, drain large ascites or effusions, correct albumin and nutrition, continue anti-TB and antiretroviral therapy; cross-match.

Evidence: ESC 2015 pericardial guideline: pericardiectomy for persistent constriction despite anti-TB therapy (expert timing 4–8 weeks). Total versus partial pericardiectomy: better long-term survival after total (reviews, e.g. IntechOpen 2023 "Constrictive pericarditis: surgical management").

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: EuroSCORE II; NYHA class (class IV carries the highest risk), nutrition, liver function. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Bleeding
  • AF
  • Chest infection

3. Serious

  • Low cardiac output needing inotropes
  • Injury to a heart chamber or coronary artery
  • Phrenic nerve injury
  • Death (about 1 in 10 in African series)

4. Specific to this operation

  • Symptoms may take weeks to improve as the heart muscle recovers
  • Bypass may be needed if a chamber tears

5. Alternatives

  • Continued anti-TB therapy and diuretics (when constriction may still resolve)
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Complete anti-TB therapy and continue antiretrovirals
  • Blood availability

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: What should a patient expect after pericardiectomy for long-standing constriction?

choices.text: Improvement over weeks, with a risk of low cardiac output early on
choices.why: The myocardium has atrophied under the shell and needs time and support.

steps.title: Median sternotomy; groin prepped for bypass
steps.body: Median sternotomy with the groins prepped and draped: femoral cannulation is the fastest route to bypass if a chamber tears. Heparin is not given unless bypass is needed. A retractor opened gently: the stiff heart tolerates traction poorly.

steps.title: Find the plane over the outflow tract; free the left ventricle first
steps.body:
Incise the thick pericardium over the aorta and right ventricular outflow until the epicardium bulges through: that is the plane. Develop it with scissors and blunt dissection, a sponge on a stick, and sharp division of bands.

Free the left ventricle before the right: releasing the right ventricle first lets it fill and pump into a still-constrained left ventricle and lungs, causing pulmonary oedema. Work from the left phrenic nerve, over the apex, down to the diaphragm, keeping a strip of pericardium on the nerve.

ask.question: Why is the left ventricle freed before the right?

choices.text: Releasing the right side first can flood a still-constrained left ventricle and cause pulmonary oedema
choices.why: The traditional order protects the lungs: the left side is decompressed first.

steps.title: Right ventricle, right atrium and the cavae; calcium and the coronaries
steps.body:
Then the right ventricle, the right atrium (thin: take care) and the bands around the inferior and superior venae cavae, as far as the right phrenic nerve. Where calcium is welded to the myocardium, leave an island rather than tear the heart. A thick, adherent epicardial peel can be scored in a grid (waffle procedure) to let the muscle expand.

Do not chase the plane over a coronary artery in the atrioventricular groove.

action.label: Remove the pericardium, phrenic to phrenic

steps.title: The heart fills: check, haemostasis, close
steps.body:
The freed ventricles visibly expand; the CVP falls. Haemostasis over the raw epicardium (warm packs, topical agents, cautery away from the coronaries). Drains to both pleural spaces if opened. Send the pericardium for histology and TB culture (GeneXpert).

Expect low cardiac output in the first days: the myocardium has been atrophied by months of constriction. Inotropes, careful filling and diuresis; continue anti-TB therapy.

ask.question: After pericardiectomy, the CVP is 8 but the cardiac output is low and the ventricle looks thin and hypokinetic. Most likely?

choices.text: Myocardial atrophy from long-standing constriction: inotropic support and cautious filling
choices.why: Low output syndrome is the commonest cause of death after pericardiectomy in African series.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Low output from an atrophied myocardium: inotropes, cautious filling, diuresis; avoid overload
  • Bleeding from raw epicardium
  • Continue anti-TB and antiretroviral therapy; send pericardium for histology and TB culture

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Africa meta-analysis 2026: low cardiac output the commonest cause of perioperative death.

ask.question: Day 1 after pericardiectomy: low output, CVP 14, a dilated thin RV. Next?

choices.text: Inotropes and diuresis, avoid more fluid
choices.why: The freed but atrophied ventricle dilates with volume; support contractility rather than fill.

asd-patch.name: Atrial septal defect closure
asd-patch.summary: Surgical patch closure of a secundum ASD with deficient rims: indications, device or surgery, the rims and Koch's triangle, bicaval bypass, patch, de-airing.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: atrial septal defect
steps.body:
A hole in the atrial septum lets blood cross from the left atrium to the right. The direction and size of the shunt are set less by the hole than by the compliance of the two ventricles: the thin RV fills more easily, so blood follows it, mostly in late diastole.

Left-to-right shunt→RA, RV and pulmonary arteries carry 1.5–3 times the systemic flow→RA and RV dilate→AF, RV failure, and in a minority pulmonary vascular disease

Types

  • Secundum (fossa ovalis): the commonest; the only type suitable for a device
  • Primum: a partial atrioventricular septal defect, with a cleft mitral valve
  • Sinus venosus: superior (with anomalous right upper pulmonary veins) or inferior
  • Coronary sinus (unroofed): rare

Clinical: often silent in childhood. A wide, fixed split S2, a pulmonary flow murmur, RV heave; ECG with incomplete RBBB and right axis (left axis suggests primum). Adults present with breathlessness, palpitations from AF/flutter, or paradoxical embolism.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

ask.question: What mainly decides how much blood crosses a large ASD?

choices.text: The relative compliance (filling) of the two ventricles
choices.why: With a large defect the atria share one pressure; flow goes to the ventricle that fills more easily, the RV.

choices.text: The size of the hole alone

steps.title: Types of ASD and where they sit
steps.body:
TypeShareWhereGoes withClosure
SecundumAbout 70–75%Fossa ovalis, mid-septumUsually isolatedDevice (good rims) or patch
Primum15–20%Low septum, just above the AV valvesCleft mitral valve (partial AV septal defect)Surgery: patch and repair of the cleft
Sinus venosus, superiorUp to about 10% (both forms)At the SVC entry, outside the fossaRight upper pulmonary vein draining to the SVC, almost alwaysSurgery: baffle the veins to the LA (patch, two-patch or Warden)
Sinus venosus, inferior(rarer)At the IVC entryRight lower pulmonary vein to the IVCSurgery
Coronary sinus (unroofed)Under 1%At the coronary sinus orificeOften a left SVC to the coronary sinusSurgery

Evidence: Proportions: 5-Minute Clinical Consult (secundum 75%, primum 15–20%, sinus venosus 5–10%, coronary sinus under 1%); Medscape: superior sinus venosus almost always with anomalous right upper pulmonary vein drainage to the SVC.

ask.question: Which ASD is almost always accompanied by anomalous pulmonary venous drainage?

choices.why: The right upper pulmonary vein drains to the SVC; the repair must baffle it to the left atrium.

steps.title: Size, and what the heart shows
steps.body:
An ASD is judged less by its millimetres than by its effect on the right heart:

FindingMeaning
Small defect, normal RA and RV in an infantOften closes on its own: the smaller the defect and the younger the child, the likelier. Review
RA and RV dilated, Qp:Qs 1.5 or moreHaemodynamically significant: close (if PVR allows)
Defect over about 38 mm or rims under 5 mmToo big or too poorly supported for a device: surgery
Adult with AF, paradoxical embolism, or symptomsClose even if older; AF may persist

Unlike a VSD or PDA, an ASD dilates the right heart: shunted blood goes RA → RV → lungs → LA and round again.

Evidence: Spontaneous closure: 5-Minute Clinical Consult. Device limits (rims over 5 mm, defect up to 38 mm): StatPearls 2025. Closure at Qp:Qs over 1.5 with RV volume overload: ESC 2020.

steps.title: The septum seen from the right atrium
steps.body:
Through a right atriotomy the fossa ovalis is the target. Know its neighbours before you place a stitch:

  • Superior / anterosuperior: the SVC orifice and, behind the septum, the aortic root (the "aortic rim")
  • Inferior: the IVC orifice with the Eustachian valve in front of it, a trap: sew the patch to it and the IVC drains into the left atrium
  • Posterior: the right pulmonary veins (a sinus venosus defect sits here, by the SVC)
  • Anteroinferior: the coronary sinus and Koch's triangle (tendon of Todaro, CS ostium, septal tricuspid annulus); the AV node lies at its apex

A secundum defect can be stitched anywhere on its rim except where the rim is deficient; never let sutures stray into Koch's triangle.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

steps.title: Case: a large secundum defect in a young woman
steps.body:
Right heart volume overload from a large secundum ASD: closure is indicated. The question is how.

Evidence: ESC 2020: with Qp:Qs over 1.5 and PVR under 3 WU closure is class I; PVR 3–5 WU, IIa; PVR 5 WU or more despite treatment, closure is contraindicated (III), except a fenestrated closure when PVR falls below 5 WU on targeted therapy (IIb). Device closure needs rims of more than 5 mm and a defect no larger than about 38 mm (StatPearls).

ask.question: What is the best option?

choices.text: Surgical patch closure: the inferior rim is too deficient for a device
choices.why: Shunt and normal PVR make closure class I; a deficient inferior (IVC) rim makes device closure unsafe, while an absent aortic rim alone is often tolerated by devices.

steps.lead: A 26-year-old woman referred from a county hospital with breathlessness on climbing stairs and palpitations. Fixed split S2, pulmonary flow murmur. ECG: incomplete RBBB. Echo: secundum ASD 34 mm, absent aortic rim and a deficient (3 mm) inferior rim, dilated RA and RV, estimated PA systolic pressure 40 mmHg. Right heart catheter: Qp:Qs 2.3, PVR 2 WU.

steps.title: Close or not; device or surgery
steps.body:
QuestionAnswer
Close?RV volume overload with Qp:Qs over 1.5: yes when PVR is under 3 WU (I) and usually at 3–5 WU (IIa). PVR 5 WU or more despite therapy: no (III)
Device?Secundum only, rims over 5 mm (the inferior/IVC and posterior rims matter most), defect up to about 38 mm
Surgery?Primum, sinus venosus, coronary sinus defects; secundum with deficient rims, very large, or with another lesion to fix (TR, anomalous veins)
When, in a child?Usually electively at 2–5 years (device or surgery); earlier if there is heart failure
Patch or stitch?Small defects with good rims: direct closure. Larger: autologous pericardial (or PTFE/Dacron) patch, so the septum is not distorted

Evidence: ESC 2020 adult congenital guideline (PVR thresholds); StatPearls 2025 (device criteria); AATS/TSRA primer (pericardium or Gore-Tex patch, running polypropylene).

steps.title: Is this patient still operable?
steps.body:
A ASD seen late, as so many are in Kenya, raises one question before any other: has the pulmonary vascular bed remodelled beyond repair? Closing a defect in a patient with fixed pulmonary vascular disease removes the "pop-off" for the right heart and shortens life.

Points to operableWarns of inoperable (Eisenmenger)
HistoryBreathless, poor growth, chest infections (high flow)Fewer infections and "better" with age; exertional cyanosis, syncope, haemoptysis
ExaminationNormal saturations; loud flow murmur; big active heartResting or exercise desaturation, clubbing; murmur fading; loud single P2; RV heave; small heart on X-ray
EchoLeft-to-right shunt throughout; dilated left heart (VSD, PDA) or right heart (ASD)Bidirectional or right-to-left shunt; RV hypertrophy; left heart no longer dilated
Catheter (the decider)PVRi under about 4 WU·m² (PVR under 3 WU in adults); PVR/SVR under 1/3; Qp:Qs 1.5 or morePVRi over 8 WU·m² (PVR 5 WU or more in adults despite treatment); PVR/SVR over about 0.4
  • Grey zone (PVRi about 4–8 WU·m²): individual decision in a team with pulmonary hypertension expertise; the response to oxygen or nitric oxide helps, though criteria for shunts are not standardised
  • Treat-and-repair (pulmonary vasodilators first, then a fenestrated or flap-valve closure) is used in selected patients but remains controversial
  • Where catheterisation is not available, a clear left-to-right shunt with a dilated left heart and normal saturations is reassuring; any desaturation or bidirectional flow needs a catheter before surgery

Evidence: 6th World Symposium: PVRi 4 WU·m² as the operability cut-off, 4–8 individual, over 8 inoperable; AHA/ATS 2015: PVRi 6–8 WU·m² individual, PVR/SVR under 1/3 operable; ESC 2020 (adults): PVR under 3 WU class I, 3–5 WU IIa, 5 WU or more only in selected cases; vasoreactivity criteria for shunts not established (ERJ Open Res 2023).

ask.question: A 7-year-old with a large ASD now has saturations of 89% at rest and bidirectional shunting on echo. Next step?

choices.text: Cardiac catheterisation with PVR measurement and vasoreactivity testing before any decision
choices.why: Desaturation and bidirectional flow suggest advanced pulmonary vascular disease; closure could be lethal if PVR is fixed.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Age, PVR and RV function, other lesions; for an adult, AF and EuroSCORE II. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pain, drains for 1–2 days
  • Atrial arrhythmias (AF, flutter), usually short-lived

3. Serious

  • Bleeding needing re-operation
  • Heart block (rare)
  • Stroke or air embolism
  • Death (well under 1% in children)

4. Specific to this operation

  • A small residual leak
  • Post-pericardiotomy syndrome: fever, chest pain, effusion in the first weeks
  • AF may persist in adults operated late

5. Alternatives

  • Device closure (secundum with adequate rims)
  • No closure: progressive RV dilatation, AF, heart failure
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Waiting time for surgery or a device
  • Echo follow-up access

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which late problem after surgical ASD closure should the family know about?

choices.text: Post-pericardiotomy syndrome: fever, chest pain and an effusion in the first weeks
choices.why: It responds to anti-inflammatories; a growing effusion needs echo and sometimes drainage.

steps.title: Median sternotomy
steps.body: Median sternotomy; in a small child keep a thymic remnant (or excise part of it) and harvest a piece of anterior pericardium for the patch before heparin. Fix it in 0.6% glutaraldehyde for a few minutes if you want it stiffer and easier to handle.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin; aortic cannula high on the ascending aorta, bicaval venous drainage (SVC directly or through the appendage, IVC low on the right atrium), with snares around both cavae so the right atrium can be opened without air entering the venous line.

Bicaval cannulation is the rule for any operation inside the right atrium, as here for an ASD.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body:
Mild hypothermia, cross-clamp and antegrade cold cardioplegia into the aortic root; tighten the caval snares. A left heart vent (through the right superior pulmonary vein or across the defect) keeps the field dry from bronchial return.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: median sternotomy, aortic and bicaval cannulation, cold cardioplegia after cross-clamping; for VSD an LA or LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein and repeat doses every 20–30 minutes.

steps.title: Right atriotomy
steps.body: Open the right atrium parallel to the atrioventricular groove, about 1 cm from it, from the appendage toward the IVC cannula; stay away from the crista terminalis and the SA node at the SVC–atrial junction. Retract the edges with stay sutures.

steps.title: Inspect the defect and its rims
steps.body:
With the atrium open and the field vented: confirm a secundum defect, measure it, and look at every rim. Check the pulmonary veins drain into the left atrium (sinus venosus defects carry anomalous right upper veins), look for a left SVC (a large coronary sinus) and for other fenestrations.

Identify the IVC orifice and the Eustachian valve before the first stitch: the inferior rim of the patch goes to the true atrial septum, not the Eustachian valve.

ask.question: Sewing the inferior edge of the patch to the Eustachian valve causes what?

choices.text: IVC blood diverted into the left atrium: cyanosis after the operation
choices.why: The Eustachian valve guards the IVC orifice; the patch must go to the septal rim, or the IVC is baffled to the left side.

steps.title: Sew in the pericardial patch
steps.body:
Trim the pericardium a little larger than the defect. Start at the inferior (IVC) end, where exposure is hardest, with a running 5-0 polypropylene suture, and run both arms up each side to meet superiorly. Stay superficial near the aortic rim (the aortic root is just behind) and away from Koch's triangle.

Before tying: de-air the left atrium: the anaesthetist inflates the lungs and blood and air are allowed out at the last stitch.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: autologous pericardium or Gore-Tex, running polypropylene; left side de-aired through the aortic root vent before the suture line is completed.

steps.title: De-air, close the atrium, release the clamp
steps.body: Before the last sutures: fill the left heart (anaesthetist inflates the lungs), let air escape through the defect or the patch edge, then tie. Close the right atriotomy in two layers of running polypropylene, release the snares, vent the aortic root and remove the cross-clamp.

steps.title: Separate from bypass; check the repair
steps.body: Rewarm, separate from bypass, transesophageal echo for a residual shunt and valve function, then decannulate and give protamine. Temporary atrial and ventricular pacing wires; one or two drains; close the pericardium loosely or leave it open.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Usually extubated within hours; early mobilisation
  • Rhythm: atrial arrhythmias; check K⁺ and Mg²⁺; pacing wires
  • Echo before discharge: residual shunt, effusion
  • Children: fluids, drugs and blood by weight with the paediatric intensivist; the adult dose tables do not apply

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: ESC 2020 adult congenital guideline; AATS/TSRA primer.

ask.question: Day 3 after ASD closure: fever, pleuritic pain, rub, small effusion, well perfused. Likely cause?

choices.why: Treat with anti-inflammatories and watch the effusion; exclude infection.

vsd-pm.name: Ventricular septal defect closure
vsd-pm.summary: Closure of a large perimembranous VSD through the right atrium and tricuspid valve: timing, operability (PVR), the His bundle, the aortic valve, patch technique.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: ventricular septal defect
steps.body:
The commonest congenital lesion, and the commonest at KNH. Systolic LV pressure drives blood into the RV and on to the lungs, so the left atrium and left ventricle carry the volume load.

Large left-to-right shunt→High pulmonary flow and pressure→Heart failure, poor growth, chest infections in infancy→Pulmonary vascular disease, then reversal (Eisenmenger)

Types (by position, seen from the RV)

  • Perimembranous: by far the commonest; below the aortic valve, under the septal tricuspid leaflet
  • Muscular: often multiple; many close spontaneously
  • Outlet (doubly committed, subarterial): below both semilunar valves; aortic cusp prolapse and regurgitation
  • Inlet: beneath the septal leaflet, as in AV septal defects

Size decides the course: a small (restrictive) defect gives a loud murmur and little else (risk: endocarditis); a large one causes heart failure in the first months and, if left, irreversible pulmonary vascular disease, often by about 1–2 years.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

ask.question: Which chambers carry the volume load of a VSD?

choices.text: The left atrium and left ventricle
choices.why: Shunted blood passes through the lungs and returns to the LA and LV; the RV ejects it straight on in systole.

choices.text: The right atrium and right ventricle

steps.title: Five types of VSD: where they sit
steps.body:
TypeOther namesWhereConduction tissueUsual surgical route
1. SubarterialOutlet, supracristal, conal, doubly committed juxta-arterialUnder the pulmonary and aortic valves; roof is the two valvesAway from the defectThrough the pulmonary trunk (or RV outflow); watch aortic cusp prolapse
2. PerimembranousParamembranous, conoventricular, membranousMembranous septum, under the septal tricuspid leaflet and the right/non-coronary cuspsPosteroinferior rim, left side of the septumRight atrium, through the tricuspid valve
3. InletAV canal typeUnder the septal tricuspid leaflet, behind the perimembranous zone; often with AV septal defectInferior and posterior (from a posterior AV node)Right atrium, through the tricuspid valve
4. MuscularTrabecularWholly surrounded by muscle: mid, apical, anterior, posterior; often multiple ("Swiss cheese")Usually remoteRight atrium; apical ones by LV apex, device, or hybrid
GerbodeLV to right atrial communicationAtrioventricular part of the membranous septum, above the tricuspid hingeClose by: the AV node regionRight atrium

Type 2 is about 80% of operated defects. Muscular defects are common at birth (about 20% overall) but many close on their own, so fewer reach surgery.

Evidence: STS Cardiothoracic Surgery Consult: types 1–4; operated proportions type 2 80%, type 1 7%, type 4 4%, type 3 2%, multiple 5%; conduction in perimembranous defects along the posteroinferior rim, on the left side. Congenital Heart Surgery Nomenclature project (Jacobs 2000) adds the Gerbode (LV–RA) type. ICD-11 (Lopez 2018) renames them outlet, central perimembranous, inlet and trabecular muscular.

ask.question: Which VSD type is most likely to cause aortic regurgitation?

choices.why: The unsupported right coronary cusp prolapses into the defect; close it even when the shunt is small.

steps.title: Size, restriction and what the heart shows
steps.body:
SizeDefect vs aortic annulusPhysiologyQp:QsEcho / clinical
SmallUnder 1/3Restrictive: high LV–RV gradient, normal RV pressureUnder 1.5Loud murmur, normal LA and LV size
Moderate1/3 to 2/3Partly restrictive1.5–3LA and LV dilated, RV pressure mildly raised
LargeOver 2/3 (about the size of the annulus)Non-restrictive: LV and RV pressures equalOver 3 (falls as PVR rises)Heart failure, failure to thrive, pulmonary hypertension

LA and LV dilatation are the echo signature of a haemodynamically important shunt: the shunted blood returns through the lungs to the left heart. A restrictive defect with normal left heart size is followed, not closed.

Beware a large defect with a small heart and little murmur in an older child: the shunt has fallen because pulmonary resistance has risen.

Evidence: Size relative to the aortic annulus: WFSA tutorial 316 (Rolo 2015). Qp:Qs bands and LA/LV enlargement as evidence of a significant shunt: STS Consult.

ask.question: A 6-year-old with a perimembranous VSD has a loud murmur, LV–RV gradient of 80 mmHg and normal LA and LV size. Plan?

choices.text: Follow up; no closure (small restrictive defect)
choices.why: No left heart volume load and normal RV pressure: watch for aortic cusp prolapse and endocarditis.

steps.title: The perimembranous defect and the conduction tissue
steps.body:
Through the tricuspid valve, a perimembranous defect lies under the septal leaflet, at the junction of its septal and anterior leaflets. Its rims:

  • Superior / anterosuperior: the aortic valve (right and non-coronary cusps) just on the other side: deep bites here catch a cusp
  • Posteroinferior: the His bundle runs along this rim, on its left ventricular side, from the apex of Koch's triangle: the danger zone
  • Septal leaflet and chordae: often attached to the rim; may need to be detached and resuspended

Rule: in the danger zone, shallow bites on the RV side, 3–5 mm back from the edge, or use the tricuspid leaflet tissue itself.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

steps.title: Case: an infant with a large perimembranous VSD
steps.body:
A large unrestrictive defect with heart failure and poor growth: close it now, before pulmonary vascular disease sets in.

Evidence: KNH (Osano et al., preprint 2025): 1,703 admissions with congenital heart disease 2016–2021, VSD the commonest; median wait for surgery 59 days; only 37.1% had the recommended operation within a year; one-year mortality 36.1%. Delay costs lives and operability.

ask.question: What next?

choices.why: Heart failure and failure to thrive despite medical therapy with a large left-to-right shunt: close it in infancy, before the pulmonary vessels remodel.

choices.text: Increase diuretics and review at 2 years

steps.lead: A 7-month-old boy, 5.2 kg (below the 3rd centile), on furosemide and spironolactone. Fast breathing, sweating with feeds, two admissions with pneumonia. Pansystolic murmur, hepatomegaly. Echo: perimembranous VSD 9 mm, unrestrictive (low gradient), dilated LA and LV, no aortic cusp prolapse. Systolic PA pressure near systemic, but the shunt is left to right throughout and he is not cyanosed.

steps.title: Who needs closure, and how
steps.body:
SituationPlan
Large VSD, heart failure, poor growthSurgical closure in infancy (usually within the first 6 months to a year); PA banding only for multiple muscular defects or a very unwell infant
LA and LV dilatation (left heart volume load), Qp:Qs 1.5 or moreClose: the key echo indication at any age, provided PVR allows
Small restrictive VSD, normal heart sizeObserve; endocarditis prevention (dental care)
Adult or older child, LV volume overloadClose if PVR is under 3 WU (I) or 3–5 WU (IIa); PVR 5 WU or more: individual decision in an expert centre (IIb)
Outlet VSD with aortic cusp prolapse or ARClose even when the shunt is small, to protect the valve
Device?Muscular defects, and selected perimembranous ones in experienced hands; heart block after device closure of perimembranous defects limits its use

Evidence: ESC 2020 (PVR thresholds for VSD as for ASD and PDA; >5 WU individual decision, IIb). Conduction risk: permanent complete heart block in 3.5% of 400 surgical closures (Azab 2013), more with large perimembranous defects and small infants.

steps.title: Is this patient still operable?
steps.body:
A VSD seen late, as so many are in Kenya, raises one question before any other: has the pulmonary vascular bed remodelled beyond repair? Closing a defect in a patient with fixed pulmonary vascular disease removes the "pop-off" for the right heart and shortens life.

Points to operableWarns of inoperable (Eisenmenger)
HistoryBreathless, poor growth, chest infections (high flow)Fewer infections and "better" with age; exertional cyanosis, syncope, haemoptysis
ExaminationNormal saturations; loud flow murmur; big active heartResting or exercise desaturation, clubbing; murmur fading; loud single P2; RV heave; small heart on X-ray
EchoLeft-to-right shunt throughout; dilated left heart (VSD, PDA) or right heart (ASD)Bidirectional or right-to-left shunt; RV hypertrophy; left heart no longer dilated
Catheter (the decider)PVRi under about 4 WU·m² (PVR under 3 WU in adults); PVR/SVR under 1/3; Qp:Qs 1.5 or morePVRi over 8 WU·m² (PVR 5 WU or more in adults despite treatment); PVR/SVR over about 0.4
  • Grey zone (PVRi about 4–8 WU·m²): individual decision in a team with pulmonary hypertension expertise; the response to oxygen or nitric oxide helps, though criteria for shunts are not standardised
  • Treat-and-repair (pulmonary vasodilators first, then a fenestrated or flap-valve closure) is used in selected patients but remains controversial
  • Where catheterisation is not available, a clear left-to-right shunt with a dilated left heart and normal saturations is reassuring; any desaturation or bidirectional flow needs a catheter before surgery

Evidence: 6th World Symposium: PVRi 4 WU·m² as the operability cut-off, 4–8 individual, over 8 inoperable; AHA/ATS 2015: PVRi 6–8 WU·m² individual, PVR/SVR under 1/3 operable; ESC 2020 (adults): PVR under 3 WU class I, 3–5 WU IIa, 5 WU or more only in selected cases; vasoreactivity criteria for shunts not established (ERJ Open Res 2023).

ask.question: A 7-year-old with a large VSD now has saturations of 89% at rest and bidirectional shunting on echo. Next step?

choices.text: Cardiac catheterisation with PVR measurement and vasoreactivity testing before any decision
choices.why: Desaturation and bidirectional flow suggest advanced pulmonary vascular disease; closure could be lethal if PVR is fixed.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Weight, nutrition, PVR, other defects; age at operation. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Drains, ICU stay of 1–3 days
  • Feeding difficulty at first

3. Serious

  • Complete heart block needing a pacemaker (a few per cent)
  • Residual VSD
  • Aortic or tricuspid valve injury
  • Pulmonary hypertensive crisis
  • Death

4. Specific to this operation

  • Temporary pacing wires
  • Echo follow-up of the aortic and tricuspid valves

5. Alternatives

  • Pulmonary artery banding (selected infants)
  • Device closure (some muscular and perimembranous defects)
  • Medical therapy only: risk of irreversible pulmonary vascular disease
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Waiting list and nutrition before surgery
  • Distance to follow-up and pacemaker services

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which risk of VSD closure is specific to the anatomy of a perimembranous defect?

choices.text: Complete heart block from injury to the His bundle
choices.why: The bundle runs along the posteroinferior rim; a pacemaker is needed if block persists.

choices.text: Phrenic nerve palsy as the main risk

steps.title: Median sternotomy
steps.body: Median sternotomy; in a small child keep a thymic remnant (or excise part of it) and harvest a piece of anterior pericardium for the patch before heparin. Fix it in 0.6% glutaraldehyde for a few minutes if you want it stiffer and easier to handle.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin; aortic cannula high on the ascending aorta, bicaval venous drainage (SVC directly or through the appendage, IVC low on the right atrium), with snares around both cavae so the right atrium can be opened without air entering the venous line.

Bicaval cannulation is the rule for any operation inside the right atrium, as here for a VSD.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body:
Mild hypothermia, cross-clamp and antegrade cold cardioplegia into the aortic root; tighten the caval snares. A left heart vent (through the right superior pulmonary vein or across the defect) keeps the field dry from bronchial return.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: median sternotomy, aortic and bicaval cannulation, cold cardioplegia after cross-clamping; for VSD an LA or LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein and repeat doses every 20–30 minutes.

steps.title: Right atriotomy
steps.body: Open the right atrium parallel to the atrioventricular groove, about 1 cm from it, from the appendage toward the IVC cannula; stay away from the crista terminalis and the SA node at the SVC–atrial junction. Retract the edges with stay sutures.

steps.title: Expose the defect through the tricuspid valve
steps.body:
Retract the anterior and septal leaflets with fine stay sutures. Look for the defect under the septal leaflet; tethering chordae may hide its edges. If they do, detach the septal leaflet 2 mm from the annulus and resuspend it at the end.

Name the rims aloud: aortic valve above, conduction tissue posteroinferiorly, the muscular septum below.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: anterior and septal tricuspid leaflets retracted with 6-0 polypropylene stay sutures.

steps.title: Patch the defect; protect the His bundle
steps.body:
A Dacron, PTFE or treated pericardial patch a little larger than the defect, on the RV side. Interrupted pledgeted sutures or a running 5-0/6-0 polypropylene.

  • Posteroinferior rim: shallow bites on the RV side, 3–5 mm from the edge (the bundle runs on the LV side of this rim)
  • Superior rim: bites through the fibrous tissue at the aortic valve hinge, without catching a cusp
  • Across the tricuspid annulus: transition sutures through the base of the septal leaflet

Test the tricuspid valve with saline and resuspend a detached leaflet. Watch the rhythm when the heart beats again.

Evidence: TSRA primer: the conduction system runs close to the posteroinferior edge: partial-thickness bites. Yoneyama 2022: in perimembranous outlet defects the conduction tissue deviates toward the LV side, which favours shallow continuous suturing.

ask.question: Where along a perimembranous VSD is the His bundle at risk?

choices.text: The posteroinferior rim, near the apex of Koch's triangle
choices.why: The bundle penetrates at the apex of Koch's triangle and runs along the posteroinferior margin of the defect.

choices.text: The superior rim, under the aortic valve

steps.title: De-air, close the atrium, release the clamp
steps.body:
Before the last sutures: fill the left heart (anaesthetist inflates the lungs), let air escape through the defect or the patch edge, then tie. Close the right atriotomy in two layers of running polypropylene, release the snares, vent the aortic root and remove the cross-clamp.

Check the rhythm off bypass: complete heart block needs temporary pacing; if it persists beyond about 7–10 days, a permanent pacemaker.

steps.title: Separate from bypass; check the repair
steps.body: Rewarm, separate from bypass, transesophageal echo for a residual shunt and valve function, then decannulate and give protamine. Temporary atrial and ventricular pacing wires; one or two drains; close the pericardium loosely or leave it open.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • ECG and rhythm: junctional ectopic tachycardia (cool, correct Mg²⁺, reduce inotropes) or heart block (pace)
  • Pulmonary hypertensive crisis: sedation, oxygen, avoid acidosis and hypercarbia; nitric oxide where available
  • Echo: residual VSD, tricuspid and aortic regurgitation
  • Children: fluids, drugs and blood by weight with the paediatric intensivist; the adult dose tables do not apply

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Azab 2013: permanent complete heart block in 3.5% of 400 closures.

ask.question: Two hours after VSD closure: heart rate 210, narrow QRS, AV dissociation, low BP. Diagnosis and first steps?

choices.text: Junctional ectopic tachycardia: cool to about 35 °C, correct Mg²⁺, reduce inotropes, consider amiodarone
choices.why: JET is common after VSD surgery; it responds to cooling, electrolytes and less catecholamine.

choices.text: Atrial flutter: DC shock at once
