pda-ics3.name: Patent ductus arteriosus ligation
pda-ics3.summary: Closure of a large PDA through a left posterolateral thoracotomy: indications, the 3rd or 4th space, the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve, test occlusion, ligation or clip.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: patent ductus arteriosus
steps.body:
The fetal duct carries RV output past the lungs into the descending aorta. After birth, rising oxygen and falling prostaglandin E2 close it within days. If it stays open, flow reverses: aorta to pulmonary artery, in systole and diastole.

Continuous left-to-right shunt→Pulmonary over-circulation, LA and LV volume load→Diastolic run-off: wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses→Heart failure; pulmonary vascular disease; endarteritis
  • Preterm: common; a hemodynamically significant duct may be treated with ibuprofen or paracetamol, or ligated when this fails
  • Term and older: rarely closes spontaneously; continuous "machinery" murmur under the left clavicle
  • Eisenmenger PDA: reversed flow to the descending aorta gives differential cyanosis: pink fingers, blue toes

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

ask.question: A large PDA with reversed shunt causes which sign?

choices.text: Differential cyanosis: blue toes, pink fingers
choices.why: Desaturated pulmonary blood enters the aorta beyond the left subclavian origin, so the lower body is cyanosed.

choices.text: Central cyanosis of the lips only

steps.title: Morphology: Krichenko types A to E
steps.body:
TypeShapeWhat it means for the surgeon
A, conicalWide aortic ampulla, narrowest at the pulmonary end; the commonestRoom for two ligatures; ideal for a device (it seats in the ampulla)
B, windowVery short and wide; the aorta almost touches the PANo length to tie: a ligature can tear it or cut through. Divide between clamps and oversew; in adults, often bypass. Hard for devices
C, tubularLong, no constrictionEasy to encircle and ligate; devices may slip
D, complexSeveral constrictionsMeasure carefully; tie or clip at the longest straight segment
E, elongatedLong, constriction far from the aortic end (on lateral angiography)Plenty of length to ligate; device sizing needs care

The classification comes from lateral angiography, but echo and CT show the same shapes. Measure the narrowest point and the length before choosing ligation, division, clip or device.

Evidence: Krichenko et al., Am J Cardiol 1989: types A (conical), B (window), C (tubular), D (complex), E (elongated), described for planning catheter occlusion.

ask.question: Which duct is most dangerous to ligate with simple ties?

choices.text: Type B, window: very short and wide
choices.why: There is no length for two ligatures; division between clamps (or bypass in adults) is safer.

steps.title: Size and haemodynamic significance
steps.body:
GradeNarrowest diameter (child or adult)Clinical picture
SilentTiny; found only on echoNo murmur, no volume load
Very smallUnder 1.5 mmOften no symptoms
Small1.5–3 mmContinuous murmur, normal heart size
ModerateOver 3 to 5 mmLA and LV dilated, wide pulse pressure; may be symptomatic
LargeOver 5 mmHeart failure, poor growth, pulmonary hypertension; risk of pulmonary vascular disease

In a preterm baby millimetres matter less than haemodynamic significance: the ratio of the duct to the baby's size, left heart dilatation, flow reversal in the descending aorta, and the clinical state.

As with a VSD, LA and LV dilatation is the sign that the shunt matters.

Evidence: Size bands from the classification table in Fernando et al. 2013 (silent; very small under 1.5 mm; small 1.5–3 mm; moderate over 3–5 mm; large over 5 mm). ESC 2020: closure in adults on haemodynamic grounds (LV volume overload, PVR under 3 WU).

steps.title: The duct, the nerves and the wrong vessels
steps.body:
From the left thoracotomy you look down on:

  • The descending aorta and distal arch, the left subclavian artery rising from it
  • The vagus nerve crossing the arch and the duct; the recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves it and hooks under the duct to climb medially: at risk at every ligation
  • The phrenic nerve further anterior, on the pericardium
  • The left pulmonary artery below the duct; the thoracic duct behind, to the left of the esophagus

The classic disasters are ligating the left pulmonary artery or the descending aorta instead of the duct, especially in a small baby where the duct is as big as the aorta. See all three vessels before tying anything.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

steps.title: Case: a large duct in a 14-month-old
steps.body:
A large symptomatic duct with left heart dilatation in a child too small for the available device: ligate it surgically.

Evidence: ESC 2020 (adults): closure is indicated on haemodynamic grounds (LV volume overload) with PVR under 3 WU; device closure is preferred when feasible. TSRA primer: in adults with a calcified duct, closure may need bypass.

ask.question: What is the plan?

choices.text: Surgical ligation through a left thoracotomy
choices.why: A large symptomatic duct with LV volume overload should be closed; if a device is not available, ligation is safe and definitive.

steps.lead: A 14-month-old girl, 7.4 kg, with poor weight gain and recurrent chest infections. Bounding pulses, continuous murmur at the left upper sternal edge. Echo: PDA 6 mm, continuous left-to-right flow, dilated LA and LV, normal arch. The cath laboratory cannot offer a device of the right size for months.

steps.title: Medicines, device or surgery
steps.body:
PatientUsual plan
Preterm, significant ductIbuprofen or paracetamol; ligation (or clip) when this fails or is contraindicated
Term infant or child, large ductDevice closure where available and the child is big enough; surgical ligation otherwise
Small, silent ductNo closure needed
Adult, calcified or aneurysmal ductDevice if feasible; otherwise surgery, often on bypass through a sternotomy
PVR 5 WU or moreIndividual decision in an expert centre (ESC IIb)

  • Treat-and-repair (pulmonary vasodilators first, then a fenestrated or flap-valve closure) is used in selected patients but remains controversial

ask.question: A 7-year-old with a large PDA now has saturations of 89% at rest and bidirectional shunting on echo. Next step?

choices.text: Cardiac catheterisation with PVR measurement and vasoreactivity testing before any decision
choices.why: Desaturation and bidirectional flow suggest advanced pulmonary vascular disease; closure could be lethal if PVR is fixed.

steps.title: Which space: 3rd or 4th?
steps.body:
3rd space4th space
Lies overThe distal arch, subclavian origin and the top of the ductThe isthmus, the duct and the upper descending aorta
SuitsNeonates and small infants; a high duct; repair that must reach the distal archMost children; the standard space for PDA ligation and coarctation repair
DrawbackCramped under the scapula in a bigger child; the descending aorta is far belowThe distal arch is further away: retract the lung down, the aorta up
If you are wrongToo high: working down a tunnelToo low (5th): the duct is out of reach behind the hilum

Both are accepted; the duct and isthmus lie behind the 3rd–4th spaces, and the choice follows the child's size and how much arch must be exposed. Counting accurately matters more than the choice.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: "ribs are counted accurately to enter the third or fourth intercostal space" for PDA; coarctation through the third or fourth. Thoracic Key: a limited posterolateral thoracotomy through the fourth space is the one more commonly used for PDA. Subbian 2024: preterm ligation through the 3rd or 4th space. Farag 2019: coarctation through the 4th space in 292 children.

ask.question: Why does accurate rib counting matter more than whether you choose the 3rd or 4th space?

choices.text: Entering the 5th space by mistake puts the duct and isthmus out of reach
choices.why: The target lies behind the 3rd–4th spaces; one space too low and you work up behind the hilum.

choices.text: The 4th space damages the phrenic nerve
It does not matter at all

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Weight and prematurity, size and calcification of the duct, lung disease. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pain
  • A chest drain for a day

3. Serious

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarse voice, feeding problems)
  • Bleeding from a torn duct
  • Chylothorax
  • Ligation of the wrong vessel (rare)
  • Death (rare outside prematurity)

4. Specific to this operation

  • Small risk of the duct reopening after ligation
  • In preterm babies, unstable blood pressure and breathing in the first day

5. Alternatives

  • Device closure
  • In preterms: ibuprofen or paracetamol
  • No closure: heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, endarteritis
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Device availability and waiting times

ask.question: Which nerve injury should be discussed before PDA ligation?

choices.text: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarse voice, swallowing)
choices.why: It hooks under the duct and is at risk at every ligation.

steps.title: Left posterolateral thoracotomy, 3rd space
steps.body:
Right lateral decubitus, left arm forward and up. A posterolateral incision from below the axilla, curving 2 cm below the tip of the scapula. Divide latissimus dorsi (or retract it in a muscle-sparing approach), spare serratus anterior where possible.

Count the ribs from inside or under the scapula (the first rib you can feel under the scapula is usually the 2nd) and enter the 3rd intercostal space on the upper border of the 4th rib. Retract the lung forward and down with a moist pack.

steps.title: Open the pleura behind the vagus; find the nerve
steps.body:
Incise the mediastinal pleura over the descending aorta, behind (posterior to) the vagus, and lift the pleural flap with the vagus forward and medially on stay sutures. The recurrent laryngeal nerve comes into view hooking under the duct. Keep it in the flap; do not dissect it bare.

Identify the aorta above and below the duct, the left subclavian artery and the left pulmonary artery.

Evidence: Thoracic Key: the parietal pleura is divided longitudinally behind the vagus (or between vagus and phrenic). TSRA primer: the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve are seen coursing over the ductus.

steps.title: Encircle the duct; test occlusion
steps.body:
Dissect the upper and lower borders of the duct with fine scissors, then pass a blunt right-angled clamp gently behind it, from below up, staying on the duct wall: the back wall is where it tears.

Test-occlude it (a vascular clamp or a ligature held, not tied) for a minute: the diastolic pressure should rise and the saturation and ECG stay steady. A fall in leg pressure or saturation means you are on the wrong vessel.

ask.question: During test occlusion the femoral (or foot) saturation probe signal disappears. What has happened?

choices.text: The descending aorta has been clamped, not the duct
choices.why: Lower-body flow stops if the clamp is on the aorta: release and re-identify the three vessels.

steps.title: Ligate: aortic end first
steps.body:
Tie two heavy non-absorbable ligatures, the aortic end first, then the pulmonary end, slowly while the anaesthetist lowers the pressure a little. In a premature or small infant a titanium clip is enough; a short, wide or older duct is safer divided between clamps and oversewn.

Check the RLN, haemostasis and the lung; close the pleura over the aorta; one chest drain (often removed early).

Evidence: Thoracic Key: two heavy Ethibond sutures; finer suture can cut through a friable duct; division between clamps and oversewing for others. TSRA primer: a clip over the aortic end, or double or triple ligation with 3-0 non-absorbable suture; older children divided between ligatures.

steps.title: Post-ligation cardiac syndrome (preterm)
steps.body:
Hours after ligation in a preterm infant: falling blood pressure, worsening oxygenation and ventilation, often needing inotropes, typically 6–12 hours after surgery.

Duct tied→LV afterload rises suddenly→Preload falls (no more ductal return)→Immature LV cannot cope→Low output, hypotension, pulmonary oedema

Recognise and prevent

  • Echo within 1 hour: left ventricular output under about 200 mL/kg/min predicts the syndrome
  • Targeted milrinone for low output: lowers afterload and supports contractility
  • Avoid escalating pure vasoconstrictors, which raise afterload further; hydrocortisone for refractory hypotension
  • Less likely after transcatheter closure, which is one reason it is growing in small preterms

In older children the opposite is seen: a transient rise in blood pressure after the diastolic run-off stops.

Evidence: Thoracic Key: onset 6–12 h, related to increased LV afterload; LVO under 200 mL/kg/min within 1 h as predictor; early targeted milrinone may ameliorate it. Sathanandam et al., Circulation 2019 (ELBW infants): clinically significant PLCS in 42% after surgical ligation vs 4% after transcatheter closure.

ask.question: Eight hours after PDA ligation, a 900 g preterm becomes hypotensive and needs more oxygen. Echo: LV output low. Best first treatment?

choices.text: Milrinone (afterload reduction and inotropy), with cautious volume
choices.why: Post-ligation cardiac syndrome is an afterload problem for an immature LV; vasoconstrictors make it worse.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Preterms: post-ligation cardiac syndrome at 6–12 h (low BP, worse oxygenation): echo LV output within 1 h; milrinone for low output, not escalating vasoconstrictors

  • Voice and swallowing: RLN injury
  • Chest drain: blood, air or chyle (milky after feeds)
  • Children: fluids, drugs and blood by weight with the paediatric intensivist; the adult dose tables do not apply

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Subbian 2024: pooled vocal cord paralysis after preterm ligation 32%; bleeding, chylothorax and pneumothorax rare.

choices.why: The thoracic duct lies close by; drain, medium-chain triglyceride feeds, and re-explore if it persists.

pda-ics4.name: Patent ductus arteriosus ligation
pda-ics4.summary: Closure of a large PDA through a left posterolateral thoracotomy: indications, the 3rd or 4th space, the vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve, test occlusion, ligation or clip.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: patent ductus arteriosus
steps.body:
The fetal duct carries RV output past the lungs into the descending aorta. After birth, rising oxygen and falling prostaglandin E2 close it within days. If it stays open, flow reverses: aorta to pulmonary artery, in systole and diastole.

Continuous left-to-right shunt→Pulmonary over-circulation, LA and LV volume load→Diastolic run-off: wide pulse pressure, bounding pulses→Heart failure; pulmonary vascular disease; endarteritis
  • Preterm: common; a hemodynamically significant duct may be treated with ibuprofen or paracetamol, or ligated when this fails
  • Term and older: rarely closes spontaneously; continuous "machinery" murmur under the left clavicle
  • Eisenmenger PDA: reversed flow to the descending aorta gives differential cyanosis: pink fingers, blue toes

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

ask.question: A large PDA with reversed shunt causes which sign?

choices.text: Differential cyanosis: blue toes, pink fingers
choices.why: Desaturated pulmonary blood enters the aorta beyond the left subclavian origin, so the lower body is cyanosed.

choices.text: Central cyanosis of the lips only

steps.title: Morphology: Krichenko types A to E
steps.body:
TypeShapeWhat it means for the surgeon
A, conicalWide aortic ampulla, narrowest at the pulmonary end; the commonestRoom for two ligatures; ideal for a device (it seats in the ampulla)
B, windowVery short and wide; the aorta almost touches the PANo length to tie: a ligature can tear it or cut through. Divide between clamps and oversew; in adults, often bypass. Hard for devices
C, tubularLong, no constrictionEasy to encircle and ligate; devices may slip
D, complexSeveral constrictionsMeasure carefully; tie or clip at the longest straight segment
E, elongatedLong, constriction far from the aortic end (on lateral angiography)Plenty of length to ligate; device sizing needs care

The classification comes from lateral angiography, but echo and CT show the same shapes. Measure the narrowest point and the length before choosing ligation, division, clip or device.

Evidence: Krichenko et al., Am J Cardiol 1989: types A (conical), B (window), C (tubular), D (complex), E (elongated), described for planning catheter occlusion.

ask.question: Which duct is most dangerous to ligate with simple ties?

choices.text: Type B, window: very short and wide
choices.why: There is no length for two ligatures; division between clamps (or bypass in adults) is safer.

steps.title: Size and haemodynamic significance
steps.body:
GradeNarrowest diameter (child or adult)Clinical picture
SilentTiny; found only on echoNo murmur, no volume load
Very smallUnder 1.5 mmOften no symptoms
Small1.5–3 mmContinuous murmur, normal heart size
ModerateOver 3 to 5 mmLA and LV dilated, wide pulse pressure; may be symptomatic
LargeOver 5 mmHeart failure, poor growth, pulmonary hypertension; risk of pulmonary vascular disease

In a preterm baby millimetres matter less than haemodynamic significance: the ratio of the duct to the baby's size, left heart dilatation, flow reversal in the descending aorta, and the clinical state.

As with a VSD, LA and LV dilatation is the sign that the shunt matters.

Evidence: Size bands from the classification table in Fernando et al. 2013 (silent; very small under 1.5 mm; small 1.5–3 mm; moderate over 3–5 mm; large over 5 mm). ESC 2020: closure in adults on haemodynamic grounds (LV volume overload, PVR under 3 WU).

steps.title: The duct, the nerves and the wrong vessels
steps.body:
From the left thoracotomy you look down on:

  • The descending aorta and distal arch, the left subclavian artery rising from it
  • The vagus nerve crossing the arch and the duct; the recurrent laryngeal nerve leaves it and hooks under the duct to climb medially: at risk at every ligation
  • The phrenic nerve further anterior, on the pericardium
  • The left pulmonary artery below the duct; the thoracic duct behind, to the left of the esophagus

The classic disasters are ligating the left pulmonary artery or the descending aorta instead of the duct, especially in a small baby where the duct is as big as the aorta. See all three vessels before tying anything.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

steps.title: Case: a large duct in a 14-month-old
steps.body:
A large symptomatic duct with left heart dilatation in a child too small for the available device: ligate it surgically.

Evidence: ESC 2020 (adults): closure is indicated on haemodynamic grounds (LV volume overload) with PVR under 3 WU; device closure is preferred when feasible. TSRA primer: in adults with a calcified duct, closure may need bypass.

ask.question: What is the plan?

choices.text: Surgical ligation through a left thoracotomy
choices.why: A large symptomatic duct with LV volume overload should be closed; if a device is not available, ligation is safe and definitive.

steps.lead: A 14-month-old girl, 7.4 kg, with poor weight gain and recurrent chest infections. Bounding pulses, continuous murmur at the left upper sternal edge. Echo: PDA 6 mm, continuous left-to-right flow, dilated LA and LV, normal arch. The cath laboratory cannot offer a device of the right size for months.

steps.title: Medicines, device or surgery
steps.body:
PatientUsual plan
Preterm, significant ductIbuprofen or paracetamol; ligation (or clip) when this fails or is contraindicated
Term infant or child, large ductDevice closure where available and the child is big enough; surgical ligation otherwise
Small, silent ductNo closure needed
Adult, calcified or aneurysmal ductDevice if feasible; otherwise surgery, often on bypass through a sternotomy
PVR 5 WU or moreIndividual decision in an expert centre (ESC IIb)

steps.title: Is this patient still operable?
steps.body:
A PDA seen late, as so many are in Kenya, raises one question before any other: has the pulmonary vascular bed remodelled beyond repair? Closing a defect in a patient with fixed pulmonary vascular disease removes the "pop-off" for the right heart and shortens life.

Points to operableWarns of inoperable (Eisenmenger)
HistoryBreathless, poor growth, chest infections (high flow)Fewer infections and "better" with age; exertional cyanosis, syncope, haemoptysis
ExaminationNormal saturations; loud flow murmur; big active heartResting or exercise desaturation, clubbing; murmur fading; loud single P2; RV heave; small heart on X-ray
EchoLeft-to-right shunt throughout; dilated left heart (VSD, PDA) or right heart (ASD)Bidirectional or right-to-left shunt; RV hypertrophy; left heart no longer dilated
Catheter (the decider)PVRi under about 4 WU·m² (PVR under 3 WU in adults); PVR/SVR under 1/3; Qp:Qs 1.5 or morePVRi over 8 WU·m² (PVR 5 WU or more in adults despite treatment); PVR/SVR over about 0.4
  • Grey zone (PVRi about 4–8 WU·m²): individual decision in a team with pulmonary hypertension expertise; the response to oxygen or nitric oxide helps, though criteria for shunts are not standardised
  • Treat-and-repair (pulmonary vasodilators first, then a fenestrated or flap-valve closure) is used in selected patients but remains controversial
  • Where catheterisation is not available, a clear left-to-right shunt with a dilated left heart and normal saturations is reassuring; any desaturation or bidirectional flow needs a catheter before surgery

Evidence: 6th World Symposium: PVRi 4 WU·m² as the operability cut-off, 4–8 individual, over 8 inoperable; AHA/ATS 2015: PVRi 6–8 WU·m² individual, PVR/SVR under 1/3 operable; ESC 2020 (adults): PVR under 3 WU class I, 3–5 WU IIa, 5 WU or more only in selected cases; vasoreactivity criteria for shunts not established (ERJ Open Res 2023).

ask.question: A 7-year-old with a large PDA now has saturations of 89% at rest and bidirectional shunting on echo. Next step?

choices.text: Cardiac catheterisation with PVR measurement and vasoreactivity testing before any decision
choices.why: Desaturation and bidirectional flow suggest advanced pulmonary vascular disease; closure could be lethal if PVR is fixed.

steps.title: Which space: 3rd or 4th?
steps.body:
3rd space4th space
Lies overThe distal arch, subclavian origin and the top of the ductThe isthmus, the duct and the upper descending aorta
SuitsNeonates and small infants; a high duct; repair that must reach the distal archMost children; the standard space for PDA ligation and coarctation repair
DrawbackCramped under the scapula in a bigger child; the descending aorta is far belowThe distal arch is further away: retract the lung down, the aorta up
If you are wrongToo high: working down a tunnelToo low (5th): the duct is out of reach behind the hilum

Both are accepted; the duct and isthmus lie behind the 3rd–4th spaces, and the choice follows the child's size and how much arch must be exposed. Counting accurately matters more than the choice.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: "ribs are counted accurately to enter the third or fourth intercostal space" for PDA; coarctation through the third or fourth. Thoracic Key: a limited posterolateral thoracotomy through the fourth space is the one more commonly used for PDA. Subbian 2024: preterm ligation through the 3rd or 4th space. Farag 2019: coarctation through the 4th space in 292 children.

ask.question: Why does accurate rib counting matter more than whether you choose the 3rd or 4th space?

choices.text: Entering the 5th space by mistake puts the duct and isthmus out of reach
choices.why: The target lies behind the 3rd–4th spaces; one space too low and you work up behind the hilum.

choices.text: The 4th space damages the phrenic nerve
It does not matter at all

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Weight and prematurity, size and calcification of the duct, lung disease. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pain
  • A chest drain for a day

3. Serious

  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury (hoarse voice, feeding problems)
  • Bleeding from a torn duct
  • Chylothorax
  • Ligation of the wrong vessel (rare)
  • Death (rare outside prematurity)

4. Specific to this operation

  • Small risk of the duct reopening after ligation
  • In preterm babies, unstable blood pressure and breathing in the first day

5. Alternatives

  • Device closure
  • In preterms: ibuprofen or paracetamol
  • No closure: heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, endarteritis
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Device availability and waiting times

coa-eea.name: Coarctation of the aorta repair
coa-eea.approach: Coarctation: resection and extended end-to-end anastomosis (4th space)
coa-eea.summary: Repair of a juxtaductal coarctation through a left thoracotomy: neonatal and later presentations, stent or surgery, the 3rd or 4th space, collaterals and the spinal cord, extended end-to-end anastomosis.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: coarctation of the aorta
steps.body:
A narrowing at the isthmus, opposite the duct: a shelf of thickened media and intima on the posterior wall, often with ductal tissue that constricts as the duct closes.

Two presentations

  • Neonate, duct-dependent: lower body perfused through the duct; when it closes, shock, acidosis and absent femoral pulses in the first weeks. Start prostaglandin E1 to reopen the duct, then repair.
  • Child or adult: upper-body hypertension, weak and delayed femoral pulses (radio-femoral delay), headaches, cold legs; collaterals through the intercostals cause rib notching
Fixed obstruction at the isthmus→LV pressure load, upper-body hypertension→Collaterals around the block→Heart failure, stroke, aortic dissection, early coronary disease

Associations: bicuspid aortic valve (common), intracranial aneurysms, Turner syndrome. Even after a perfect repair, hypertension and recoarctation need lifelong follow-up.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

ask.question: A 3-week-old is brought in shocked with absent femoral pulses. First drug?

choices.why: Reopening the duct restores lower-body perfusion in duct-dependent coarctation; repair follows once the baby is resuscitated.

steps.title: The isthmus, the collaterals and the spinal cord
steps.body:
Through the left chest: the distal arch with the left subclavian artery, the ligamentum (or duct), the coarctation, and the dilated aorta below it. The vagus and recurrent laryngeal nerve cross the arch; the thoracic duct lies behind and to the right.

  • Collaterals: enlarged, thin-walled intercostal arteries and chest wall vessels; they bleed from the incision onward and need control, not wholesale ligation
  • Spinal cord: in a child with poor collaterals, clamping the aorta can leave the cord ischaemic; protect it (short clamp time, avoid hyperthermia, keep distal pressure)

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

steps.title: Case: hypertension in a 9-year-old
steps.body:
Discrete juxtaductal coarctation with a significant gradient and hypertension: repair it.

Evidence: ESC 2020: in adults, repair is indicated for hypertension with an increased gradient; percutaneous stenting is preferred to surgery when technically feasible (Rev Esp Cardiol commentary). Children and small patients: surgery, since a stent cannot be dilated to adult size.

ask.question: Best treatment for this boy?

choices.text: Surgical resection with extended end-to-end anastomosis
choices.why: A child of 24 kg would outgrow a stent; a discrete coarctation with a normal arch is repaired through a left thoracotomy.

steps.lead: A 9-year-old boy, 24 kg, referred with headaches and a blood pressure of 150/95 mmHg in the right arm; femoral pulses weak and delayed. Echo: discrete coarctation beyond the left subclavian artery, continuous Doppler flow with a diastolic tail, bicuspid aortic valve without stenosis. CT angiogram: isthmus 4 mm, normal transverse arch, intercostal collaterals.

steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Age (neonates carry more recoarctation), arch size, collaterals, LV function. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Pain, drains
  • High blood pressure for days to weeks

3. Serious

  • Paraplegia (rare)
  • Recoarctation needing balloon or surgery
  • Recurrent laryngeal nerve injury
  • Chylothorax
  • Bleeding

4. Specific to this operation

  • Paradoxical hypertension and abdominal pain in the first days
  • Lifelong blood pressure and imaging follow-up; aortic valve if bicuspid

5. Alternatives

  • Stent (older patients, suitable anatomy)
  • Balloon angioplasty (limited role)
  • No repair: hypertension, heart failure, stroke, dissection
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Access to CT or MRI follow-up
  • Long-term BP control

ask.question: Which rare but devastating risk of coarctation repair must be discussed?

choices.text: Paraplegia from spinal cord ischaemia during clamping
choices.why: Rare (0% in a modern series, about 0.4% historically) but material to any patient.

steps.title: Left posterolateral thoracotomy, 4th space
steps.body:
Right lateral decubitus, left arm forward and up. A posterolateral incision from below the axilla, curving 2 cm below the tip of the scapula. Divide latissimus dorsi (or retract it in a muscle-sparing approach), spare serratus anterior where possible.

Count the ribs from inside or under the scapula (the first rib you can feel under the scapula is usually the 2nd) and enter the 4th intercostal space on the upper border of the 5th rib. Retract the lung forward and down with a moist pack.

In an older child the chest wall collaterals bleed: control them as you go; the intercostal muscle may be several millimetres thick with dilated vessels.

steps.title: Mobilise the arch, the subclavian and the descending aorta
steps.body:
Open the pleura over the aorta behind the vagus. Mobilise the distal transverse arch (to beyond the left carotid), the left subclavian artery, and the descending aorta well below the coarctation. Ligate and divide the ductus or ligamentum. Control one or two pairs of intercostal arteries with loops if needed; avoid dividing them.

Mobility is what makes a tension-free anastomosis.

steps.title: Clamp: distal arch and descending aorta
steps.body:
Small dose of heparin. Proximal clamp across the distal arch, beyond the left carotid, taking the left subclavian origin; distal clamp on the descending aorta below the dilated segment. Note the time: the cord depends on collaterals while the aorta is clamped.

  • Keep the patient mildly cool (about 35 °C), never hyperthermic
  • Keep the clamp time short (aim for under about 20–30 minutes)
  • Poor collaterals or a long repair: consider distal perfusion (left heart bypass)

Evidence: Spinal cord injury after coarctation repair is rare (0% in Farag 2019; historically about 0.4% in a large survey, Brewer 1972) but devastating; risk rises with long clamp times and poor collaterals.

ask.question: Which patient is at most risk of paraplegia during coarctation clamping?

choices.text: One with few collaterals and a long clamp time
choices.why: Good collaterals carry blood to the cord around the clamps; without them, time and temperature decide.

steps.title: Excise the coarctation and the ductal tissue
steps.body: Divide the aorta above and below the narrowing and excise the whole coarctation with all ductal tissue (left behind, it constricts and causes recoarctation). For an extended repair, incise the underside of the arch proximally, toward or beyond the left carotid origin, and cut the descending aorta obliquely to match.

steps.title: Extended end-to-end anastomosis
steps.body:
Bring the descending aorta up to the arch. Running polypropylene (7-0 in a neonate, 5-0 or 4-0 in an older child), back wall first from inside, then the front wall. Release the distal clamp first (to de-air and check the suture line), then the proximal clamp slowly.

Measure arm and leg pressures: the gradient should be gone. Check the RLN and the thoracic duct region for chyle; drain, close.

Evidence: TSRA primer: end-to-end anastomosis with running polypropylene, 7-0 in neonates to 4-0 in young adults; extended resection with an arch incision for a hypoplastic distal arch.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Paradoxical hypertension: beta-blocker or nitroprusside early, then oral antihypertensives
  • Legs: power and sensation as soon as awake (cord ischaemia)
  • Abdominal pain or distension (mesenteric arteritis): delay feeds, control BP
  • Drain: chyle; voice: RLN
  • Children: fluids, drugs and blood by weight with the paediatric intensivist; the adult dose tables do not apply

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Farag 2019: 14% on antihypertensives at follow-up; recoarctation 9.9%.

ask.question: Day 1 after coarctation repair: BP 165/100, abdominal pain, legs moving well. Next?

choices.text: Treat the paradoxical hypertension (beta-blocker or nitroprusside), withhold feeds, examine the abdomen
choices.why: Post-coarctectomy hypertension and mesenteric arteritis go together; control BP and rest the gut.

tof-repair.name: Tetralogy of Fallot repair
tof-repair.approach: Complete repair: VSD patch, RVOT resection, ± transannular patch
tof-repair.summary: Complete repair of tetralogy: the four features, tet spells, timing and late presentation, shunt first or repair, the z-score debate, VSD closure, RVOT relief and the transannular patch.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: tetralogy of Fallot
steps.body:
One developmental error, anterior and cephalad deviation of the outlet septum, produces all four features:

  • Malalignment VSD: large, non-restrictive, under the aorta
  • RV outflow tract obstruction: infundibular muscle, a small valve and annulus, sometimes small branch PAs
  • Overriding aorta: straddling the defect
  • RV hypertrophy: the RV pumps at systemic pressure
Equal RV and LV pressures (large VSD)→RVOT obstruction sets the shunt→More obstruction: right-to-left, cyanosis→Polycythaemia, clubbing, squatting, spells

The spectrum runs from a "pink tet" (mild obstruction, net left-to-right) to severe cyanosis or pulmonary atresia. Untreated, about 55% survive 5 years and 30% 10 years.

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

Evidence: Merck Manual: four components, shunt direction set by RVOT obstruction; untreated survival 55% at 5 and 30% at 10 years.

ask.question: What sets the degree of cyanosis in tetralogy?

choices.text: The severity of RV outflow tract obstruction
choices.why: The VSD is always large; the harder it is to eject into the PA, the more RV blood goes to the aorta.

choices.text: The degree of aortic override alone

steps.title: Hypercyanotic (tet) spell: what to do
steps.body:
Agitation, crying or dehydration → infundibular spasm and falling SVR → more right-to-left shunt → deeper cyanosis, which drives more hyperpnoea and acidosis. Break the cycle:

  1. Calm the child; knee-chest position (raises SVR and venous return); 100% oxygen
  2. Morphine to stop hyperpnoea; IV fluid bolus to fill the RV
  3. Raise SVR: phenylephrine (1–5 µg/kg IV) or vasopressin
  4. Beta-blocker (propranolol, or esmolol infusion) to relax the infundibulum
  5. Sedation, intubation and ventilation if refractory (beware falling SVR on induction); correct acidosis
  6. A spell is an indication for early surgery: repair or a shunt

Evidence: Boston Children's CICU: knee-chest, oxygen, morphine, volume, phenylephrine 1–5 µg/kg, beta-blockade; operative repair often indicated after recurrent or even single spells.

ask.question: A 9-month-old with tetralogy is deeply cyanosed and hyperpnoeic after crying. Oxygen and knee-chest have not helped. Next?

choices.text: Morphine and a fluid bolus, then phenylephrine to raise SVR
choices.why: Stop the hyperpnoea, fill the RV and raise systemic resistance so less blood shunts right to left.

steps.title: The anatomy the repair must respect
steps.body:
• The VSD lies under the aortic valve; its posteroinferior rim carries the His bundle (perimembranous extension), as in an isolated perimembranous VSD
  • The infundibulum: hypertrophied septal and parietal bands; resect enough, but not the moderator band or the septal attachments of the tricuspid valve
  • The pulmonary valve and annulus: measured with Hegar dilators against normal values (z-score)
  • The coronaries: look before any ventriculotomy; a major coronary (for example the LAD arising from the right coronary) crossing the RV outflow changes the plan (conduit or limited incision)

The model is an adult heart: in a child the relations are the same and everything is smaller.

steps.title: Case: a 3-year-old with tetralogy
steps.body:
Late presentation is the rule here. Complete repair is still the aim; the question is whether the pulmonary arteries and annulus allow it.

Evidence: Schaffner et al. 2022: 165 humanitarian patients (many from sub-Saharan Africa), median age 4.5 years at repair: no early deaths in 161 complete repairs; transannular patch in 38%; preserved valve function linked to shorter ventilation and ICU stay.

ask.question: Best plan?

choices.why: Good-sized branch PAs and no coronary obstacle: a symptomatic child with spells should have complete repair; a shunt first is for unsuitable anatomy or a very small, sick infant.

choices.text: BT shunt and repair at 10 years

steps.lead: A 3-year-old girl, 11 kg, from Kisii, referred with cyanosis since infancy, squatting after play and two spells this year. SpO₂ 74%, clubbing, single S2, harsh ejection murmur. Hb 19 g/dL. Echo: tetralogy with a large malalignment VSD, infundibular and valvar stenosis, pulmonary annulus 9 mm (z-score about −2), confluent branch PAs of good size, left arch, no major coronary across the RVOT.

steps.title: Repair, shunt first, and keeping the valve
steps.body:
QuestionAnswer
When?Elective complete repair usually at about 2–6 months (earlier for spells or severe cyanosis); a late presenter is repaired when seen
Shunt first?Small or sick neonates, very small PAs, complex anatomy or a coronary across the RVOT: modified BT shunt (or RVOT/duct stent), repair later
Keep the valve?Preserve the annulus when it can be opened enough; a transannular patch relieves obstruction at the cost of free pulmonary regurgitation and later RV dilatation
Which z-score?No single cut-off: z-scores depend on the normal dataset used. Decide on the annulus achieved and the residual gradient after valvotomy
Success off bypassLow residual RV pressure (RV:LV ratio well under systemic; many accept up to about 0.7) and no significant residual VSD on TOE

Evidence: Merck: elective repair at 2–6 months; shunt or RVOT stent for low birth weight or complex anatomy. Awori et al. (EJCTS 2013; WJPCHS 2018, from Nairobi): the same z-score means very different annulus sizes across normal datasets, so a rigid z-score cut-off for a transannular patch is unreliable.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Age and weight, cyanosis and haematocrit, PA size, coronary anatomy. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • ICU for a few days
  • Drains, pacing wires
  • Some desaturation at first if a PFO is left open

3. Serious

  • Low cardiac output from a stiff RV ("restrictive physiology")
  • Junctional ectopic tachycardia
  • Complete heart block
  • Residual VSD or RVOT obstruction needing re-operation
  • Death (under 5% for uncomplicated repair)

4. Specific to this operation

  • Pulmonary regurgitation, especially after a transannular patch: lifelong follow-up and likely pulmonary valve replacement later
  • Late arrhythmias

5. Alternatives

  • BT shunt or RVOT stent first, repair later
  • No surgery: progressive cyanosis, spells, stroke, brain abscess, early death
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Waiting time; spells while waiting (propranolol)
  • Follow-up echo access for decades

ask.question: What must the family understand about a transannular patch?

choices.text: It leaves pulmonary regurgitation; most will need a pulmonary valve later in life
choices.why: The repair is not the last operation: lifelong follow-up of the RV.

choices.text: It is a cure with no follow-up

steps.title: Median sternotomy
steps.body: Median sternotomy; in a small child keep a thymic remnant (or excise part of it) and harvest a piece of anterior pericardium for the patch before heparin. Fix it in 0.6% glutaraldehyde for a few minutes if you want it stiffer and easier to handle.

steps.title: Cannulation: aorta and both cavae
steps.body:
Heparin; aortic cannula high on the ascending aorta, bicaval venous drainage (SVC directly or through the appendage, IVC low on the right atrium), with snares around both cavae so the right atrium can be opened without air entering the venous line.

Bicaval cannulation is the rule for any operation inside the right atrium, as here for tetralogy.

steps.title: Cross-clamp and cardioplegia
steps.body:
Mild hypothermia, cross-clamp and antegrade cold cardioplegia into the aortic root; tighten the caval snares. A left heart vent (through the right superior pulmonary vein or across the defect) keeps the field dry from bronchial return.

Evidence: AATS/TSRA primer: median sternotomy, aortic and bicaval cannulation, cold cardioplegia after cross-clamping; for VSD an LA or LV vent through the right superior pulmonary vein and repeat doses every 20–30 minutes.

steps.title: Right atriotomy
steps.body: Open the right atrium parallel to the atrioventricular groove, about 1 cm from it, from the appendage toward the IVC cannula; stay away from the crista terminalis and the SA node at the SVC–atrial junction. Retract the edges with stay sutures.

steps.title: Close the VSD through the right atrium
steps.body: Through the tricuspid valve (retract or detach the septal leaflet) close the VSD with a Dacron or pericardial patch, baffling the LV to the aorta. Shallow bites on the RV side at the posteroinferior rim (His bundle); along the superior rim, sutures pass close to the aortic valve. The muscular rim toward the outlet is sewn through the hypertrophied septal band.

steps.title: Open the RV outflow: resect, valvotomy, measure
steps.body: Through the right atrium and tricuspid valve, or a limited infundibular incision: divide and resect the obstructing septal and parietal bands. Through the pulmonary trunk: commissurotomy of the fused valve. Then pass Hegar dilators across the annulus and compare with the expected size for the child's body surface area.

steps.title: Transannular patch, if the annulus is too small
steps.body:
If the annulus remains too small: extend the incision across the annulus onto the pulmonary trunk and close it with a pericardial transannular patch, keeping the RV incision as short as possible. A monocusp can reduce early regurgitation.

Off bypass: measure RV and LV pressures and check for a residual VSD on TOE. A high RV:LV ratio means residual obstruction to relieve before leaving theatre.

ask.question: What is the long-term price of a transannular patch?

choices.text: Free pulmonary regurgitation, leading to RV dilatation and later pulmonary valve replacement
choices.why: Opening the annulus removes the valve function; the RV dilates over years.

steps.title: De-air, close the atrium, release the clamp
steps.body:
Before the last sutures: fill the left heart (anaesthetist inflates the lungs), let air escape through the defect or the patch edge, then tie. Close the right atriotomy in two layers of running polypropylene, release the snares, vent the aortic root and remove the cross-clamp.

Leave a small patent foramen ovale in a hypertrophied, stiff RV: it lets the right heart off-load early (at the cost of some desaturation).

steps.title: Separate from bypass; check the repair
steps.body: Rewarm, separate from bypass, transesophageal echo for a residual shunt and valve function, then decannulate and give protamine. Temporary atrial and ventricular pacing wires; one or two drains; close the pericardium loosely or leave it open.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Restrictive RV: low output with high CVP and a small, stiff RV; keep preload, avoid high airway pressures, milrinone; early extubation helps
  • JET: cool to about 35 °C, correct Mg²⁺ and K⁺, reduce catecholamines, amiodarone; atrial pacing faster than the JET
  • Echo: residual VSD, RVOT gradient, pulmonary regurgitation, effusions; chylothorax
  • Children: doses by weight with the paediatric intensivist

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Merck: perioperative mortality under 5% for uncomplicated repair.

ask.question: 6 h after TOF repair: CVP 16, BP low, small RV on echo with forward diastolic flow in the PA, ascites. Problem?

choices.why: A stiff hypertrophied RV fills poorly; support with preload, milrinone, low airway pressures, and let the PFO decompress the right heart.

pal-bt.name: Palliative operations
pal-bt.summary: The modified BT shunt for too little pulmonary blood flow: indications, the innominate artery and right PA, shunt sizing, saturations and shunt thrombosis.

steps.title: Why a shunt: too little pulmonary blood flow
steps.body:
A systemic-to-pulmonary shunt adds pulmonary blood flow when the RV outflow cannot: tetralogy with small PAs or in a sick infant, pulmonary atresia, critical pulmonary stenosis, tricuspid atresia and other single-ventricle circulations.

Too little flow to the lungs→Cyanosis, acidosis (or duct-dependent: prostaglandin E1)→PTFE tube from a systemic artery to a PA→Saturations about 75–85%, PAs grow

The balance is delicate: too small a shunt leaves the baby blue; too big floods the lungs and steals diastolic flow from the coronaries and the gut.

ask.question: A shunt that is too large for the baby causes what?

choices.text: Pulmonary over-circulation with diastolic steal: low diastolic pressure, coronary and gut ischaemia
choices.why: Blood runs off into the lungs throughout diastole; coronary perfusion and mesenteric flow fall.

steps.title: Innominate artery, right PA and the nerves
steps.body: KNH practice: median sternotomy, with a graft from the innominate artery or the right subclavian artery to the right pulmonary artery; the exact technique varies by consultant. The right PA is reached medial to the SVC, between the SVC and the ascending aorta. Through a thoracotomy (classical), from the subclavian artery to the ipsilateral PA. Protect the phrenic and vagus nerves (and the recurrent laryngeal nerve hooking the subclavian on the right).

steps.title: Case: a blue 6-week-old
steps.body: Tetralogy with very small PAs, too small and sick for complete repair: a modified BT shunt now, repair later.

ask.question: Shunt size for a 3.4 kg baby?

choices.why: About 1 mm per kg in small infants: 3–3.5 mm for 3–4 kg; 4 mm for larger infants. Oversizing raises the risk of death from over-circulation.

steps.lead: A 6-week-old, 3.4 kg, increasingly cyanosed (SpO₂ 62%), poor feeding. Echo: tetralogy with severe infundibular stenosis, a hypoplastic annulus and branch PAs of 3 mm; the duct has closed.

steps.title: Shunt size, route and risk
steps.body:
PointPractice
Size by weightAbout 1–1.2 mm per kg in neonates and small infants: 3 mm under about 3 kg, 3.5 mm about 3–4 kg, 4 mm for bigger infants; older children larger (consultant and unit practice). Use the calculator below
Check the PAThe graft should not be bigger than the branch PA it feeds; a small PA with a big graft floods one lung
RouteKNH: sternotomy, innominate or right subclavian artery to the right PA (bypass on standby, easy to take down at repair); thoracotomy elsewhere
AlternativesDuctal stent (duct-dependent), RVOT stent or balloon (tetralogy), early complete repair
RiskNot a small operation: mortality around 9% in neonates and infants in one series; early thrombosis about 9%

Evidence: Dirks et al., EJCTS 2013 (32 shunts): sizes 3 mm 25%, 3.5 mm 59%, 4 mm 16%; median 1.21 mm/kg; mortality 9.4%, thrombosis 9.4% within 24 h; lower weight and larger shunt per kg predicted death.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Weight and age, diagnosis (single ventricle higher risk), shunt size per kg. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • ICU
  • Drain

3. Serious

  • Shunt thrombosis (sudden desaturation, loss of the murmur)
  • Over-circulation and low diastolic pressure
  • Phrenic nerve injury
  • Death (around 1 in 10 in some infant series)

4. Specific to this operation

  • A second operation (complete repair or next stage) is planned
  • Aspirin until the next operation

5. Alternatives

  • Ductal or RVOT stent
  • Early complete repair where anatomy allows
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Access to oxygen saturation monitoring and aspirin at home

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which complication of a BT shunt is an emergency the parents should recognise?

choices.text: Shunt blockage: the baby becomes suddenly bluer
choices.why: Thrombosis is commonest early; sudden desaturation needs immediate assessment.

steps.title: Median sternotomy
steps.body: Median sternotomy; in a small child keep a thymic remnant (or excise part of it) and harvest a piece of anterior pericardium for the patch before heparin. Fix it in 0.6% glutaraldehyde for a few minutes if you want it stiffer and easier to handle.

steps.title: Sew the shunt: innominate end, then PA end
steps.body:
Heparin (about 100 U/kg; check the unit protocol). Side-biting clamp on the innominate (or right subclavian) artery; bevel the PTFE tube and sew it end-to-side with running 7-0 or 8-0 polypropylene. Then a clamp on the right PA (watch saturations: the baby may not tolerate PA clamping), and the distal anastomosis.

Open the shunt: saturations should rise to about 75–85% and the diastolic pressure fall a little. A thrill should be felt over the tube.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Heparin early (unit protocol), then aspirin
  • Target saturations about 75–85%; falling saturation or loss of the shunt murmur: shunt thrombosis, an emergency (heparin, echo, theatre or cath)
  • Diastolic pressure and lactate: over-circulation; avoid hyperventilation and high oxygen, which drop PVR further
  • Children: doses by weight

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Dirks 2013: early thrombosis 9.4%, mortality 9.4% in 32 infants.

ask.question: 12 h after a BT shunt, SpO₂ falls from 82% to 60% and the continuous murmur has gone. Next?

choices.text: Heparin bolus, urgent echo and return to theatre or the cath lab
choices.why: Acute shunt thrombosis is life-threatening; restore flow quickly.

pal-band.name: Palliative operations
pal-band.summary: Pulmonary artery banding for too much pulmonary blood flow: indications, Trusler's rule, on-table pressures and saturations, position and migration.

steps.title: Why band: too much pulmonary blood flow
steps.body:
A band restricts pulmonary blood flow and pressure when the defect cannot be closed safely yet: multiple muscular ("Swiss cheese") VSDs, a very small or septic infant, single-ventricle circulations with unrestricted flow, or to prepare (train) the LV before a late arterial switch.

Large left-to-right shunt→High PA flow and pressure→Band on the trunk→Less flow and pressure: heart failure settles, lungs are protected

ask.question: Why band rather than repair an infant with multiple muscular VSDs?

choices.text: Many apical muscular VSDs are hard to close completely in infancy and some close with time
choices.why: The band protects the lungs while the child grows; some muscular defects close spontaneously.

choices.text: Banding is safer for the conduction system in every VSD

steps.title: How tight? Trusler's rule and the pressures
steps.body:
CirculationBand circumference (Trusler)
Two ventricles, left-to-right shunt (VSDs)20 mm + 1 mm per kg
Mixing lesions (single ventricle, TGA with VSD)24 mm + 1 mm per kg
Large ASD or large PAAdd 1–2 mm

Then adjust on the table: distal PA pressure down to about a third to a half of systemic, systemic pressure rising a little, and acceptable saturations (about 90% in a two-ventricle child, 75–85% when there is mixing). Loosen if the saturation drops, the distal PA collapses or the heart slows.

Evidence: Trusler rules (Pedi Cardiology summary): 20 mm + 1 mm/kg for left-to-right shunts, 24 mm + 1 mm/kg for mixing; add 1–2 mm with a large ASD or PA; tighten until distal PA pressure is about 50% of systemic when pulmonary hypertension is present; loosen for distal PA collapse, cyanosis or bradycardia.

ask.question: Trusler's band circumference for a 5 kg infant with multiple VSDs (biventricular)?

choices.why: 20 mm + 1 mm/kg × 5 kg = 25 mm, then adjusted to the pressures and saturations.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Weight, sepsis, the underlying lesion. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • ICU
  • Drain

3. Serious

  • Band too tight (cyanosis) or too loose (heart failure persists)
  • Band migration onto a branch PA
  • Pulmonary valve distortion
  • Death

4. Specific to this operation

  • A further operation to remove the band and repair the heart is planned
  • Branch PA may need repair at debanding

5. Alternatives

  • Primary repair if possible
  • Medical therapy (risk of pulmonary vascular disease)
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Growth monitoring while waiting for the definitive repair

ask.question: Why will a banded child need another operation?

choices.text: The band is palliation: the defect still needs closing and the band removed
choices.why: Banding protects the lungs while the child grows; definitive repair follows.

steps.title: Median sternotomy
steps.body: Median sternotomy; in a small child keep a thymic remnant (or excise part of it) and harvest a piece of anterior pericardium for the patch before heparin. Fix it in 0.6% glutaraldehyde for a few minutes if you want it stiffer and easier to handle.

steps.title: Place the band on the main trunk
steps.body:
Through a sternotomy (or left thoracotomy): pass the tape (Teflon or PTFE) around the main pulmonary trunk, between the aorta and the PA, midway between the valve and the bifurcation. Mark the calculated circumference and tighten in steps while watching the pressures and saturations; then fix the band to the adventitia so it cannot migrate.

  • Too proximal: distorts the pulmonary valve
  • Too distal: migrates onto the branches (usually the right PA), stenosing one lung
  • Too tight: cyanosis and bradycardia; too loose: no protection

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Saturations and BP: too tight = cyanosis, bradycardia, RV failure; too loose = continued failure
  • Echo gradient across the band daily at first
  • Children: doses by weight

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

Evidence: Trusler rules: loosen for distal PA collapse, cyanosis or bradycardia.

ask.question: After banding, a 4 kg infant is bradycardic and saturations have fallen to 70% (biventricular). Next?

choices.why: Excessive restriction causes cyanosis and RV pressure overload; loosen and re-measure.

aiod-abf.name: Aorto-iliac occlusive disease
aiod-abf.summary: Both groins, the infrarenal aorta, retroperitoneal tunnels behind the ureters, bifurcated graft, femoral anastomoses.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: aorto-iliac occlusive disease
steps.body:
Atherosclerosis at the aortic bifurcation, where flow divides and shear stress is low: plaque, then stenosis, then thrombosis of the distal aorta and iliac arteries, often in smokers in their 40s–60s. Collaterals (lumbar to iliolumbar and circumflex iliac; internal thoracic to inferior epigastric; SMA to IMA through the arc of Riolan) keep the legs alive.

Plaque at the bifurcation→Stenosis→Thrombosis: occluded distal aorta and iliacs→Collaterals→Claudication (buttock, thigh, calf)
Collaterals insufficient→Rest pain, ulcers, gangrene (chronic limb-threatening ischaemia)

Leriche syndrome: buttock and thigh claudication, absent femoral pulses, erectile dysfunction. Ankle–brachial index: 0.90 or less is peripheral arterial disease; 1.40 or more means non-compressible (calcified) arteries.

TASC IIAorto-iliac lesions (summary)Usual first choice
ACIA stenoses; a short (≤3 cm) EIA stenosisendovascular
Bshort infrarenal aortic stenosis; unilateral CIA occlusion; EIA stenoses 3–10 cm; unilateral EIA occlusion sparing the internal iliac and CFAendovascular
Cbilateral CIA occlusions; bilateral EIA stenoses 3–10 cm; EIA disease into the CFA; heavily calcified EIA occlusionopen in fit patients; endovascular increasingly
Dinfrarenal aorto-iliac occlusion; diffuse disease of the aorta and both iliacs; unilateral CIA + EIA occlusion; bilateral EIA occlusionsopen (aortobifemoral); CERAB in experienced hands

In Africa think also of HIV-associated vasculopathy (young patients, acute thrombosis or occlusions, often presenting late with critical ischaemia) and Takayasu arteritis (young women, aorta and its branches; control inflammation before surgery).

Treatment: for everyone, best medical therapy: stop smoking (varenicline), antiplatelet, statin, blood pressure and diabetes control; supervised exercise for claudication. Revascularise chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, and claudication that still limits life after exercise and medical therapy, by shared decision. Treat the inflow (aorto-iliac) before the outflow.

Evidence: TASC II (Norgren et al., J Vasc Surg 2007). ESVS 2024 claudication guideline (Nordanstig et al.): ABI thresholds, smoking cessation, individualised revascularisation for claudication. Global Vascular Guidelines 2019 for CLTI (Conte et al.): endovascular-first for moderate-to-severe aorto-iliac disease; open reconstruction for extensive disease in average-risk patients. HIV vasculopathy: Robbs and Paruk (Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2010; 226 patients, mean age 36) and Van Marle et al. (S Afr J Surg; over 90% presented with Fontaine III/IV, primary amputation 32%). Takayasu in Africa: Genga, Oyoo and Adebajo (Curr Rheumatol Rep 2018).

Grading the ischaemia (chronic):

FontaineRutherford (category)Clinical pictureObjective (Rutherford)
I0asymptomaticnormal treadmill test
IIa (over 200 m)1 mildclaudicationcompletes treadmill; ankle pressure after exercise over 50 mmHg but at least 20 mmHg below resting
IIb (under 200 m)2 moderate, 3 severeclaudicationcategory 3: cannot complete treadmill; ankle pressure after exercise under 50 mmHg
III4ischaemic rest painresting ankle pressure under 40 mmHg, toe pressure under 30 mmHg
IV5 minor, 6 major tissue lossulcer, gangreneresting ankle pressure under 60 mmHg, toe pressure under 40 mmHg

Rutherford 4–6 is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI). Acute limb ischaemia has its own Rutherford grading: I viable; IIa marginally threatened (no or minimal sensory loss, no weakness); IIb immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond the toes, rest pain, mild or moderate weakness); III irreversible (anaesthetic, paralysed, no venous Doppler signal).

Ankle-brachial index: 0.90 or less is PAD; 1.40 or more is non-compressible (calcified, common in diabetes and renal failure): use toe pressures.

Best medical therapy is for everyone with PAD, and the first treatment for claudication:

  • Stop smoking: counselling at every visit, with varenicline (or bupropion, nicotine replacement).
  • Antithrombotic: a single antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel); consider low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily with aspirin in symptomatic PAD and after revascularisation if bleeding risk is low.
  • High-intensity statin: LDL under 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and at least a 50% fall (ESVS 2024).
  • Blood pressure under 130/80 mmHg (ACE inhibitor or ARB); diabetes control (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists); foot care.
  • Supervised exercise: 30–45 minutes of walking to near-maximal pain, at least 3 times a week, for at least 12 weeks.

When to revascularise: claudication only when it stays lifestyle-limiting despite best medical therapy and exercise, decided with the patient (never for asymptomatic disease); CLTI (rest pain, ulcer, gangrene): prompt assessment for revascularisation to save the limb; acute ischaemia IIa urgently, IIb as an emergency, III amputation.

Evidence: Rutherford 1997 standards (J Vasc Surg 1997;26:517-38) and Fontaine, as tabulated in current reviews. ACC/AHA 2024 PAD guideline (Gornik et al.): single antiplatelet, rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin, high-intensity statin, BP under 130/80, supervised exercise at least 3 times a week for 12 weeks; revascularisation for claudication only if lifestyle-limiting despite therapy. ESVS 2024 (Nordanstig et al.): LDL under 1.4 mmol/L; varenicline first-line; individualised decisions. COMPASS (Lancet 2018) and VOYAGER PAD (NEJM 2020) for low-dose rivaroxaban.

ask.question: A 50-year-old smoker has buttock claudication, absent femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction. Where is the disease?

choices.text: The distal aorta and both iliac arteries (Leriche syndrome)
choices.why: Buttock claudication and absent femoral pulses place the obstruction above the groins; erectile dysfunction reflects poor internal iliac flow.

steps.title: The aortic bifurcation, iliacs and femoral arteries
steps.body:
The aorta divides at L4 (the level of the iliac crests) into the common iliac arteries, each dividing over the sacroiliac joint into the internal iliac (pelvis, buttock) and the external iliac, which becomes the common femoral artery under the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point and divides 3–5 cm lower into the superficial femoral and profunda femoris. The profunda is the key collateral to the leg when the SFA is occluded.

Protect: the ureters (crossing the iliac bifurcations: graft tunnels pass behind them), the iliac veins behind the arteries, the hypogastric plexus (sexual function), the IMA, and in the groin the femoral vein medially and the femoral nerve laterally.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

steps.title: Case: Leriche syndrome with rest pain
steps.body:
TASC II D (infrarenal aorto-iliac occlusion) with chronic limb-threatening ischaemia in a fit patient: aortobifemoral bypass, the most durable reconstruction. Endovascular reconstruction (CERAB) is an alternative in expert centres.

Before surgery: stop smoking, statin and antiplatelet, check the coronaries and the renal function; confirm the femoral run-off (profunda patent) on CT angiography. Test for HIV.

Evidence: de Vries and Hunink (J Vasc Surg 1997, meta-analysis): aortic bifurcation graft 5-year limb patency 91% for claudication and 87.5% for critical ischaemia; operative mortality 4.4%, systemic morbidity 12.1%. A 2021 meta-analysis of extensive aorto-iliac disease (Cardiovasc Intervent Radiol; 9,319 patients): open repair 5-year primary patency 88% vs 71% for standard endovascular treatment, with higher 30-day mortality (3% vs 0.8%).

ask.question: What is the most durable reconstruction for this fit patient with a TASC II D aorto-iliac occlusion?

choices.why: Five-year limb patency is about 90% (de Vries and Hunink, 1997); endovascular results for TASC D are improving (CERAB) but standard stenting is less durable (about 71% at 5 years).

steps.lead: A 54-year-old man, a matatu owner who smokes 20 a day. Two years of buttock and thigh claudication at 100 m, now rest pain in the right foot at night and erectile dysfunction. No femoral pulses. ABI 0.38 right, 0.52 left. CT angiography: the aorta occluded from just below the IMA, both common iliacs occluded, the external iliacs reconstituting; common femoral and profunda arteries patent; SFA patent. HIV-negative; creatinine normal; echo normal.

steps.title: Which reconstruction? Aortobifemoral, axillobifemoral, femorofemoral or endovascular
steps.body:
The choice rests on the extent of disease (unilateral or bilateral, how far up the aorta, the common femorals), the patient (fitness for laparotomy, the abdomen, life expectancy, infection) and the inflow for an extra-anatomic graft.

Aortobifemoral bypass

  • Choose for: a fit patient with extensive bilateral aorto-iliac disease or aortic occlusion (TASC C/D); failed endovascular treatment
  • Avoid when: unfit for general anaesthesia and laparotomy; a hostile abdomen; (relative) retroperitoneal fibrosis, horseshoe kidney, severe cardiac disease
  • Patency at 5 years: about 86–91% per limb
  • Main risks: operative mortality about 4% in older series; sexual dysfunction; graft infection; aortoenteric fistula

Axillobifemoral bypass

  • Choose for: bilateral aorto-iliac occlusion in a patient unfit for laparotomy; a hostile abdomen (several laparotomies, a stoma, radiation); an infected aortic graft or aortoenteric fistula after the graft is removed
  • Avoid when: inflow disease in the subclavian or axillary artery (compare both arm pressures, image the arch branches, use the arm with the higher pressure); a fit claudicant (poorer patency)
  • Patency at 5 years: about 50–75% (63% primary in one series)
  • Main risks: graft thrombosis; disruption of the axillary anastomosis with arm strain; infection along the tunnel

Femorofemoral cross-over

  • Choose for: unilateral iliac occlusion with a healthy donor iliac (or one stented first); high risk or hostile abdomen; failed iliac stenting
  • Avoid when: untreated disease in the donor iliac; bilateral disease; (relative) marked obesity
  • Patency at 5 years: about 70% primary, 85% secondary
  • Main risks: groin infection; steal from the donor leg (rare)

Endovascular (kissing stents, CERAB)

  • Choose for: most TASC A–C lesions, and increasingly D in experienced centres
  • Avoid when: heavy calcified occlusion into the common femoral (hybrid: femoral endarterectomy plus stent); occlusion up to the renal arteries; no access
  • Patency at 5 years: covered stents about 75% (COBEST); CERAB 82% at 3 years
  • Main risks: access complications; stent occlusion; reintervention

Evidence: de Vries and Hunink (J Vasc Surg 1997): aortic bifurcation grafts, 5-year limb patency 91% (claudication) and 87.5% (CLI), mortality 4.4%. Martin and Katz (Am J Surg 2000): axillofemoral primary patency 63% at 5 years. Park et al. (Vasc Specialist Int 2017): femorofemoral 70% primary, 85% secondary at 5 years; donor-iliac disease was treated first when present. COBEST (J Vasc Surg 2016); CERAB (Taeymans, J Vasc Surg 2018). Indications and contraindications: StatPearls/Medscape reviews of each operation.

ask.question: A 70-year-old with a right common iliac occlusion, a normal left iliac on CT, and severe COPD has rest pain in the right foot. Stenting has failed. Which bypass?

choices.text: Femorofemoral cross-over from the left groin
choices.why: Unilateral disease with a healthy donor iliac is the classic indication; it avoids a laparotomy and has better patency than an axillofemoral graft.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Cardiac and respiratory fitness. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Ileus
  • Groin lymph leak or infection

3. Serious

  • Graft infection
  • Limb occlusion
  • Colonic ischaemia
  • Aortoenteric fistula (late)
  • Death

4. Specific to this operation

  • Sexual dysfunction

5. Alternatives

  • Endovascular (kissing stents, CERAB)
  • Axillobifemoral if unfit
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Cost; follow-up

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which late complication should the ABF patient know to report?

choices.text: Gastrointestinal bleeding (aortoenteric fistula) or a groin lump or infection
choices.why: Late graft complications present this way.

steps.title: Expose both femoral bifurcations
steps.body:
Vertical incisions over the femoral pulses (or where they should be: the mid-inguinal point). Expose the common femoral artery from the inguinal ligament down, and control the SFA and the profunda (its first branches too). Tie the lymphatics (lymph leaks and infection are the groin's complications). Feel the CFA for plaque: an endarterectomy or profundaplasty may be needed where the graft is sewn.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

steps.title: Laparotomy; the infrarenal aorta below the left renal vein
steps.body:
Midline laparotomy (or left retroperitoneal). Expose the infrarenal aorta just below the left renal vein, where it is usually soft enough to clamp: the occlusion often reaches the IMA, and above it the aorta is patent.

End-to-end anastomosis (divide the aorta, oversew the distal stump) is better haemodynamically and lies flatter behind the duodenum; end-to-side keeps flow to the IMA and internal iliacs when the external iliacs are occluded (pelvic and colonic perfusion).

steps.title: Retroperitoneal tunnels to the groins, behind the ureters
steps.body: From the groin and the aorta, a finger (then a tunnelling instrument) creates a tunnel on the front of the iliac arteries, behind the ureter, under the inguinal ligament, to meet in the groin. A graft limb placed in front of the ureter can compress it (hydronephrosis).

ask.question: Why must the limbs of an aortobifemoral graft pass behind the ureters?

choices.text: A graft in front of the ureter can compress it and cause hydronephrosis
choices.why: Tunnel along the front of the iliac arteries, under (behind) the ureter; the ureter then lies in front of the graft.

steps.title: Proximal anastomosis, then the femoral anastomoses
steps.body: Heparin; clamp. A bifurcated Dacron graft (commonly 16 × 8 mm or 14 × 7 mm, matched to the aorta), the body kept short so the bifurcation sits low and the limbs do not kink. Proximal anastomosis (3-0 polypropylene), pass the limbs through the tunnels, then each femoral anastomosis end-to-side onto the CFA (5-0 polypropylene), extended onto the profunda (profundaplasty) if the SFA is occluded or the profunda origin narrowed. Flush before completing each.

steps.title: Release one limb at a time; check the feet and the colon
steps.body:
Release each limb slowly (declamping hypotension). Feel for pulses in the grafts and at the feet (Doppler signals), look at the sigmoid colon. Close the retroperitoneum over the graft (away from the duodenum), then the groins in layers without dead space.

Early complications: bleeding, limb thrombosis, distal embolism (trash foot), colonic ischaemia, groin infection or lymph leak. Late: anastomotic false aneurysm at the groin, graft infection, limb occlusion from outflow disease.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Graft and foot Doppler hourly at first
  • Groin wounds
  • Colon: bloody diarrhoea

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 1 after ABF: right foot cold, no Doppler signal. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant: limb occlusion needs thrombectomy
choices.why: Early limb thrombosis is a technical problem until proven otherwise.

steps.title: Case: critical ischaemia with a hostile abdomen and poor lungs
steps.body:
An aortic operation is too risky (her lungs, the frozen abdomen): an extra-anatomic bypass from the axillary artery avoids the abdomen and the aortic clamp. Choose the side with the better arm pressure (and no subclavian stenosis). Less durable than an aortobifemoral graft.

ask.question: Before an axillobifemoral bypass, what must be checked in the donor arm?

choices.text: Equal arm pressures and no subclavian or axillary stenosis on the chosen side
choices.why: A stenosed donor artery starves the graft and the arm; a pressure difference over about 20 mmHg suggests subclavian stenosis.

steps.lead: A 71-year-old woman, rest pain and a heel ulcer on the right, ABI 0.3 both sides; aorto-iliac occlusion on CT. Severe COPD on home oxygen; three previous laparotomies and a colostomy. Brachial pressures equal on both arms; no subclavian stenosis on CT.

Femorofemoral cross-over

  • Choose for: unilateral iliac occlusion with a healthy donor iliac (or one stented first); high risk or hostile abdomen; failed iliac stenting
  • Avoid when: untreated disease in the donor iliac; bilateral disease; (relative) marked obesity
  • Patency at 5 years: about 70% primary, 85% secondary
  • Main risks: groin infection; steal from the donor leg (rare)

Endovascular (kissing stents, CERAB)

  • Choose for: most TASC A–C lesions, and increasingly D in experienced centres
  • Avoid when: heavy calcified occlusion into the common femoral (hybrid: femoral endarterectomy plus stent); occlusion up to the renal arteries; no access
  • Patency at 5 years: covered stents about 75% (COBEST); CERAB 82% at 3 years
  • Main risks: access complications; stent occlusion; reintervention

Evidence: de Vries and Hunink (J Vasc Surg 1997): aortic bifurcation grafts, 5-year limb patency 91% (claudication) and 87.5% (CLI), mortality 4.4%. Martin and Katz (Am J Surg 2000): axillofemoral primary patency 63% at 5 years. Park et al. (Vasc Specialist Int 2017): femorofemoral 70% primary, 85% secondary at 5 years; donor-iliac disease was treated first when present. COBEST (J Vasc Surg 2016); CERAB (Taeymans, J Vasc Surg 2018). Indications and contraindications: StatPearls/Medscape reviews of each operation.

choices.why: Unilateral disease with a healthy donor iliac is the classic indication; it avoids a laparotomy and has better patency than an axillofemoral graft.

ask.question: Why is axillobifemoral chosen despite poorer patency?

choices.text: It avoids a laparotomy and aortic clamp in a high-risk patient
choices.why: Extra-anatomic bypass trades durability for lower operative risk.

steps.title: Expose both femoral bifurcations
steps.body:
Vertical incisions over the femoral pulses (or where they should be: the mid-inguinal point). Expose the common femoral artery from the inguinal ligament down, and control the SFA and the profunda (its first branches too). Tie the lymphatics (lymph leaks and infection are the groin's complications). Feel the CFA for plaque: an endarterectomy or profundaplasty may be needed where the graft is sewn.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

steps.title: Expose the first part of the axillary artery
steps.body:
A horizontal incision 2 cm below the middle third of the clavicle. Split the pectoralis major in the line of its fibres, divide the clavipectoral fascia (and the pectoralis minor if needed); the axillary vein lies in front and below, the brachial plexus cords above and behind. Control the artery medial to pectoralis minor.

The anastomosis goes on the first part of the artery, the graft running along the artery for a few centimetres before turning down (so arm abduction does not tear it off).

steps.title: Subcutaneous tunnel down the mid-axillary line; the cross-over
steps.body: A long tunneller, through one or two counter-incisions, subcutaneously in the mid-axillary line (not over the costal margin, where it kinks), down to the right groin. A ringed (externally supported) PTFE graft, 8 mm. Then a femorofemoral limb in a suprapubic subcutaneous tunnel to the left groin.

steps.title: Release, check the flow, close
steps.body: Complete the femoral anastomoses, flush, release. A graft pulse along the chest wall and at both groins; Doppler signals at the feet. The patient must not lie on the graft side or wear tight belts over it.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • No BP cuff on the donor arm; do not lie on the graft side
  • Graft pulse along the chest wall; feet Doppler

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Which instruction protects an axillobifemoral graft?

choices.text: No BP cuff on the donor arm and do not lie on the graft side
choices.why: External compression can thrombose the graft.
