aiod-endo.name: Aorto-iliac occlusive disease
aiod-endo.summary: Bilateral femoral access, crossing and re-entry, simultaneous covered stents at the bifurcation.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: aorto-iliac occlusive disease
steps.body:
Atherosclerosis at the aortic bifurcation, where flow divides and shear stress is low: plaque, then stenosis, then thrombosis of the distal aorta and iliac arteries, often in smokers in their 40s–60s. Collaterals (lumbar to iliolumbar and circumflex iliac; internal thoracic to inferior epigastric; SMA to IMA through the arc of Riolan) keep the legs alive.

Plaque at the bifurcation→Stenosis→Thrombosis: occluded distal aorta and iliacs→Collaterals→Claudication (buttock, thigh, calf)
Collaterals insufficient→Rest pain, ulcers, gangrene (chronic limb-threatening ischaemia)

Leriche syndrome: buttock and thigh claudication, absent femoral pulses, erectile dysfunction. Ankle–brachial index: 0.90 or less is peripheral arterial disease; 1.40 or more means non-compressible (calcified) arteries.

TASC IIAorto-iliac lesions (summary)Usual first choice
ACIA stenoses; a short (≤3 cm) EIA stenosisendovascular
Bshort infrarenal aortic stenosis; unilateral CIA occlusion; EIA stenoses 3–10 cm; unilateral EIA occlusion sparing the internal iliac and CFAendovascular
Cbilateral CIA occlusions; bilateral EIA stenoses 3–10 cm; EIA disease into the CFA; heavily calcified EIA occlusionopen in fit patients; endovascular increasingly
Dinfrarenal aorto-iliac occlusion; diffuse disease of the aorta and both iliacs; unilateral CIA + EIA occlusion; bilateral EIA occlusionsopen (aortobifemoral); CERAB in experienced hands

In Africa think also of HIV-associated vasculopathy (young patients, acute thrombosis or occlusions, often presenting late with critical ischaemia) and Takayasu arteritis (young women, aorta and its branches; control inflammation before surgery).

Treatment: for everyone, best medical therapy: stop smoking (varenicline), antiplatelet, statin, blood pressure and diabetes control; supervised exercise for claudication. Revascularise chronic limb-threatening ischaemia, and claudication that still limits life after exercise and medical therapy, by shared decision. Treat the inflow (aorto-iliac) before the outflow.

Evidence: TASC II (Norgren et al., J Vasc Surg 2007). ESVS 2024 claudication guideline (Nordanstig et al.): ABI thresholds, smoking cessation, individualised revascularisation for claudication. Global Vascular Guidelines 2019 for CLTI (Conte et al.): endovascular-first for moderate-to-severe aorto-iliac disease; open reconstruction for extensive disease in average-risk patients. HIV vasculopathy: Robbs and Paruk (Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2010; 226 patients, mean age 36) and Van Marle et al. (S Afr J Surg; over 90% presented with Fontaine III/IV, primary amputation 32%). Takayasu in Africa: Genga, Oyoo and Adebajo (Curr Rheumatol Rep 2018).

Grading the ischaemia (chronic):

FontaineRutherford (category)Clinical pictureObjective (Rutherford)
I0asymptomaticnormal treadmill test
IIa (over 200 m)1 mildclaudicationcompletes treadmill; ankle pressure after exercise over 50 mmHg but at least 20 mmHg below resting
IIb (under 200 m)2 moderate, 3 severeclaudicationcategory 3: cannot complete treadmill; ankle pressure after exercise under 50 mmHg
III4ischaemic rest painresting ankle pressure under 40 mmHg, toe pressure under 30 mmHg
IV5 minor, 6 major tissue lossulcer, gangreneresting ankle pressure under 60 mmHg, toe pressure under 40 mmHg

Rutherford 4–6 is chronic limb-threatening ischaemia (CLTI). Acute limb ischaemia has its own Rutherford grading: I viable; IIa marginally threatened (no or minimal sensory loss, no weakness); IIb immediately threatened (sensory loss beyond the toes, rest pain, mild or moderate weakness); III irreversible (anaesthetic, paralysed, no venous Doppler signal).

Ankle-brachial index: 0.90 or less is PAD; 1.40 or more is non-compressible (calcified, common in diabetes and renal failure): use toe pressures.

Best medical therapy is for everyone with PAD, and the first treatment for claudication:

  • Stop smoking: counselling at every visit, with varenicline (or bupropion, nicotine replacement).
  • Antithrombotic: a single antiplatelet (aspirin or clopidogrel); consider low-dose rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily with aspirin in symptomatic PAD and after revascularisation if bleeding risk is low.
  • High-intensity statin: LDL under 1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL) and at least a 50% fall (ESVS 2024).
  • Blood pressure under 130/80 mmHg (ACE inhibitor or ARB); diabetes control (SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 agonists); foot care.
  • Supervised exercise: 30–45 minutes of walking to near-maximal pain, at least 3 times a week, for at least 12 weeks.

When to revascularise: claudication only when it stays lifestyle-limiting despite best medical therapy and exercise, decided with the patient (never for asymptomatic disease); CLTI (rest pain, ulcer, gangrene): prompt assessment for revascularisation to save the limb; acute ischaemia IIa urgently, IIb as an emergency, III amputation.

Evidence: Rutherford 1997 standards (J Vasc Surg 1997;26:517-38) and Fontaine, as tabulated in current reviews. ACC/AHA 2024 PAD guideline (Gornik et al.): single antiplatelet, rivaroxaban 2.5 mg twice daily plus aspirin, high-intensity statin, BP under 130/80, supervised exercise at least 3 times a week for 12 weeks; revascularisation for claudication only if lifestyle-limiting despite therapy. ESVS 2024 (Nordanstig et al.): LDL under 1.4 mmol/L; varenicline first-line; individualised decisions. COMPASS (Lancet 2018) and VOYAGER PAD (NEJM 2020) for low-dose rivaroxaban.

ask.question: A 50-year-old smoker has buttock claudication, absent femoral pulses and erectile dysfunction. Where is the disease?

choices.text: The distal aorta and both iliac arteries (Leriche syndrome)
choices.why: Buttock claudication and absent femoral pulses place the obstruction above the groins; erectile dysfunction reflects poor internal iliac flow.

steps.title: The aortic bifurcation, iliacs and femoral arteries
steps.body:
The aorta divides at L4 (the level of the iliac crests) into the common iliac arteries, each dividing over the sacroiliac joint into the internal iliac (pelvis, buttock) and the external iliac, which becomes the common femoral artery under the inguinal ligament at the mid-inguinal point and divides 3–5 cm lower into the superficial femoral and profunda femoris. The profunda is the key collateral to the leg when the SFA is occluded.

Protect: the ureters (crossing the iliac bifurcations: graft tunnels pass behind them), the iliac veins behind the arteries, the hypogastric plexus (sexual function), the IMA, and in the groin the femoral vein medially and the femoral nerve laterally.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

steps.title: Case: bilateral common iliac occlusions and disabling claudication
steps.body:
TASC II C (bilateral common iliac occlusions) with lifestyle-limiting claudication after 6 months of supervised walking and best medical therapy. Endovascular first: kissing stents at the bifurcation (covered balloon-expandable stents do better in occlusions and complex lesions), or a CERAB reconstruction. Open surgery stays available if it fails.

Evidence: COBEST (J Vasc Surg 2011 and 2016): covered stents gave better freedom from restenosis than bare stents, especially in TASC C/D lesions (5-year patency 74.7% vs 62.5%). CERAB (Taeymans et al., J Vasc Surg 2018; 89% TASC D): 3-year primary patency 82%. ESVS 2024: primary stenting for iliac occlusions; covered stents may be considered for TASC C/D.

ask.question: Why treat this claudicant at all, and why endovascular first?

choices.text: Symptoms still limit his life after exercise and best medical therapy; for iliac occlusions, stenting is effective and less invasive, with surgery in reserve
choices.why: Revascularisation for claudication is individualised after conservative therapy fails; for common iliac occlusions (TASC B–C), primary stenting has good patency and low morbidity.

choices.text: To prevent amputation, which is likely within a year

steps.lead: A 61-year-old man, ex-smoker (stopped a year ago), diabetic. Buttock and calf claudication at 80 m despite 6 months of supervised exercise, statin and aspirin; he is a farmer and cannot work. ABI 0.62 and 0.58. CT: both common iliac arteries occluded (5 cm each), the aorta above and the external iliacs below healthy; not heavily calcified.

steps.title: Which reconstruction? Aortobifemoral, axillobifemoral, femorofemoral or endovascular
steps.body:
The choice rests on the extent of disease (unilateral or bilateral, how far up the aorta, the common femorals), the patient (fitness for laparotomy, the abdomen, life expectancy, infection) and the inflow for an extra-anatomic graft.

Aortobifemoral bypass

  • Choose for: a fit patient with extensive bilateral aorto-iliac disease or aortic occlusion (TASC C/D); failed endovascular treatment
  • Avoid when: unfit for general anaesthesia and laparotomy; a hostile abdomen; (relative) retroperitoneal fibrosis, horseshoe kidney, severe cardiac disease
  • Patency at 5 years: about 86–91% per limb
  • Main risks: operative mortality about 4% in older series; sexual dysfunction; graft infection; aortoenteric fistula

Axillobifemoral bypass

  • Choose for: bilateral aorto-iliac occlusion in a patient unfit for laparotomy; a hostile abdomen (several laparotomies, a stoma, radiation); an infected aortic graft or aortoenteric fistula after the graft is removed
  • Avoid when: inflow disease in the subclavian or axillary artery (compare both arm pressures, image the arch branches, use the arm with the higher pressure); a fit claudicant (poorer patency)
  • Patency at 5 years: about 50–75% (63% primary in one series)
  • Main risks: graft thrombosis; disruption of the axillary anastomosis with arm strain; infection along the tunnel

Femorofemoral cross-over

  • Choose for: unilateral iliac occlusion with a healthy donor iliac (or one stented first); high risk or hostile abdomen; failed iliac stenting
  • Avoid when: untreated disease in the donor iliac; bilateral disease; (relative) marked obesity
  • Patency at 5 years: about 70% primary, 85% secondary
  • Main risks: groin infection; steal from the donor leg (rare)

Endovascular (kissing stents, CERAB)

  • Choose for: most TASC A–C lesions, and increasingly D in experienced centres
  • Avoid when: heavy calcified occlusion into the common femoral (hybrid: femoral endarterectomy plus stent); occlusion up to the renal arteries; no access
  • Patency at 5 years: covered stents about 75% (COBEST); CERAB 82% at 3 years
  • Main risks: access complications; stent occlusion; reintervention

Evidence: de Vries and Hunink (J Vasc Surg 1997): aortic bifurcation grafts, 5-year limb patency 91% (claudication) and 87.5% (CLI), mortality 4.4%. Martin and Katz (Am J Surg 2000): axillofemoral primary patency 63% at 5 years. Park et al. (Vasc Specialist Int 2017): femorofemoral 70% primary, 85% secondary at 5 years; donor-iliac disease was treated first when present. COBEST (J Vasc Surg 2016); CERAB (Taeymans, J Vasc Surg 2018). Indications and contraindications: StatPearls/Medscape reviews of each operation.

ask.question: What should a patient know about kissing stents compared with bypass?

choices.text: Less invasive, with a higher chance of restenosis and repeat procedures
choices.why: Durability is lower than aortobifemoral bypass for extensive disease.

steps.title: Bilateral femoral access; cross the occlusions
steps.body:
Ultrasound-guided retrograde puncture of both CFAs; sheaths; heparin. Cross each occlusion with a hydrophilic wire and catheter, preferably intraluminally; if subintimal, re-enter the true lumen in the aorta below the renal arteries (a re-entry device, or a brachial approach from above). Confirm the true lumen with contrast before dilating.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

steps.title: Kissing stents: deploy together, inflate together
steps.body: Predilate. Position two balloon-expandable (covered) stents side by side, their tops level just above the bifurcation (the "new carina"), and inflate them simultaneously so neither crushes the other. Extend with further stents distally if needed, stopping short of the internal iliac origins where possible. Completion angiogram: no residual stenosis, no dissection, no rupture (have a covered stent and an occlusion balloon ready).

ask.question: During iliac stenting the patient suddenly has back pain and hypotension. Most likely cause and first move?

choices.text: Iliac rupture: inflate a balloon at the site to control bleeding, then place a covered stent
choices.why: Rupture is rare but lethal; always have an occlusion balloon and covered stents on the shelf.

steps.title: Closure, antiplatelet, surveillance
steps.body: Closure devices or manual pressure. Dual antiplatelet therapy for a period, then single; statin; stay off tobacco. Walking resumes the next day; duplex surveillance of the stents. Recurrence is treated endovascularly again, or by aortobifemoral bypass.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Puncture sites; distal pulses
  • Back pain and falling Hb: retroperitoneal bleed

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Two hours after iliac stenting: back pain, BP falling, Hb down. Next?

choices.text: Suspect a retroperitoneal bleed or rupture: call, resuscitate, CT or angiography
choices.why: Access or iliac injury bleeds into the retroperitoneum.

aaa-infra.name: Abdominal aortic aneurysm
aaa-infra.summary: Transperitoneal open repair of an infrarenal aneurysm: neck, iliacs, clamps, sac, tube graft, closure.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: abdominal aortic aneurysm
steps.body:
What fails is the media. Elastin is broken down (matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages and smooth muscle cells), smooth muscle cells die, and chronic inflammation involves the adventitia. The infrarenal aorta has the fewest vasa vasorum and the least elastin: most aneurysms start there. Risk factors: age, male sex, smoking (the strongest modifiable), family history, hypertension; diabetes is, oddly, protective.

Elastin degradation, loss of smooth muscle→Dilatation→Wall tension rises with radius (Laplace: T = P × r)→More dilatation, faster growth→Rupture

An aneurysm is a diameter of 3.0 cm or more. Growth accelerates as it enlarges; rupture risk climbs steeply above 5.5 cm:

Diameter1-year risk of (probable) rupture, untreated
5.5–5.9 cm9.4%
6.0–6.9 cm10.2% (19.1% at 6.5–6.9)
7.0 cm or more32.5%

Repair thresholds: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women (smaller aortas rupture at smaller diameters), rapid growth (about 1 cm a year, confirmed), or symptoms (tenderness, back pain). Below that, surveillance: early repair of 4.0–5.5 cm aneurysms did not improve survival.

The neck decides the operation:

Type (SVS 2021)Where the aneurysm startsProximal clamp and repair
Infrarenala healthy neck of 10–15 mm or more below the lowest renal arteryinfrarenal clamp; EVAR usually possible
Short neckneck 4–10 mmoften suprarenal clamp; EVAR marginal
Juxtarenalat the renal arteries (neck 4 mm or less), not involving themsuprarenal clamp, anastomosis at the renal origins; or fenestrated EVAR
Pararenal / paravisceral ("suprarenal")involving the renal arteries, up to (pararenal) or including (paravisceral) the SMAsupracoeliac clamp, renal and visceral reconstruction; or fenestrated/branched EVAR
Thoracoabdominal extent IVup to the coeliac axis or diaphragmatic hiatusthoracoabdominal repair

In Africa aortic aneurysms present younger and more often from infection or HIV-associated vasculitis (saccular, at atypical sites, sometimes multiple); many present ruptured. Always consider an infective (mycotic) aneurysm: fever, raised inflammatory markers, a saccular or lobulated shape, periaortic gas or fluid.

Evidence: rupture rates: Lederle et al., JAMA 2002 (198 patients refusing or unfit for repair). Small aneurysms: UK Small Aneurysm Trial 12-year follow-up (Powell et al., Br J Surg 2007: no survival difference, HR 0.90) and ADAM (NEJM 2002: RR 1.21). Thresholds and surveillance: ESVS 2024 (Wanhainen et al.). Anatomical definitions: SVS reporting standards (Oderich et al., J Vasc Surg 2021). HIV-associated aneurysms: Nair et al. (J Vasc Surg 1999; mean age 30, often multiple, atypical sites). African AAA: Wu, J West Afr Coll Surg 2022.

Normal sizes and when to act. An aneurysm is a permanent dilatation to at least 1.5 times the expected normal diameter.

ArteryNormal adult (typical)AneurysmalUsual threshold to repair
Ascending aortaabout 2.2–3.6 cmdilated above 22 mm/m² (ESC)5.5 cm; 5.0 cm with risk factors, bicuspid root phenotype or Marfan; 4.5 cm if the aortic valve is being operated on
Descending thoracicabout 2.0–3.0 cmdilated above 16 mm/m² (ESC)TEVAR at 5.5 cm with suitable anatomy (ESC 2024); 6.0 cm (ACC/AHA 2022)
Infrarenal aortaabout 1.5 cm (women), 1.7 cm (men) over 503.0 cm or more5.5 cm (men), 5.0 cm (women); growth of about 1 cm a year; symptoms
Common iliacabout 1 cmabout 1.8–2.0 cm and more (definitions vary)4.0 cm (ESVS 2024, raised from 3.5 cm)
Poplitealabout 0.5–0.9 cmover 1.5 cm or 1.5 × normal2.0 cm, or smaller with thrombus and embolism or poor run-off (SVS 2022)

Evidence: definition of aneurysm as 1.5 × normal: SVS/ISCVS reporting standards (Johnston et al., J Vasc Surg 1991); normal infrarenal diameters (AAFP 2006). Thoracic indexing and thresholds: ESC 2024 (Mazzolai et al.) and ACC/AHA 2022 (Isselbacher et al.). Iliac threshold: ESVS 2024 (Recommendation 135). Popliteal: SVS 2022 (Farber et al.). Normal ranges for the iliac and popliteal arteries are typical values, not guideline cut-offs.

ask.question: Why does an aneurysm grow faster as it gets bigger?

choices.text: Wall tension rises with the radius (Laplace's law), so the larger the aneurysm, the greater the stress on an already weakened wall
choices.why: T = P × r: at the same blood pressure a 6 cm aneurysm carries twice the wall tension of a 3 cm aorta. That is why growth and rupture risk accelerate with size.

choices.text: Thrombus lining the sac weakens it

steps.title: The infrarenal aorta and its neighbours
steps.body:
From above down on the front of the aorta: the coeliac trunk (T12/L1), the SMA about 1 cm lower, the renal arteries (L1/L2, the right passing behind the IVC), the left renal vein crossing in front of the aorta just below the SMA (the upper limit of the infrarenal neck), the IMA from the left front at L3, and the bifurcation at L4.

What to protect: the left renal vein above the neck (and a retroaortic or circumaortic variant, which tears when clamping); the duodenum (3rd and 4th parts) over the aneurysm; the IVC to the right and the iliac veins behind the iliac arteries (the left common iliac vein runs behind the right common iliac artery): encircling the iliac arteries tears them; the ureters crossing the iliac bifurcations; the superior hypogastric plexus on the left of the aorta and over the left common iliac (dissect on the right to preserve ejaculation); the lumbar arteries behind, which back-bleed into the opened sac.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

ask.question: Which vein lies behind the right common iliac artery and is torn by careless encircling of that artery?

steps.title: Case: a 6.2 cm infrarenal aneurysm in a fit 64-year-old
steps.body:
Read the case above. The steps that follow are his operation.

Decision: a 6.2 cm aneurysm (1-year rupture risk about 10%) in a fit man: repair. Open or EVAR? EVAR has lower early mortality, but the benefit is lost over the years, it needs lifelong imaging surveillance and more reinterventions, and late rupture occurs. For a fit 64-year-old with a long life expectancy and limited access to CT surveillance, open repair is a sound choice; EVAR is equally valid where surveillance is reliable.

Evidence: EVAR-1 (Lancet 2016; mean follow-up 12.7 years): EVAR lower total and aneurysm-related mortality in the first 6 months, but after 8 years higher aneurysm-related mortality (mainly from sac rupture) and more reinterventions. OVER (NEJM 2019) and DREAM (NEJM 2010): long-term survival similar. ESVS 2024: EVAR remains the preferred modality in most patients, weighing durability, life expectancy, and patient preference.

ask.question: What is the main long-term drawback of EVAR compared with open repair?

choices.text: The need for lifelong imaging surveillance and reinterventions, with a risk of late rupture
choices.why: EVAR excludes the sac without removing it; endoleaks and migration can re-pressurise it. EVAR-1 showed more reinterventions and higher late aneurysm mortality after 8 years.

Creatinine normal; echo EF 60%; he walks 3 km a day. He lives 4 hours from the nearest CT scanner.

aaa-juxta.summary: No infrarenal neck: renal vein, suprarenal clamp, anastomosis at the renal arteries, clamp moved down.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: abdominal aortic aneurysm
steps.body:
What fails is the media. Elastin is broken down (matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages and smooth muscle cells), smooth muscle cells die, and chronic inflammation involves the adventitia. The infrarenal aorta has the fewest vasa vasorum and the least elastin: most aneurysms start there. Risk factors: age, male sex, smoking (the strongest modifiable), family history, hypertension; diabetes is, oddly, protective.

Elastin degradation, loss of smooth muscle→Dilatation→Wall tension rises with radius (Laplace: T = P × r)→More dilatation, faster growth→Rupture

An aneurysm is a diameter of 3.0 cm or more. Growth accelerates as it enlarges; rupture risk climbs steeply above 5.5 cm:

Diameter1-year risk of (probable) rupture, untreated
5.5–5.9 cm9.4%
6.0–6.9 cm10.2% (19.1% at 6.5–6.9)
7.0 cm or more32.5%

Repair thresholds: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women (smaller aortas rupture at smaller diameters), rapid growth (about 1 cm a year, confirmed), or symptoms (tenderness, back pain). Below that, surveillance: early repair of 4.0–5.5 cm aneurysms did not improve survival.

The neck decides the operation:

Type (SVS 2021)Where the aneurysm startsProximal clamp and repair
Infrarenala healthy neck of 10–15 mm or more below the lowest renal arteryinfrarenal clamp; EVAR usually possible
Short neckneck 4–10 mmoften suprarenal clamp; EVAR marginal
Juxtarenalat the renal arteries (neck 4 mm or less), not involving themsuprarenal clamp, anastomosis at the renal origins; or fenestrated EVAR
Pararenal / paravisceral ("suprarenal")involving the renal arteries, up to (pararenal) or including (paravisceral) the SMAsupracoeliac clamp, renal and visceral reconstruction; or fenestrated/branched EVAR
Thoracoabdominal extent IVup to the coeliac axis or diaphragmatic hiatusthoracoabdominal repair

In Africa aortic aneurysms present younger and more often from infection or HIV-associated vasculitis (saccular, at atypical sites, sometimes multiple); many present ruptured. Always consider an infective (mycotic) aneurysm: fever, raised inflammatory markers, a saccular or lobulated shape, periaortic gas or fluid.

Evidence: rupture rates: Lederle et al., JAMA 2002 (198 patients refusing or unfit for repair). Small aneurysms: UK Small Aneurysm Trial 12-year follow-up (Powell et al., Br J Surg 2007: no survival difference, HR 0.90) and ADAM (NEJM 2002: RR 1.21). Thresholds and surveillance: ESVS 2024 (Wanhainen et al.). Anatomical definitions: SVS reporting standards (Oderich et al., J Vasc Surg 2021). HIV-associated aneurysms: Nair et al. (J Vasc Surg 1999; mean age 30, often multiple, atypical sites). African AAA: Wu, J West Afr Coll Surg 2022.

Normal sizes and when to act. An aneurysm is a permanent dilatation to at least 1.5 times the expected normal diameter.

Evidence: definition of aneurysm as 1.5 × normal: SVS/ISCVS reporting standards (Johnston et al., J Vasc Surg 1991); normal infrarenal diameters (AAFP 2006). Thoracic indexing and thresholds: ESC 2024 (Mazzolai et al.) and ACC/AHA 2022 (Isselbacher et al.). Iliac threshold: ESVS 2024 (Recommendation 135). Popliteal: SVS 2022 (Farber et al.). ask.question: Why does an aneurysm grow faster as it gets bigger?

choices.text: Wall tension rises with the radius (Laplace's law), so the larger the aneurysm, the greater the stress on an already weakened wall
choices.why: T = P × r: at the same blood pressure a 6 cm aneurysm carries twice the wall tension of a 3 cm aorta. That is why growth and rupture risk accelerate with size.

choices.text: Thrombus lining the sac weakens it

steps.title: The infrarenal aorta and its neighbours
steps.body:
From above down on the front of the aorta: the coeliac trunk (T12/L1), the SMA about 1 cm lower, the renal arteries (L1/L2, the right passing behind the IVC), the left renal vein crossing in front of the aorta just below the SMA (the upper limit of the infrarenal neck), the IMA from the left front at L3, and the bifurcation at L4.

What to protect: the left renal vein above the neck (and a retroaortic or circumaortic variant, which tears when clamping); the duodenum (3rd and 4th parts) over the aneurysm; the IVC to the right and the iliac veins behind the iliac arteries (the left common iliac vein runs behind the right common iliac artery): encircling the iliac arteries tears them; the ureters crossing the iliac bifurcations; the superior hypogastric plexus on the left of the aorta and over the left common iliac (dissect on the right to preserve ejaculation); the lumbar arteries behind, which back-bleed into the opened sac.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

choices.text: The left common iliac vein (near the confluence of the IVC)

steps.title: Case: a juxtarenal aneurysm with no neck
steps.body:
No infrarenal neck (under 4 mm): a standard EVAR cannot seal. The options are open repair with a suprarenal clamp, or a fenestrated stent graft (FEVAR, custom-made or off-the-shelf, where available). At standard surgical risk, either is reasonable; chimney grafts are for emergencies or bailout.

Protect the kidneys: preoperative hydration, avoid nephrotoxins, keep suprarenal clamp time short, cold renal perfusion if it will exceed about 25 minutes.

Evidence: ESVS 2024: for complex AAA at standard risk, open or endovascular repair based on fitness, anatomy and preference; fenestrated/branched EVAR first line at high surgical risk; parallel (chimney) grafts only in emergencies or as bailout. Jongkind et al. (J Vasc Surg 2010; 1,256 open juxtarenal repairs): 30-day mortality 2.9%, new dialysis 3.3%.

ask.question: Where must the proximal clamp go for this juxtarenal aneurysm?

choices.text: Above the renal arteries (between the renals and the SMA, or above the SMA)
choices.why: There is no healthy infrarenal aorta to clamp; the anastomosis is made at the level of the renal ostia, then the clamp is moved onto the graft below them to restore renal flow.

steps.title: The infrarenal aorta and its neighbours
steps.body:
From above down on the front of the aorta: the coeliac trunk (T12/L1), the SMA about 1 cm lower, the renal arteries (L1/L2, the right passing behind the IVC), the left renal vein crossing in front of the aorta just below the SMA (the upper limit of the infrarenal neck), the IMA from the left front at L3, and the bifurcation at L4.

What to protect: the left renal vein above the neck (and a retroaortic or circumaortic variant, which tears when clamping); the duodenum (3rd and 4th parts) over the aneurysm; the IVC to the right and the iliac veins behind the iliac arteries (the left common iliac vein runs behind the right common iliac artery): encircling the iliac arteries tears them; the ureters crossing the iliac bifurcations; the superior hypogastric plexus on the left of the aorta and over the left common iliac (dissect on the right to preserve ejaculation); the lumbar arteries behind, which back-bleed into the opened sac.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

ask.question: Which vein lies behind the right common iliac artery and is torn by careless encircling of that artery?

choices.text: The left common iliac vein (near the confluence of the IVC)
choices.why: The iliac veins lie behind and slightly to the right of the arteries; the left common iliac vein crosses behind the right common iliac artery to reach the IVC. Clamp the iliacs without encircling them.

steps.title: Case: a pararenal aneurysm through the left flank
steps.body:
The renal arteries arise from the aneurysm: the proximal anastomosis must be above them, incorporating the visceral and renal origins. The left retroperitoneal approach gives the best access to the aorta above the renal arteries and up to the hiatus, and avoids a hostile abdomen (her previous laparotomy).

Alternatives: fenestrated or branched EVAR at high risk, where available.

Evidence: Sicard et al. (J Vasc Surg 1995, randomised, 145 patients): the retroperitoneal approach had less ileus and shorter ICU stay; Cambria et al. (1990, 113 patients) found no important difference. ESVS 2024: the approach is chosen on patient factors and surgeon preference. Jongkind et al. 2010: renal dysfunction after complex open repair was common (median 18%).

ask.question: Why the left flank (retroperitoneal) approach here?

choices.text: It exposes the aorta above the renal arteries up to the hiatus and avoids her scarred abdomen
choices.why: The left retroperitoneal route gives direct access to the para- and supravisceral aorta (dividing the left crus) and stays out of the peritoneal cavity; the right renal artery is harder to reach from this side.

choices.text: It gives better access to the right iliac artery
It is quicker for infrarenal aneurysms
It avoids the need for a suprarenal clamp

steps.lead: A 66-year-old woman, hypertensive, a previous laparotomy for a perforated duodenal ulcer. CT angiography: a 6.5 cm aneurysm that involves both renal artery origins and reaches 1 cm below the SMA; the coeliac and SMA origins are healthy; eGFR 55.

ask.question: Which open AAA risk should be discussed with a sexually active man?

choices.text: Sexual dysfunction from injury to the hypogastric plexus
choices.why: The autonomic nerves over the left common iliac and aortic bifurcation can be injured.

steps.title: Left flank incision; the retroperitoneal plane
steps.body: Right side down, the left shoulder rotated back about 60°, the pelvis flatter (the "corkscrew" position), the table broken at the flank. Incision from the tip of the 11th rib posteriorly, obliquely to the lateral edge of the rectus sheath below the umbilicus; resect or enter the bed of the 11th rib. Divide the abdominal muscles; stay outside the peritoneum, sweeping it, the colon and the spleen forward. Take the left kidney forward with them (exposing the posterior aorta and the left renal artery) or leave it in place.

steps.title: Expose the neck and the visceral aorta
steps.body: Through the left retroperitoneum: sweep the left kidney (or leave it posterior), the colon and the spleen forward; divide the left crus of the diaphragm to reach the supracoeliac aorta. The left renal artery is the landmark: follow it to the aorta. Expose the coeliac, SMA and both renal origins.

steps.title: Heparin, clamp distally, then proximally
steps.body:
Heparin (about 70–100 U/kg). Clamp the iliac arteries first (so that debris from the sac goes nowhere), then the supracoeliac aorta at the hiatus: the liver, bowel and kidneys are all ischaemic; work fast, and perfuse the kidneys with cold crystalloid. Tell the anaesthetist before clamping: afterload rises; before releasing, fluid and vasoconstrictor ready.

Evidence: ESVS 2024: consider cold renal perfusion when the suprarenal clamp time is expected to exceed about 25 minutes. In a systematic review of 1,256 open juxtarenal repairs (Jongkind et al., J Vasc Surg 2010), 30-day mortality was 2.9% and 3.3% needed new dialysis.

steps.title: Open the sac, clear the thrombus, stop the back-bleeding
steps.body:
Open the aneurysm longitudinally on its right anterior surface (away from the IMA), T-ing the incision at the neck and at the bifurcation. Scoop out the laminated thrombus. Oversew the lumbar arteries from inside with figure-of-eight 2-0 or 3-0 sutures; back-bleeding from the IMA: if it bleeds briskly (good collaterals) oversew its origin from inside; if the flow is poor and the colon may depend on it, keep a button for reimplantation.

Evidence: ESVS 2024: routine IMA reimplantation is not recommended; consider it when pelvic and colonic perfusion is doubtful (both internal iliacs diseased or excluded, previous colectomy, poor back-bleeding). Colonic ischaemia after open repair presents with bloody diarrhoea, acidosis or distension: sigmoidoscopy early.

steps.title: Sew in the graft
steps.body: Bevelled proximal anastomosis: the graft cut obliquely so that its suture line incorporates the coeliac, SMA and right renal origins as one patch (a Carrel patch), sewn with 3-0 polypropylene. The left renal artery is reimplanted as a button or bypassed with a side-arm. Move the clamp down onto the graft below the visceral origins in sequence: the viscera, then each kidney.

ask.question: Before tying the distal anastomosis, why flush the graft?

choices.text: To wash out air, thrombus and debris that would otherwise embolise to the legs or pelvis
choices.why: Brief release of the iliac, then aortic clamps flushes the graft; debris left in it embolises to the feet ("trash foot") or the pelvis.

choices.text: To test the proximal anastomosis only

steps.title: Cold renal perfusion; reimplant the left renal
steps.body:
With the supracoeliac clamp on and the sac opened, place balloon perfusion catheters into both renal ostia and infuse cold crystalloid (about 4 °C, commonly Ringer's lactate with mannitol, per unit protocol) intermittently; visceral ischaemia time is the other clock: keep it short.

After the bevelled proximal suture line, the left renal artery goes onto a side-arm or as a button reimplanted into the graft; restore flow to the viscera and right kidney first by moving the clamp down onto the graft.

Evidence: ESVS 2024 (Rec 125): consider cold renal perfusion when suprarenal clamp time exceeds about 25 minutes. The perfusate temperature and composition vary by centre.

steps.title: Release, close the sac over the graft, check the colon and the feet
steps.body:
Release the clamps one leg at a time, slowly, with the anaesthetist (declamping hypotension). Protamine if needed. Close the sac over the graft and then the posterior peritoneum, so the graft never touches the duodenum (aortoenteric fistula). Look at the sigmoid colon (pink, peristalsing, a mesenteric pulse) and the feet (pulses, colour) before closing.

Check both kidneys (colour, a pulse in each renal artery) and the bowel; urine output and lactate overnight.

ask.question: Why close the aneurysm sac and peritoneum over the graft?

choices.text: To keep the graft away from the duodenum and prevent an aortoenteric fistula
choices.why: Direct contact between the graft suture line and the duodenum can erode into the bowel months or years later: a catastrophic bleed.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Serial haematocrit and abdominal girth KNH practice; bladder pressure when triggered proposed
  • Colonic ischaemia: bloody diarrhoea, rising lactate: sigmoidoscopy
  • Feet: trash foot
  • Kidneys after supra- or juxtarenal clamps

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 1 after rupture repair: girth rising, urine 10 mL/h despite filling, airway pressures rising. Next?

choices.text: Measure bladder pressure and call the consultant: compartment syndrome
choices.why: Oliguria despite filling with a tense abdomen: more fluid makes it worse.

aaa-evar.summary: Femoral access, marking the renal arteries, main body, gate, limbs, completion angiogram, surveillance.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: abdominal aortic aneurysm
steps.body:
What fails is the media. Elastin is broken down (matrix metalloproteinases from macrophages and smooth muscle cells), smooth muscle cells die, and chronic inflammation involves the adventitia. The infrarenal aorta has the fewest vasa vasorum and the least elastin: most aneurysms start there. Risk factors: age, male sex, smoking (the strongest modifiable), family history, hypertension; diabetes is, oddly, protective.

Elastin degradation, loss of smooth muscle→Dilatation→Wall tension rises with radius (Laplace: T = P × r)→More dilatation, faster growth→Rupture

An aneurysm is a diameter of 3.0 cm or more. Growth accelerates as it enlarges; rupture risk climbs steeply above 5.5 cm:

Diameter1-year risk of (probable) rupture, untreated
5.5–5.9 cm9.4%
6.0–6.9 cm10.2% (19.1% at 6.5–6.9)
7.0 cm or more32.5%

Repair thresholds: 5.5 cm in men, 5.0 cm in women (smaller aortas rupture at smaller diameters), rapid growth (about 1 cm a year, confirmed), or symptoms (tenderness, back pain). Below that, surveillance: early repair of 4.0–5.5 cm aneurysms did not improve survival.

steps.title: Case: EVAR in a man with COPD
steps.body:
Anatomy suits EVAR: a neck of at least 10–15 mm, not too angled or conical, of a diameter the device can seal (usually 18–32 mm), and iliac access vessels wide enough for the sheath (about 7 mm or more for most devices). His lungs make a laparotomy and a long aortic clamp riskier: EVAR avoids both.

The contract: lifelong surveillance (CT or duplex) for endoleaks and migration, and a greater chance of a secondary procedure.

Evidence: EVAR-1 (Lancet 2016): lower early mortality with EVAR, lost over time; more reinterventions. ESVS 2024: EVAR is the preferred modality in most patients with suitable anatomy; for a ruptured AAA, EVAR is the first option when anatomy allows (Class I). IMPROVE (BMJ 2014 and 2017): 30-day mortality 35.4% vs 37.4% for an endovascular strategy vs open repair in rupture, with better 3-year survival (48% vs 56% mortality) and quality of life.

ask.question: Which anatomical feature is essential for a standard EVAR?

choices.text: A healthy infrarenal neck long enough for a seal (usually at least 10–15 mm), not too angled or conical
choices.why: The stent graft seals by radial force against normal aorta below the renal arteries; a short, wide, angled or thrombus-lined neck causes type I endoleak and failure.

choices.text: Lifelong imaging surveillance for endoleak and migration
choices.why: EVAR-1: more reinterventions over time; surveillance detects them.

steps.title: Femoral access; mark the renal arteries
steps.body:
Ultrasound-guided puncture of both common femoral arteries (over the femoral head), preclosure sutures placed (or a surgical cut-down in calcified or small arteries). Heparin. A stiff wire to the thoracic aorta; an angiogram with a marker catheter, the image angled to open the neck, to mark the lowest renal artery.

Note: the reference CT ends at the 4th lumbar vertebra; the iliac and femoral vessels and the groins are drawn to typical adult dimensions below it.

steps.title: Deploy the main body below the lowest renal; cannulate the gate; the limbs
steps.body: Introduce the main body through one groin, align its top marker just below the lowest renal artery, and deploy (suprarenal fixation, where the device has it, sits across the renal arteries without covering them). Cannulate the contralateral gate from the other groin, confirm you are inside the graft, and deploy the contralateral limb, then the ipsilateral limb, landing both in the common iliac arteries above the internal iliac origins. Balloon the seal zones and junctions.

ask.question: The completion angiogram shows contrast filling the sac from around the top of the graft. What is it, and what now?

choices.text: A type I (proximal seal) endoleak: treat it now (balloon, proximal cuff or anchors)
choices.why: Type I and III endoleaks pressurise the sac and must be fixed; a type II (from lumbars or IMA) is usually observed.

steps.title: Completion angiogram, closure, lifelong surveillance
steps.body:
Completion angiogram: both renal arteries patent, no type I (seal) or type III (junction) endoleak, both internal iliacs perfused. Close the arteries. Surveillance: CT angiography (or contrast ultrasound) at about 30 days, then by protocol, lifelong: sac growth means an endoleak until proven otherwise.

EndoleakSourceAction
Iseal zone (proximal a, distal b)treat
IIlumbar arteries or IMA back-fillingobserve; treat if the sac grows
IIIjunction or fabric teartreat
IVgraft porosityresolves
Vendotension (growth without visible leak)investigate

taa-open.name: Thoracic aortic aneurysm
taa-open.summary: Left thoracotomy, CSF drainage, left heart bypass, intercostal reattachment, interposition graft.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: thoracic aortic aneurysm
steps.body:
Medial degeneration (loss of smooth muscle cells, fragmented elastic fibres, pooled proteoglycans) weakens the wall. Causes: heritable (Marfan syndrome, Loeys-Dietz, familial, bicuspid aortic valve), degenerative/atherosclerotic (the descending aorta in older smokers with hypertension), and inflammatory or infective: syphilitic aortitis (ascending and arch; obliterative endarteritis of the vasa vasorum) and Takayasu arteritis (young women), both seen in Africa.

Medial degeneration→Dilatation→Laplace: tension rises with radius→Dissection or rupture

Hinge points: the risk of rupture or dissection jumps at about 6.0 cm in the ascending and 7.0 cm in the descending aorta, so repair is advised before them: ascending 5.5 cm (5.0 cm in Marfan, or with risk features, or in experienced teams), descending 5.5 cm for TEVAR with suitable anatomy (ESC 2024; ACC/AHA 2022 uses 6.0 cm for descending and thoracoabdominal), thoracoabdominal 6.0 cm, or growth of 0.5 cm in a year (0.3 cm a year for 2 years).

Crawford extent of thoracoabdominal aneurysm: I (left subclavian to above the renals), II (left subclavian to the bifurcation: the largest, highest spinal risk), III (distal thoracic to the bifurcation), IV (below the diaphragm), V (distal thoracic to above the renals, Safi).

steps.title: Case: a descending aneurysm in Marfan syndrome
steps.body:
Marfan syndrome with a 5.8 cm descending aneurysm: open repair. TEVAR is not advised in heritable aortopathies (the stent graft's radial force on fragile tissue, progressive dilatation of the landing zones, retrograde dissection) except as a bridge or in emergencies.

Plan: left thoracotomy, left heart bypass (distal aortic perfusion), CSF drainage, reattachment of critical intercostals, mild hypothermia.

Evidence: 2022 ACC/AHA: TEVAR is preferred for descending aneurysms with suitable anatomy in the absence of Marfan, Loeys-Dietz or vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. Coselli et al. (J Vasc Surg 2002, randomised, extent I/II): CSF drainage reduced paraplegia or paraparesis from 13.0% to 2.6%.

ask.question: Why open repair rather than TEVAR in this patient?

choices.text: Marfan syndrome: stent grafts in heritable aortopathy risk landing-zone dilatation, endoleak and retrograde dissection
choices.why: Guidelines reserve TEVAR in Marfan and related syndromes for emergencies or as a bridge; open repair is durable.

choices.text: The aneurysm is too small for TEVAR
TEVAR causes more paraplegia in young patients

ask.question: Which risk must be discussed before open descending thoracic aneurysm repair?

choices.why: A defining risk of thoracic aortic surgery.

steps.title: CSF drain, double-lumen tube, left thoracotomy
steps.body:
Before induction: a lumbar CSF drain (L3–L4), keeping the pressure at 10–15 mmHg or less during and after the repair. A double-lumen tube (left lung deflated), arterial lines in the right arm and a leg (for distal pressure), motor evoked potentials where available. Right lateral decubitus, hips rotated back (femoral access).

Left posterolateral thoracotomy through the 5th or 6th space (a second, lower space or rib section for a long aneurysm).

action.label: Place the drain; open the chest

steps.title: Left heart bypass; sequential clamping
steps.body:
Left heart bypass: drain oxygenated blood from the left inferior pulmonary vein (or LA appendage) and return it by a centrifugal pump to the distal aorta or a femoral artery, with low-dose heparin. The kidneys, gut and the cord below the clamps are perfused while the aneurysm is repaired, and the heart is unloaded when the aorta is clamped.

Clamp proximally (between the left carotid and subclavian, or distal to the subclavian if there is a neck), and distally in the mid-descending aorta. Keep the proximal MAP 80–100 mmHg and the distal pressure above about 60 mmHg.

Evidence: Coselli et al. (Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2023) protection bundle: CSF pressure below 15 mmHg during clamping, left heart bypass, reattachment of T7/8 to L1/2 intercostals, MAP 80–100 mmHg, spinal perfusion pressure at least 60 mmHg, haemoglobin at least 10 g/dL, mild hypothermia 32–34 °C.

steps.title: Open the aneurysm, reattach intercostals, sew in the graft
steps.body: Open the aneurysm longitudinally, oversew back-bleeding upper intercostals, and reattach the critical lower intercostals (T8–T12, especially large, back-bleeding pairs) to the graft as an island or with a small side graft. Proximal anastomosis with 3-0 or 4-0 polypropylene (felt strip if fragile, as in Marfan), then move the clamp down; then the distal anastomosis. Flush, de-air, release slowly.

ask.question: After an extensive descending repair the patient wakes with weak legs. First moves?

choices.text: Raise the MAP (above about 90 mmHg), drain CSF to below 10 mmHg, correct anaemia and hypoxia
choices.why: Delayed spinal cord ischaemia often recovers if spinal perfusion pressure (MAP minus CSF pressure) is restored quickly.

choices.text: Lower the blood pressure to protect the anastomoses

steps.title: Spinal cord watch; the drain
steps.body: Hourly leg checks for 48–72 hours; MAP targets, CSF drainage by protocol (watch for headache and for blood in the CSF: subdural haematoma), then clamp and remove the drain. Other complications: bleeding, renal failure, left recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy (hoarseness), chylothorax, pneumonia.

steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

  • Kidneys, lungs (thoracotomy)

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Six hours after thoracic aortic repair: new bilateral leg weakness. First action?

choices.text: Raise MAP, drain CSF to target, keep Hb up, call immediately
choices.why: Spinal cord ischaemia can recover if perfusion pressure is restored quickly.

steps.title: Case: a degenerative descending aneurysm in an older man
steps.body:
TEVAR: a 6.4 cm degenerative aneurysm in a 71-year-old with COPD, with landing zones of at least 20 mm of healthy aorta at both ends and iliac access that takes the sheath. The proximal landing needs coverage of the left subclavian artery (zone 2): revascularise it first (carotid-subclavian bypass or transposition), which lowers stroke, arm ischaemia and spinal cord risk.

Evidence: VALOR (J Vasc Surg 2008): 30-day mortality 2.1% with TEVAR vs 7.9% with open repair (historical controls), paraplegia 1.5% and stroke 3.6% after TEVAR. Cheng et al. (JACC 2010, 5,888 patients): TEVAR lower 30-day mortality (OR 0.44) and paraplegia (OR 0.42), no long-term survival difference. SVS 2009 (Matsumura et al.): routine revascularisation before elective TEVAR that covers the left subclavian (weak recommendation); strongly recommended with a LIMA graft or dominant left vertebral. Spinal cord injury meta-analysis (Ann Cardiothorac Surg 2023; 61,962 patients): descending aneurysms 2.0% after TEVAR and after open repair.

ask.question: The landing zone requires covering his left subclavian, and his left vertebral is dominant. What should be done?

choices.text: Revascularise the left subclavian (carotid-subclavian bypass or transposition) before or at the TEVAR
choices.why: Covering the subclavian with a dominant left vertebral risks posterior-circulation stroke, arm ischaemia and spinal cord ischaemia; revascularisation is strongly recommended in this setting.

steps.title: Access, angiography, deploy, completion
steps.body:
A CSF drain if the coverage is long (over about 20 cm), the previous abdominal aorta has been repaired, or the subclavian and hypogastric supply is compromised. Femoral access (percutaneous with preclosure, or a cut-down; an iliac conduit if the vessels are small). A pigtail from the other groin or the left arm; an angiogram in the left anterior oblique projection to open the arch.

Advance the stent graft over a stiff wire, place its covered edge at the planned zone, lower the blood pressure (systolic about 90–100 mmHg or rapid pacing) and deploy; balloon the seal zones only if needed. Completion angiogram: no type I endoleak, the carotids patent.

steps.title: Neurology checks; surveillance
steps.body: Leg and arm checks, MAP above 80–90 mmHg for the first days, drain management. Surveillance imaging at about 1 month, then yearly: endoleak, migration, sac growth, retrograde dissection.

steps.title: The ascending aorta and the arch
steps.body: The ascending aorta runs from the sinotubular junction to the innominate artery, inside the pericardium, with the SVC and right atrium on its right, the pulmonary trunk in front and to the left, the right pulmonary artery behind. The left brachiocephalic vein crosses in front of the arch branches. A hemiarch repair replaces the underside of the arch (the lesser curve) without reimplanting the head vessels.

steps.title: Case: syphilitic aortitis with an ascending aneurysm
steps.body:
A 5.6 cm ascending aneurysm reaching the arch, symptomatic (chest pain), from syphilitic aortitis: replace the ascending aorta and the hemiarch under hypothermic circulatory arrest with antegrade cerebral perfusion. Treat the syphilis (intravenous penicillin), check the coronary ostia (ostial stenosis is typical) and the aortic valve (regurgitation from root dilatation).

Evidence: 2022 ACC/AHA: ascending repair at 5.5 cm or more, or when symptomatic; hemiarch replacement when the aneurysm extends into the arch. Syphilitic aortitis involves the ascending aorta in about half and the arch in a third; untreated, symptomatic disease has a high mortality (ICVTS 2012). Hypothermia classification (Yan et al. 2013): moderate 20.1–28 °C, used with antegrade cerebral perfusion.

ask.question: Which coronary lesion is characteristic of syphilitic aortitis?

choices.text: Ostial stenosis of the coronary arteries
choices.why: Aortitis thickens the intima at the root, narrowing the ostia; it needs to be addressed at surgery (endarterectomy, patch or bypass).

steps.lead: A 52-year-old man, 3 months of central chest pain and a hoarse voice. CT: a 5.6 cm ascending aneurysm with wall calcification, extending to the proximal arch; aortic root 3.9 cm; mild aortic regurgitation. TPHA positive, VDRL 1:32. Coronary angiography: a 70% ostial stenosis of the left main.

ask.question: Which risk is specific to hemiarch repair under circulatory arrest?

choices.why: Brain protection (antegrade cerebral perfusion, hypothermia) reduces but does not remove it.

steps.title: Sternotomy; axillary cannulation; cool
steps.body: Median sternotomy. Arterial cannulation of the right axillary artery (through an 8 mm graft sewn end-to-side), which later provides antegrade cerebral perfusion; venous drainage from the right atrium; an LV vent. Cool on bypass to moderate hypothermia (about 24–28 °C). Cross-clamp below the innominate; cardioplegia (antegrade, or into the ostia if there is aortic regurgitation).

steps.title: Proximal anastomosis; circulatory arrest and the hemiarch
steps.body: Excise the aneurysm; proximal anastomosis to the sinotubular junction (4-0 polypropylene, felt if needed). At target temperature, stop the pump, clamp the innominate, and perfuse the brain antegrade through the axillary graft (about 10 mL/kg/min, right radial pressure 40–60 mmHg). Remove the clamp, bevel the open distal anastomosis along the underside of the arch. Restart perfusion through the graft, de-air, clamp the graft, rewarm; complete the proximal work.

steps.title: Rewarm, wean, and treat the syphilis
steps.body: Rewarm slowly (no more than 10 °C gradient, not above 37 °C), wean, protamine, haemostasis (coagulopathy after circulatory arrest: platelets, fibrinogen). Neurological assessment on waking. Penicillin for tertiary syphilis (14 days intravenously for cardiovascular syphilis, per local protocol), and follow-up imaging of the remaining arch and descending aorta.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the cardiac core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Neurological assessment on waking
  • Coagulopathy after circulatory arrest: platelets, fibrinogen
  • Penicillin for cardiovascular syphilis

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After hemiarch repair: oozing, platelets 60, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L. Next?

choices.why: Correct the coagulopathy of circulatory arrest before re-exploring.

ali-emb.name: Acute limb ischaemia
ali-emb.summary: Rutherford grading, heparin, femoral embolectomy with a Fogarty catheter, source search, and four-compartment fasciotomy.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: acute limb ischaemia
steps.body:
A sudden loss of limb perfusion threatening viability, presenting within 2 weeks. Embolus (from the heart: AF, mitral stenosis, a mural thrombus after MI, endocarditis) lodges at a bifurcation, most often the common femoral; thrombosis in situ occludes a diseased artery or bypass graft, and the limb often has collaterals. In Kenya add rheumatic AF and HIV-associated arterial thrombosis in the young.

Occlusion→Muscle and nerve ischaemia→Irreversible after about 6 hours of severe ischaemia→Reperfusion: swelling, compartment syndrome, K⁺ and myoglobin release

The 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulselessness, perishing cold, paraesthesia, paralysis. Sensory loss and weakness are the ones that decide urgency.

RutherfordSensory lossWeaknessDoppler (art / vein)Action
I viablenonenoneaudible / audibleurgent imaging, revascularise
IIa marginally threatenedtoes or nonenoneinaudible / audiblerevascularise urgently
IIb immediately threatenedbeyond the toes, rest painmild to moderateinaudible / audibleemergency revascularisation
III irreversibleprofound, anaestheticparalysis, rigorinaudible / inaudibleamputation

Evidence: Rutherford et al. (J Vasc Surg 1997) categories, as adopted by the ESVS 2020 acute limb ischaemia guideline (Björck et al., Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg 2020).

ask.question: Which finding moves acute limb ischaemia from Rutherford IIa to IIb?

choices.text: Sensory loss beyond the toes, rest pain or muscle weakness
choices.why: IIb is immediately threatened: emergency revascularisation.

steps.title: The femoral bifurcation to the trifurcation
steps.body:
The common femoral artery lies at the mid-inguinal point and divides 3–5 cm lower into the superficial femoral (down the adductor canal to the hiatus) and the profunda femoris. The popliteal artery lies deep in the popliteal fossa, then divides into the anterior tibial (through the interosseous membrane into the anterior compartment, becoming the dorsalis pedis) and the tibioperoneal trunk (posterior tibial, behind the medial malleolus, and peroneal).

A single transverse femoral arteriotomy reaches all of these with a Fogarty catheter: proximally into the iliac, distally down the superficial femoral and profunda, and to the trifurcation.

steps.title: Case: a cold right leg in rheumatic AF
steps.body:
Rutherford IIb embolic occlusion at the femoral bifurcation. Heparin now, then emergency femoral embolectomy; the history and the normal left leg make an embolus likely, so imaging need not delay theatre. Plan a fasciotomy: ischaemia beyond 6 hours with motor loss.

Evidence: Heparin on diagnosis: 70–100 IU/kg (or 5000 IU) bolus then an infusion (ESVS 2020, as summarised in Endovascular Today 2026). Clinical decision without imaging for a clear embolus with a normal contralateral limb is accepted practice.

ask.question: What is the first treatment, given in the emergency department?

choices.text: Unfractionated heparin: a bolus then an infusion
choices.why: Heparin stops propagation of clot while theatre is arranged.

steps.lead: A 34-year-old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis and AF, off warfarin for 2 months (could not afford INR checks). 8 hours of a painful, cold, white right leg. No femoral pulse on the right; a normal left leg. Numb to the ankle; cannot move her toes well. No Doppler signal at the ankle; venous signal present.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Cardiac state (AF, recent MI), renal function, time since onset. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Groin wound problems
  • Swelling of the leg

3. Serious

  • Amputation despite surgery
  • Death
  • Reperfusion injury: high potassium, kidney injury
  • Compartment syndrome needing fasciotomy

4. Specific to this operation

  • Fasciotomy wounds left open, closed or grafted later
  • Lifelong anticoagulation if embolic from AF

5. Alternatives

  • Catheter-directed thrombolysis (IIa, no contraindication)
  • Primary amputation if irreversible
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • INR monitoring access for warfarin
  • HIV testing in the young

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which risk is specific to revascularising a limb ischaemic for many hours?

choices.text: Reperfusion injury: compartment syndrome, high potassium and kidney injury
choices.why: Restoring flow to dead or injured muscle releases potassium and myoglobin.

steps.title: Expose the common femoral bifurcation; control; transverse arteriotomy
steps.body: A vertical groin incision over the femoral artery (local anaesthesia is possible in a frail patient). Control the common femoral, superficial femoral and profunda with slings. Heparin is already running. A transverse arteriotomy just above the bifurcation (closed primarily without narrowing); a longitudinal one if the artery is diseased and will need a patch.

steps.title: Fogarty embolectomy: proximal, then distal; check back-bleeding
steps.body:
The embolus often extrudes. Proximally: a 5F Fogarty catheter into the iliac until pulsatile inflow returns. Distally: a 3–4F catheter down the superficial femoral and the profunda, passed beyond the clot, the balloon inflated gently with saline and withdrawn steadily while the inflation is adjusted to the vessel. Repeat until two clean passes and good back-bleeding. Flush with heparinised saline.

Over-inflation damages the intima, causing dissection and later stenosis. If the catheter will not pass or flow stays poor, image on the table (angiogram) and explore the below-knee popliteal to direct the catheter into each tibial artery.

ask.question: After embolectomy, which sign shows the distal arteries are clear?

choices.text: Brisk back-bleeding and two clean catheter passes, confirmed by a completion angiogram or Doppler signals
choices.why: Back-bleeding alone can come from collaterals; confirm with imaging or pedal Doppler.

choices.text: The patient says the pain is better
The foot is warm within a minute

steps.title: Clot out; close the arteriotomy; check the foot
steps.body:
The clot is withdrawn. Close the transverse arteriotomy with interrupted or running 5-0 polypropylene, flushing before the last sutures. Check Doppler signals at the posterior tibial and dorsalis pedis; a completion angiogram where available.

Send the clot for histology (myxoma, infection) and look for the source: ECG, echocardiogram (left atrial thrombus, valves, vegetations).

steps.title: Four-compartment fasciotomy through two incisions
steps.body:
After revascularisation of severe or prolonged ischaemia, reperfusion swells the muscle inside unyielding fascia. Prophylactic fasciotomy when ischaemia exceeded about 6 hours with neuromotor deficit; therapeutic when compartment syndrome appears (pain on passive stretch, tense calf, falling sensation).

  • Anterolateral incision: midway between the tibial crest and the fibula; open the anterior and lateral compartments either side of the intermuscular septum; protect the superficial peroneal nerve in the lower third
  • Posteromedial incision: 1–2 cm behind the posteromedial border of the tibia; protect the great saphenous vein and saphenous nerve; open the superficial posterior compartment, then detach soleus from the tibia to open the deep posterior compartment

Long incisions through skin and fascia; leave open, dress (or negative pressure); close or graft at 3–7 days. Dead muscle is debrided.

Evidence: Fasciotomy for severe ischaemia lasting more than 6 hours (compartment syndrome in up to 30% of revascularisations; Endovascular Today 2026 summary of ESVS 2020). Two-incision technique and the diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure under 30 mmHg threshold: AO Surgery Reference.

ask.question: Which compartment is most often missed through a single lateral incision?

choices.why: It lies behind the interosseous membrane and soleus; reach it through the posteromedial incision by detaching soleus from the tibia.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Hourly foot Doppler and compartment checks (pain on passive stretch, tense calf)
  • Reperfusion: K⁺, CK, myoglobinuria; urine output; alkalinise urine per unit
  • Heparin infusion, then anticoagulation for AF; echo for the source

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Six hours after embolectomy: severe calf pain on passive toe movement, tense calf. Next?

choices.why: Clinical compartment syndrome needs decompression without waiting for pressure readings.

fp-gsv.name: Infrainguinal bypass and amputation
fp-gsv.summary: CLTI staging (WIfI, GLASS, PLAN), BEST-CLI and BASIL-2, vein harvest, femoral and below-knee popliteal anastomoses, surveillance.

steps.title: Pathophysiology: femoropopliteal disease and chronic limb-threatening ischaemia
steps.body:
The superficial femoral artery at the adductor canal is the commonest site of leg atherosclerosis. Collaterals from the profunda reconstitute the popliteal: alone, an SFA occlusion usually causes calf claudication. Add tibial disease, diabetes or a wound, and the limb becomes threatened (rest pain, ulcer, gangrene: Rutherford 4–6).

Stage the limb (WIfI: wound, ischaemia, foot infection) and the anatomy (GLASS); decide by the PLAN: Patient risk, Limb severity, ANatomy. Best medical therapy for every patient.

Evidence: Global Vascular Guidelines on CLTI (Conte et al., Eur J Vasc Endovasc Surg / J Vasc Surg 2019): WIfI, GLASS, PLAN; great saphenous vein the preferred conduit.

ask.question: An isolated SFA occlusion usually causes which symptom?

choices.why: Profunda collaterals reconstitute the popliteal; rest pain or tissue loss needs more extensive disease.

steps.title: Case: rest pain and a heel ulcer; good saphenous vein
steps.body:
CLTI with a long SFA occlusion, a patent popliteal and good run-off, a fit patient and a good single-segment great saphenous vein: femoral to below-knee popliteal bypass with reversed vein.

Evidence: BEST-CLI (Farber et al., NEJM 2022): with adequate single-segment GSV, surgery reduced major adverse limb events or death (42.6% vs 57.4%). BASIL-2 (Bradbury et al., Lancet 2023): for infrapopliteal disease, an endovascular-first strategy gave better amputation-free survival (death or major amputation 53% vs 63%). The two are complementary: anatomy and conduit decide.

ask.question: Which conduit gives the best patency to the below-knee popliteal?

choices.text: The patient's own great saphenous vein
choices.why: Autologous vein outperforms prosthetic grafts below the knee.

choices.text: Cephalic vein from the arm, always

steps.lead: A 66-year-old man, diabetic, ex-smoker. 3 months of rest pain in the right foot, a 2 cm heel ulcer. ABI 0.35; toe pressure 25 mmHg. CT angiogram: SFA occluded from its origin to the adductor hiatus, the popliteal reconstituted above the knee, two-vessel run-off. Duplex: great saphenous vein 3.5–4 mm throughout.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Cardiac and renal risk, frailty, WIfI stage. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Wound problems along the vein harvest
  • Leg swelling

3. Serious

  • Graft occlusion
  • Amputation
  • MI
  • Death
  • Graft infection

4. Specific to this operation

  • Duplex surveillance of the graft
  • Further procedures to keep the graft open

5. Alternatives

  • Angioplasty or stenting (BASIL-2, anatomy permitting)
  • Medical therapy alone
  • Primary amputation
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Access to duplex surveillance
  • Wound care at home

ask.question: Which commitment comes with a vein bypass?

choices.text: Graft surveillance with duplex scans and possible further procedures
choices.why: Vein graft stenoses are found and fixed before occlusion.

steps.title: Harvest the great saphenous vein; reverse it
steps.body: Mark the vein with duplex. Harvest through continuous or skip incisions, ligating tributaries with fine ties without narrowing the vein. Gently distend with heparinised saline and check for leaks. Reverse the vein so its valves do not obstruct flow (or leave it in situ and cut the valves with a valvulotome).

steps.title: Femoral and below-knee popliteal anastomoses; tunnel
steps.body: Expose the common femoral bifurcation (inflow) and the below-knee popliteal through a medial incision behind the tibia (retract gastrocnemius back). Heparin. Tunnel the vein deep to sartorius and behind the knee (anatomic tunnel) without twisting. End-to-side anastomoses at both ends (6-0 polypropylene distally), the toe of the distal anastomosis cut to avoid narrowing.

steps.title: Completion imaging; graft surveillance
steps.body: Check a pulse in the graft and pedal Doppler signals; a completion angiogram or duplex for kinks, residual valves and the distal anastomosis. Duplex surveillance of vein grafts (for example at 1, 3, 6 and 12 months) finds stenoses before they occlude. Antiplatelet and statin for life.

ask.question: Why are vein grafts followed with duplex scanning?

choices.text: To detect stenoses in the graft before it occludes, when they can be fixed
choices.why: Most vein graft failures after the first month come from intimal hyperplasia at anastomoses or valve sites.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Graft pulse and pedal Doppler hourly at first
  • Leg wound and swelling (reperfusion oedema)
  • Antiplatelet and statin; glucose control

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: Day 1 after fem-pop bypass: the graft pulse is lost and the foot is cold. Next?

choices.text: Call the consultant: early graft thrombosis needs return to theatre
choices.why: Early failure is usually technical: inflow, twist, or the distal anastomosis.

amp-levels.name: Infrainguinal bypass and amputation
amp-levels.summary: Choosing the level, staged guillotine amputation in sepsis, below-knee amputation with a long posterior flap, rehabilitation.

steps.title: Choosing the level: as distal as will heal
steps.body:
The level is chosen by perfusion (will it heal?), infection (is all dead and infected tissue removed?) and function (will this patient walk?).

LevelUseNote
Toe or raydry gangrene or osteomyelitis of one or two toesneeds adequate foot perfusion; revascularise first
Transmetatarsalforefoot loss, three or more toespreserves a weight-bearing foot; more revisions than BKA but better walking
Below-kneeunreconstructable foot, heel or midfoot sepsisthe knee makes prosthetic walking far easier
Through-kneeBKA not healable, long stump wantedend-bearing; for non-walkers it balances well in sitting
Above-kneeno healable distal level, flexion contracture, bed-boundmost reliable healing; walking with a prosthesis much harder

More proximal levels cost more energy to walk, so a vascular patient is far more likely to walk on a below-knee than an above-knee prosthesis. In sepsis, a guillotine amputation first (ankle level), then a definitive level once the infection settles.

Evidence: Global Vascular Guidelines 2019 (amputation in CLTI); Waters et al. (J Bone Joint Surg Am 1976): energy cost of walking rises with the level of amputation; transmetatarsal versus below-knee: more revisions but higher ambulation after TMA (published series).

ask.question: Why is a below-knee amputation preferred to an above-knee one when both would heal?

choices.text: Keeping the knee makes walking with a prosthesis much more likely and less tiring
choices.why: Energy cost and prosthetic success fall steeply with an above-knee level.

steps.title: Case: wet gangrene of the foot in a diabetic
steps.body: Septic, unsalvageable foot: resuscitate, antibiotics, and a guillotine ankle amputation today to control sepsis; a below-knee amputation in 3–5 days once the sepsis settles, if the popliteal pulse and skin at that level allow healing.

ask.question: What is the first operation?

choices.text: A guillotine amputation at the ankle to control sepsis, then a definitive level later
choices.why: Staging avoids closing a stump in infected tissue.

steps.lead: A 58-year-old man, poorly controlled diabetes. Wet gangrene of the forefoot spreading to the midfoot, crepitus, foul smell; temperature 39 °C, glucose 24 mmol/L. Popliteal pulse palpable; no foot pulses.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Cardiac and renal risk; sepsis. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Wound healing problems
  • Phantom sensations and pain

3. Serious

  • Revision to a higher level
  • Death
  • Loss of the other leg later

4. Specific to this operation

  • Rehabilitation and a prosthesis over months
  • Staged operation in sepsis

5. Alternatives

  • Revascularisation if the limb is salvageable
  • Palliative care
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Access to and cost of a prosthesis
  • Home adaptations

ask.question: What should a patient know before a below-knee amputation?

choices.text: Healing may need revision; walking with a prosthesis takes months of rehabilitation
choices.why: Realistic expectations and the risk to the other leg are part of consent.

choices.text: The other leg is never at risk

steps.title: Below-knee amputation: long posterior flap
steps.body: Mark the anterior incision at the level of bone section, about 12–15 cm below the knee joint (or 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity); the long posterior flap (Burgess) is about as long as the leg is wide at that level. Divide the tibia, bevel its anterior edge, cut the fibula 1–2 cm shorter. Ligate the anterior tibial, posterior tibial and peroneal vessels; pull down, divide and let retract the tibial nerve. Trim the soleus bulk; fold the gastrocnemius flap forward over the bone; close without tension; a soft dressing or rigid removable dressing to prevent knee flexion contracture.

ask.question: Why is the fibula cut shorter than the tibia?

choices.text: So the fibular end does not press into the stump and the socket
choices.why: A long fibula is prominent and painful in the prosthesis.

steps.title: Stump care, rehabilitation, the other leg
steps.body: Pain control (including phantom pain), glucose and nutrition, wound checks. Prevent knee flexion contracture: lie prone, keep the knee straight, early physiotherapy. Stump shaping, then prosthetic fitting at about 6–8 weeks. Examine and protect the other foot: the risk to the second leg is high. Secondary prevention.

steps.title: ICU and post-operative care
steps.body:
Start with the vascular core, the lab schedule and the escalation table; then this operation's own points.

Specific to this operation

  • Sepsis control: glucose, antibiotics, fluids
  • Stump wound; knee kept straight (prevent flexion contracture)
  • Phantom pain: early, multimodal analgesia

Labs

  • Day 1 morning: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice

Doses: electrolytes, vasoactive drugs.

ask.question: After BKA the patient lies with the knee bent on a pillow. Why correct it?

choices.text: A knee flexion contracture prevents prosthetic walking
choices.why: Keep the knee straight and start physiotherapy early.
