avf-rc.name: Arteriovenous fistula (dialysis access)
avf-rc.summary: Access planning (KDOQI 2019 Life-Plan), radiocephalic fistula, maturation and its failure.

steps.title: Why a fistula: access for haemodialysis
steps.body:
Haemodialysis needs blood flow of about 300–400 mL/min, three times a week, for years. A fistula joins an artery to a superficial vein: the vein arterialises (dilates and thickens) over weeks until it can be needled. Compared with a graft (PTFE) it has fewer infections and interventions; compared with a tunnelled catheter, far less bacteraemia and central vein stenosis.

KDOQI 2019 replaced "fistula first" with "patient first": an ESKD Life-Plan for every patient with progressive CKD (eGFR 15–20), choosing the access that fits that patient's expected course: forearm first, distal to proximal, non-dominant arm, protecting veins (no cannulas or blood tests in the planned arm).

Maturation: the old rule of 6s (at 6 weeks: flow 600 mL/min, diameter 6 mm, no more than 6 mm deep). KDOQI 2019 defines maturity by function: dialysis with two needles in more than two-thirds of sessions over 4 consecutive weeks.

Evidence: KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Vascular Access: 2019 Update (Lok et al., Am J Kidney Dis 2020): ESKD Life-Plan; no absolute minimum vessel diameter (vessels under 2 mm need careful evaluation); selective pre-operative ultrasound for high-risk patients; maturation assessed at 4–6 weeks; rope-ladder cannulation preferred. Rule of 6s: earlier KDOQI guidance.

ask.question: What did KDOQI 2019 change about access planning?

choices.text: From "fistula first" to a patient-first ESKD Life-Plan
choices.why: The access is chosen for the patient's expected life course, not a fistula at any cost.

steps.title: Case: planning access before dialysis starts
steps.body: Progressive CKD with an eGFR of 14: create access now so it matures before dialysis. A good forearm cephalic vein and radial artery: radiocephalic fistula on the non-dominant arm. If it fails or the vein is poor: brachiocephalic, then a transposed brachiobasilic, then a graft.

ask.question: Which access is first for this man?

choices.text: A radiocephalic fistula in the right (non-dominant) forearm
choices.why: Distal first preserves proximal sites for later; the non-dominant arm leaves the dominant hand free on dialysis.

steps.lead: A 45-year-old man, hypertensive nephropathy, eGFR 14 and falling, not yet on dialysis; left-handed. Allen test normal. Ultrasound of the right arm: radial artery 2.4 mm, forearm cephalic vein 2.8 mm and continuous to the elbow; no previous cannulas.

steps.title: Consent: what to discuss with this patient
steps.body:
1. The patient's own risk: Vessel quality, diabetes, age, previous lines. Quote the figure, not a textbook average.

2. Common

  • Failure to mature
  • Bruising, swelling

3. Serious

  • Steal syndrome (hand ischaemia)
  • Thrombosis
  • Infection
  • Nerve injury
  • High-output heart failure (rare, large upper-arm fistulas)

4. Specific to this operation

  • Weeks before it can be used; further procedures to help maturation

5. Alternatives

  • Graft
  • Tunnelled catheter
  • Peritoneal dialysis
  • Conservative kidney care
  • No operation, and what that means

6. Recovery

  • ICU, then ward; drains; walking from day 1
  • Return to normal activity over weeks
  • Follow-up in clinic

7. Kenya-specific

  • Protect the arm: no cannulas or blood pressure cuffs
  • Dialysis access and cost

Template and how to use it: CTICU protocol, consent.

ask.question: Which serious early complication must be explained before a brachial fistula?

choices.text: Steal syndrome: hand ischaemia needing urgent correction
choices.why: Commoner with brachial inflow, diabetes and age.

steps.title: Radiocephalic fistula at the wrist (Brescia–Cimino)
steps.body: Local or regional anaesthesia. A longitudinal incision between the radial artery and the cephalic vein at the wrist. Mobilise the vein, ligate its distal end and divide it; dilate gently. Expose the radial artery under the deep fascia, control it, open 6–8 mm. Swing the vein to the artery: vein end to artery side, 7-0 polypropylene. A thrill should be felt at once.

steps.title: Maturation: the forearm vein arterialises
steps.body:
Over 4–6 weeks the cephalic vein dilates and thickens. Examine it at 4–6 weeks: a continuous thrill, a soft pulse (not hammering), a straight segment long enough for two needles, superficial enough to feel.

The rule of 6s: at 6 weeks a mature fistula has
Flow600 mL/min or more
Diameter6 mm or more
Depthno more than 6 mm under the skin
Whenassessed at 6 weeks

KDOQI 2019 defines maturity by use: the fistula supports dialysis with two needles in more than two-thirds of sessions over 4 consecutive weeks. The rule of 6s stays a useful bedside and duplex check.

Not maturing by 6 weeks: duplex ultrasound. A juxta-anastomotic stenosis (the commonest cause in the forearm): balloon angioplasty or revision. Competing side branches stealing flow: ligate. A deep vein: superficialise. A small, diseased artery: a more proximal fistula.

Evidence: Rule of 6s: earlier KDOQI vascular access guidance (as summarised by the Renal Fellow Network). KDOQI 2019 update (Lok et al., Am J Kidney Dis 2020): functional definition of maturation; assess at 4–6 weeks.

choices.text: A juxta-anastomotic stenosis: ultrasound, then balloon angioplasty or revision
choices.why: The commonest cause of failure to mature in the forearm.

avf-bc.name: Arteriovenous fistula (dialysis access)
avf-bc.summary: Brachiocephalic fistula at the elbow; steal syndrome.

steps.title: Why a fistula: access for haemodialysis
steps.body:
Haemodialysis needs blood flow of about 300–400 mL/min, three times a week, for years. A fistula joins an artery to a superficial vein: the vein arterialises (dilates and thickens) over weeks until it can be needled. Compared with a graft (PTFE) it has fewer infections and interventions; compared with a tunnelled catheter, far less bacteraemia and central vein stenosis.

KDOQI 2019 replaced "fistula first" with "patient first": an ESKD Life-Plan for every patient with progressive CKD (eGFR 15–20), choosing the access that fits that patient's expected course: forearm first, distal to proximal, non-dominant arm, protecting veins (no cannulas or blood tests in the planned arm).

Maturation: the old rule of 6s (at 6 weeks: flow 600 mL/min, diameter 6 mm, no more than 6 mm deep). KDOQI 2019 defines maturity by function: dialysis with two needles in more than two-thirds of sessions over 4 consecutive weeks.

Evidence: KDOQI Clinical Practice Guideline for Vascular Access: 2019 Update (Lok et al., Am J Kidney Dis 2020): ESKD Life-Plan; no absolute minimum vessel diameter (vessels under 2 mm need careful evaluation); selective pre-operative ultrasound for high-risk patients; maturation assessed at 4–6 weeks; rope-ladder cannulation preferred. Rule of 6s: earlier KDOQI guidance.

ask.question: What did KDOQI 2019 change about access planning?

choices.text: From "fistula first" to a patient-first ESKD Life-Plan
choices.why: The access is chosen for the patient's expected life course, not a fistula at any cost.

steps.title: Brachiocephalic fistula at the elbow
steps.body: A transverse incision in the antecubital fossa. The cephalic vein (or the median cubital vein, giving outflow to both cephalic and basilic) to the brachial artery, end to side, with an arteriotomy limited to 4–6 mm to reduce steal. The bicipital aponeurosis is divided; the median nerve lies medial to the artery.

ask.question: Six hours after a brachiocephalic fistula the hand is cold, painful and numb. Diagnosis and action?

choices.text: Access-related hand ischaemia (steal): urgent assessment; ligation or a flow-reducing or DRIL procedure
choices.why: Severe steal with neurological signs is an emergency; it is commoner with brachial fistulas, in diabetics and the elderly.

steps.title: Transposed brachiobasilic fistula
steps.body: When the cephalic vein is unusable. The basilic vein runs deep to the fascia in the upper arm beside the medial cutaneous nerve of the forearm and the median nerve: mobilise it along the arm through a long medial incision (or several), then tunnel it superficially and laterally so it can be needled, and join it to the brachial artery. One or two stages.

TriggerThink of

cticu-cardiac.name: CTICU protocol
cticu-cardiac.summary: The unit protocol: labs, rounds, escalation, cardiac, thoracic and vascular cores, doses, consent and governance.

steps.title: Arrival, haemodynamics, bleeding, ventilation
steps.body:
Arrival (first 30 min)

  • Structured handover: surgeon, anaesthetist, nurse: the operation, bypass and clamp times, how the heart came off bypass, drugs running, pacing, drains
  • ABG, Hb, K⁺, glucose, lactate, ACT or coagulation screen, chest X-ray, ECG; test the epicardial pacing wires

Haemodynamics

  • MAP 65–80 mmHg; higher after CABG with carotid disease, lower with a friable aortic suture line
  • Noradrenaline for vasodilatation, adding adrenaline for low output: the anaesthetist's choice KNH practice (doses)
  • Low output: preload, rhythm and pacing first; then inotrope; then IABP. Never miss tamponade

Bleeding

  • Re-explore for more than 400 mL in the first hour, more than 300 mL/h for 2–3 h, more than 200 mL/h for 4 h, a sudden gush, or tamponade physiology
  • Correct temperature, protamine (by ACT), platelets, fibrinogen, calcium first; do not strip the drains
  • Transfuse restrictively: Hb under 7.5 g/dL (TRICS III) guideline

Ventilation

  • Extubate within 6 h when warm, awake, not bleeding, stable, with good gases guideline

Evidence: ERAS Cardiac Society guidelines (Engelman et al., JAMA Surg 2019): early extubation, glucose, multimodal analgesia, AKI prevention. TRICS III (Mazer et al., NEJM 2017): restrictive threshold 7.5 g/dL non-inferior.

ask.question: When is re-exploration indicated for bleeding?

choices.text: More than 400 mL in the first hour, or sustained high output, or tamponade
choices.why: Correct coagulopathy and temperature, but these thresholds call for the surgeon.

steps.title: Rhythm, kidneys, glucose, analgesia, day 1
steps.body:
Rhythm

  • K⁺ 4.0–5.0 mmol/L; keep Mg²⁺ replete (doses)
  • AF in 20–40%, peaking on days 2–3: beta-blocker prophylaxis, rate or rhythm control; anticoagulate if it lasts beyond 48 h, once bleeding allows

Kidneys, glucose, analgesia, delirium

  • AKI prevention: perfusion pressure, no nephrotoxins, urine output (KDIGO)
  • Glucose under 10 mmol/L (180 mg/dL) guideline
  • Paracetamol-based multimodal analgesia; avoid NSAIDs
  • Screen for delirium (CAM-ICU); mobilise early

Day 1

  • Day-1 labs: FBC, UEC, LFTs, Ca, Mg, PO₄ KNH practice
  • Drains out when output is low and serous
  • Sit out, walk, physiotherapy

Evidence: KDIGO AKI guideline 2012; ERAS Cardiac 2019 (glucose under 180 mg/dL, AF prophylaxis).

ask.question: Target K⁺ after cardiac surgery?

choices.why: Low K⁺ and Mg²⁺ provoke AF and ventricular arrhythmias.

steps.title: Anticoagulation after valve surgery
steps.body:
Mechanical valve

  • Day 1 morning, or once bleeding has stopped: enoxaparin (Clexane), bridging to warfarin KNH practice
  • First INR 72 h after the first warfarin dose, then as the dose is adjusted KNH practice
  • Stop enoxaparin when the INR is in the target range for the valve type, position and risk factors guideline; in range on two consecutive days proposed
Prosthesis thrombogenicityNo risk factorRisk factor*
Low (e.g. St Jude, On-X, Carbomedics, Medtronic Hall, ATS)2.53.0
Medium (other bileaflet valves)3.03.5
High (tilting disc such as Björk-Shiley; caged ball such as Starr-Edwards)3.54.0

Target INR. *Risk factors: mitral or tricuspid replacement, previous thromboembolism, AF, mitral stenosis of any degree, LVEF under 35%.

Tissue valve, repair, rheumatic AF

  • Tissue mitral valve or mitral repair: warfarin for 3 months guideline
  • Rheumatic AF: warfarin, not rivaroxaban (INVICTUS) guideline
  • Continue secondary penicillin prophylaxis after rheumatic valve surgery

Evidence: ESC/EACTS 2021 valvular heart disease guideline (INR targets by prosthesis and patient risk factors; VKA after bioprosthetic MVR or repair for 3 months). INVICTUS (Connolly et al., NEJM 2022).

ask.question: A mechanical mitral valve in a patient with AF: INR target (medium-thrombogenicity bileaflet)?

choices.why: ESC/EACTS 2021: medium thrombogenicity 3.0, plus 0.5 with a risk factor such as mitral position or AF.

cticu-thoracic.summary: The unit protocol: labs, rounds, escalation, cardiac, thoracic and vascular cores, doses, consent and governance.

steps.title: Arrival, analgesia, lungs, fluids
steps.body:
Arrival

  • Chest X-ray: expansion, drain position, mediastinum, surgical emphysema; ABG; Hb
  • Check that the regional block works: paravertebral, erector spinae or epidural

Analgesia is lung function

  • Block + paracetamol ± NSAID (kidneys permitting), low opioid
  • Sit up and walk on day 0–1; physiotherapy, incentive spirometry
  • Sputum retention: physio, then bedside bronchoscopy, then minitracheostomy

Fluids, rhythm, VTE

  • Euvolaemic to restrictive; no liberal crystalloid
  • AF: continue beta-blockers, keep K⁺ and Mg²⁺ replete
  • LMWH + mechanical prophylaxis; extended prophylaxis for high-risk cancer resections

Evidence: ERAS Society / ESTS guidelines for enhanced recovery after lung surgery (Batchelor et al., Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 2019).

ask.question: Why is regional analgesia central after thoracotomy?

choices.text: Pain prevents coughing, leading to sputum retention and pneumonia
choices.why: Analgesia is lung function.

steps.title: Drains, air leak, pneumonectomy
steps.body:
Drains

  • One drain after lobectomy; no routine suction guideline
  • Record the air leak every shift: none, on cough, continuous
  • Remove when there is no air leak and non-chylous output is up to 450 mL/24 h guideline
  • Prolonged air leak: more than 5 days

Read the drain

  • Serous: expected
  • Blood: over the thresholds, re-explore
  • Turbid or salivary after esophagectomy: leak
  • Milky: chyle (send triglycerides)

Pneumonectomy

  • No suction on the pneumonectomy drain (clamped or balanced)
  • Strict fluids: post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema is rare but often fatal
  • BPF at days 7–14 (right side, after chemoradiation, TB stump): lie operated side down, drain the space, bronchoscopy

Evidence: Batchelor 2019 (drain removal up to 450 mL/24 h, no routine suction). Post-pneumonectomy pulmonary oedema: Parquin et al. (Eur J Cardiothorac Surg 1996); Campisi (Shanghai Chest).

ask.question: When can a chest drain come out after lobectomy?

choices.text: No air leak and non-chylous output up to 450 mL/24 h
choices.why: ERAS lung 2019.

steps.title: Open aortic surgery: Hct, girth, compartment syndrome
steps.body:
Open aortic surgery

  • Hourly urine output; foot pulses and Doppler; wounds
  • Serial haematocrit 6-hourly for 24 h, then daily KNH practice
  • Abdominal girth at the umbilicus against a marked line, every 4–6 h KNH practice
  • When girth rises, the abdomen is tense, after rupture or massive transfusion, or with oliguria despite filling: bladder pressure proposed

Why bladder pressure: clinical examination misses raised abdominal pressure (sensitivity about 40–60%), and oliguria after a clamp may be hypovolaemia, AKI or compartment syndrome: fluid worsens the last. Foley, 25 mL saline, zero at the mid-axillary line, read at end-expiration. Intra-abdominal hypertension is 12 mmHg or more; compartment syndrome over 20 mmHg with new organ failure: decompress.

  • Colonic ischaemia: bloody diarrhoea or rising lactate: sigmoidoscopy
  • Trash foot: distal emboli
  • AKI after juxta- or suprarenal clamping

Evidence: WSACS 2013 definitions (Kirkpatrick et al., Intensive Care Med 2013). Kirkpatrick et al. (Can J Surg 2000): clinical examination sensitivity 40–56%. ACS after endovascular repair of rupture: 17–21% in studies with proper definitions, mortality 47% (J Vasc Surg meta-analysis). ESVS 2024 AAA guideline.

ask.question: Why can oliguria after AAA repair be dangerous to treat with fluid alone?

choices.text: It may be abdominal compartment syndrome, which fluid worsens
choices.why: Measure bladder pressure when girth rises or oliguria persists despite filling.

steps.title: Spinal cord, bypass grafts, endovascular
steps.body:
Spinal cord (TAA, TEVAR)

  • MAP target 80–90 mmHg or more
  • CSF drain at 10–12 mmHg; hourly leg checks
  • New weakness: raise MAP, drain CSF, keep Hb up, call immediately

Bypass and endovascular

  • Graft and foot Doppler signals hourly at first; groin wounds (lymph leak, infection)
  • Axillobifemoral: no BP cuff on the donor arm; do not lie on the graft side
  • Puncture sites: haematoma; back pain and a falling Hb: retroperitoneal bleed
  • EVAR and TEVAR: contrast AKI; post-implantation fever

Evidence: ESVS 2024 AAA guideline; ESC 2024 and ACC/AHA 2022 aortic guidelines (spinal cord protection, CSF drainage).

steps.title: Electrolytes: K⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, PO₄
steps.body:
Doses as in Medscape Reference, the unit standard KNH practice, prepared from KNH stock. Targets are the unit's; limits are the product label's.

Potassium: KCl 15% (2 mmol/mL; 10 mL = 20 mmol)

Target after cardiac surgery 4.0–5.0 mmol/L guideline. Never undiluted, never as a push.

Serum K⁺Maximum rateMax / 24 h
2.5 or more10 mmol/h, at no more than 40 mmol/L200 mmol
Under 2.0 with ECG changes or paralysisup to 40 mmol/h, continuous ECG400 mmol

Peripheral bag: 10 mL KCl 15% (20 mmol) in 500 mL 0.9% saline = 40 mmol/L; 250 mL/h gives 10 mmol/h. Use saline, not dextrose, when urgent. Hold if urine is under 0.5 mL/kg/h or creatinine is rising. Concentrated central-line syringes: unit to decide proposed

Magnesium: MgSO₄

Target after cardiac surgery 1.0 mmol/L or more proposed

DeficiencyDose
Mild1 g IM every 6 h for 4 doses
Severe5 g (about 20 mmol) in 1 L 5% dextrose or 0.9% saline IV over 3 h

Dilute 50% MgSO₄ to 20% or less for IV use; no faster than 150 mg/min. Severe renal impairment: no more than 20 g in 48 h. Pharmacy to confirm the vial strength stocked.

Calcium: calcium gluconate 10% (10 mL = 1 g, about 2.3 mmol Ca)

Target ionised Ca 1.1–1.3 mmol/L.

Ionised CaDose
1.0–1.2 (mild)1–2 g IV over 2 h
Under 1.0, no tetany0.5 mg/kg/h IV, up to 2 mg/kg/h; no more than 3–4 g over 4 h

Maximum 50–100 mg/min as a push, 200 mg/min as an infusion. Not in the same line as bicarbonate or phosphate. Pharmacy to confirm whether the mg/kg/h rate is elemental calcium.

Phosphate

Serum PO₄Dose, IV over 4–6 h
Under 0.16 mmol/L (0.5 mg/dL)0.5 mmol/kg
0.16–0.32 mmol/L (0.5–1 mg/dL)0.25 mmol/kg

Potassium phosphate if K⁺ is low, sodium phosphate otherwise; caution in renal impairment. Milder deficits: unit to set proposed

Evidence: Medscape Reference (calcium gluconate, sodium phosphates IV); potassium chloride and magnesium sulfate prescribing information (product labels, as followed by Medscape).

ask.question: Maximum KCl rate for K⁺ 2.8 mmol/L without ECG changes?

choices.text: 10 mmol/h, at no more than 40 mmol/L
choices.why: The label limit for K⁺ 2.5 or more; up to 40 mmol/h only with ECG monitoring for severe hypokalaemia with ECG changes.

steps.title: Noradrenaline and adrenaline infusions
steps.body:
One standard syringe for both: 4 mL of the 1 mg/mL vial (4 mg) + 46 mL 5% dextrose = 50 mL at 80 µg/mL, central line only. Label clearly: the two syringes look the same. The choice of drug and dose is the anaesthetist's KNH practice

Noradrenaline

Start 8–12 µg/min and titrate to MAP; maintenance usually 2–4 µg/min. mL/h = µg/min × 0.75

steps.title: Consent: seven parts for every operation
steps.body:
PartContent
1. The patient's own riskEuroSCORE II or STS PROM (cardiac); ppoFEV1, ppoDLCO and Thoracoscore (thoracic); fitness and cardiac risk (vascular)
2. Common risksOccur often; discussed with everyone
3. Serious risksRare but life-changing: death, stroke, paraplegia, amputation
4. Specific to this operationThe choices and risks only this operation has
5. AlternativesOther operations, endovascular, medical therapy, no operation
6. RecoveryICU and ward days, drains, return to work, long-term medicines, follow-up
7. Kenya-specificINR access, pregnancy on warfarin, penicillin prophylaxis, blood availability, cost, distance to follow-up

A structured aid for the conversation: it does not replace the signed KNH consent form. Material risks are those this patient would want to know, not only the frequent ones.

ask.question: What makes a risk material?

choices.text: It is one this patient would want to know, not only a frequent one
choices.why: Serious rare risks (paraplegia, stroke) are material even when uncommon.

choices.text: Only risks the surgeon worries about
None if the form is signed
